papers.title: Spectral signatures of hidden order and hidden quantum critical points
papers.abstract: Hidden-order phases elude the conventional Ginzburg-Landau framework: although they spontaneously break symmetry, their order remains invisible to standard local two-point correlators. Instead, they are typically characterized by nonlocal (string) order parameters and are believed to underlie a range of exotic quantum states, such as symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases. While hidden correlations have previously been detected through nonlocal observables in quantum gas microscope experiments, in realistic solid-state systems multipoint observables are typically inaccessible and the signatures of hidden order remain largely unexplored. In this work, we show that hidden order in doped spin chains can be directly probed through dynamical two-point response functions measurable by resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) and neutron scattering. Focusing on a minimal model, we numerically identify clear spectral fingerprints of both the hidden-order phase, its associated hidden quantum critical point as well as a specific group of gapless SPT phases. Complementing our numerical results with analytical insights, we uncover the microscopic origin of these spectral signatures and demonstrate how they emerge from the interplay between spin and charge degrees of freedom. Together, our results establish spectroscopy as a practical probe of hidden order and gapless SPT phases and provide a unified understanding of the low-energy physics governing these unconventional quantum phases.

papers.title: Dual and lensed AGN at sub-arcsecond separations uncovered by ERIS
papers.abstract: We present the first results of the ongoing INAF GTO program focused on the search of sub-arcsecond dual AGN, carried out with the near-infrared integral-field unit SPIFFIER of the Enhanced Resolution Imager and Spectrograph (ERIS) at the ESO Very Large Telescope, operating in adaptive-optics mode with a laser guide star. We report integral field spectroscopy with the low-resolution gratings (R ~ 5000 - 5600) of 34 multiple AGN candidates selected from the Gaia Data Release 3 source catalog via the Gaia Multi-Peak (GMP) method, which preferentially identifies luminous unobscured AGN at sub-arcsecond separations. The targets span the redshift range 0.7 < z < 3.4 and exhibit projected angular separations between ~0.2'' and ~0.9'', corresponding to physical separations of ~1.7-7.8 kpc. Of the 34 observed systems,13 (~40 %) are resolved into multiple AGN-like components; 18 (~53 %) are classified as AGN plus foreground star superpositions, one as a single AGN, and two as systems with an AGN primary and an unclassified secondary component. Among the multiple AGN systems, we confirm six dual AGN at projected separations of 0.26'' - 0.80'' (2.2 - 6.7 kpc), in the redshift range z = 0.68 - 1.57, and with velocity offsets in the range Δv ~ 290 - 950 km/s. We also identify seven gravitationally lensed quasars, only one of which was previously known, including four doubly imaged and three quadruply imaged systems. These results substantially enlarge the census of spectroscopically confirmed compact multiple AGN systems at z > 0.5 and demonstrate the efficiency of ERIS-SPIFFIER for the systematic characterization of sub-arcsecond dual and lensed AGN candidates.

papers.intro:
In hierarchical models of galaxy formation, major mergers are expected to be frequent, especially at high redshift, and to strongly shape galaxy morphology, star formation activity, and chemical evolution (White and Rees, 1978a), while also involving the supermassive black holes (SMBHs) residing at the centers of the merging galaxies (Begelman et al., 1980; Volonteri et al., 2003; White and Rees, 1978b). Hydrodynamical simulations indicate that these mergers drive substantial gas inflows toward the central regions of galaxies, fueling both intense star formation and accretion onto SMBHs, likely triggering active galactic nucleus (Mayer et al., 2007, AGN;) activity. Following the merger, the central SMBHs of the progenitor galaxies sink toward the center of the common remnant via dynamical friction, eventually forming a gravitationally bound pair (Colpi, 2014). The subsequent evolution toward coalescence can require extended timescales, of the order of ∼\sim1 Gyr (Volonteri et al., 2021, e.g.), before the final inspiral produces gravitational-wave (GW) emission. Consequently, pairs of SMBHs at kpc-scale separation within the same host are predicted to be a natural phase of this evolutionary path, particularly at early epochs (Volonteri et al., 2003). When both SMBHs are actively accreting material from the surroundings, the system is observed as a dual AGN (Steinborn et al., 2016; Rosas-Guevara et al., 2019; Volonteri et al., 2022), with projected separations ranging from tens of kpc down to sub-kpc scales (De Rosa et al., 2019). Compact dual AGN systems are therefore direct observational tracers of late-stage mergers and SMBH–host galaxy co-evolution, offering a unique laboratory for studying merger-driven gas accretion, AGN feedback in disturbed environments, and the dynamical processes that drive two SMBHs toward coalescence. The final inspiral and merger of such SMBH pairs are expected to produce GW signals in the nHz regime, already probed by pulsar timing arrays (Arzoumanian et al., 2018; Agazie et al., 2023, PTA;), and at mHz frequencies detectable by the upcoming Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (Amaro-Seoane et al., 2023; Colpi et al., 2024, LISA;).

Cosmological simulations predict that dual AGN at separations below 10 kpc represent a non-negligible fraction of the overall AGN population, reaching up to a few percent at z>0.5z>0.5, where the galaxy merger rate is significantly higher than in the local Universe (Volonteri et al., 2021; Steinborn et al., 2016; Rosas-Guevara et al., 2019). Despite these theoretical expectations, and more than a decade of dedicated observational searches, the number of spectroscopically confirmed dual AGN at sub-kpc to few-kpc separations remains small (Chen et al., 2022; Mannucci et al., 2022; Mannucci et al., 2023; Ciurlo et al., 2023; Scialpi et al., 2024; Scialpi et al., 2026a), the deficit being particularly severe beyond the local Universe (De Rosa et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2022; Mannucci et al., 2022). A full list of all spectroscopically confirmed dual AGN at z>0.5z>0.5 will be presented by Scialpi et al. (2026b). Resolving two AGN separated by less than one arcsecond requires either space-based imaging or ground-based adaptive-optics (AO)-assisted observations, both of which are observationally expensive and have historically been applied to small samples. Furthermore, late-stage mergers are often associated with increased column densities and dust obscuration (Koss et al., 2018; Blecha et al., 2018; Ricci et al., 2017; Barrows et al., 2023), making it harder to detect both nuclei even when the spatial resolution is sufficient. As a result, wide-separation systems and low-redshift pairs dominate current observational samples (De Rosa et al., 2019, e.g.), leaving the compact merger regime largely unexplored.

Systematic searches for close dual AGN have employed a variety of indirect and direct techniques. Early approaches exploited double-peaked narrow emission lines in spatially integrated spectra as a signature of two kinematically distinct nuclei (Zhou et al., 2004; Comerford et al., 2009, e.g.), though such features can also arise from gas rotation, disturbed kinematics, or AGN-driven outflows, leading to significant contamination. Radio-selected samples (Fu et al., 2015), mid-infrared pre-selection (Satyapal et al., 2017; Pfeifle et al., 2019), and quasar clustering studies (Hennawi et al., 2006; Hennawi et al., 2010) have each contributed to the identification of dual AGN. Recently, Jing et al. (2026) identified 1020 quasar pairs with separations >2​″>2\arcsec in the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) DR1 quasar sample (DESI Collaboration et al., 2026), with a redshift distribution peaking at z∼1z\sim 1–2.5. These approaches often probe relatively wide separations or specific AGN populations, and therefore do not provide a complete census of the merging SMBH population. papers.title: MatchCityLoc: Aerial Localization in LoD City Models via Surface Normal Matching
papers.abstract: Autonomous Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) navigation in urban environments requires precise pose estimation. Because Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals are often unreliable in cities, visual localization serves as a crucial complement. Within this domain, textureless Level-of-Detail (LoD) city models provide a lightweight and privacy-preserving substitute for heavy 3D textured meshes. However, localizing against abstract geometry is challenging. Existing pipelines typically score 2D silhouette overlaps, which can suffer from severe geometric ambiguities. We present MatchCityLoc, a framework that shifts this paradigm to direct feature matching from a noisy 6-DoF pose prior. By extracting surface normals from the query image using a zero-shot foundation model and matching them against rendered LoD normals, we establish explicit 3D-to-2D correspondences. This enables a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) pose solve, which we iteratively refine through a render-and-match loop. Experiments demonstrate strong pose recall and accurate translation and rotation among the evaluated off-the-shelf LoD-based methods with very few renderings. By bridging the modality gap between aerial imagery and texture-free geometry, MatchCityLoc enables accurate localization using lightweight, privacy-preserving city models.

UAV play a crucial role in modern applications ranging from infrastructure inspection and search and rescue [28, 2] to autonomous landing [11]. Operating in these complex environments often requires precise and robust aerial visual localization. While drones are equipped with Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs), GNSS (GNSS) does not provide full pose information and its signals are often degraded in complex environments. Therefore, UAV must rely on onboard cameras to determine their pose.

UAV play a crucial role in modern applications ranging from infrastructure inspection and search and rescue [28, 2] to autonomous landing [11]. Operating in these complex environments often requires precise and robust aerial visual localization. While drones are equipped with Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs), GNSS (GNSS) does not provide full pose information and its signals are often degraded in complex environments. Therefore, UAV must rely on onboard cameras to determine their pose.

Traditional visual localization methods depend heavily on dense 3D maps or photogrammetry models [25, 20, 30]. While accurate, these representations are exceedingly memory-intensive and expensive to acquire. They also pose significant privacy concerns due to their high-fidelity textures [36, 19]. Alternatively, orthographic geodata provides a more storage-efficient option [5, 3]. However, using orthophotos introduces a massive view gap. Orthophotos capture the scene from a strict nadir perspective, whereas UAV navigate with highly diverse viewpoints. This perspective discrepancy, coupled with the lack of detailed 3D facade geometry and vulnerability to radiometric shifts like cast shadows, makes orthophoto-based matching challenging.

These models are globally available, lightweight, and inherently privacy-preserving since they discard visual textures [36, 31, 10]. Despite these advantages, localization remains geometrically ambiguous. LoD-Loc [36] and LoD-Loc v2 [35] align predicted wireframes or silhouettes with 2D renderings (Fig. 1a). LoD-Loc v3 [22] adds instance segmentation, while SemCityLoc [18] incorporates semantic surfaces and depth-based 3D cues to improve the pose-scoring landscape. Concurrent PlanarCityLoc [4] goes further by grounding matched planes in 3D for pose refinement, but first establishes coarse alignment through render-and-score search. We instead match surface normals directly from the supplied pose prior and lift the matches to 3D, bypassing this initial alignment search.

We address this ambiguity geometrically, introducing an iterative “render-and-match” approach (Fig. 1b). Rather than relying on exhaustive silhouette alignment, MatchCityLoc solves the localization problem geometrically by performing direct 2D-2D feature matching between the UAV image and the LoD city model. At first glance, direct feature matching might seem intractable because LoD models lack visual textures. Our core insight is that surface orientation bridges this modality gap. By extracting normal predictions from the UAV image and matching them against rendered surface normal maps from the LoD models, we can establish highly accurate correspondences. Surface normals intrinsically encode robust geometric cues that are invariant to lighting and texture. This allows us to leverage off-the-shelf foundation feature matching models [7, 23, 14, 6] to find dense matches without any domain-specific training.

papers.title: On the Fragility of Tasks under Composition: Implicit Budgeting in Language Models
papers.abstract: Modern language models are increasingly asked to handle several tasks within a single prompt. Doing so requires solving each task correctly while integrating the resulting answers into a coherent response. In this paper, we identify a fundamental limitation in this process, where models make substantially more errors when tasks are composed, even when they can solve every constituent task reliably in isolation. This degradation cannot be fully explained by the accumulation of independent errors. Across both open-weight models and the frontier model Claude Opus 5, our findings instead point to an implicit thinking budget underlying this effect. In particular, under composition, models use substantially fewer tokens per task than in isolation, even when the full sequence remains well within the context window. Tasks that require longer solution traces in isolation are consequently more $\textit{fragile}$ under composition, i.e., models make more errors on prompts containing these tasks. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than they need and waste compute. However, by grouping tasks according to their fragility, the implicit budgeting can be manipulated to reduce token usage by $43$\% across a range of math and linguistic tasks while also preserving accuracy.

papers.intro:
A single prompt often asks a language model to do several things at once, such as answering a handful of questions, solving a set of math problems, or following a list of instructions before writing one response. Common benchmarks, however, still test models one task at a time (Rein et al., 2023; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Gema et al., 2025). As scores on these benchmarks saturate, they may overstate how robust the underlying capabilities are. We ask whether a model that reliably solves a task on its own can still solve it when other tasks share the prompt.

A single prompt often asks a language model to do several things at once, such as answering a handful of questions, solving a set of math problems, or following a list of instructions before writing one response. Common benchmarks, however, still test models one task at a time (Rein et al., 2023; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Gema et al., 2025). As scores on these benchmarks saturate, they may overstate how robust the underlying capabilities are. We ask whether a model that reliably solves a task on its own can still solve it when other tasks share the prompt.

One natural explanation is error accumulation. If each task fails with nonzero probability, solving many at once fails more often. Prior work has found this phenomenon when models are tasked to do familiar reasoning steps (Press et al., 2023; Dziri et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2026) or follow several instructions at once (Harada et al., 2025; Vasileva, 2026). However, accumulation is only half of the story. Because composition in these settings also changes the structure and token demands of the task, it remains unclear whether the model’s ability to solve each constituent task degrades as well, and what mechanism drives that degradation.

To investigate the question, we analyze the effect of composition on each constituent task of a composition. We start by establishing that this per-task degradation exists at all. For that, we select tasks the model solves correctly in isolation, which establishes that the requisite capability is present. We then leave those tasks unchanged and simply concatenate them within a single prompt. This design separates degradation under increased task load from baseline solvability on the constituent tasks.

Across state-of-the-art open models, as well as the frontier model Claude Opus 5, we find substantial performance degradation when more previously solved tasks are concatenated within the same prompt. The drop in accuracy is substantially larger than what the constituent tasks’ isolated error rates would predict, and is consistent across both mathematical and linguistic domains. We characterize this degradation along two dimensions. 1) Failures concentrate on a subset of fragile tasks that, for a given model, remains stable across sampling noise and composition sizes. These tasks also have longer reasoning traces in isolation. 2) As more tasks are presented together, models systematically reduce the reasoning tokens devoted to each task, even though no explicit per-task token constraint is imposed. This reduction follows a clear scaling pattern, with reasoning per task decreasing approximately as a power law with composition size. papers.title: Predicting Linear Relational Decodability Without the Relation
papers.abstract: Linear relational embeddings (LREs) approximate a language model's subject-to-object mapping with an affine function. Their faithfulness varies enormously across relations, from near zero for person_father to the ceiling for country_capital_city. We investigate the factors that contribute to this variation and demonstrate that it can be significantly predicted from a readout that is not aware of the underlying relation. To do so, we propose a novel form of the Jacobian lens, the entity lens. Whereas the Jacobian lens is estimated across all tokens and concepts, the entity lens EL_t is trained to predict what the model will output for an entity of type t under the neutral prompt "{} is known for"; e.g., we train ELs for countries and persons. After estimating an entity lens, we measure how highly it ranks the model's answer for a relation without using any relation-specific information in estimation and prediction. Across 28 relations of the LRE dataset on Olmo-3-7B this relation-agnostic score correlates with LRE faithfulness at $ρ= 0.7355$ (p < .01). This suggests that linear decodability is largely a property of what a subject's representation already carries, rather than of the relation being decoded. Moving the unit of analysis from the relation to the individual fact, we conclude that new relation datasets and analysis methods are needed to address several problems in existing datasets, most prominently semantically weak first tokens (e.g., most predicted universities' first token is "University") and reference competition (e.g., the LLM confuses obscure actor names with competing non-actor entities that have the same last name). Our full pipeline is available at https://github.com/jonasrohw/entity-lens

Hernandez et al. (2024) showed that a language model’s mapping from a subject to the object of a relation is often well approximated by an affine function of the subject’s hidden state, a linear relational embedding (LRE). papers.title: Towards Autonomous Bricklaying Using Boston Dynamics Spot
papers.abstract: Mobile legged robots offer unique advantages for on-site construction, including the ability to traverse unstructured terrain, climb stairs, and operate independently between spatially separated work zones. This paper presents a proof-of-concept system for autonomous brick stacking using a Boston Dynamics Spot quadrupedal robot equipped with a manipulator arm. The system operates between a supply area and an assembly area, using AprilTag fiducials for localization and autowalk missions for navigation. Target brick positions and orientations are specified in CAD software and exported directly for robotic execution. We evaluate placement accuracy through ten repeated assemblies of a curved four-layer wall comprising 14 wooden bricks. Results show mean translation errors below 10 mm and mean yaw errors below 1.5 degrees, while the overall RMSE across all runs is 27.72 mm (translation) and 2.06 degrees (rotation). The system was also tested outdoors with stairs between the two areas. The workflow is modular and easily extendable to different wall geometries.

papers.intro:
The construction industry is undergoing a transition towards greater automation, driven by rising housing demand, skilled labor shortages, and persistent safety concerns on construction sites. Yet, compared to sectors such as automotive and logistics, construction has seen limited productivity gains, with annual improvement rates of only 1 %1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} against an industry average of 2.8 %2.8\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} [1]. On-site robotic automation has been proposed as one means to address these challenges [2]. Despite this potential, the deployment of robotic systems on construction sites remains limited [3]. Existing approaches face significant constraints. Large gantry systems require infrastructure that often exceeds the scale of the structure being built. Wheeled and tracked mobile platforms struggle with rough terrain, stairs, and cluttered site conditions. These constraints have confined most successful automation efforts to off-site prefabrication; yet construction fundamentally remains an on-site process where varying conditions resist complete pre-planning. Recent advances in commercial legged robotics have produced platforms capable of traversing stairs, uneven terrain, and human-centric spaces [4]. This makes them suited to the multi-level, cluttered environments of real construction sites, where wheeled and tracked platforms face fundamental access constraints. Prior work has demonstrated legged manipulation for general pick-and-place tasks [5, 6], but application to construction assembly has not been explored. To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has quantitatively evaluated the accuracy with which a legged robot can execute a brick-stacking task.

This paper presents a proof-of-concept for what we term the MARA (MARA) workflow: a distributed construction process in which a legged mobile manipulator autonomously traverses between spatially separated supply and assembly areas, picking and placing bricks according to a specified layout. The approach is evaluated using a Boston Dynamics Spot quadrupedal robot equipped with a manipulator arm. Target brick positions are modeled in Rhino, a CAD (CAD) program, and exported directly for robotic assembly. The system localizes by referencing each manipulation operation to a locally visible fiducial marker, thereby decoupling placement accuracy from global odometry drift. Placement accuracy is evaluated through ten repeated assemblies of a curved four-layer wall, reporting translational and rotational errors across layers.

papers.title: Gaussian process-based Bayesian imaging of bolometric (sub-)millimetre data
papers.abstract: Widefield single-dish telescopes operating at (sub-)mm wavelengths ($λ\sim 4$~mm to 350~$μ$m) tend to feature much faster mapping speeds than radio interferometers at the same wavelengths, and are more suitable for measuring signals on larger spatial scales. However, the data are dominated by atmospheric fluctuations on large scales and by photon and instrumental noise on smaller scales, making it difficult to recover the true astronomical sky. We build on maria-nifty, a Gaussian process-based Bayesian imaging framework for reconstructing sky maps from single-dish telescope data, implemented on top of Numerical Information Field Theory (NIFTy). It uses modular generative models to efficiently separate the astronomical signal from atmospheric emission while providing pixel-wise uncertainty quantification for the reconstructed sky maps. Moreover, our method cleanly separates individual astrophysical signals, even though they are superposed on the sky. Following its successful validation on synthetic time-ordered data generated using the maria software, we apply it to real data observed with the MUSTANG-2 bolometric array on the 100-meter Green Bank Telescope. For the galaxy cluster RXJ1347.5-1145, we separate the extended cluster emission from the compact source at its centre and obtain a smoother map with fewer artefacts compared to a standard maximum-likelihood reconstruction using the same data. The JAX-based implementation and GPU acceleration provide the basis for applying the method to the vastly larger datasets that the next generation of single-dish telescopes will deliver.

papers.intro:
Widefield sub-millimetre and mm-wave single-dish telescopes (at frequencies ∼\sim90–950 GHz) feature faster mapping speeds and are more sensitive to large angular scales than their interferometric counterparts at the same wavelengths (Frayer, 2017; Plunkett et al., 2023). This makes them particularly well suited to observing extended emission, such as the thermal Sunyaev–Zeldovich (SZ) effect, which is a signal due to inverse Compton scattering of photons from the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) off hot (∼108\sim 10^{8} K) electrons in reservoirs of hot thermal plasma such as found in galaxy clusters (Sunyaev & Zeldovich 1972; see Mroczkowski et al., 2019 for a review). One way to probe the SZ effect is through large bolometric array detectors such as MUSTANG-2, a 223-detector array on the 100-meter Green Bank Telescope (GBT) that provides ≈9​″\approx 9\arcsec angular resolution continuum mapping in a broad bandwidth centred around a frequency of 93 GHz (see Dicker et al. 2014a; Dicker et al. 2014b for more detail).

However, ground-based bolometric observations are dominated by the emission of the atmosphere. Fluctuations of the water vapour along the line of sight cause a signal that follows a steep, Kolmogorov-like temporal power spectrum (Lay, 1997; Errard et al., 2015) and varies on short timescales as the telescope scans across the sky (Morris et al., 2022; Morris et al., 2025). While the atmosphere dominates on large scales, where it exceeds the astronomical signal by several orders of magnitude, the data on smaller scales are limited by photon and instrumental noise (Hill & Kusaka, 2024). Separating these contributions from the subdominant astronomical signal is the central challenge in recovering the true sky.

Separating these contributions from the subdominant astronomical signal is the central challenge in recovering the true sky.

Traditional map-making methods remove the atmospheric contribution before the creation of the map. In doing so, a common mode or the leading principal components of the focal plane are subtracted from the observed data, which are then high-pass filtered and binned into a map (Perotto et al., 2020; Romero et al., 2020). This efficiently suppresses the atmosphere, but it also removes the astronomical signal on angular scales comparable to the size of the field of view (FOV) and beyond. It also requires a transfer function, which has to be calibrated with simulations. Maximum-likelihood map-makers reduce this loss by describing the atmosphere as correlated noise with an estimated covariance, which results in flatter transfer functions (Dünner et al., 2013; Naess et al., 2025). However, these are not very well constrained on large modes, which leads to large-scale gradients in the map, commonly referred to as “bowling”. Examples may be found in Romero et al. (2020) and Orlowski-Scherer et al. (2022), among others, who used the minkasi11 1 https://github.com/sievers/minkasi mapper to reconstruct the sky from MUSTANG-2 observational data.

papers.title: Density Saturation and Autocorrelation Characteristics of Interlayer Exciton Ensembles in MoSe$_2$/WSe$_2$ Heterostructures
papers.abstract: We investigate interlayer excitons in MoSe$_2$/WSe$_2$ heterostructures using time-resolved photoluminescence and second-order autocorrelation measurements across a wide range of excitation powers and bath temperatures. By analyzing the photoluminescence amplitude and lifetime of the interlayer exciton state with the lowest emission energy, we extract a corresponding density-temperature diagram. The extracted exciton density exhibits a saturation at approximately $10^{13}$cm$^{-2}$, consistent with values predicted for a Mott transition of interlayer exciton ensembles in van der Waals heterostructures. Moreover, possible interpretations beyond the Mott transition are discussed. We further test whether the density limit is accompanied by a departure from classical photon statistics. The second-order autocorrelation measurements reveal that the photoluminescence maintains an emission characteristic of $g^{(2)}(0) \approx 1$ from low exciton densities up to the maximum reachable density in the investigated exciton ensembles consistent with the lowest-energy exciton ensemble obeying Poissonian statistics.

papers.intro:
In recent years, the discovery of two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides has opened new routes for exploring excitonic phenomena in reduced dimensional systems. Particularly, interlayer excitons (IXs) formed across the interface of a MoSe2/WSe2 van-der-Waals heterostack exhibit unique optical properties [4], including a large exciton binding energy of several hundred meV, a permanent out-of-plane dipole moment, long diffusion lengths, and a long photoluminescence lifetime on the order of 100 ns [9, 28]. The long lifetime suggests that IXs can fully thermalize to an excitonic ground state for sufficiently long detection times, which makes them attractive for the exploration of many-body phenomena at sufficiently high interlayer exciton densities and low enough temperatures [9, 28, 31, 37, 15, 5]. The density determines the effective strength of interactions between individual IXs and is an important parameter in the buildup of collective behavior [9]. At low exciton densities, the interactions are weak and the overall exciton system behaves like a dilute gas of independent particles [18]. As the density increases, exciton-exciton and exciton-charge carrier interactions can become significant, which eventually leads to spectral broadening and shifts of the photoluminescence characteristics and a modification of the ensemble lifetime [10, 2]. At sufficiently high exciton densities, exciton ensembles are expected to undergo a transition to a correlated exciton phase, where a macroscopic coherence builds up first in individual puddles and then across the full exciton ensemble at low enough temperatures [9, 37, 5].

The creation of thermalized high-density ensembles in optically pumped systems remains challenging. Effects such as exciton-exciton repulsion and temperature-driven diffusion locally redistribute the excitons into regions of lower density. To overcome these limitations, various approaches, including electrostatic trapping via tailored gate geometries [12, 29, 30, 14], strain engineering [17], and non-Gaussian optical excitation schemes [36] have been pursued to modulate the overall excitonic potential landscape and to locally increase the exciton density of thermalized excitons. Still, the Mott transition marks the natural density limit of exciton ensembles, since it creates a balance between bound and free charge carriers [23, 43, 26, 25, 35, 33, 20, 1, 16]. Close to the Mott transition, small changes in carrier density can result in significant changes in the excitonic properties, such as a change in the binding energy and the absorption characteristics [34]. For IXs, the Mott-transition has so far been reported in terms of spectral broadening of the photoluminescence [14, 38, 41, 3], an significant increase of the IX-related diffusivity and photoconductance [41, 39], as well as a reduction of the photoluminescence lifetime [38]. However, whether the Mott transition is the only mechanism limiting the achievable exciton density in optically pumped ensembles, as opposed to, e.g., filling of localized and moiré states, as well as a photo-doping induced renormalization of moiré- and disorder-induced modulations of the potential landscape, effectively impacting exciton ensembles, remains an open question. Moreover, a clear connection between the density limit of an IX ensemble and its photon emission statistics has not been demonstrated yet: does the saturated, high-density state still emit photons independently in a Poissonian statistics, or does the onset of a possible Mott transition or a correlated many-body phase leave a signature in the second-order correlation function g(2)​(τ)g^{(2)}(\tau)?

Here, we present time-resolved photoluminescence measurements of IXs in MoSe2/WSe2 heterostructures for a large range of excitation powers and bath temperatures. We model the decay dynamics of the observed IX-related photoluminescence by extracting the amplitude and lifetime of the time-resolved traces to estimate the exciton densities for a given temperature. We observe that the exciton density of the lowest energy peak saturates and that the maximum exciton density on two different samples equals (2.4±0.1)×1013(2.4\pm 0.1)\times 10^{13} cm-2 and (5.6±0.7)×1012(5.6\pm 0.7)\times 10^{12} cm-2, respectively. The values are consistent with a predicted Mott transition for IXs in MoSe2/WSe2 heterostructures [9]. Moreover, we investigate the second-order autocorrelation function g(2)​(τ)g^{(2)}(\tau) of the excitonic photoluminescence, with τ\tau the time delay between two photon emission processes. We find g(2)​(0)≈1g^{(2)}(0)\approx 1 within the given time resolution for the energetically lowest interlayer exciton state across the investigated density-temperature diagram. This Poissonian emission behavior persists throughout the investigated temperature range, namely from 1.7K up to 12K. Our results suggest that the Poissonian emission behavior prevails across the whole phase-diagram of interlayer excitons, ranging from an ideal gas of excitons at high temperatures to coherent, degenerate many-body ensembles at low temperature and high densities [9, 31, 37, 15, 5].

papers.title: Pulse Shape Model for a Light Enhanced Phonon Detector
papers.abstract: COSINUS has tested prototype NaI-based cryogenic scintillating calorimeters with a composite design, in which the transition edge sensor (TES) is fabricated on a separate carrier crystal coupled to the NaI target. Measurements with the composite detectors showed deviations from the known pulse shape description for cryogenic calorimeters and did not reveal an identifiable nuclear recoil population during a neutron calibration. In this work we present a new pulse shape model which provides an explanation to these observations and that laid the foundation for the development of the final COSINUS phonon detector design named remote TES (remoTES). We demonstrate that the first COSINUS detector prototypes featured a phonon channel with signal enhancement by light absorption in the carrier, namely a light enhanced phonon detector. This design offers for the first time the chance to use a single channel phonon detector for particle discrimination. We present recent results using a novel pulse shape fitting method based on the Bayesian inference software package BAT.jl.

papers.intro:
Cryogenic calorimeters are detectors widely employed for rare event searches in particle physics, e.g. for dark matter and neutrino scattering detection, because of their exceptional energy resolution at low energies [21, 9, 3, 22, 32, 23, 7, 12, 2, 20, 15]. They consist of a selected target material, the absorber, coupled to an ultra sensitive temperature device fabricated on its surface, the sensor. They are employed to measure the energy deposited by a particle interaction in the absorber and converted into phonons. About 30 years of development of TES-based cryogenic calorimeters have been carried out at the Max Planck Institute for Physics, starting from the work of W. Seidel et al. [31] which led to the foundation of the CRESST [3, 8, 1], COSINUS [11] and NUCLEUS [7] experiments. The refined fabrication process of tungsten TES (W-TES) produces detectors that are among the most sensitive cryogenic calorimeters for rare event searches worldwide [3, 8, 1]. Some target materials are considered unsuitable for cryogenic applications because of their softness, low melting point or hygroscopicity. For instance, NaI must be stored and handled only in air-tight containers with controlled nitrogen atmosphere and it cannot withstand the evaporation of a W-TES because of the high temperature required [6]. Nevertheless, the COSINUS experiment is developing NaI cryogenic scintillating calorimeters (NaI-CSCs) to cross-check the results of the DAMA/LIBRA experiment using the same target material and an event-by-event discrimination of nuclear recoils from other events [6]. To this aim, in an early stage, COSINUS adopted a workaround and evaporated the TES on a different crystal, named carrier. The carrier was placed in thermal contact with the absorber, e.g. by gluing it on the absorber surface [6], see Fig. 1. This composite design, which also preserves the absorber from the TES fabrication process, was previously successfully employed by CRESST-II [5], but using the same material for absorber and carrier, i.e. CaWO4.

The combination of an absorber made from NaI and a carrier of a different material (e.g. CaWO4, CdWO4, Al2O3, Si) led to two observations in the COSINUS composite prototypes: a different pulse shape with respect to the reference model for this type of detectors (Pröbst et al. [28], see appendix) and the lack of identification of nuclear recoil events in the data taken during irradiation with neutron sources. Since nuclear recoils produce less scintillation light than electron recoils due to quenching, they are expected to populate a separate band in the light yield versus energy plane. As discussed in this work, both observations can be understood as a consequence of scintillation light absorption in the carrier crystal. This insight motivated the transition from the carrier-based composite prototype concept to the final COSINUS detector design, the remoTES [4].

The focus of the present work, however, is the interpretation of the earlier carrier-based composite prototypes. We show that these detectors can be understood as light-enhanced phonon detectors, in which the TES measures a superposition of the absorber-phonon signal and an additional phonon signal generated by scintillation-light absorption in the carrier. In this way, an accidental experimental finding is turned into an opportunity for single-channel particle discrimination. In Sec. 5, we present a pulse shape model fit to the NaIce2 and NaIce6 data based on Bayesian inference, which validates the model, demonstrates its effectiveness for neutron-event discrimination, and yields new insights on the detector response. We conclude in Sec. 6.

papers.title: Singular Linear Differential-Algebraic Equations with Constant Coefficients Necessarily Admit Non-Computable Solutions
papers.abstract: If a regular linear differential-algebraic equation has a unique solution, this solution is known to be Turing computable. In contrast, this paper shows that singular linear differential-algebraic equations exhibit fundamentally different computability properties. More precisely, we show that for every linear differential-algebraic equation (LDAE) with constant computable coefficients, there exists a computable input function with strong regularity properties such that the LDAE admits a unique solution, yet this solution is not Turing computable. In fact, the solution is non-computable at certain computable times.

LDAEs are a widely accepted tool for modeling constrained dynamical systems [1] in numerous applications, such as power systems, nonlinear circuits or control systems [2, 3, 4, 5]. In general, they can be viewed as a combination of an ordinary differential equation (ODE) with some algebraic equations relating the single components of the independent variable 𝕩\mathbb{x}. LDAEs usually arise when a physical process is modeled by an ODE whose state variables are subject to additional constraints. A typical example of such an algebraic constraint arises when a mass point, whose motion is described by Newton’s ODEs, is restricted to a certain subspace. Another typical example arises from Kirchhoff’s circuit laws, which restrict the voltages and currents in a electrical network to follow certain rules (cf. also the example in Section IV-C).

The vast majority of LDAEs that appear in practical applications require numerical methods to compute an approximation of the solution. Since digital computers are the primary platform for such computations, a fundamental question is whether solutions of LDAEs are generally Turing computable [6, 7]. The central question is whether it is possible to compute an approximation of the solution under an effective control of the approximation error. papers.title: Debiased Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Amortized Bayesian Semi-Parametric Inference
papers.abstract: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) have recently gained popularity as an end-to-end approach to amortized Bayesian inference. Yet, their statistical behavior for semi-parametric targets, such as means under missingness or causal effects, remains poorly understood. In this work, we develop theoretical foundations for debiased PFNs to perform inference on finite-dimensional targets in general semi-parametric settings. First, we show that, despite being Bayes-optimal with respect to the target, an idealized PFN can exhibit a posterior concentration rate that implicitly depends on the concentration rates of (latent) nuisance functions and can become slower as the prior becomes more diverse. Then, to speed up the target posterior concentration rates, we introduce two generic debiasing strategies based on efficient influence functions: (i) a label correction and (ii) a prior correction. Finally, we show that the debiased PFNs (i) & (ii) possess concentration rates that asymptotically match a convergence rate given by traditional frequentist bias-corrected estimators. In this way, we establish a novel connection between amortized Bayesian inference with PFNs and frequentist semi-parametric efficiency theory. Under additional assumptions, this allows us to guarantee local and global optimality of PFN-based estimators (namely, the Bernstein-von Mises property and minimax optimality, respectively). Therefore, our work provides guidelines for designing debiased PFNs for semi-parametric inference with principled and provable asymptotic guarantees.

papers.title: Don't Skip the Baseline: A Controlled Comparison of Dynamic Expert Skipping in MoEs
papers.abstract: A growing body of work proposes dynamic expert-skipping methods for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that adjust the number of experts activated per token during inference, aiming to preserve model quality while further reducing the number of active parameters. These methods have added calibrated importance scores, inter-expert similarity metrics, or learned per-token allocators in order to identify experts to skip. However, different calibration regimes, different reductions in the effective number of experts, and evaluation suites make comparisons difficult. We classify four representative prior methods into a unified taxonomy and benchmark them against a natural, simple baseline: statically reducing the number of experts $k$ (i.e., same reduced $k$ across all layers and tokens). We provide a fair comparison of these methods at matched expert-compute budget, on two modern MoEs (Gemma4-26B-A4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B) in a text-only setting and a contemporary vision-language model (Qwen3-VL) in a multimodal setting. Surprisingly, we find that the simple baseline is hard to outperform consistently across models, modalities, benchmarks, and calibration settings. The methods we benchmark often underperform the baseline and achieved gains, when present, are minor. We further find that the effective $k$ achieved (or optimized for) in calibration can diverge from the effective $k$ in testing, resulting in over- or under-estimating the compute at inference time. Based on these findings, we recommend a calibration-free per-modality static $k$ reduction and validate this on a held-out model and modality. We further argue that a static control at matched measured compute is the baseline any dynamic skipping method must beat.

We therefore focus on the question: given a trained model, can we reduce the active number of experts while preserving quality by reducing this kk during inference, potentially dynamically per token and/or per layer?

Static, fixed-kk MoE inference has clear practical advantages: it is simple to implement, requires no additional calibration (i.e., selecting kk given an input token and layer), and, most importantly, matches the routing behavior learned during training. It further produces predictable, uniform compute and memory-access patterns across tokens. However, research has shown that not every token requires the same number of experts (Lu et al., 2024). As a result, different approaches have been proposed to optimize inference costs by varying kk. These approaches include static pruning, which permanently reduces the set of available experts to conserve memory, and (dynamic) skipping, which instead varies the number of active experts per token at inference time. Yang et al. (2025b) describe three benefits dynamic skipping can offer over fixed-kk inference: first, it reduces the total number of computations performed during each forward pass. Second, in small-batch scenarios, it reduces the number of unique experts active, lowering memory bandwidth requirements. Third, in a distributed deployment scenario, it can reduce communication overhead and improve load balancing.

papers.title: Convergence of stochastic gradient descent for learning linear neural networks
papers.abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is the cornerstone of modern deep learning, yet its theoretical convergence properties remain poorly understood in non-convex settings. To address this gap, we study SGD dynamics in deep linear neural networks - simplified models that retain key non-convex characteristics while remaining analytically tractable. Building on recent results for gradient descent, we extend convergence guarantees to SGD under regularized squared loss. We establish almost sure boundedness of SGD iterates. Using the framework of asymptotic pseudotrajectories from stochastic approximation theory, our analysis establishes then, for both deterministic and adaptive step-size choices, convergence of SGD to the set of critical points under mild conditions (without relying on Lipschitz properties or whitened data). To our knowledge, this is the first work providing almost sure convergence guarantees for SGD in deep linear networks, bridging the gap between theoretical optimization and practical stochastic training.

papers.title: Metal-poor molecular clouds in dwarf galaxies at parsec-scale resolution
papers.abstract: Understanding how stars form at low metallicity is challenging because carbon monoxide (CO) emission, which usually probes the molecular gas reservoir, is faint, and tends to be concentrated in parsec-scale clumps. To overcome this difficulty, in order to study the molecular clouds in metal-poor environments, we have acquired CO(2-1) ALMA maps at 3-4 pc resolution of four nearby dwarf galaxies with nebular (O/H) metallicities ranging from roughly 1/9 Z_sun to 1/3 Z_sun. Significant CO signal in the cubes has been identified through two masks, a ``strict'', high-confidence, mask and a ``broad'' one for better completeness. The former traces the cores of the clouds, while the latter includes fainter emission in the vicinity of the cores. Through a cloud-finding algorithm applied to the two sets of masked cubes, we have identified more than 200 molecular clouds across the sample, with roughly 50 in NGC3109, at 1/9 Z_sun, the lowest metallicity parsec-scale cloud population yet observed. The best-fit size-linewidth relations for the resolved clouds are similar among all galaxies, with a slope like the Milky Way (MW), but with lower velocity dispersion at a given cloud size. For a fixed CO-to-H_2 MW conversion factor, the cloud virial ratios tend to be large, and show a weak increasing trend with increasing cloud size, and decreasing apparent surface densities and metallicity. We find evidence for faint but significant CO emission outside CO-bright cores, spanning similar velocities to those observed in the cores. We attribute this to effective shielding by gas and dust, despite the low metallicities of our sample, since the CO tends to be cospatial with dust as traced by far-infrared emission.

This balancing act is observed at the macroscopic level as a low efficiency for the conversion of gas into stars.

The problem of probing the connection of star formation with molecular gas at low metallicity is the inability to probe molecular clouds in a metal-poor environment. The relatively high abundance of carbon monoxide (CO) in spiral galaxies makes it a common proxy of H2, because it can be easily excited within cold molecular clouds, thanks to low critical density and low excitation energy in the ground-state rotational transition. However, the presence of CO emission as a tracer for the molecular gas depends primarily on shielding. While self-shielding of H2 is highly efficient, occurring even at H2 column densities as low as NH2N_{\mathrm{H2}} ∼1014\sim 10^{14} cm-2 (de Jong et al. 1980), self-shielding of CO and cross-shielding of CO by H2 are inefficient processes. Thus, additional shielding of CO from FUV radiation by dust is necessary to maintain significant CO content. At low metallicity, C and O abundances and the dust-to-gas ratios are reduced (Aniano et al. 2020, e.g.,), leading to diminishing protection of CO against photodissociation.

papers.title: Small Collisions, Big Impact: The Sensitivity of Atmospheric Temperatures to Collision-Induced Absorption
papers.abstract: Collision-induced absorption (CIA) data are relevant to determining atmospheric temperatures and, in turn, the habitability of a diverse set of planetary atmospheres. However, these data remain sparse across broad wavelength and temperature ranges. Nevertheless, multiple, sometimes disagreeing, sources of experimental and theoretical data can be available for the same CIA pair. In this paper, we assess the impact of these varying sources on atmospheric temperatures and the limitations that the available data coverage can introduce. In order to inform future measurements and calculations, we test additional cases with extrapolated wavelength and temperature ranges. We first introduce a measure of the importance of CIA opacities depending on pressure and temperature by calculating the Rosseland mean with and without each CIA pair's contribution. Secondly, we employ each CIA source in a radiative transfer model of idealised atmospheres which maximise the effect of the CIA pair of interest. Our findings highlight the uncertainties related to the current data. Temperature differences between CIA data sources range from $\sim$10\,K when sources overlap in wavelength and temperature coverage to >100\,K when spectral gaps or temperature limits differ. Spectral windows or narrow temperature coverage can also hinder the model's convergence of the temperature profile. This work aims to provide guidance on the selection of CIA opacity datasets for atmospheric modelling and to identify the wavelength and temperature regimes in which further laboratory measurements and theoretical calculations are most urgently needed. We publish all our findings in detail in the form of an accessible website.

papers.intro:
Collision-Induced Absorption (CIA) arises from the interaction of colliding molecules — supermolecular complexes — which induce a transient dipole moment in otherwise non-polar species (Frommhold, 2006, e.g.). The absorption coefficient of these transitions scales with the collision frequency, and hence with the square of the gas density (or, more precisely, the product of the densities of the colliding partners). CIA thus becomes a dominant source of opacity only in high-pressure environments ≳1\gtrsim 1 bar. Crucially, this mechanism allows symmetric molecules such as N2\text{N}_{2}, H2\text{H}_{2}, and CH4\text{CH}_{4} to act as potent greenhouse gases, filling spectral windows left open by molecular absorption.

This absorption mechanism is fundamental to our understanding of diverse planetary climates. On the Archean Earth, N2\text{N}_{2}-H2\text{H}_{2} absorption has been invoked to maintain habitable temperatures despite the Faint Young Sun (Kasting, 2013; Wordsworth and Pierrehumbert, 2013). Similarly, the warming of Early Mars to allow for liquid water is often attributed to reducing atmospheres stabilised by CO2\text{CO}_{2}-H2\text{H}_{2} and CO2\text{CO}_{2}-CH4\text{CH}_{4} interactions (Ramirez et al., 2014; Wordsworth et al., 2017; Turbet et al., 2020). papers.title: The SIMPLIFI Survey: Polarization of Dense Filaments with SOFIA III. Relative orientations of antenna temperature gradients with the magnetic field in the DR21 molecular cloud
papers.abstract: We investigate magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence in the DR21 molecular cloud using far infrared polarimetry from SOFIA HAWC+ and molecular spectroscopy from the Nobeyama 45~m telescope. The Velocity Channel Gradient (VChG) method is applied to thin velocity slices of the 12CO and 13CO J=1-0 emission to determine the antenna temperature gradients and their orientations in the plane of the sky. The relative orientations of the gradients with respect to the magnetic field position angles enable an evaluation of theoretically predicted alignment of elongated, turbulent eddies for Alfvenic, fast and slow modes and self-gravity. The projected Rayleigh statistic is calculated for both the full cloud and 6 regions of interest to provide a quantitative assessment of these alignments. Our analysis finds mostly parallel alignment of the gradient direction and the local magnetic field orientation in the Main Ridge of DR21 that comprises most of the cloud mass. While parallel alignment can result from fast MHD modes or cloud collapse, previous studies show spectroscopic evidence for the large scale collapse of the DR21 cloud, which supports self-gravity as the primary cause of the observed parallel alignment. One of the six sub-filaments that are connected to the Main Ridge exhibits mostly perpendicular alignment of the position angles of the gradient and magnetic field. These perpendicular relative orientations may be a product of Alfven and slow modes in a magnetized, sub-Alfvenic medium even if the sub-filament is accreting onto the Main Ridge.

papers.intro:
The dynamics of the molecular interstellar medium in the Milky Way are characterized by fluctuating densities and velocities over spatial scales ranging from ∼\sim0.001 pc to tens of pc. For scales larger than 1 pc, the Mach numbers are generally greater than 2, indicative of supersonic turbulence. But such gas motions also interact with the interstellar magnetic field that threads molecular clouds. This interaction can modify the characteristics of the flow if the motions are sub-Alfvénic, σv/\sigma_{v}/VA<<1, where σv\sigma_{v} is the velocity dispersion and VA=|B|/(4​π​ρ)1/2(4\pi\rho)^{1/2} is the Alfvén velocity, |B||{\rm B}| is the magnetic field strength, and ρ\rho is the mass volume density of the gas. Under sub-Alfvénic conditions, the turbulent eddies are predicted to become elongated and aligned with the orientation of the magnetic field (Goldreich and Sridhar, 1995; Lazarian and Vishniac, 1999; Hu et al., 2020). Observationally, this feature of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence is recognized as an anisotropy of velocity and density structure functions and the alignment of localized gradients of gas properties with the local magnetic field orientation (Heyer et al., 2008; Esquivel and Lazarian, 2011; Heyer and Brunt, 2012; Burkhart et al., 2014). Such gas properties include molecular column densities (Planck Collaboration et al., 2016), velocity centroids (González-Casanova and Lazarian, 2017), and molecular line brightness temperatures over narrow velocity channels (Lazarian and Yuen, 2018; Hu et al., 2019; Heyer et al., 2020).

But such gas motions also interact with the interstellar magnetic field that threads molecular clouds. This interaction can modify the characteristics of the flow if the motions are sub-Alfvénic, σv/\sigma_{v}/VA<<1, where σv\sigma_{v} is the velocity dispersion and VA=|B|/(4​π​ρ)1/2(4\pi\rho)^{1/2} is the Alfvén velocity, |B||{\rm B}| is the magnetic field strength, and ρ\rho is the mass volume density of the gas. Under sub-Alfvénic conditions, the turbulent eddies are predicted to become elongated and aligned with the orientation of the magnetic field (Goldreich and Sridhar, 1995; Lazarian and Vishniac, 1999; Hu et al., 2020). Observationally, this feature of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence is recognized as an anisotropy of velocity and density structure functions and the alignment of localized gradients of gas properties with the local magnetic field orientation (Heyer et al., 2008; Esquivel and Lazarian, 2011; Heyer and Brunt, 2012; Burkhart et al., 2014). Such gas properties include molecular column densities (Planck Collaboration et al., 2016), velocity centroids (González-Casanova and Lazarian, 2017), and molecular line brightness temperatures over narrow velocity channels (Lazarian and Yuen, 2018; Hu et al., 2019; Heyer et al., 2020).

The DR21 molecular cloud has been a popular and important target for studies of the molecular interstellar medium and star formation. It is located within the Cygnus star forming complex (Downes and Rinehart, 1966; Dickel et al., 1978) at a heliocentric distance of 1.4±\pm0.08 kpc (Rygl et al., 2012). DR21 is superposed upon the W75 molecular cloud, also residing within the Cygnus complex, that may indicate the two clouds are colliding (Dickel et al., 1978). As measured by the Herschel Observatory using PACS and SPIRE bands, the total mass of the cloud is 2×\times104 M⊙ (Hennemann et al., 2012). The massive clump, DR21 Main, harbors a compact HII region. This star formation activity powers a massive (3000 M⊙), energetic (2×\times1048 ergs) molecular outflow (Garden et al., 1991). In addition, an explosive, dispersal outflow is present in the DR21 Main clump (Guzmán Ccolque et al., 2024). DR21 (OH) is another active, star forming clump within the DR21 cloud with multiple dense cores and molecular outflows (Zapata et al., 2012). Such internal feedback activity may modify the local magnetic field geometry or increase the gas velocities to super-Alfvénic values that effectively reduces the impact of the magnetic field on the gas.

Previous studies of DR21 have explored the magnetic field strength and geometry. Koley et al. (2021) measured Zeeman splitting of the 1665 MHz and 1667 MHz OH lines toward the photodissociation region in DR21 Main. From these data, they calculate a line of sight magnetic field strength of 0.13 milli-gauss. The mass to magnetic flux ratio is calculated assuming an abundance of OH molecules and assumed angles of the magnetic field direction with respect to the line of sight. The mass to magnetic flux ratios range from 6.6 to 1.1, which imply that the magnetic field can not support the DR21 Main clump against its own self-gravity. In addition, the magnetic energy density of the cloud is lower than the turbulent energy density by factors of 4 to 13 for this set of assumed angles. From these results, it appears that the magnetic field is not dynamically important in this stage of the evolution of DR21 Main.

papers.title: Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting grows a dense scene from a sparse initialization through adaptive density control (ADC), driven by per-Gaussian statistics gathered during rendering. These statistics pass a frustum-based visibility filter blind to occlusion: fully occluded Gaussians still count as observed, diluting the averaged gradient signal and suppressing densification precisely where geometry is occluded. We correct this with an occlusion-aware filter that restricts densification statistics to views in which a Gaussian actually contributes, and replace the criterion's raw view-count normalizer with an average-contribution one. Integrated into a StopThePop-based framework, the two together improve every image-quality metric over the occlusion-blind baseline on occlusion-heavy scenes (up to 6% lower LPIPS), at less than half the Gaussians a view-count normalizer requires. Under the longer schedules these large scenes require, the count stays bounded where most criteria diverge, and on smaller benchmarks our method stays competitive at a fraction of the competitors' count.

papers.intro:
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [13] represents a milestone in 3D scene reconstruction and novel-view synthesis. It introduced a large multi-component system, with a tile-based rasterizer and adaptive density control (ADC) purpose-built for the new representation. Follow-up works improve these components largely in isolation, many focusing on ADC, which is essential for growing a dense reconstruction from the sparse initialization. However, we find that the accumulation of the densification statistics at the root of all ADC decisions has a fundamental flaw: the frustum-based visibility filter that gathers them tests only whether a Gaussian could appear in a view, not whether it actually contributes to the rendered image. A fully occluded Gaussian yields zero gradients, yet the filter still counts its view in the criterion’s denominator, dragging the average down and stalling densification wherever geometry is occluded. The resulting under-densification grows with the degree of occlusion and degrades quality most where high detail and occlusion co-occur. Large, occlusion-heavy scenes such as multi-room apartments are affected most severely (Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting). We correct this with an occlusion-aware visibility filter that updates a Gaussian’s statistics only from views in which it is actually rendered; densification then reaches occluded regions whenever their level of detail requires it.

papers.title: An efficient approach to electron-phonon coupling calculations of heterostructures within an all-electron framework
papers.abstract: A major challenge in calculating electron-phonon coupling at interfaces from first principles is the prohibitive computational cost due to the large supercells involved. Here, we present an efficient approach, which builds the electron-phonon matrix of weakly bound heterostructures from the properties of the isolated layers. The two key ingredients, the dynamical matrices and the potential response, are constructed in two steps. In the expansion step, these quantities are folded from the unit cells onto the supercell through an exact Fourier mapping. In the addition step, the interatomic force constants and the potential responses of the heterostructure are assembled blockwise from the corresponding quantities of the isolated layers, neglecting the weak interlayer contribution. The method is implemented in the electron-phonon module of the all-electron full-potential code exciting, enabling efficient calculations of the electron-phonon self-energy. We demonstrate the approach for the phonon dispersion and spectral functions of bilayer WSe$_2$ and pyridine/MoS$_2$, in comparison with exact reference calculations.

papers.intro:
Stacking two-dimensional materials into weakly bound van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures has become a powerful route to tune electronic and optical properties beyond those of the individual layers [12, 24]. In this regard, transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) are prominent building blocks [22], whether combined with one another into multilayered structures or interfaced with organic molecules to form hybrid inorganic organic systems (HIOS) [36, 19, 3, 6]. These systems host rich phenomena, from interlayer and moiré excitons in multilayer TMDCs [20] to interfacial charge transfer, hybrid and charge-transfer excitons, and strong electron-phonon coupling (EPC) in HIOS [28, 35, 2, 5, 15, 16, 4].

For the quantitative modeling of various excitations, many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) has become the standard for describing electron-electron and electron-hole interactions, through the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} approximation for quasiparticle (QP) band structures and the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) for optical excitations [15, 4], respectively. Likewise, a consistent treatment of self-energy effects from EPC within MBPT [9, 8, 17, 25, 26, 23, 14, 30] has become routine for semiconductors [14] and more recently, has been demonstrated to be substantial also in HIOS [11, 10, 16]. For complex systems, however, and in particular for interfaces, which typically require large supercells, the computational cost of MBPT renders its application often prohibitive. This not only applies to G​WGW and BSE, but also to the investigation of EPC effects, since one needs phonon calculations for the complete heterostructure. For the electronic and optical properties, this cost has motivated an expansion and addition screening (EAS) method for the non-interacting polarizability of vdW heterostructures [37, 21, 29], a key ingredient in both G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} and BSE calculations. In this work, we extend this idea to EPC, an approach we refer to as EA-EPC. We have implemented it in the all-electron code exciting [18, 27], which is based on the (linearized) augmented planewave + local orbital (L)APW+LO method. The central quantity of this calculation is the EPC matrix, which depends on the dynamical matrix and the potential response upon the displacements of the nuclei. Our method constructs these ingredients for the heterostructure in the two steps that give it its name. In the expansion step, the dynamical matrix and potential response of each layer are mapped onto the supercell of the heterostructure. In the addition step, the contributions of the individual layers are combined into those of the full system. If the interaction between the layers is weak, this construction recovers the EPC of the heterostructure from calculations of its constituents alone, at a fraction of the computational cost of a full supercell treatment.

papers.title: The Culture Within: Towards Mechanistic Understanding of Cultural Reasoning in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate across culturally diverse settings, yet existing evaluations largely measure cultural behavior at the output level. We introduce CultureLens, a reference-grounded benchmark and mechanistic study of how LLMs use cultural information. CultureLens contains 9,261 scenarios across 75 countries and systematically varies country, value, true-norm, and contradictory-norm evidence. Across Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-3-12B, and Qwen-3.5-27B, stating a contradictory norm lowers aligned answers by 32-47 percentage points, even when the model answers correctly from the country alone. Mechanistically, models default to Anglophone norms when no country is given. The failure under a contradictory norm is not one of missing knowledge, as blocking the norm inside the model restores the correct answer in most cases. Models accept a stated norm according to how it is presented and not whether it is true, which leaves them most exposed to errors in retrieved content. Supervised fine-tuning with contradictory-norm examples raises aligned answers under a contradictory norm to 85-93%, including on unseen countries, at a small cost under a true norm.

papers.intro:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across countries and communities with different social expectations, values, and norms. A response that seems reasonable in one cultural context may be inappropriate or unhelpful in another. Recent work shows that LLMs exhibit uneven cultural knowledge and behavior across countries, languages, and value systems (DURMUS et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2024; Myung et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024). Other work goes beyond factual cultural knowledge to whether models adapt their judgments and responses when culturally relevant context is provided (Shi et al., 2024; Rao et al., 2025). Yet they evaluate only model outputs.

A response that seems reasonable in one cultural context may be inappropriate or unhelpful in another. Recent work shows that LLMs exhibit uneven cultural knowledge and behavior across countries, languages, and value systems (DURMUS et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2024; Myung et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024). Other work goes beyond factual cultural knowledge to whether models adapt their judgments and responses when culturally relevant context is provided (Shi et al., 2024; Rao et al., 2025). Yet they evaluate only model outputs.

Cultural competence involves not only knowledge of cultural contexts, but also the ability to interpret and act appropriately within them (Deardorff, 2006). For LLMs, this raises the question of whether cultural knowledge that is internally available guides behavior, since a model may encode a norm without relying on it (Elazar et al., 2021). In deployment, models rarely answer from the country alone. Prompts also carry cultural claims from users and retrieved documents (Lewis et al., 2020), which may be outdated, stereotyped, or wrong (Pan et al., 2023), and models often defer to stated context over their own knowledge (Longpre et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2024) and agree with users’ beliefs (Sharma et al., 2024). A stated norm that contradicts what the model knows about a country thus tests whether its cultural knowledge survives a conflicting claim. A wrong answer may mean that the knowledge was absent, or that it was present and overridden, which behavioral evaluation cannot distinguish. Recent mechanistic work identifies cultural information in activations, neurons, and sparse features (Yu et al., 2026; Yamamoto et al., 2026; Zou et al., 2026), motivating a study of how these relate to culturally situated behavior.

CultureLens contains 9,261 scenarios across 75 countries and varies country, value, true-norm, and contradictory-norm evidence, testing what a model knows, whether it uses correct evidence, and whether it can tell correct evidence from incorrect, in both a two-option choice and open-ended generation. Using probes and causal interventions on the stated norm, we then study why models abandon a correct country-based answer under a contradictory norm. We test whether the outcome is decided before the model answers, locate where the norm takes over, determine whether the model’s knowledge is lost or overridden, and examine what governs compliance. Finally, we fine-tune models on reference answers and examine how their behavior changes.

papers.title: Optimizing Flexibility and Commitments: Partially-Adaptive Multi-Stage Matrix Assembly Layout Design Problem
papers.abstract: Matrix assembly layouts provide manufacturing flexibility under product variety and demand volatility through locally reconfigurable production stations. Periodic redesign exploits this flexibility, yet existing models allow only annual revisions. Finer calendars expose a flexibility-commitment trade-off: advance layout commitments support coordination, supplier agreements, and discounts. We introduce the layout revision timing problem, jointly choosing revision points and committed layout sequences under demand uncertainty while production adapts within those layouts. We formulate it as a partially adaptive multistage stochastic program with two complementary extensions. Our cost-based extension places the economic value of advance commitment in the objective rather than prescribing revision budgets; our scenario-adaptive extension adapts revision timing to revealed information. For station-use minimization, we establish a cost decomposition across commitment intervals, yielding an exact dynamic program that reuses station subproblem solutions across model variants and parameter settings. As a more general alternative, we develop an integer L-shaped method strengthened by monotonicity-based cuts for budgeted formulations and enhanced cuts exploiting this decomposition. On automotive instances, including scenario trees with nearly 10,000 nodes, our combined model's average savings in expected station-use cost at the base-case discount reach 4.99% versus full adaptivity and 28.65% versus full commitment. Scenario adaptivity is most valuable when demand paths diverge and discounts justify commitment on some paths but not others, as in electrification-driven scenarios.

papers.intro:
Matrix assembly layouts have emerged as a prominent response to the growing need for production systems that can accommodate high product variety, volatile demand, evolving sustainability requirements, and rapid changes in products and production technologies. These pressures are particularly visible in automotive manufacturing, where rising customization and the transition across powertrain technologies have intensified the need for flexible production. Consistent with this shift, the AMS/ABB Automotive Manufacturing Outlook Survey 2025 identifies the transition toward more flexible and modular manufacturing processes as one of the principal strategies being pursued by automotive manufacturers [6].

Consistent with this shift, the AMS/ABB Automotive Manufacturing Outlook Survey 2025 identifies the transition toward more flexible and modular manufacturing processes as one of the principal strategies being pursued by automotive manufacturers [6].

Matrix assembly layouts are particularly suited to production segments with high product variety and heterogeneous workloads and task requirements. In these unpaced systems, modular workstations are arranged in a grid, and automated guided vehicles (AGVs) transport products between stations. Rather than following a common station sequence, each product is transported along a customized route that visits only the stations needed to perform its required tasks. A matrix segment can be integrated into a broader production system rather than operated as a standalone facility [8, 13]. Figure 1 illustrates a representative matrix layout: the pink line traces one possible product-specific AGV route, while the buffer station represents an interface between the matrix segment and the surrounding production system.

In these unpaced systems, modular workstations are arranged in a grid, and automated guided vehicles (AGVs) transport products between stations. Rather than following a common station sequence, each product is transported along a customized route that visits only the stations needed to perform its required tasks. A matrix segment can be integrated into a broader production system rather than operated as a standalone facility [8, 13]. Figure 1 illustrates a representative matrix layout: the pink line traces one possible product-specific AGV route, while the buffer station represents an interface between the matrix segment and the surrounding production system.

The physical structure of a matrix layout provides several complementary forms of flexibility. Routing flexibility arises because a task may be assigned to alternative stations, whereas operation flexibility arises because task sequences may vary subject to precedence constraints rather than being fixed in advance. There is also volume flexibility because production capacity can be adjusted through local station-level changes as demand changes. The same modularity allows the layout to respond locally to disruptions without requiring the entire production line to be shut down. Together, these capabilities form the operational basis for dynamic layout planning, in which the matrix segment can be periodically redesigned in response to changes in product mix, demand conditions, or station availability over the product lifecycle.

In current practice, matrix assembly layout design is undertaken at the tactical level of the facility-planning hierarchy, after the main production segments have been identified and before operational production decisions are made. The planning horizon typically covers the product lifecycle and may, for instance, span five years. Major layout reconfigurations are generally coordinated between consecutive production years, for example during planned maintenance periods such as end-of-summer shutdowns [2]. Within this horizon, the planner selects a layout configuration for each production year, comprising the active station set and the task-to-station assignment. The configuration is determined before the year’s actual demand is known; once demand is observed, the operational planning step determines production quantities within the selected configuration.

Existing dynamic matrix-layout planning models formalize this planning process on an annual time grid and show that periodic redesign can yield efficiency gains under both deterministic and stochastic demand [2, 3]. Figure 2, synthesized from these models, depicts the corresponding annual planning template. Each production year contains a pre-demand layout-planning substage (S), in which the layout configuration is selected based on aggregated demand forecasts, followed by a post-demand operational substage (O), in which production quantities are determined after demand is realized. We refer to the pre-demand substage as strategic to distinguish its information timing from that of post-demand operational recourse. At this annual resolution, the stochastic formulation requires the selected configuration to permit feasible production under every demand realization represented for the year. This structure captures an important source of value: matrix layouts can be redesigned over time as demand changes. However, because admissible revision times are fixed at annual boundaries rather than optimized, these models cannot fully exploit the local reconfigurability that distinguishes matrix layouts from traditional serial assembly lines. In particular, they cannot evaluate whether an intermediate layout revision would better adapt the layout to demand patterns that emerge within the year. Beyond these missed revision opportunities, the annual representation also limits the feasibility statement delivered by the model: it verifies feasibility for demand and capacity measured at the annual planning unit, but it does not certify feasibility for a finer operational calendar in which the same annual demand may be distributed unevenly across shorter intervals.
