Planning at this finer resolution makes it possible to respond to seasonal or regime-driven demand patterns that are obscured by annual aggregation. Yet revising the plan at every opportunity may leave insufficient time to prepare the resulting configuration changes. Station activation may require hiring personnel, installing equipment, and arranging infrastructure, whereas task reassignment may require worker training, equipment movement, and validation. We refer to the interval between consecutive selected revision points as a commitment: at the earlier revision point, the planner fixes the sequence of layout configurations for the intervening periods until the next revision, providing time to coordinate their implementation. Beyond this coordination benefit, longer commitments can create economic value through longer-term arrangements, such as supplier agreements, bulk purchasing terms, or priority delivery.

papers.title: P-ONE-1: the first detector line of the Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment
papers.abstract: Neutrino telescopes instrument optically transparent media with three-dimensional arrays of photosensors to detect Cherenkov radiation induced by neutrino interactions within or near the instrumented volume. The small cross-sections of the weak interaction and the low neutrino fluxes above TeV energies require vast detector volumes, which only natural media on Earth can realistically provide. Spurred by the detection of the first neutrino sources by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a new generation of neutrino telescopes is emerging to increase the global instrumented volume and detection sensitivity. The Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment (P-ONE) aims to install such a telescope in the Northeast Pacific Ocean, building on established neutrino telescope design targets in collaboration with Ocean Networks Canada (ONC). This article presents the design, integration, and testing of the first P-ONE line, P-ONE-1, in preparation for its deployment and integration into ONC's deep-sea observatory NEPTUNE. Alongside the detector design and integration methods, we detail in-air and in-water system-level validation performed at several test sites in Canada, culminating in the successful construction of P-ONE-1 and its preparation for deployment.

papers.intro:
Neutrino astronomy aims to detect and characterize sources of high-energy neutrinos in the universe. The elusiveness of neutrinos, being solely weakly interacting, and the low expected fluxes above TeV energies make this a challenging task; however, the detection of the first point sources and neutrinos from our Galaxy by IceCube [1, 2, 3]and the ultra-high-energy neutrino by KM3NeT [4] have demonstrated that it is possible and that a new era of astronomy is accessible with increased detection statistics.

Neutrino astronomy aims to detect and characterize sources of high-energy neutrinos in the universe. The elusiveness of neutrinos, being solely weakly interacting, and the low expected fluxes above TeV energies make this a challenging task; however, the detection of the first point sources and neutrinos from our Galaxy by IceCube [1, 2, 3]and the ultra-high-energy neutrino by KM3NeT [4] have demonstrated that it is possible and that a new era of astronomy is accessible with increased detection statistics.

The main detection signature is Cherenkov light emitted by the relativistic charged secondary particles produced in neutrino interactions. Above the TeV scale, the resulting event morphologies range from cascades of a few tens of meters to muon tracks of several kilometers. Resolving these topologies, while collecting sufficient statistics from the faint astrophysical flux, requires instrumented volumes on cubic-kilometer scales. The challenge is to instrument such a volume densely enough to reject atmospheric and environmental backgrounds, yet sparsely enough to reach the necessary target mass. Moving beyond the discovery of an astrophysical flux towards detailed characterization of source populations and production mechanisms therefore calls for a new generation of detectors that build on the experience of IceCube and KM3NeT while improving particle identification, timing, background suppression, and angular resolution.

The Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment (P-ONE) [5] is a new initiative to achieve greater precision and deep-sea reliability through novel technologies. P-ONE aims to detect astrophysical neutrinos at or above the TeV scale using Pacific Ocean water as the detection medium. With low optical scattering in seawater, the objective is to boost the angular resolution of detected neutrino events by a factor of four compared to IceCube [6, 7], thus increasing the sensitivity to neutrino point sources [8]. It is also located in the Northern Hemisphere, placing the Galactic Plane and Galactic Center within its sensitive region by detecting up-going neutrinos through the Earth. This reduces atmospheric background, which enhances sensitivity. With this, P-ONE aims to complement the high-energy neutrino sky coverage together with other experimental efforts in the world, among them KM3NeT in the Mediterranean Sea [9], GVD in Lake Baikal [10], built and proposed upgrades of IceCube [11, 12], and proposed initiatives in the South China Sea [13, 14, 15].

papers.title: Braid spaces have no geodesic loops
papers.abstract: The braid spaces are defined as universal metric coverings of the standard complex spaces, branched over certain hyperplane arrangements. We describe a natural family of convex functions on braid spaces and use them to prove that braid spaces contain no geodesic loops. This statement is a consequence of the well-known conjecture that every braid space is CAT(0).

papers.title: Magnetic-Field-Induced Darkening of Bright Excitons in a MoWSe$_2$ Monolayer Alloy
papers.abstract: Magnetic fields are widely used to brighten spin-forbidden dark excitons, but the inverse effect on an optically bright exciton has remained largely unexplored. We demonstrate the complementary phenomenon of magnetic-field-induced darkening of a bright exciton in Mo$_{0.68}$W$_{0.32}$Se$_2$. At 4.2 K, an in-plane magnetic field up to 25 T activates a dark-exciton line 14.2$\pm$1.3 meV below the bright exciton while suppressing the bright-exciton emission by about 85\%. A bright-dark mixing model quantitatively captures the coupled energy and intensity evolution with an effective in-plane $g$ factor of $|g_{\parallel}|=5.2\pm0.2$. Alloying is crucial to the effect, as it brings the system close to the bright-dark crossover, where a small bright-dark splitting is combined with unusually strong in-plane magnetic coupling. This places the system in a regime where field-induced level repulsion raises the bright-like branch and strongly depletes its thermal population. These results identify a general route to magnetic control of exciton populations through engineering of the bright-dark hierarchy.

papers.title: Superconducting weak links at substrate steps in bilayer nickelate films
papers.abstract: Ambient-pressure superconductivity above 40 K has been realized in bilayer nickelate thin films on SrLaAlO$_4$ (001), yet resistive measurements often exhibit incomplete zero-resistance states and/or two-step superconducting transitions of unresolved origin. We show that these features arise from superconducting weak links at substrate step-terrace structures. A direct correlation between the azimuthal-angle-dependent two-step transition and step-terrace orientation establishes this connection, further supported by atomic-scale visualization of structurally disrupted regions at step terraces. Modeling the films as pristine (weak-link) regions with higher (lower) transition temperature reproduces essential features of the two-step transition using both a simple model and finite-element simulations. Transport measurements further reveal a strong dependence of transition characteristics - and even the occurrence of superconductivity itself - on average terrace width. These results identify step-induced weak links as the microscopic origin of two-step transitions in bilayer nickelate films, providing a framework for understanding anisotropic and percolative transport, and a route to superconducting devices.

papers.title: GRADUS: Discovering and Recovering Agent Lessons from the Environment's Latent Syllabus
papers.abstract: Training LLM agents for policy-constrained tool environments, such as an airline backend with booking, refund, and cancellation policies, requires tasks that exercise the environment's rules individually and in combination. Existing synthesis pipelines let a model propose tasks and retain only those it immediately solves, biasing training data toward easier behaviors. We introduce Gradus (Graded Rungs of Ascending Difficulty from an Underlying System), which decouples what a task should teach from the concrete task and solution used to teach it. Without seed tasks, Gradus treats a fixed environment as a latent syllabus, extracting guarded behavioral operators that capture how actions depend on current conditions and how their effects reshape subsequent decisions. It composes these operators into increasingly demanding tasks while using corpus-level feedback to target missing outcome combinations. Crucially, Gradus jointly calibrates tasks and solutions against the environment: execution feedback identifies which side to refine while preserving the intended behavioral requirements. Verification thus becomes a recovery signal rather than a terminal filter, coupling coverage-guided exploration with the preservation of difficult examples. From off-the-shelf backbones, the resulting curriculum lifts a 30B model from 59% to 89% on $τ^2$-Bench and from 47% to 83% on CAR-Bench with an Opus 4.5 proposer, and to 76% and 62%, respectively, with an open-weight Qwen3-235B proposer. These results show the value of jointly controlling which behaviors are explored and which survive into verified training data.

Training LLMs to act as agents requires data spanning diverse tool use, reasoning demands, and multi-turn interactions. Recent synthesis pipelines build generalist agents by generating tasks, workflows, and even entire environments at scale (Lyu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026). Recent synthesis pipelines build generalist agents by generating tasks, workflows, and even entire environments at scale (Lyu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026). These efforts broaden the range of situations agents encounter. A complementary problem arises when the environment is already given: how can we construct a curriculum that prepares an agent for the full range of behaviors required by that particular environment?

A fixed environment contains substantially more training structure than its list of APIs suggests. Depending on the current state and operating policies, the same action may be permitted, denied, or require additional steps. For example, in an airline booking environment, whether a cancellation is permitted depends on the cabin class, the time since booking, and whether travel insurance covers the stated reason, so the same request may end up with different agent behaviors in different states. Moreover, an earlier action may change the conditions governing later decisions. Constructing training data from this environment structure presents two coupled challenges: deciding which behaviors to teach and producing valid tasks and solutions that teach them.

papers.title: Multi-View Latent Action Pretraining for Cross-Embodiment Robot Learning from Videos
papers.abstract: Action-free videos are an appealing substitute for costly teleoperated data. Latent action models (LAMs) turn videos into a supervision signal by inferring abstract actions between frames. Existing LAMs observe a single camera view, which resolves 6D robot actions only ambiguously missing out-of-plane movements and potential occlusions. We propose a LAM that ingests synchronized multi-camera views using cross-attention to resolve depth and occlusions before compressing them into latent actions. The latent actions are fed into a policy in which a latent expert and an action expert are coupled by sequential flow matching around a frozen VLM backbone. We further evaluate in strict cross-embodiment settings where task-specific demonstrations come from other embodiments. We show that dual-view LAM pretraining improves the decodability of ground-truth 6D actions by 17% compared to single-view, while scaling single-view data by two orders of magnitude is not sufficient to fully recover out-of-plane motions. The downstream policy improves success rate by +13.5% compared to +6.2% for single-view LAM. A single cross-embodiment is sufficient for skill transfer, and adding a second viewpoint outperforms adding up to four further embodiments. The results transfer to hardware where demonstrations come from a human hand improving success rate by +20% over action-only policies in 850 rollouts. We show that video and robot data are complementary, and that benefits of learning from video are task-dependent. Website: https://learnsyslab.github.io/multiview_latent_action_pretraining/
papers.intro:
Data availability remains a limiting factor for learning robot policies. Recent works propose leveraging action-free video data that contains semantically rich information, which can aid robots in long-term task planning. One approach infers latent actions from videos using an inverse dynamics model (IDM), and conditions a downstream policy on those latents [1, 2, 3]. The latent actions are an abstract representation describing the transition dynamics in the video. Downstream policy success highly depends on how well the latent actions predict real robot actions. A number of approaches have been proposed to improve this transferability, including grounding latent actions in real robot actions or states[4, 5] and visual pre-processing approaches [6, 7, 8]. However, we show that existing single-view approaches cannot sufficiently recover the full 6D poses that define robot actions. Single views capture actions only ambiguously: out-of-plane motion is underdetermined and parts of the scene may be occluded.

The latent actions are an abstract representation describing the transition dynamics in the video. Downstream policy success highly depends on how well the latent actions predict real robot actions. A number of approaches have been proposed to improve this transferability, including grounding latent actions in real robot actions or states[4, 5] and visual pre-processing approaches [6, 7, 8]. However, we show that existing single-view approaches cannot sufficiently recover the full 6D poses that define robot actions. Single views capture actions only ambiguously: out-of-plane motion is underdetermined and parts of the scene may be occluded.

We therefore propose a Latent Action Model (LAM) that ingests synchronized multi-camera views and attends to image patches across viewpoints—recovering depth and occlusion a single camera leaves ambiguous—before compressing them into a latent action. We demonstrate that this spatial awareness leads to better recoverability of 6D robot actions compared to single-view approaches. Crucially, multiple views are only required during LAM pretraining to improve latent action quality, but not during the policy learning stage where only a single external camera and wrist view are used.

papers.title: Testing Associative Creativity in Humans and Multimodal LLMs with Difficult-to-Name Visual Stimuli
papers.abstract: We investigate associative creativity in descriptions of abstract visual stimuli by humans and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). While conceptual association is central to human communication, it remains unclear how humans and models adapt when visual stimuli become increasingly difficult to map onto familiar semantic concepts. We evaluate several state-of-the-art MLLMs and human participants along two dimensions of creativity, originality and effectiveness, using two datasets with controlled manipulations of difficulty. SilCC varies naming difficulty through progressively more complex combinations of abstract shapes, and PixCC varies difficulty through increasing levels of random visual noise. Results show that humans produce more diverse associative descriptions than MLLMs, including greater semantic distance, higher entropy, and more novel expressions relative to reference lexica. As difficulty increases, effectiveness declines in SilCC, and humans increasingly shift from holistic associations to descriptions of low-level visual properties in PixCC.
papers.intro:
Humans use conceptual associations to describe novel experiences, overcome communicative challenges, and convey meaning even when the precise vocabulary is unavailable. For example, a toddler encountering an airplane for the first time might describe it as a “bird”. Such conceptual mapping reflects a fundamental mechanism of human cognition and has been linked to domain-specific performance across a range of tasks (Beaty and Kenett, 2023).

For example, a toddler encountering an airplane for the first time might describe it as a “bird”. Such conceptual mapping reflects a fundamental mechanism of human cognition and has been linked to domain-specific performance across a range of tasks (Beaty and Kenett, 2023).

Recent research on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has begun to examine and benchmark their capacity to produce creative descriptions of different kinds of input images (see following section). However, it remains unclear how such systems respond to stimuli of increasing difficulty, particularly in cases when associations become less straightforward due to increased visual complexity, reduced resemblance to familiar objects, or reduced ‘degree of objecthood’ (Feldman, 2003). In principle, several outcomes are conceivable: Systems with strong associative capabilities may continue to connect visual inputs to meaningful semantic concepts despite increased difficulty. Alternatively, they may shift their descriptive strategies, relying less on higher-level associations and more on low-level, objective properties of the stimulus. Finally, their ability to generate meaningful descriptions may deteriorate altogether. To date, these possibilities have not been systematically examined in either humans or generative systems.

In this work, we examine the associative abilities of several state-of-the-art MLLMs using established criteria for creativity, namely originality and effectiveness (Runco and Jaeger, 2012). For this, we collect and annotate two datasets of abstract shapes with controlled manipulations of naming difficulty. In SilCC, difficulty is varied through the complexity of abstract shape combinations; in PixCC, it is varied through increasing levels of random visual noise. Using these datasets, we analyze how naming behavior changes as difficulty increases and compare human and MLLM performance in producing original and effective descriptions. We assess effectiveness by testing whether descriptions adequately capture the visual input, and originality through measures of semantic diversity and naming variation. In PixCC, we also account for strategies that circumvent associative descriptions when noise weakens the link between visual stimuli and familiar semantic concepts.

papers.title: Polarity Blindness in LLM Safety: A Systematic Study of Negation, Antonym Substitution, and Adversarial Framing
papers.abstract: Negation remains a persistent challenge for language models across NLP tasks and modalities. We show that this weakness can undermine LLM safety guardrails through a structural vulnerability we term polarity blindness: the failure to recognize harmful intent after polarity-altering linguistic transformations. We study two forms of polarity inversion: grammatical negation and antonym replacement, and use synonym replacement as a polarity-preserving control. We further test whether an adversarial textual wrapper amplifies these failures. Using a 260-prompt benchmark across 10 state-of-the-art LLMs and 3 languages (English, Spanish, Czech), stratified by harmfulness potential and evaluated on a validated 0-5 harm scale, we find that polarity blindness affects most evaluated models, with mean harm scores reaching 4.12 for the most vulnerable model. The effect persists across typologically differing negation systems, suggesting that polarity blindness reflects a broader limitation in semantic robustness rather than a language- or grammar-specific failure.

papers.intro:
Negation remains a persistent challenge for NLP systems despite decades of study and its universality across languages (Déprez and Espinal, 2020). Negation detection (Abuhammad and Ahmed, 2023) is central in domains such as clinical NLP (Martinis et al., 2024), and failures under negation have been documented across tasks, domains, and modalities. This broader phenomenon, often referred to as the “negation problem” or “negation blindness” (Vrabcová et al., 2025), suggests that language models struggle to reliably reason over polarity-altering linguistic constructions. In this work, we investigate whether these weaknesses have implications for LLM safety.

In this work, we investigate whether these weaknesses have implications for LLM safety.

Unlike prior work on negation in toxicity detection, we study the opposite failure. In toxicity classification, negation can cause benign content to be incorrectly flagged as toxic (Hosseini et al., 2017; Alexiou and Mertoguno, 2023). In contrast, we study whether polarity inversion11 1 Polarity inversion reverses an expression’s meaning through operations such as negation or antonym replacement. causes safety guardrails to underdetect harmful intent. We term this vulnerability polarity blindness: the failure of LLM safety mechanisms to recognize harmful intent under polarity-inverting transformations. Although these transformations alter surface polarity, the resulting prompts may preserve harmful intent in context, making this connection an empirical question rather than a direct consequence of prior toxicity-detection findings.

papers.title: Edit in Sync: Unified End-to-End Audio-Visual Editing for Human-Centric Videos
papers.abstract: Human-centric audio-visual editing requires precise alignment of lip movements, gestures, and expressions with speech. Existing methods process inputs through independent video and audio pipelines, preventing cross-modal interaction between visual editing and audio dubbing. Many of these pipelines further rely on mask-based inpainting. As a result, they suffer from poor lip-audio synchronization, cumulative pipeline errors, and an inherent mask-size dilemma. We present AVE, the first unified end-to-end framework that jointly performs reference-guided person swapping, insertion, and deletion across both audio and video modalities without requiring spatial masks. To overcome data scarcity, we design a synthesis pipeline and introduce AVE-Dataset, the first audio-visual editing dataset to provide 100K pairs with appearance and voice references. By combining Synthetic-to-Real reconstruction with preliminary audio warm-up, our framework transcends synthetic pipeline limits and mitigates audio-video token imbalance. AVE outperforms modality-separate audio-visual editing pipelines in editing realism, temporal consistency, and audio-visual alignment.

papers.intro:
Content editing has long been an important topic in both visual and audio fields. Representative visual editing tasks include object removal [57, 58, 13, 34], insertion [1, 46, 53, 21], and replacement [35, 12, 51], while audio editing commonly involves voice conversion [22, 29], source separation [44, 30, 32], and speech content editing [36, 41]. Despite progress in both modalities, independent audio-visual editing remains insufficient for human-centric scenarios where visual events and speech are intrinsically coupled across lip movements, facial expressions, and bodily actions [27, 16]. Human-centric editing such as insertion, removal, and replacement should be reflected coherently in both modalities, with consistent subject presence, identity, and timing [14, 26]. Thus, joint human-centric audio-visual editing has emerged as a key multimodal frontier and the primary focus of this work.

However, training such a unified framework is severely constrained by data scarcity. A common workaround is to reformulate editing as a self-supervised mask-and-reconstruct task [7, 14, 26], where the target subject and speech are masked to reconstruct the original content from the remaining context. Yet, such mask-dependent training imposes strict spatial constraints that often erase fine motion cues and surrounding context, causing visual artifacts and temporal instability. To improve reference adherence across diverse visual and acoustic contexts, we construct cross-pair multimodal references by retrieving the target identity across distinct scenes or synthesizing it with generative augmentations, providing reliable identity and timbre guidance while preventing copy-and-paste shortcuts. Through multi-stage visual and acoustic filtering, we assemble AVE-Dataset, comprising 100K curated audio-visual pairs that support unified character Delete, Insert, and Swap.

By taking complete source audio-video signals directly as input AVE preserves full spatiotemporal and acoustic context, producing harmoniously synchronized output under multimodal conditions. AVE builds on a joint audio-video backbone [31], utilizing its bidirectional cross-modal attention for synchronized editing across modalities. To handle complex multimodal inputs, we introduce a Modality-Aware Sync-RoPE design that assigns role-specific positional coordinates to source, target, and reference tokens. This preserves source-target temporal correspondence while aligning audio and video along a shared timeline. Furthermore, we introduce a multi-stage training curriculum with bidirectional supervision: forward supervision (from a real source to a synthetic target) teaches the intended editing operations, while the backward direction exposes the model to real target distributions. Together with audio warm-up, bidirectional joint adaptation, and quality-focused refinement, this curriculum mitigates synthesis artifacts and enables the mask-free editor to bootstrap beyond the quality ceiling of its synthetic training data.

papers.title: Matrix-Game 4.0: Harnessing Video Models for Real-Time Playable Game Worlds
papers.abstract: Moving from controllable videos to genuinely playable worlds requires persistent world state, executable game rules, and low-latency interaction. We outline a roadmap for the next generation of Matrix-Game that separates game execution from visual generation through an executable game harness, and introduce Matrix-Game 4.0 as the first system built on this design. A lightweight game engine maintains world state and executes interaction rules, a multimodal coding agent translates player ideas into game code and dynamic scene captions, and a renderer based on autoregressive video model transforms engine-rendered low-poly proxies into detailed visuals, conditioned on dynamic captions and memory references. This framework provides continuous guidance for visual generation and enables natural-language creation and modification of scenes and gameplay. Our renderer is trained on aligned low-poly and high-fidelity video pairs and distilled into a causal generator that generates in four-frame chunks with one or two denoising steps. Together with targeted inference optimizations, Matrix-Game 4.0 enables 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on a single NVIDIA RTX5090 with a key-press-to-display latency of 112ms. Single-step generation achieves 83FPS steady-state throughput with 18.2GiB of peak GPU memory usage. With fixed prompts, steady-state throughput also reaches 67FPS on an RTX5080 and 58FPS on an RTX5070Ti. We demonstrate customizable shooter and driving games with engine-enforced mechanics, and release code, model weights, and low-poly game assets to support research and creation of playable game worlds.

More fundamentally, diffusion models primarily learn statistical correlations: visual realism does not necessarily imply causal or physical understanding. Following Roman Jakobson’s tripartite classification Jakobson (2021), the language-to-visual mapping in text- and image-to-video (TI2V) generation can be viewed as intersemiotic translation. We argue that current video generators are not yet vision foundation models for world modeling: much of their semantic understanding and apparent intelligence comes from upstream multimodal language models (MLLMs) or text encoders, while diffusion acts more like a renderer. Yet addressing these limitations alone is insufficient: genuinely playable worlds also require real-time generation with low interaction latency, meaningful game mechanics and rich interactions beyond navigation, and shared world state for multiplayer interaction. These considerations motivate an architecture where an external system maintains persistent world state and executes interaction rules, while the video model focuses on visual rendering.

We introduce Matrix-Game 4.0, a framework that places a video generation model within an external harness to separate game logic from visual generation. The system has three components (Figure 2). The multimodal coding agent translates player ideas into runnable game code and scene descriptions. The game engine maintains world state, executes interaction rules, and renders simplified geometry as structural rendering (i.e. low-poly proxy). The video generation model transforms this proxy into detailed frames with materials, lighting, and atmosphere. At runtime, player actions update the engine state; the engine outputs proxy frames and structural, motion, and dynamic semantic conditions; and the video generation model renders the detailed frames displayed to the player. These continuous external guidance from the game engine provides a basis for correct rendering, such that the game no longer relies on the video generation model’s memory to maintain world state or execute rules. Our main contributions are as follows: • Real-time, playable video generation on a single consumer GPU. Matrix-Game 4.0 enables 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090, with 112 ms of key-press-to-display latency. Single-step denoising achieves 83 FPS steady-state generation throughput with approximately 18.2 GiB of peak GPU memory usage, making video-model-driven games practical for local deployment and real-time interaction. (Table 3) With fixed prompts, single-step generation also reaches approximately 67 FPS on an RTX 5080 and 58 FPS on an RTX 5070 Ti, extending deployment to consumer GPUs with 16 GiB of memory. • A roadmap toward playable worlds. We outline Matrix-Game V4’s roadmap, separating game execution from visual generation through an executable harness. It combines a lightweight engine for world-state maintenance and rule execution, a multimodal agent for creating and modifying gameplay and scenes, and an autoregressive video model for real-time rendering, advancing from controllable videos to playable and extensible worlds. • A reusable pipeline spanning data, training, and runtime. We integrate data collection of paired proxy-detailed frames and dynamic captions, model training for video rendering, few-step autoregressive distillation, and efficient real-time inference. • An open-source foundation for generative games. We open-source Matrix-Game 4.0 at launch. For researchers, it provides a reusable technical foundation for further exploration of this emerging paradigm, combining executable game harnesses with video-model-based rendering. For game developers, it offers a concrete preview of how coding agents and neural rendering can support future game-development workflows, while lowering the barrier to prototyping and customizing scenes, interactions, and gameplay through natural-language instructions.

papers.title: One-Ring Bourgain Alternative And A 5-Decimal Bound On The Dimension Of Harmonic Measure
papers.abstract: Improving theorems of Bourgain and Badger--Genschaw, we prove that the Hausdorff dimension of harmonic measure on any domain in $\mathbb{R}^3$, $\mathbb{R}^4$, and $\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n\geq3$ is at most $3-10^{-5}$, $4-10^{-7}$, and $n-(n-1)^{-(2n+6.12\sqrt{n})}$, respectively. The previous bounds in dimensions $3$ and $4$ were $3-10^{-15}$ and $4-10^{-26}$, while Bishop conjectures that the sharp bound is $n-(n-1)^{-1}$. The main difficulty in optimizing Bourgain's method is estimating non-additive $s$-dimensional Hausdorff-type contents when $s<n$ is close to $n$. Previous arguments used net contents associated to a fixed $m$-adic lattice, with $m$ large depending on $n$. We redevelop the dimension theory using pairwise disjoint cubes in general position and obtain a new estimate showing that one thin ring without large holes surrounding a cube makes it unlikely for Brownian motion to reach the cube before exiting the domain. A key feature of the construction is that the holes are round rather than rectangular. We also propose ten challenges on the dimension of harmonic measure that may provide accessible targets en route to Bishop's conjecture.

papers.title: Pulsar J1909+0749 and Supernova Remnant G42.1-0.2: A case of a pulsar that has exited the shell of its associated supernova remnant
papers.abstract: (Abridged) The ATNF pulsar catalogue features only 63 pulsars that are possibly associated with a supernova remnant (SNR). Even rarer is the scenario in which the pulsar has escaped the physical extent of its corresponding SNR. We aim to identify the serendipitously discovered shell-type object G42.1-0.2 as a SNR. The known pulsar (PSR) J1909+0749 lies well outside the shell of SNR G42.1-0.2, but it has a cometary tail pointing towards the centre of the SNR; we propose that the SNR and the pulsar originated from the same supernova explosion. By measuring the flux densities of the shell G42.1-0.2 from ${\sim}$200 MHz to ${\sim}$6 GHz, we establish the nonthermal nature of its emission. With the characteristic age of the pulsar, its distance from the Sun estimated from the dispersion measure (DM), and the angular separation between the pulsar and the centre of the shell, we infer the evolutionary state of the SNR and the transverse velocity of the pulsar. Using proper motion measurements, we compare the SNR-pulsar direction with the velocity of the pulsar. The radio spectral index of the shell is $-0.36 \pm 0.08$, confirming that the emission is primarily nonthermal synchrotron. The proper motion measurements are not well constrained, but the amplitude and the direction are consistent with the interpretation that the SNR and the pulsar are associated. If the characteristic age and the DM-based distance represent the true age and the true distance of the pulsar and the SNR, then the standard evolution equations suggest that the SNR must still be in the Sedov-Taylor phase, evolving in a medium with a density of about 1.5 cm$^{-3}$. In addition, as a result of the PSR-SNR association, the transverse velocity of the pulsar PSR J1909+0749 is estimated to be ${\sim}1460~\mathrm{km\,s}^{-1}$, ranking it among the highest transverse velocities observed for pulsars in the Milky Way.

papers.intro:
The ejected matter from a supernova (SN) explosion expands and sweeps up the material in the surrounding interstellar medium (ISM), forming what we call a supernova remnant (SNR). SNRs inject momentum and energy into the ISM and enhance the turbulent gas pressure and the metallicity (Cox, 2005; Dubner and Giacani, 2015; McEwen et al., 2016; Yamada et al., 2017; Koo et al., 2020, e.g.,). While the feedback effects due to SNRs and their progenitor SN explosions on star-formation are routinely included—either directly or indirectly—in high-resolution galaxy-scale simulations (Scannapieco et al., 2012; Chaikin et al., 2023, e.g.,), the initial conditions are poorly constrained as of yet, making the simulations overly sensitive to the initial conditions (Li et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2024, e.g.,). This is partly due to the challenges in determining the physical parameters of SNRs through observations.

This is partly due to the challenges in determining the physical parameters of SNRs through observations.

Notably, determining the distance to a SNR reliably is still a difficult task to achieve, despite its fundamental importance in estimating the SNR’s size, expansion velocity, kinetic energy, age, and evolutionary state. Although advances have been made recently (Ranasinghe and Leahy, 2022, e.g.,) in moving beyond the inadequate Σ−D\Sigma{-}D (surface brightness to distance) relationship (Green, 2005), the majority of SNRs still lack reliable distance measurements.

Exacerbating the situation is the fact that the current catalogs of SNRs in the Milky Way (Ferrand and Safi-Harb, 2012; Green, 2025), which contain fewer than 400 objects, are estimated to be at most ∼30{\sim}30% complete (Li et al., 1991; Ranasinghe and Leahy, 2022). In essence, our knowledge of the physical parameters of Galactic SNRs comes from an under-sampled population whose distances are reliable only for a minority, potentially potentially distorting our understanding of their true Galaxy-wide characteristics.

A likely byproduct of a SN event of the core-collapse (CC) type, which is responsible for at least 70% of the SN events (Tammann et al., 1994; Diehl et al., 2006, e.g.,), is a rapidly rotating neutron star known as a pulsar (Heger et al., 2003, PSR; e.g.,). A characteristic age of the pulsar, which may be used as a proxy for its true age (see, e.g., Gaensler and Frail, 2000, for caveats), can be derived using the time-period and its derivative. In addition, the distance to the pulsar can be inferred using the dispersion measure (DM) and an electron density model of the Galaxy (Yao et al., 2017, e.g.,). Consequently, if a pulsar is associated with a SNR, then the age and the distance of the remnant can be regarded as those of the pulsar.

However, SNR-PSR associations are not commonly found. According to the ATNF pulsar catalogue (Manchester et al., 2005), there are only 63 possible associations of pulsars and SNRs in the Milky Way at the moment. Of these, only 44 associations are considered to be confirmed. The low number of confirmed SNR-PSR associations is because of two reasons. First, pulsars may continue radiating for millions of years, whereas SNRs have a much shorter mean lifetime of the order of 10510^{5} yr (Frail et al., 1994). Second, pulsars can have kick velocities as high as ∼1000​km​s−1{\sim}1000\penalty\ \mathrm{km\,s}^{-1} (Cordes et al., 1993; Chatterjee et al., 2009), which may be large enough for the pulsar to escape even its corresponding SNR shell. The Mouse (Yusef-Zadeh and Bally, 1987) is one well-known example of such a scenario. Recently, a similar SNR-PSR association has been discovered by MeerKAT, which was named the Mini Mouse (Motta et al., 2023). Only a handful of such cases are known in which the pulsar escaped the shell of its sibling SNR: e.g., the Mushroom (Kargaltsev et al., 2017), the Frying Pan (Kesteven et al., 1987; Camilo et al., 2009) and the Canon Ball (Schinzel et al., 2019).

First, pulsars may continue radiating for millions of years, whereas SNRs have a much shorter mean lifetime of the order of 10510^{5} yr (Frail et al., 1994). Second, pulsars can have kick velocities as high as ∼1000​km​s−1{\sim}1000\penalty\ \mathrm{km\,s}^{-1} (Cordes et al., 1993; Chatterjee et al., 2009), which may be large enough for the pulsar to escape even its corresponding SNR shell. The Mouse (Yusef-Zadeh and Bally, 1987) is one well-known example of such a scenario. Recently, a similar SNR-PSR association has been discovered by MeerKAT, which was named the Mini Mouse (Motta et al., 2023). Only a handful of such cases are known in which the pulsar escaped the shell of its sibling SNR: e.g., the Mushroom (Kargaltsev et al., 2017), the Frying Pan (Kesteven et al., 1987; Camilo et al., 2009) and the Canon Ball (Schinzel et al., 2019).

In this paper, we report one more such association in which the pulsar has escaped the confines of its SNR shell. We discovered, by chance, a shell centred at the Galactic coordinates l∼42.1​°l{\sim}42.1\degree, b∼−0.2​°b{\sim}-0.2\degree with a diameter of ∼11′{\sim}11^{\prime} and a cometary nebula pointing linearly away from the shell in the continuum images of the SARAO MeerKAT Galactic Plane Survey (Goedhart et al., 2024, SMGPS;). The shell has not been identified by any study yet. Furthermore, one corner of the cometary nebula is positionally coincident with the known pulsar PSR J1909+0749 (see Fig. 1). We hypothesize that the shell is a SNR and that the pulsar was born in the same progenitor SN explosion as of the shell. In Sect. 2, we describe the data and the methods used in this study. In Sect. 3, we present the evidence supporting our hypothesis and discuss the implications of the SNR-PSR association in Sect. 4. We conclude with a short summary in Sect. 5.

papers.title: Tracking multiscale liquid crystal order with high harmonic spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Can high-harmonic generation track how microscopic intermolecular interactions give rise to macroscopic order? We address this question in the thermotropic liquid crystal 4-cyano-4'-n-pentylbiphenyl, a model system with a well-defined nematic-to-isotropic transition. Using a temperature-controlled flat jet, we show that polarization-resolved high-harmonic generation driven by mid-infrared strong-field pulses is highly sensitive to liquid-crystal order. In the nematic phase, the harmonic yield forms a four-lobed angular pattern with twofold rotational symmetry and is strongest when the driving-field polarization is perpendicular to the molecular director; this anisotropy vanishes in the isotropic liquid. A tight-binding model parameterized by first-principles calculations attributes this response to intermolecular orbital hybridization in short-range antiparallel molecular arrangements. Temperature-dependent measurements across multiple harmonic orders resolve the same first-order phase transition, with each harmonic order exhibiting a distinct optical sensitivity. A multiscale model combining the microscopic response, Landau-de Gennes orientational correlations and phase matching explains this behaviour through the interplay between orientational correlation lengths and harmonic coherence lengths. High-harmonic generation therefore links local electronic coupling to mesoscopic order and macroscopic propagation, providing an all-optical probe of multiscale organization in soft matter.

papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Time Series Foundation Models for Electrical Load Forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate electrical load forecasting supports power-system operation across countries, regions, cities, and buildings, but repeated development of target-specific models is costly. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) provide reusable pretrained backbones, although multi-domain pretraining may not fully capture load-specific characteristics. This paper compares pretrained inference, full fine-tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) in terms of forecasting accuracy and adaptation efficiency across four electrical load aggregation levels. MOIRAI 1.0 Large serves as the primary backbone, while Chronos-2 assesses whether the findings transfer across model families. The evaluation covers both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings and examines whether compact adaptation provides consistent gains over strong pretrained checkpoints. Pretrained foundation models outperform the implemented seasonal naive and XGBoost baselines across the evaluated aggregation levels. On MOIRAI Large, rank-16 LoRA reduces normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) by 7.5% on average while updating 3.146 million parameters, about 1% of the model, and retains most of the improvement from full fine-tuning. Chronos-2 achieves lower pretrained NMAE than MOIRAI, while its relative adaptation gains remain smaller overall. OOD results show that adaptation benefits vary by target, with the clearest gains for the local-area series and several buildings. Overall, LoRA provides a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off when adaptation yields a meaningful gain over a strong pretrained checkpoint.

papers.intro:
Accurate electrical load forecasting is essential for reliable and economically viable power-system operation. Short-term forecasts inform generation scheduling, balancing and reserve decisions, market participation, demand response, and the operation of local energy systems and buildings. Forecasting difficulty also changes with aggregation: national and regional demand is comparatively smooth, while city and building loads are more strongly affected by weather, occupancy, operating schedules, and local equipment behavior [1, 2].

Short-term forecasts inform generation scheduling, balancing and reserve decisions, market participation, demand response, and the operation of local energy systems and buildings. Forecasting difficulty also changes with aggregation: national and regional demand is comparatively smooth, while city and building loads are more strongly affected by weather, occupancy, operating schedules, and local equipment behavior [1, 2].

In practice, many systems, market areas, customer groups, and buildings require individual load forecasts. Conventional forecasting approaches can provide strong local performance, but they often require models to be trained separately for individual series or datasets [3]. As the number of forecasting targets grows, model configuration and training must therefore be repeated across more series. For comparison, a weekly seasonal naive model provides a meaningful reference because electrical load exhibits daily, weekly, and seasonal structure, with many series showing strong weekly repetition. Gradient-boosted trees provide a supervised machine-learning alternative using lagged load and external covariates [4]. Both approaches can be effective, but target-specific models and feature pipelines limit their scalability across large forecasting collections.

Time series foundation models (TSFMs) offer a reusable pretrained alternative. TSFMs aim to transfer temporal representations learned from large and heterogeneous datasets. MOIRAI, a TSFM, provides a universal and covariate-aware architecture for forecasting across frequencies and dimensions [5]. Chronos formulates forecasting as token prediction [6], and Chronos-2 extends this model family to univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed forecasting [7]. Recent peak-aware evaluation across area-code, secondary-substation, and low-voltage-feeder levels found that Chronos-2 performed strongly during high-demand periods across all three distribution-grid aggregation levels [8]. A strong pretrained checkpoint can therefore provide zero-shot forecasts, meaning forecasts without target-specific training, across diverse electrical load series.

The remaining question is how much downstream adaptation such a pretrained model requires for electrical load forecasting. Three practical options exist: (i) pretrained inference applies the pretrained checkpoint without downstream training; (ii) full fine-tuning specializes the complete model by updating all model parameters; and (iii) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) provides an intermediate option by freezing the pretrained backbone and learning compact low-rank updates in selected transformations [9]. Quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) combines low-rank adaptation with a quantized backbone [10], and weight-decomposed low-rank adaptation (DoRA) decomposes weight updates into directional and magnitude components [11]. The present work focuses on LoRA because the primary question is not which parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) variant performs best, but whether compact adaptation retains sufficient forecasting accuracy to provide an operationally attractive alternative to full fine-tuning. The value of LoRA therefore depends on whether it retains the relevant accuracy gains of full fine-tuning while updating far fewer task-specific parameters.

papers.title: Primal-Dual Adaptive Subgradient Methods
papers.abstract: We propose adaptive primal-dual subgradient methods for constrained convex optimization. Our first method applies an AdaGrad-style step-sizes to the dual problem and recovers primal solutions by averaging the associated Fenchel-type oracle outputs. It achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$ convergence for the dual objective residual, primal objective residual, and feasibility gap in the nonsmooth regime, while automatically improving to $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$ when the dual objective is smooth. We further develop an accelerated variant, which retains the $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$ nonsmooth rate while achieving $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$ convergence in the smooth regime under mild assumptions. These guarantees require no prior knowledge of the underlying regularity. We demonstrate the empirical performance of the proposed methods on optimal transport and semidefinite relaxation of the Max-Cut problem.

Duchi et al. (Duchi et al., 2011) introduced AdaGrad, pioneering adaptive step sizes based on accumulated gradient norms. While originally developed for online and stochastic optimization, this mechanism has subsequently been used to obtain universal methods that adapt to different smoothness and noise regimes (Levy, 2017). In particular, AcceleGrad (Levy et al., 2018) combines AdaGrad-style adaptation with acceleration, attaining guarantees for both smooth and nonsmooth convex optimization without prior knowledge of the smoothness regime or its constants. AdaGrad-type adaptation has also been extended to constrained optimization using projection and proximal operations. Kavis et al. (Kavis et al., 2019) proposed UniXGrad for constrained convex optimization, while Bach and Levy (Bach and Levy, 2019) developed a universal Mirror-Prox method for variational inequalities. Both methods use extra-gradient-type updates and adapt to smooth and nonsmooth regimes as well as deterministic and stochastic oracles. Antonakopoulos et al. (Antonakopoulos et al., 2021) further developed adaptive extra-gradient methods for min-max optimization and games. Ene et al. (Ene et al., 2021) developed universal adaptive methods for constrained convex optimization based on adaptive projected updates, including accelerated variants, while Wang and Yurtsever (Wang and Yurtsever, 2026) developed universal adaptive methods for composite objectives. In contrast, our methods address constrained problems through their unconstrained dual and require only Fenchel-type oracles, rather than projections onto or proximal updates over the constraint set.

His universal gradient methods adapt to unknown Hölder smoothness regime and constants through an inexact line-search strategy. Yurtsever et al. (Yurtsever et al., 2015) extended this approach to constrained convex optimization using a primal-dual framework with Fenchel-type oracles, providing guarantees for both the objective residual and feasibility gap. Their methods, however, rely on an inexact line-search strategy that requires objective evaluations and can be costly or impractical when such evaluations are expensive. Moreover, they require a target accuracy to be specified in advance and converge only to a neighborhood determined by this accuracy, making it difficult to run them to arbitrary accuracy without prior knowledge of the convergence regime. Our methods retain the same primal-dual oracle framework while avoiding line searches, objective evaluations, and a prescribed target accuracy, and adapt automatically to the underlying smoothness regime.

papers.title: Characterizing Cross-Relay Generalization Failure in Machine Learning-Based Power System Protection
papers.abstract: Machine learning-based fault detectors are often evaluated at the relay locations used for training, although local voltage and current measurements vary across power networks. This work investigates cross-relay generalization for binary detection of faults anywhere in the network using local measurements, rather than line-selective tripping. Using 50 ms windows from a simulated 110 kV transmission network, we evaluate a multilayer perceptron across all 64 source target combinations of eight relays and five random seeds. A shared simulation-level split and source-only threshold selection provide a controlled held-out evaluation without target-specific calibration. Despite nearly unchanged mean F1-scores (0.730 within-relay versus 0.734 cross-relay), the mean false-positive rate (FPR) increases from 0.088 to 0.341, while the mean false-negative rate decreases from 0.399 to 0.318. The change is strongly directional: models trained at Bus 2 relays yield a mean FPR of 0.670 at Bus 1 and Bus 3 relays, compared with 0.096 for cross-relay transfers within the same bus group. Linear probing indicates that learned representations retain coarse bus-group information, while exploratory class-conditional latent distribution analysis shows no consistent monotonic association with transfer errors. These findings demonstrate that aggregate metrics can conceal location-structured changes in false-alarm behavior, highlighting the importance of evaluating error types separately when assessing cross-relay generalization.

papers.title: Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-Set Diffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks
papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion models iteratively denoise a noisy sequence of categorical data such as text, enabling any-order generation with self-correction and in-filling capabilities. This makes them promising candidates for reasoning, planning, and constrained-generation tasks like coding and math. Yet masked and uniform diffusion erase a token's identity in a single corruption event, so their noisy states cannot explicitly represent partially resolved uncertainty in which several alternatives remain plausible. We close this gap with Binary Discrete Diffusion, a family of continuous-time discrete-diffusion processes whose noisy state is a set of candidate tokens per position, represented as a binary membership vector. Binary diffusion changes candidate sets through additions and removals, allowing information to be lost and recovered gradually while the diffusion state itself represents partial uncertainty. On Sudoku-Extreme, Boxoban, and graph coloring, the symmetric formulation of binary diffusion consistently outperforms strong, well-tuned masked and uniform baselines under matched architectures and controlled training, sampling, and tuning budgets, with its largest gains on the hardest instances, while remaining competitive on language modeling (Text8, TinyStories, OpenWebText). These results support candidate sets as an effective intermediate representation for iterative reasoning and show that the corruption kernel can materially change the computation learned by the reverse model.

Unlike autoregressive generation, decisions need not follow a fixed left-to-right order and can be revised later, while many positions can be updated in parallel (Schiff et al., 2025; Sahoo et al., 2024; Gong et al., 2025). These properties make discrete diffusion attractive for reasoning, planning, and constrained generation (Ye et al., 2025; Wewer et al., 2025). Yet sample quality at finite inference budgets remains challenging, motivating work on ordering, remasking, planned denoising, and search (Kim et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2026). We instead focus on a complementary axis: the corruption process itself. How much can be gained by changing the corruption process, and in particular the intermediate representation on which denoising operates? Logic and planning are useful testbeds: they impose global constraints, admit exact solve-rate evaluation, and scale cleanly in difficulty at manageable computational cost, while sharing structure with coding, mathematics, and biological design (Sahoo et al., 2026; Avdeyev et al., 2023; Stärk et al., 2024). papers.title: Continual Concept Personalization in Diffusion Models via Residual-Space Adaptation
papers.abstract: Text-to-image personalization aims to equip pretrained diffusion models with the ability to learn user-specific concepts from only a few reference images. Existing methods, however, typically train each concept independently or assume that all concepts are available simultaneously. In practical applications, concepts often arrive sequentially, requiring models to continually learn new subjects, objects, or styles while minimizing interference with previously acquired concepts. We address this continual concept personalization setting by extending residual-space adaptation to the stochastic adaptation process of pretrained diffusion models. Our work achieves the highest concept fidelity among competing continual personalization methods while maintaining near-zero forgetting. Beyond these empirical gains, the learned residual-space dynamics reveal where adaptation capacity is concentrated within the diffusion model. Restricting adaptation to the identified layers by our method preserves nearly the same performance while reducing the number of trainable parameters by up to 72\%, demonstrating that residual-space dynamics can identify the layers that contribute most to continual concept personalization and directly guide more parameter-efficient adaptation.
papers.intro:
Recent text-to-image models such as Stable Diffusion [17, 15] and FLUX [11] have enabled high-quality image synthesis from natural language descriptions, making generative models increasingly accessible to end users. Their flexibility has further motivated personalization methods that adapt pretrained models to user-specific concepts, subjects, objects, or artistic styles from only a few examples.

Recent text-to-image models such as Stable Diffusion [17, 15] and FLUX [11] have enabled high-quality image synthesis from natural language descriptions, making generative models increasingly accessible to end users. Their flexibility has further motivated personalization methods that adapt pretrained models to user-specific concepts, subjects, objects, or artistic styles from only a few examples.

Personalization methods commonly rely on parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques such as LoRA [9] to adapt pretrained diffusion models to new concepts. Most existing approaches [7, 14, 10, 21] perform a separate fine-tuning procedure for every concept, and subsequently merge the resulting adapters into a unified personalized model. In many practical scenarios, however, concepts are acquired sequentially over time as new subjects, objects, or styles become available. Under this setting, whenever a new concept is introduced, the expensive merging procedure must be repeated to reconstruct the final personalized model. As the number of concepts grows, this repeated merging process becomes increasingly inefficient. This motivates continual concept personalization, where a single model is updated incrementally to incorporate new concepts while preserving previously acquired ones. The main obstacle to continual concept personalization is interference: learning new concepts can degrade performance on previously learned concepts. At the same time, the fixed model capacity must be used parsimoniously to preserve sufficient adaptation capacity for future concepts. Several continual learning methods [4, 19, 12, 1] achieve low levels of interference by constraining the parameter update to a pre-computed safe subspace. The most successful among these rely on layer-wise input statistics to characterize the safe subspace. This procedure cannot be directly extended to stochastic backbones, thus limiting its applicability in image generation tasks. In this work, we bridge this gap, extending residual-space adaptation to stochastic diffusion models for continual concept personalization. In particular, our starting point is an adapted version of DyRA [1] into diffusion models, a recent method which we choose for its elegant formulation and explicit theoretical guarantees. We also introduce a novel systematic evaluation framework for continual concept personalization and show that the resulting residual-space dynamics reveal layerwise specialization, providing a practical tool for guiding parameter-efficient adaptation.

papers.title: Sage-A1.5: From Long-Horizon Execution to Scientific Exploration with Capability Composition
papers.abstract: In this report, we introduce Sage-A1.5, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model that builds on A1 to advance long-horizon problem solving through adaptive capability composition. Compared with A1, Sage-A1.5 learns not only to solve individual tasks, but also to organize work and revise its approach during execution. Sage-A1.5 highlights three improvements: agentic orchestration, verification, and open scientific discovery. First, agentic orchestration extends single-agent execution through task delegation and parallel collaboration among subagents with isolated contexts, enabling complex tasks to be decomposed and addressed concurrently and supporting efficient execution while reducing interference across concurrent subagents. Second, agentic verification strengthens long-horizon reliability through progress checking, evidence validation, and reflective strategy revision, allowing the agent to recognize unproductive search paths and pursue alternative approaches. Third, open scientific discovery extends agentic capabilities beyond answering predefined questions to conducting exploratory research, connecting scientific inquiry with interactive analysis and inspectable research artifacts. We showcase these capabilities through complicated agentic tasks and multidisciplinary scientific applications. Besides, we hope Sage-A1.5 provides the community with an accessible foundation for open scientific discovery, offering a practical path from long-horizon task execution to collaborative, verifiable, and inspectable scientific exploration.

papers.intro:
In our earlier work, we introduced Agents-A1 [1], a 35B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agent model that improves long-horizon task performance by scaling the agent horizon rather than model parameters. We built a knowledge–action infrastructure [2] that connects external knowledge, tool calls, observations, and verification feedback, producing training trajectories with an average length of 45K tokens. Agents-A1 [1] showed strong performance in multi-step search, scientific reasoning, instruction following, and tool use, matching or exceeding trillion-parameter models on several benchmarks. These results established a practical path toward capable long-horizon agents at a smaller model scale.

Recent progress [3, 4, 5, 2] demonstrates that strong domain skills alone are not enough for complicated tasks. Software engineering, machine learning optimization, and scientific research often require agentic model to manage related subtasks, compare different approaches, and revise decisions as new evidence becomes available. A single agentic model working step by step may struggle with a growing context, slow exploration, and errors that affect later decisions. Longer execution also does not always lead to better results: an agent may repeat unproductive searches, build on unsupported assumptions, or accept a conclusion before checking all the evidence. Further progress therefore requires not only stronger intrinsic agentic capabilities and broader skills, but also better ways to organize agent work and check progress. Task delegation, parallel collaboration, evidence review, and strategy revision should become learned model capabilities rather than depend only on fixed rules in an external framework.

To address these challenges, we introduce Sage-A1.5, a 35B MoE agent model built on Agents-A1, with two key capabilities: Agentic Orchestration and Agentic Verification. 1) Agentic Orchestration allows the model to decide how to divide work, delegate subtasks to parallel subagents with separate contexts, and combine their findings toward a shared goal. 2) Agentic Verification allows the model to recognize when progress has stalled or an important conclusion needs checking, review the available evidence and assumptions, and adjust its next actions. At inference time, this verification takes place within the model’s own reasoning and tool-use process, without an online supervisor or a separate verification tool. These capabilities offer the community a scalable technical pathway for translating model capabilities into agentic capabilities. As shown in Fig. 1, despite having only 35B parameters, Sage-A1.5 outperforms the substantially larger Kimi-K3 [4], GLM-5.3 [6], and GPT-5.6-sol [5] on FrontierScience-Olympiad [7], CMT [8], PinchBench [9], and IFBench [10], while remaining competitive with them on SWE-Bench Pro [11] and BrowseComp [12]. Moreover, Sage-A1.5 matches or surpasses the equally sized Agents-A1 [1] and Ornith-1.5 [13] on all twelve benchmarks.

papers.title: Generic finiteness of solutions to parametrized systems of generalized polynomial inequalities
papers.abstract: We study parametrized systems of $\mathit{generalized}$ polynomial inequalities, $(c \circ x^B) \in C$, for a positive variable vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^n_>$, a $\mathit{real}$ exponent matrix $B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$, a positive parameter vector $c \in \mathbb{R}^m_>$, and a positive, blunt coefficient cone $C \subset \mathbb{R}^m_>$. This setting includes (i) generalized polynomial equations, $A \, (c \circ x^B) = 0$, arising e.g. from power-law dynamical systems with real exponents (and involving a real coefficient matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n' \times m}$), and (ii) generalized semi-algebraic sets. Our main result guarantees the generic finiteness of solutions modulo unavoidable exponential fibers. Building on a framework for parametrized $\mathit{polynomial}$ systems developed by Müller and Regensburger, we reformulate the problem as a system of $\mathit{binomial}$ equations on the coefficient set $P = C \cap Δ\subseteq \mathbb{R}^m_>$, where $Δ$ is a product of (standard) simplices. Solvability is governed by the monomial-dependency subspace $D$. Using elementary arguments from analysis and topology, including a logarithmic boundary analysis and Sard's theorem, we control the accumulation of solutions on the boundary and in the interior of $P$. We show that, if $\dim P \le \dim D$, then generically in both the measure-theoretic and topological sense, there are finitely many solutions on $P$ (and hence finitely many exponential fibers of solutions in $\mathbb{R}^n_>$). As an application, we prove generic finiteness of steady states (within forward-invariant sets) for parametrized power-law dynamical systems with real exponents.
papers.intro:
Parametrized power-law dynamical systems (with real, not necessarily integer exponents) are used to model a variety of chemical, biological (e.g. ecological or epidemiological), economic, and engineering processes. For example, they arise from (chemical) reaction networks with (generalized) mass-action kinetics; see e.g. [14, 15, 8] and [20, 21]. The analysis of their steady states leads to parametrized systems of generalized polynomial equations and inequalities, given by finite sums of monomial terms (where a monomial term is a monomial times a positive parameter).

Solution sets of (generalized) polynomial systems may consist of infinite exponential fibers. Hence, generic finiteness questions are both natural and subtle: one seeks conditions ensuring that, for generic parameter values, only finitely many solution fibers occur. By “generic” we mean that finiteness holds almost everywhere and is robust; that is, the “good” parameter set is open and dense, and the “bad” set has Lebesgue measure zero.

papers.title: Automated optimization of solar energetic particle acceleration and transport parameters against five-spacecraft observations of the 9 October 2021 event
papers.abstract: Solar energetic particle (SEP) events threaten space infrastructure, yet physics-based prediction models depend on numerous poorly constrained free parameters. We introduce the Fujitsu Solar Energetic particle Intelligent Tuning and Evaluation Network (SEITEN), which couples the SUSANOO MHD model of CME propagation to SEPIF, a diffusive shock acceleration and focused transport model, through the shock conditions SUSANOO supplies, and automatically optimizes the free parameters of the particle model against the SEP event of 9 October 2021. The mean free path and the injection efficiency vary independently along each magnetic field line and heliolongitudinal bin, giving a 19-dimensional problem solved by quasi-Monte Carlo sampling followed by a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. The optimized model reproduces proton flux profiles at five spacecraft with a mean absolute error of $\approx 0.45$ in $\log_{10}$ flux, and the inferred mean free paths show a clear east-west structure; these are effective parameters conditional on the assumed transport geometry. Six independent runs show that whether mean free paths or injection efficiencies dominate depends on the MHD shock strength, and that injection efficiencies differ by orders of magnitude between MHD configurations despite nearly identical fit quality. Joint MHD-SEP parameter estimation is therefore a necessary next step towards generalized, operational SEP forecasting.

papers.intro:
Solar energetic particle (SEP) events present a significant radiation hazard to aviation, spaceborne electronics, and human space exploration, particularly for missions venturing beyond Earth’s magnetosphere such as the near-future expeditions to the Moon and Mars [1]. The more human society relies on space infrastructure, the more essential space weather forecasting becomes, particularly the accurate prediction of the onset, peak intensity, and duration of SEP events. While empirical models and machine learning approaches offer rapid forecasts [2, 3], physics-based understanding is still essential for the complex chain of mechanisms, from particle acceleration at solar flares and coronal mass ejection (CME)-driven shocks to transport through the heliosphere, and to predict the full spatial and temporal distribution of particle fluxes in an event of a severity that modern technological society has not yet faced, but eventually will.

In recent years, sophisticated physics-based modelling chains that couple magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of the solar corona and solar wind with particle transport codes, such as PARADISE [4, 5] coupled with EUHFORIA [6, 7], iPATH [8, 9, 10] coupled with AWSoM [11], M-FLAMPA [12] operating within the SOFIE model coupled with AWSoM-R [13], and EPREM [14] within the EMMREM framework, have been developed. These models solve the focused transport equation to simulate particle transport processes including pitch-angle diffusion, cross-field diffusion, and adiabatic cooling. The same transport model has since been coupled to a different MHD background: the iPATH acceleration and transport modules have been driven by EUHFORIA to model individual multi-spacecraft events, energetic storm particle events observed by Solar Orbiter, and, with its successor model, inverse velocity dispersion signatures [15, 16, 17]. Such pairings of one particle transport model with alternative MHD backgrounds bear directly on the present study, in which we quantify how much the inferred SEP parameters depend on the MHD background rather than on the transport physics. More recently, forecasting-oriented variants have also emerged, such as PARASOL [18], which augments the PARADISE transport model with a semi-analytical foreshock description derived from self-consistent acceleration simulations. Complementary observation-driven frameworks, such as SPREAdFAST [19, 20], characterize CME-driven coronal shocks directly from extreme-ultraviolet imaging and couple them to particle acceleration and transport models to forecast SEP fluxes in the inner heliosphere. However, a fundamental challenge remains in the operational application of these models. They rely on numerous free parameters that are often hard to constrain by observations. In particular, the properties of the seed particle population and the transport coefficients significantly influence the resulting SEP time profiles [1]. For instance, slight variations in the assumed injection energy or scattering mean free path can lead to orders-of-magnitude differences in predicted fluxes. Consequently, current physics-based simulations often require ad-hoc manual tuning of these parameters to reproduce past events observed near Earth, hindering their generalization for predictive purposes.

Palmerio et al.[26] successfully modelled the onset of this event by coupling the WSA-Enlil MHD model with the SEPMOD test-particle code. They addressed the limitation of missing early-stage acceleration in MHD models by introducing a “fixed source” injection at the inner boundary, scaled empirically by flare and CME parameters. However, the spatial form of these fixed sources is prescribed rather than inferred: the injection is applied over a circular patch centred on the mapped flare site or on the CME nose, with an axisymmetric profile whose width is set by the patch radius. Such a prescription cannot represent the non-uniformity of the actual injection region along the shock front. Furthermore, the determination of injection parameters in such models generally relies on empirical scalings rather than optimization based on the physical transport processes themselves.

papers.title: Semantic Observability for Autonomous Systems Diagnostics
papers.abstract: Modern distributed microservice deployments generate massive volumes of heterogeneous, multi-format observability logs across physically and logically partitioned infrastructure. Isolating root causes during cascading failures remains an arduous task for Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), bottlenecked by manual keyword filtering and disjointed temporal correlation across monitoring dashboards. We introduce Semantic Observability, an autonomous multi-agent framework that unifies disparate log streams into a dynamic, queryable Property Graph Database. By modeling physical infrastructure topologies, logical software dependencies, and chronological event sequences as attributed nodes and directed relations, it bridges the semantic gap inherent in flat, unstructured log repositories. Building on this unified substrate, we deploy a stateful multi-agent system orchestrated through Directed Cyclic Graphs (DCGs). The system autonomously navigates the topology, applying causal graph algorithms and temporal back-traversal to isolate the precise blast radius of anomalies. The pruned subgraph is then interpreted by a Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning engine to generate contextualized, code-level Root Cause Analyses (RCA) and actionable remediations. This paper establishes the foundational system architecture, formal relational ontology, and multi-agent control loops of Semantic Observability. We show conceptually how the framework eliminates ambient telemetry noise, reduces Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR), compresses LLM token consumption, and prevents structural hallucinations. We also specify an open-source validation framework on standard benchmarks (LogHub and Train-Ticket), laying the groundwork for a forthcoming companion paper on exhaustive quantitative evaluation and production benchmarking.
papers.intro:
The cloud-native paradigm shift has transformed software systems from monolithic units into distributed meshes of microservices, serverless tasks, and ephemeral container fleets. While this architecture provides horizontal elasticity and modularity, it complicates system observability. When a localized subsystem failure occurs—such as database disk saturation or network contention—it rarely manifests in isolation. Instead, it cascades downstream, producing service timeouts, connection-pool exhaustions, and anomalous HTTP 500 status codes across independent application tiers.

In contemporary Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practice [1], engineers triage incidents by correlating three primary telemetry pillars: metrics, distributed traces, and logs. Among these, logs provide the highest granularity of execution state. However, extracting causal insights during critical outages is hindered by three structural limitations:

1. Heterogeneity and Semantic Fragmentation: Log events originate from diverse entities (e.g., bare-metal hosts, Kubernetes pods, proxy gateways, and relational databases) and are emitted in disparate syntactic formats (e.g., unstructured text, Apache Common Log Format, Syslog, and arbitrary JSON). Existing centralized logging aggregators (e.g., Elasticsearch, ClickHouse) treat logs as indexable flat text or tabular documents, discarding relational topology and physical host context. 2. High Cognitive Overhead in Spatial-Temporal Correlation: Correlating events across independent machines requires an engineer to manually assemble a mental model of execution across multiple dimensions: Which container executed on this host? Which upstream endpoint invoked this downstream RPC? What log event transpired immediately preceding the database thread exhaustion? 3. Failure Modes of Standard LLM and Vector RAG Approaches: Direct application of Large Language Models (LLMs) via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over flat log files is ineffective for large-scale operations. Dense semantic vector spaces cannot capture strict graph topologies, causality, or microsecond-level chronological sequences. This leads to context window saturation, substantial API operational costs, and hallucinations where unrelated errors are erroneously diagnosed as causal antecedents.
