papers.title: Suppression and reemergence of directional transport across the ferromagnetic transition in SrRuO$_3$
papers.abstract: SrRuO$_3$ is a canonical itinerant ferromagnet that continues to serve as a fertile platform for exploring spin-orbit coupled transport and topological responses in correlated oxide metals. Here, we investigate a (110)-oriented epitaxial SrRuO3 thin film on DyScO$_3$, where crystallographic anisotropy allows for symmetry-resolved charge transport along orthogonal in-plane directions. We uncover two principal findings. First, the resistance above the Curie temperature $T_{c,on}\approx 165$ K exhibits strong anisotropy, consistent with directionally dependent spin-fluctuation scattering. Below $T_{c,on}$, this anisotropy nearly vanishes, despite persistent structural inequivalence, due to isotropic electron-magnon and electron-electron scattering processes. Second, the application of a magnetic field reveals a striking directional contrast in the linear magnetoresistance (MR): it remains negative and saturates along [001], but changes sign and becomes positive along $[1\bar{1}0]$ below $T_0=145$ K. In contrast, the quadratic MR term is identical for both directions and peaks near $T_{\mathrm{OHE}}^*=155$ K, where the ordinary Hall coefficient crosses zero, consistent with carrier compensation under a two-band scenario. A sign change in the anomalous Hall signal at $T_{\mathrm{AHE}}^*=150$ K is consistent with a temperature-dependent redistribution of Berry-curvature contributions near the Fermi level. These results establish ferromagnetic ordering as the primary driver of the observed directional magnetotransport in SrRuO$_3$.

papers.title: Leviathan: a very massive, extended sub-millimetre galaxy spectroscopically confirmed at $\rm z = 4.05$
papers.abstract: We present Leviathan, a sub-millimetre galaxy (SMG) spectroscopically confirmed at $z=4.051$ with JWST/NIRSpec. Modelling 31 bands of photometry from the rest-frame ultraviolet to the millimetre, we find a stellar mass of $\log(M_\star/M_\odot)=11.34^{+0.15}_{-0.22}$, making Leviathan one of the most massive spectroscopically confirmed galaxies at $z>4$, yet consistent with $Λ$CDM for a star-formation efficiency of approximately 20%. Although SMGs are often thought to be building the dense cores of compact quiescent galaxies, Leviathan is extended, with a rest-frame $0.9\,μ\mathrm{m}$ half-light radius of 4.3 kpc. Spatially resolved SED fitting gives a half-mass radius of $3.1\pm0.4$ kpc, consistent with its size in rest-frame $1.5\,μ\mathrm{m}$ imaging. This is three times larger than quiescent galaxies of the same mass, but consistent with the size-mass relation of star-forming galaxies at $4<z<5$ extrapolated to $M_\star=10^{11.3}M_\odot$. Leviathan forms stars on the main sequence (approximately $400\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$) with dust spread across its disc. Both its stellar mass and dust are more extended than those of $z\approx3$ SMGs. Alongside GN20.2b, which has a similar mass and star-formation rate but is three times smaller, these show that massive dusty galaxies at $z\approx4$ can have very different stellar structures, and that not all have their stellar mass concentrated in a compact core.

papers.title: SN 2023iop: An Extreme 1987A-like Supernova and the Death of Very Massive Stars
papers.abstract: Supernova (SN) 1987A showed that some hydrogen-rich core-collapse supernovae (SNe) rise slowly to peak, defining a distinct subclass. Wide-field surveys have uncovered more extreme members, such as OGLE-2014-SN-73, SN 2020faa, and SN 2023vbw, that challenge neutrino-driven explosion models. We present ultraviolet-to-infrared, radio, X-ray, and spectropolarimetric observations of SN 2023iop at $z = 0.1020$, the most extreme 87A-like event to date. It rose for $\gtrsim88$ rest-frame days to $M_r \approx -20.1$ mag, also placing it among the hydrogen-rich superluminous SNe, and radiated $\gtrsim4\times10^{50}$ erg. Its spectra resemble those of typical Type II SNe and remain photospheric at $\sim330$ days post-maximum. Continuum polarization of 0.8-1.0% indicates an aspherical system. Hydrogen-rich pair-instability supernova (PISN) models of a $190~M_\odot$ star reproduce the light-curve up to 150 days after peak, but not the late-time emission. A late-time spectrum shows a feature near 7300 Å, tentatively identified as [Ni II] $λ$7378. The implied $\approx0.02~M_\odot$ of stable $^{58}$Ni is reached only in the most massive PISN models. The low-mass host galaxy ($\sim10^{8.2}~M_\odot$) is consistent with a metal-poor progenitor as required by the PISN channel. Fallback accretion reproduces the light-curve morphology, but not the colors. We consider a pair-instability explosion the most plausible scenario, with the late-time light-curve excess powered by circumstellar interaction, which shows no signatures in the spectra. SN 2023iop shows that the most luminous 87A-like events occupy an underexplored region of massive-star evolution.

The observational landscape of hydrogen-rich core-collapse Type II supernovae [199, 10, SNe II;] was fundamentally altered by the discovery of SN 1987A. At the time, stellar-evolution calculations and models of SN II light curves generally favored extended red-supergiant progenitors for H-rich explosions [96, 12, e.g.,]. However, SN 1987A was traced to the compact blue supergiant Sanduleak −69∘​202-69^{\circ}202 [14, 234], demonstrating that core collapse can also occur in a markedly different evolutionary state.

Recent years have seen the discovery of extreme transients that share the defining photometric characteristics of the 87A-like subclass while extending its properties to much higher luminosities and longer characteristic timescales. Three well-studied examples of this extreme population are OGLE-2014-SN-073 [295, hereafter called OGLE-73;], SN 2020faa [324, 251], and SN 2023vbw [131]. OGLE-73 displayed an unusually broad light curve and a high peak luminosity, suggesting a remarkably large ejecta mass and explosion energy [295]. Similarly, SNe 2020faa and 2023vbw exhibited sustained high luminosity that challenged conventional radioactive-decay models, implying that an additional, more potent energy source was at play [324, 251, 131]. Whether the three extreme events represent the high-luminosity tail of the classical 87A-like population or a physically distinct class of explosions remains unclear.

These extraordinary objects have necessitated the exploration of powering mechanisms beyond standard explosion mechanisms and radioactive decay [295, 160, 219, 202, 80, 251]. One candidate is the pair-instability supernova (PISN) mechanism, thought to occur in stars with helium core masses between ∼65\sim 65 and 130​M⊙130\,M_{\odot}, where the production of electron-positron pairs leads to thermonuclear disruption and Ni56{}^{56}\mathrm{Ni} yields of up to several 10​M⊙10~M_{\odot} [101, 17, 242, 160]. Alternatively, a magnetar central engine can inject rotational energy into the ejecta via magnetic multipole radiation [154, 77, 80, 295, 219, 218]. Fallback accretion provides another potential engine, where gravitational potential energy is released as material accretes onto the central compact remnant following a failed or partial shock revival [202, 295]. Finally, “hidden” circumstellar-matter (CSM) interaction might also boost luminosity if the interaction occurs within an asymmetric disk or torus embedded beneath the optically thick photosphere. In this scenario, the CSM interaction zone is within the optically thick photosphere and is not directly observed, masking the characteristic narrow emission lines of Type IIn SNe [276, 211, 251].

Furthermore, distinguishing observationally between PISN, magnetar-powered, fallback-powered, and hidden-CSM-interaction scenarios remains a primary challenge owing to the lack of unique spectral signatures in the photospheric phase and the degeneracy of light-curve models. papers.title: The environments of type Ibn supernovae: evidence for a strong Wolf-Rayet star component
papers.abstract: Characterisation of progenitor stars of supernovae (SNe) poses several challenges. Direct observations of progenitors are based on serendipitious archival observations and are only possible for nearby events. Indirect methods include inferring nickel mass from the light curves or oxygen masses from the SN's nebular phase, both of which are tools to constrain the progenitor's initial mass. Alternatively, environments of SNe have been used as a proxy for the progenitor's age and metallicity. The progenitor channel of type Ibn SNe is a hotly debated topic. The mass-loss and the formation of He-rich circumstellar medium requires strong envelope stripping of the progenitor star. For core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe), this requires strong stellar wind mass losses, i.e. a Wolf-Rayet (WR) star, or binary interaction with a companion star. Here, we analyse a sample of host galaxies of type Ibn SNe that have been observed with MUSE. We use H$α$ emission to infer the transient's association to star formation and derive the local metallicity with commonly used strong line diagnostic. We find that the sample of SNe are highly associated with star formation in the host galaxy, typically situated within one of the brightest HII regions in the host galaxy. The NCR distribution of H$α$ pixels in SN Ibn environments strongly resembles that of WR stars, and shows a stronger preference to SF compared to other core-collapse SN types. Metallicity measurements show typically sub-solar metallicity in the SN environments.

papers.intro:
A central question in the study of supernovae (SNe) is the connection of SN classes to their respective progenitors. While some stars have been observed before their eventual cataclysmic end, this approach always requires some degree of luck and has been achieved in only a handful of cases. The most famous example is the blue supergiant Sk -69 202 in the Large Magellanic Cloud that exploded as SN 1987A and was observed by surveys in the preceding decades (West, Lauberts, Jorgensen, & Schuster, 1987). More recently, pre-explosion images were obtained for SN 2019yvr, which showed a yellow supergiant as the likely progenitor star (Kilpatrick et al., 2021). Pre-explosion imaging is also limited by current instrumentation as individual stars become harder to distinguish with distance.

The evolution of the explosion itself may glean us information about the star that produced it. 56Ni created during the SN explosion decays into 56Co, which produces much of the light curve of the SN. By estimating the amount of 56Ni produced in the explosion from the light curve shape, the mass of the progenitor may be constrained. During later phases the photospehere of the SN recedes and the SN enters its nebular phase. In this phase, information on the progenitor may be constrained with oxygen abundances derived from the oxygen emission lines (Kuncarayakti et al., 2015).

In this phase, information on the progenitor may be constrained with oxygen abundances derived from the oxygen emission lines (Kuncarayakti et al., 2015).

Observationally the least time-critical method is the use of SN environments as an information source for the progenitor; here the SN itself is a contaminant for observations. Progenitors of core-collapse SNe (CCSNe) are massive and short-lived stars. The lifespan is not long enough for them to disperse from the original group of stars with which they were originally born. Therefore, by studying the immediate stellar environments of SNe information on the progenitor may be constrained. Stellar population age and gas-phase metallicity of the interstellar medium (ISM) directly hint at the lifespan and metallicity of the progenitor.

papers.title: Understanding the formation of alpha-Fe bimodality in the Milky Way using constrained cosmological simulations of the Local Group
papers.abstract: We use a novel suite of constrained cosmological simulations of the Local Group to investigate the formation of alpha--Fe bimodalities in stellar discs of Milky Way analogues. In agreement with past studies using the Auriga model, we show that in our simulations the high-alpha sequence forms in a merger-induced starburst, which further quenches star formation, allowing the new stellar populations to form at low [alpha/Fe]. Producing a bimodality that is prominent at large radii, with a significant [alpha/Fe] gap and overlapping metallicity as in the Milky Way, requires the quenching of star formation across all radii where the bimodality is observed. The quenching can be achieved either with a galaxy-wide starburst, or with a retrograde merger reducing angular momentum in the outer disc and allowing more efficient dilution by the metal-poor gas in the circumgalactic medium (CGM). We show that mergers can also tilt the disc, changing the direction of galactic outflows and enriching a larger volume of the CGM with galactic metals, leading to low [alpha/Fe] scatter in the subsequently formed low-alpha sequence. We argue that the slopes in [alpha/Fe] of the two alpha sequences are crucial in narrowing down the mechanism that leads to their formation. We additionally uncover an indirect role that mergers play in enhancing the accretion of metal-poor gas onto galaxies. The smoothly accreted gas can dominate the gas content in the CGM and aid in the formation of distinct chemical sequences, especially at the low-metallicity end.

Chemo-dynamical studies based on surveys like Gaia (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2018; Gaia Collaboration et al., 2021), APOGEE (Majewski et al., 2017) and GALAH (Buder et al., 2025) have been revealing a complex picture regarding the formation and structure of the Milky Way. One particular peculiarity of the Milky Way’s stars that has received significant attention is the bimodality in the α\alpha-element – metallicity plane, observed in the Solar neighbourhood (Bensby et al., 2003; Fuhrmann, 2011). The high and low-α\alpha populations appear to correlate kinematically with the thick and thin disc, respectively (Haywood et al., 2013). The high-α\alpha population consists mainly of old stars on kinematically hot orbits with some amount of rotational support, while the low−α-\alpha population is kinematically cold and consists mostly of younger stars (Adibekyan et al., 2011; Recio-Blanco et al., 2014; Hayden et al., 2015; Queiroz et al., 2023), although recent studies by Nepal et al. (2024), Gent et al. (2024) and Borbolato et al. (2025) suggest that the two populations did not form sequentially but were coevolving. Other studies have also found overlap in age of the stars in the low and high-α\alpha sequences (Hayden et al., 2017; Mackereth et al., 2017). Interestingly, the majority of the low-α\alpha population appears to have formed in the past 10 Gyr and high-α\alpha population relatively quickly between 9 and 12 Gyr ago (Snaith et al., 2014; Silva Aguirre et al., 2018). Several hypotheses have been proposed to explain the origin of the two-α\alpha sequences. In the “two-infall” model (Chiappini et al., 1997; Chiappini et al., 2001), the high-α\alpha sequence forms during an early phase of rapid gas accretion and star formation, followed by a later, more extended accretion episode that forms the low-α\alpha disc from lower-metallicity gas. The time delay between these episodes ensures a decline in [α\alpha/Fe], while metal dilution in the second episode of gas infall produces the overlap in metallicity between the two sequences. “Parallel” models, in which the thin and thick discs form at the same time but with different rates (Grisoni et al., 2017), have also been proposed; however, reproducing the age distribution of old stars appears to favour the two-infall model, with a separation between the two infall episodes of approximately 3–5 Gyr (Spitoni et al., 2019; Spitoni et al., 2021; Spitoni et al., 2024). The intense star formation in the first infall episode could be related to the Gaia Enceladus/Sausage (GES) merger or to the establishment of the Galactic bar (Haywood et al., 2018b).

Cosmological simulations provide a way to connect these chemical evolution models to realistic assembly histories of Milky Way-like galaxies within CDM. A common trend emerging from several studies is that the high-α\alpha sequence requires an early phase of efficient star formation and rapid gas consumption, followed by a reduction in the star formation rate, with the low-α\alpha sequence forming quiescently from lower-metallicity gas. In some simulations, this transition is driven by a gas-rich merger, which can both trigger intense star formation and supply low-metallicity gas (Grand et al., 2018; Buck, 2020; Beane, 2025). In others, the main ingredient is not the merger itself, but the subsequent infall of metal-poor gas from the circumgalactic medium, which dilutes the star-forming gas and allows the low-α\alpha sequence to form at low metallicity (Parul et al., 2025; Orkney et al., 2025). These results suggest that mergers may trigger or facilitate the formation of the low-α\alpha sequence, but that they are not necessarily the only source of the metal-poor gas required in its formation.

Using NIHAO-UHD simulations, Buck (2020) find that a gas-rich minor merger can naturally produce a chemical bimodality by diluting the metallicity of the star-forming gas after the high-α\alpha sequence is in place (see also Grand et al. 2018). They argue this process is likely not uncommon in disc galaxies. By contrast, Mackereth et al. (2018) find in EAGLE simulations that Milky Way-like bimodality is rare and requires unusually rapid early mass growth followed by later gas infall, suggesting that the Milky Way may have had an atypical formation history. papers.title: Orbital Parameters for 65 Wide Binary Systems: no evidence for gravitational anomaly at low acceleration
papers.abstract: We use a Monte Carlo analysis to study whether wide binaries can be represented by bound Newtonian orbits, and, if this is the case, whether the distribution of the orbital parameters agrees with expectations. The potential orbits are classified according to the $χ^2$ probability of representing star coordinates, parallaxes, velocity components and masses. We apply this analysis to 44 systems previously published, to which we add 26 wide binaries, consisting of twin low-mass (M) stars. We find orbital solutions for 65 systems, and derive the distribution of their orbital parameters. For one system composed of M-type stars, no Newtonian bound solution can be found; however, this pair is a member of the young Argus association and therefore not a suitable target. The remaining four systems that cannot be fit were already identified as likely disrupted binaries. The uncertainty in the separation between the components, given by the parallax error, is by far the dominant error source, and the main limitation of the present analysis, affecting especially the determination of the orbits' inclination angle and phase. Newtonian dynamics describe well our sample. When dividing the sample into two subsamples, according to the mutual acceleration, the eccentricity and periastron distributions agree with theoretical expectations; inclination and phase are distorted by the parallax-limited separation, more strongly in the high-acceleration (37 systems) than in the low-acceleration ($A_N < 10^{-9} m s^{-2}$, 28 systems) subsample, which is opposite to what a gravitational signal would produce. In particular the ratio between observed velocity difference and circular velocity does not show any excess for the low acceleration sample. When parametrized as a boost $γ$ parameter to the velocity, $0.95 < γ<1.05 (1 σ)$, fully consistent with Newton also for the low acceleration sample.

papers.intro:
Detached binaries are the simplest example of a cluster of stars. As such, they have been used in the past for a number of studies, for instance, to test stellar evolution models (Barrientos and Chanamé 2021; Espinoza-Rojas et al. 2021) or to study the effect of planetary systems on photospheric abundances (Spina et al. 2021). Wide binaries (WBs), in addition, offer a unique opportunity to test gravity in the low-acceleration regime. WBs in fact experience gravitational accelerations comparable to those in the outer regions of galaxies, however, dark matter does not significantly influence their dynamics, as its density is known to be negligible in the solar neighborhood (Söding et al. 2025). A further advantage of WBs is that their dynamics is well understood. They can be treated as isolated systems because the differential acceleration exerted by the Galaxy on the two stars is negligible. Similar low accelerations can be found, for instance, in the outer regions of globular clusters. However, these systems exhibit complex dynamical behaviour, including tidal tails and internal rotation, which makes them poorly suited as probes for testing Newtonian gravity.

However, these studies have reached conflicting conclusions on whether Newtonian gravity best reproduces the observations.

Another line of research focuses on the study of 3D solutions, by adding precise and accurate radial velocities to the Gaia data. High-quality radial velocities are essential for identifying and removing multiple systems from the samples (e.g., cases where a third body orbits one of the WB stars), and, when combined with Gaia DR3 parallaxes and proper motions, they allow the orbits of binaries to be constrained (Saglia et al. 2025). These authors analysed HARPS (Mayor et al. 2003) archival spectra for 32 WBs, finding that 31 of them could be represented with a viable bound Newtonian solution. Radial velocities have also been used by Chae (2025), who selected Gaia’s best-quality radial velocities and a Bayesian approach to compare Newtonian and MOdified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) solutions, finding that the latter are preferred for separations beyond 2 kAU. Similar conclusions were reached by Chae (2026), who applied a Bayesian analysis to the HARPS sample published by Saglia et al. (2025). A similar analysis was repeated for a new sample of 36 low acceleration (acceleration <10−9​m​s−2<10^{-9}ms^{-2}) WBs (Chae et al. 2026) finding that for all systems, irrespective of their acceleration, Newtonian gravity is not the preferred solution. Finally, Pasquini et al. (2026) analysed a sample of 12 wide binaries with large separations (greater than 13,000 AU) and found that for three systems no bound Newtonian orbits were possible. However, these binaries have extremely large separations and are therefore expected to be disrupted by interactions with the Galaxy or by encounters with other stars (Hamilton and Modak 2024). In their study, Pasquini et al. (2026) pointed out that low mass systems could be ideal targets because these binaries experience low accelerations for much smaller star separations, making therefore the probability of being disrupted by interactions with Galactic tides or third bodies negligible.

papers.title: KMOS Spectroscopic Follow-up of 16 Star Cluster Candidates of the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy
papers.abstract: The Sagittarius (Sgr) dwarf spheroidal galaxy hosts several known globular clusters and numerous additional cluster candidates identified toward its crowded central regions. Establishing the nature of these candidates is difficult because apparent spatial and astrometric structure can arise from the underlying Sgr population. We investigate sixteen Minni stellar-cluster candidates with KMOS spectroscopy to determine whether the observed stars are compatible with Sgr and whether any candidate field shows evidence for a distinct stellar system. We analyse H-band KMOS spectra of 341 targets from the VVVX-GalCen Spectroscopic Survey, deriving radial velocities (RVs) and empirical metallicities. We compare these with an independent Sgr spectroscopic sample and use VVVX photometry and Gaia DR3 astrometry to test for localized stellar excesses relative to local control fields. Of the 341 KMOS targets, 256 (75%) have RVs within the adopted Sgr interval, and their metallicities broadly overlap the Sgr comparison population. No field shows statistically compelling kinematic evidence for a distinct system after accounting for the multiple candidates examined. Minni 329 shows the strongest spatial excess, but this is not significant after multiple-testing correction and is not accompanied by significant central concentration. The KMOS targets predominantly trace the Sgr population, but Sgr compatibility alone does not confirm the individual candidates as distinct stellar clusters. None of the sixteen fields can be confirmed as a separate stellar system with the present data, although this does not establish that the original candidates are spurious. Deeper imaging and larger spectroscopic samples are required to determine their physical nature.

papers.intro:
The Sagittarius (Sgr) dwarf spheroidal galaxy is one of the clearest examples of the ongoing accretion of a satellite by the Milky Way. Since its discovery (Ibata et al., 1994), its main body and extended tidal debris have been traced over a large area of the sky (Majewski et al., 2003; Newberg et al., 2003; Belokurov et al., 2006; Correnti et al., 2010; Vasiliev et al., 2021). Its stellar populations and associated globular clusters therefore provide important constraints on the formation and disruption of the Sgr system and its contribution to the Galactic halo.

Since its discovery (Ibata et al., 1994), its main body and extended tidal debris have been traced over a large area of the sky (Majewski et al., 2003; Newberg et al., 2003; Belokurov et al., 2006; Correnti et al., 2010; Vasiliev et al., 2021). Its stellar populations and associated globular clusters therefore provide important constraints on the formation and disruption of the Sgr system and its contribution to the Galactic halo.

Several clusters have been securely associated with Sgr, including NGC 6715 (M54), Arp 2, Terzan 7, Terzan 8, Palomar 12, and Whiting 1, together with systems associated with its tidal debris (Law and Majewski, 2010; Forbes and Bridges, 2010; Bellazzini et al., 2020). Near-infrared surveys have subsequently enabled searches for fainter stellar systems in the crowded region surrounding the Sgr main body. Using VVV/VVVX photometry together with Gaia EDR3 astrometry, Minniti et al. (2021a); Minniti et al. (2021b) examined 41 Minni candidate stellar overdensities projected toward Sgr. Of these, 20 were classified as new Sgr clusters or strong cluster candidates, whereas the remaining 21 were considered inconclusive or unconfirmed. Some of the latter may represent chance fluctuations in the dense Sgr field, although genuine low-mass or spatially extended systems could also be difficult to confirm through conventional spatial-overdensity and colour–magnitude analyses. Confirmation of even a subset of these candidates as distinct stellar systems would substantially increase the known cluster population associated with the Sgr progenitor.

Some of the latter may represent chance fluctuations in the dense Sgr field, although genuine low-mass or spatially extended systems could also be difficult to confirm through conventional spatial-overdensity and colour–magnitude analyses. Confirmation of even a subset of these candidates as distinct stellar systems would substantially increase the known cluster population associated with the Sgr progenitor.

The physical nature of these candidates remains uncertain. Their identification was based on combinations of spatial overdensities, proper motions (PMs), colour–magnitude diagram (CMD) morphology, and, in some cases, RR Lyrae stars. Subsequent photometric studies characterized several candidates and estimated their ages, metallicities, and luminosities under the assumption that they represent genuine stellar systems (Garro et al., 2021). However, Piatti (2021) showed that the physical reality of these systems must be assessed individually. Using field-star-decontaminated CMDs and spatial stellar distributions, the study found the strongest evidence for Minni 332, with weaker indications for Minni 342, Minni 348, and Minni 349. Minni 341 was identified as a possible young cluster, whereas Minni 335, Minni 343, and Minni 344 could not be confirmed as stellar aggregates. More generally, the study showed that stellar fluctuations in the composite Sgr field can produce apparent overdensities and CMD features resembling those expected for a stellar cluster. Proper-motion and CMD compatibility with Sgr must therefore be distinguished from evidence that a candidate constitutes a physically distinct stellar system. Nevertheless, the Minni systems continue to enter recent inventories of the Sgr cluster population. For example, Wang et al. (2026) included the 20 objects identified in the VVVX studies in an updated compilation of Sgr-associated globular clusters, although radial velocities (RVs) and proper motions remain unavailable for the Minni objects in that compilation.

papers.title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence
papers.abstract: Cross helicity, the velocity--magnetic-field correlation, is an ideal invariant of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics and constrains energy cascades and magnetic-field generation. Although cross helicity typically decays via visco-resistive effects, we analytically demonstrate that it grows exponentially in sheared inhomogeneous turbulence. This cross-helical shear instability is confirmed using three-dimensional numerical simulations. Growth requires a nonzero gradient of the Reynolds--Maxwell stress to produce turbulent cross helicity; this production overcomes effective losses when shear exceeds a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities.

papers.title: The clumpy fraction of galaxies at $z=1-9$ with JADES: evidence for a mass-dependent transition in clump origin
papers.abstract: We measure the fraction of clumpy galaxies ($f_{\rm clumpy}$) over the redshift range $z=1-9$ and stellar masses $\log_{10}(M_\star/{\rm M_\odot}) \geq 8$ using JWST/NIRCam imaging from JADES. We define clumps as compact off-centre surface-brightness peaks with characteristic sizes of a few hundred parsecs, and develop a dendrogram-based clump-finding method with astrodendro to identify them directly in rest-frame UV, blue, and optical images. Clump-detection completeness is quantified through injection-recovery simulations, which we use to define ($M_\star$, $z$)-dependent 50 per cent completeness-limited $f_{\rm clumpy}$, alongside a probability-weighted completeness-corrected statistic for comparison. For the full sample, the blue and optical $f_{\rm clumpy}$ reach $\approx55$ per cent at $z\approx1-2$ and decline to $\lesssim5$ per cent by $z\approx8-9$, while the UV fraction remains higher at $\approx12$ per cent. At $z\approx1-2$, $f_{\rm clumpy}$ increases strongly with stellar mass, from $\approx35$ per cent in the lowest-mass bin to $\approx85$ per cent at $\log_{10}(M_\star/{\rm M_\odot})\geq10$. Most clumpy galaxies host only one or two robustly detected off-centre clumps, while higher-multiplicity systems occur preferentially in massive, strongly star-forming galaxies at low to intermediate redshift. Comparison with major merger rates suggests that mergers could account for a substantial fraction of low-mass ($\log_{10}(M_\star/{\rm M_\odot})<8.5$), high-redshift clumpy galaxies, while the observed fractions in more massive systems ($\log_{10}(M_\star/{\rm M_\odot})>9$) require an additional in situ clump-formation channel. Our results are consistent with a transition from merger-dominated clumpy morphologies at early times and low stellar masses to an increasing contribution from in situ clump-formation channels, such as disc instabilities, in more massive systems.

papers.intro:
Observations of star-forming galaxies have revealed that they often exhibit irregular morphologies with distinct kiloparsec-scale substructures called clumps (Elmegreen et al., 2005; Elmegreen et al., 2007; Förster Schreiber et al., 2011a; Förster Schreiber et al., 2011b; Genzel et al., 2011; Wisnioski et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2012; Wuyts et al., 2012; Ikeda et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2025). The majority of these clumps are bright in the rest-frame ultraviolet (UV) and are found to be sites of intense star formation (Guo et al., 2018; Huertas-Company et al., 2020; Vanzella et al., 2021; Sattari et al., 2023; Kalita et al., 2025b; Claeyssens et al., 2025), with the fraction of clumpy galaxies peaking at redshift z≈2z\approx 2 (Guo et al., 2015; Shibuya et al., 2016; Mawatari et al., 2026; Sok et al., 2026b; de la Vega et al., 2026, e.g.,), coinciding with the peak of the cosmic star formation rate density (Madau and Dickinson, 2014). The stellar mass growth history of galaxies over cosmic time is governed by the combination of star formation and the accretion of satellites through galaxy mergers (Oser et al., 2010; Duncan et al., 2019; Duan et al., 2025; Puskás et al., 2025, e.g.,). Consequently, the observed clump population may comprise a mixture of physically distinct structures, including disc fragments, compact star clusters, filamentary star-forming regions, minor satellites, and merger-induced star-forming features (Mandelker et al., 2017; Mandelker et al., 2018; Nakazato et al., 2024, e.g.,). With recent JWST observations (Harikane et al., 2025; Sok et al., 2026b; de la Vega et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026, e.g.,) revealing a large number of clumpy systems at z>3z>3, a natural question arises regarding the in situ or ex situ origin of these substructures, particularly as a function of redshift, stellar mass, and rest-frame wavelength.

The majority of these clumps are bright in the rest-frame ultraviolet (UV) and are found to be sites of intense star formation (Guo et al., 2018; Huertas-Company et al., 2020; Vanzella et al., 2021; Sattari et al., 2023; Kalita et al., 2025b; Claeyssens et al., 2025), with the fraction of clumpy galaxies peaking at redshift z≈2z\approx 2 (Guo et al., 2015; Shibuya et al., 2016; Mawatari et al., 2026; Sok et al., 2026b; de la Vega et al., 2026, e.g.,), coinciding with the peak of the cosmic star formation rate density (Madau and Dickinson, 2014). The stellar mass growth history of galaxies over cosmic time is governed by the combination of star formation and the accretion of satellites through galaxy mergers (Oser et al., 2010; Duncan et al., 2019; Duan et al., 2025; Puskás et al., 2025, e.g.,). Consequently, the observed clump population may comprise a mixture of physically distinct structures, including disc fragments, compact star clusters, filamentary star-forming regions, minor satellites, and merger-induced star-forming features (Mandelker et al., 2017; Mandelker et al., 2018; Nakazato et al., 2024, e.g.,). With recent JWST observations (Harikane et al., 2025; Sok et al., 2026b; de la Vega et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026, e.g.,) revealing a large number of clumpy systems at z>3z>3, a natural question arises regarding the in situ or ex situ origin of these substructures, particularly as a function of redshift, stellar mass, and rest-frame wavelength.

The main formation mechanisms proposed by observational studies and simulations include: (i) fragmentation (e.g., disc instabilities), and (ii) mergers. A leading model for in situ clump formation is gravitational collapse in gas-rich turbulent systems, including disc fragmentation (Agertz et al., 2009; Dekel et al., 2009; Ceverino et al., 2010; Genel et al., 2012; Tamburello et al., 2015; Inoue et al., 2016; Mayer et al., 2016; Renaud et al., 2021; van Donkelaar et al., 2022; Mayer et al., 2025), but also fragmentation within dense inflowing filaments (taking place in the galaxy) or circumgalactic medium (CGM) overdensities which could contribute to this early clump or cluster population (Mandelker et al., 2017; Mandelker et al., 2018; van Donkelaar et al., 2026, see, e.g.,). Here, in situ refers to the clump forming locally within or around the galaxy, irrespective of whether the material from which it formed was supplied by the CGM or inflowing filaments, rather than to the accretion of a pre-existing stellar system. Violent disc instability (VDI) is commonly used to describe fragmentation in continuously gas-fed, marginally stable discs that do not reach equilibrium due to ongoing cold accretion (Dekel et al., 2009; Bournaud et al., 2014; Mandelker et al., 2017; Krumholz et al., 2018, e.g.,). At high redshift, these discs form by cosmological accretion of cold gas from the intergalactic medium (Birnboim and Dekel, 2003; Kereš et al., 2005; Bournaud and Elmegreen, 2009; Nelson et al., 2013), and due to their high gas fractions and disc masses (Tamburello et al., 2015; Renaud et al., 2021; van Donkelaar et al., 2022; Mayer et al., 2025, e.g.,), as well as low or marginal Toomre Q stability parameters (Toomre 1964; Q≲1Q\lesssim 1 across most of the disc), the gas collapses under gravitational instabilities and creates clumps. Recent analytical work extends this framework beyond the characteristic fastest-growing Toomre mode, predicting an intrinsic spectrum of clump masses and sizes from the full range of unstable modes (Ferrara et al., 2026). This fragmentation picture is consistent with the high gas fractions observed or inferred in high-zz galaxies (Tacconi et al., 2010; Tacconi et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022; Parlanti et al., 2023; Danhaive et al., 2025), as well as the prevalence of disc-like morphologies (Ferreira et al., 2023; Kartaltepe et al., 2023) and rotationally supported gas-rich systems revealed through spectroscopy (Förster Schreiber et al., 2011a; Förster Schreiber et al., 2011b; Förster Schreiber et al., 2018; Wisnioski et al., 2011; Wisnioski et al., 2019; Übler et al., 2019; Rizzo et al., 2024; Rowland et al., 2024; Danhaive et al., 2025; Cescon et al., 2026). These observations do not directly demonstrate fragmentation, but show that many high-redshift galaxies host extended gas-rich discs where gravitational instabilities can develop, potentially aided by turbulence or external perturbations. Resolved studies at cosmic noon further reveal extended molecular gas discs and clumpy spiral or ring structures with ordered kinematics, in some cases accompanied by evidence for radial gas inflows (Nestor Shachar et al., 2025; Parlanti et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026, e.g.,). Ex situ origins of clumps include minor or major mergers and the accretion of satellites such as dwarf galaxies (Di Matteo et al., 2008; Puech, 2010; Calabrò et al., 2019; Estrada-Carpenter et al., 2024; Nakazato et al., 2024). Galaxy interactions can also trigger clump formation within the gas of the interacting systems through tidal forces, gas compression, and induced turbulence (Teyssier et al., 2010; Renaud et al., 2014; Renaud et al., 2022; Puskás et al., 2026, e.g.,). Recent JWST observations suggest that even very minor interactions (mass ratio ≲1/10\lesssim 1/10) may trigger clump formation, extending this channel below the range typically considered in merger studies (de la Vega and Mobasher, 2026). High-resolution simulations further show that mergers can drive gas fragmentation and the formation of compact star-forming regions and star clusters (Renaud et al., 2015; Lahén et al., 2022, e.g.,). The merger-related clump formation channel is supported by the increasing frequency of galaxy mergers with redshift (Mundy et al., 2017; Duncan et al., 2019; Dalmasso et al., 2024; Duan et al., 2025; Puskás et al., 2025), particularly at lower stellar masses. Accreted satellites can leave remnants within the host galaxy, which was found both in simulations (Mandelker et al., 2017, e.g.,) and indicated by observations (Ribeiro et al., 2017; Zanella et al., 2019). Metallicity variations relative to the gas within the disc of the host galaxy can provide a further diagnostic, although negative offsets can arise from either satellite accretion or metal-poor gas accretion and the subsequent triggering of in situ clump formation (Estrada-Carpenter et al., 2025; Sok et al., 2025; Sok et al., 2026a, e.g.,). Previous studies argued that fragmentation-driven clump formation is more efficient at cosmic noon than at higher redshift due to larger discs, however, recent observations and simulations (see, e.g., Mayer et al. 2025 at z≈7.6z\approx 7.6) pushed its relevance further back in redshift. Mergers may become increasingly important compared to internal fragmentation at higher redshifts and lower masses. However, the competing effects of these clump formation mechanisms at z>3z>3 and at different stellar masses are still unclear and require a large statistical sample to address this properly.

papers.title: Community Lessons from builders of infrared multi-object spectrographs
papers.abstract: We present a summary of lessons learned from our community on the design and construction of infrared multi-object spectrographs. As members of the Magellan Infrared Multi-Object Spectrograph (MIRMOS) development team, we were motivated to learn about the most common troubles faced by our colleagues and incorporate measures in our design and assembly plan to address known issues. The lessons are compiled as a result of interviews we carried out with members of the instrument development teams for several multi-object infrared spectrographs. We found considerable overlap in the lessons learned for building this type of instrument; many of which relate to the cryogenic operation of the instruments. In this paper, we will present the compilation of general and specific lessons which we found relevant for the successful development of MIRMOS or any other future cryogenic instruments.

papers.title: UIBK-Embedding: Effective Text Retrieval by Unifying Dense and Late-Interaction Retrieval
papers.abstract: Dense bi-encoders and late-interaction retrievers are usually treated as alternatives, yet they fail on different queries: one vector captures what a text is about, token-level matching finds its exact entities and phrases. Using both today means two models, two indexes and a score-fusion step. We present UIBK-Embedding-v1, a 179M-parameter English encoder that produces both representations in one pass and scores them with one unmodified MaxSim. The dense embedding is written into the list of token vectors as three extra vectors, and a one-dimensional tag keeps the two kinds of vectors from matching each other, so that plain MaxSim equals the token-level MaxSim plus a weighted dense cosine. The model therefore runs in a standard late-interaction index without changes; we test it with PLAID. A shared 18-layer trunk with a separate 4-layer top per head, and a cross-encoder distilled into the fused score, turn the two heads into one retriever. On BEIR, UIBK-Embedding-v1 reaches 59.79 nDCG@10. This is 2.57 points above LateOn, the strongest model of its size, and 2.10 points above it when both models read documents of the same length; UIBK-Embedding-v1 is ahead on all 15 datasets. On a decontaminated version of BEIR it stays ahead on average (61.55 against 60.36) and on 8 of 12 datasets. Among the 156 models with complete BEIR results in the MTEB results repository, only models with at least 1.5B parameters score higher. Code, model weights, and a technical blog post are available at https://github.com/DataScienceUIBK/uibk-embedding , https://huggingface.co/DataScience-UIBK/uibk-embedding-v1 , and https://huggingface.co/blog/abdoelsayed/uibk-embedding-v1 .

papers.intro:
Neural retrievers encode documents offline and compare them with the query at search time, and two families of models dominate. Dense bi-encoders compress a text into a single vector and score a query–document pair with one cosine (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Reimers and Gurevych, 2019; Wang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2024; Abdallah et al., 2026b). Late-interaction models keep one vector per token and score a pair with MaxSim, the sum over the query tokens of their best-matching document token (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020; Santhanam et al., 2022b; Santhanam et al., 2022a). The two are usually presented as a choice between a small index and better generalisation (Thakur et al., 2021).

The two families do not make the same mistakes. Figure 1 compares a dense model and a ColBERT model that we fine-tuned from the same backbone on the same data. The dense model is better where a long query has to be matched as a whole, as in argument retrieval, and the late-interaction model is better where a single entity or phrase decides, as in the open-domain question answering. Their scores are complementary. Systems exploit this complementarity today through hybrid retrieval: two models, two indexes, two searches, and a fusion step such as reciprocal rank fusion (Cormack et al., 2009). Models that return several representations at once (Chen et al., 2024; Günther et al., 2025) save the second encoder, but every representation still has its own index and its own scoring function.

In this work we introduce UIBK-Embedding, a retriever that holds a dense head and a late-interaction head in one encoder and adds their scores inside a standard late-interaction index (Figure 2d). Specifically, we make the following contributions: (1) For the representation, we store the dense sentence vector as three extra vectors, the slots, in the list of token vectors, and give every vector a one-dimensional tag with opposite signs for tokens and slots. Inside MaxSim a token then never selects a slot and a slot never selects a token, so the unmodified MaxSim returns the token-level score plus a weighted dense cosine (§4.2). The index and the scorer need no change: the model is saved as a ColBERT model and runs in PLAID (Santhanam et al., 2022a) through PyLate (Chaffin and Sourty, 2025). (2) For the architecture, the two heads share the first 18 layers of ModernBERT-base (Warner et al., 2025) and each has its own copy of the last four, which raises the score of each head on its own by about one point. The dense head uses the latent-attention pooling of NV-Embed (Lee et al., 2025), here on an encoder-only model (§4.1). (3) For the training, we distil a cross-encoder into the fused score, the score that is used at inference, in addition to the losses of each head (§4.3). Ablations show the contribution of the two heads, of the fused distillation and of the main training choices (§7). (4) UIBK-Embedding-v1 has 179M parameters and reaches 59.79 nDCG@10 on BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021) and 70.55 on NanoBEIR (Zeta Alpha, 2024), evaluated with the public MTEB implementation (Muennighoff et al., 2023). It is 2.57 points above LateOn (Sourty et al., 2026), the strongest model of its size, 2.10 points above it at equal document length, and ahead of it on all 15 datasets. On the decontaminated BEIR of Sourty et al. (2026) it reaches 61.55, against 60.36 for LateOn, and is ahead on 8 of the 12 datasets. See Tables 2 and 3 for details.

papers.title: EMBER: Predicting TCR--pMHC Binding Without a Docked Complex
papers.abstract: We propose EMBER, a structure-based framework for TCR--pMHC binding prediction that eliminates the need for a predicted docked complex, and with it the placement error that dominates such predictions. Traditional structure-based predictors utilize the co-folded complex structure of the receptor and the antigen and interpret binding from its contact surface. Consequently, every downstream feature inherits any deviation the structure-prediction tool introduced. Methodologically, EMBER folds the TCR and pMHC independently, encodes them as SE(3)-invariant residue graphs, and compares their learned representations without constructing a shared coordinate frame. A relative pose is therefore not an input of the model, so placement error cannot propagate into the prediction. Computationally, EMBER preprocesses $O(N{+}M)$ monomer folds where a complex-based predictor needs $O(NM)$ operations. Experimentally, under epitope-disjoint evaluation with six retrained baselines, EMBER is first on every metric under all four folding tools, by 0.9 to 14.4% in micro-AUROC, 18.5 to 25.3% in micro-AUPRC and 10.6 to 24.1% in MCC. Its ranking is also up to 85% more stable across folding tools.

papers.title: Random $C^*$-subalgebras
papers.abstract: Given a discrete countable group $Γ$, we introduce the concept of random subalgebras of the reduced group $C^*$-algebra $C_r^*(Γ)$. This extends the existing theory of invariant random subgroups and the one of invariant random subalgebras of the group von Neumann algebra ${\rm L}(Γ)$. As applications, we provide a characterisation of $C^*$-simplicity, a condition for amenability of the group and show the existence and uniqueness of a maximal nuclear $Γ$-invariant unital $C^*$-subalgebra of $C^*_r(Γ)$. Moreover, we give a topological characterisation of exactness of any separable unital $C^*$-algebra. Finally, we study exotic random subalgebras of $C^*_r(Γ)$ and super-exotic random subalgebras of ${\rm L}(Γ)$, that is, random subalgebras which do not arise purely from random subgroups of $Γ$ and not from random subalgebras of $C^*_r(Γ)$, respectively.

papers.title: Coevolution of Dust Growth and Gravitational Instability in Massive Protostellar Disks
papers.abstract: Massive protostellar disks are expected to sustain high accretion rates through gravitational instability, while dust growth may modify their opacity, cooling efficiency, and stability. Conversely, the time-dependent and nonaxisymmetric structures produced by gravitational instability may regulate the local conditions for dust growth. However, the coupled evolution of dust growth and gravitational instability in massive protostellar disks has not yet been explored self-consistently. We present two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations that follow gas dynamics, dust growth, and opacity-dependent radiative cooling in a massive protostellar disk. We find that dust grains rapidly grow to millimeter-centimeter sizes shortly after disk formation, substantially reducing the infrared opacity. The enhanced cooling promotes disk fragmentation and produces more frequent accretion-driven luminosity outbursts than in a model without dust growth, with durations and peak luminosities comparable to those observed in massive protostars. Dust growth is broadly regulated by the fragmentation-limited size in dense disk regions, whereas newly formed outer disk regions and low-density regions deviate from this limit because of finite collision timescales and dust transport. These results suggest that dust growth may facilitate episodic accretion and fragmentation, while gravitationally unstable disk structures in turn regulate the dust growth process.

papers.intro:
Massive stars exert a profound influence on their surrounding environments through intense radiation of ≳104​L⊙\gtrsim 10^{4}\>L_{\odot} and supernova explosions. Understanding how such massive stars form is therefore a fundamental problem [8, e.g.,]. Massive protostars emit strong radiation that inhibits further mass accretion onto the protostar. As a consequence, it has long been recognized that spherically symmetric accretion from molecular cloud cores imposes an upper limit on the final stellar mass (∼40​M⊙\sim 40\>M_{\odot}) [58, 49, 120, e.g.,]. To mitigate such radiative feedback and enable continued mass supply onto the protostar, the presence of accretion disks around massive protostars has been proposed [124, 53, 55, 88, 99, e.g.,]. In recent years, high-angular-resolution observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) have proposed evidence for the presence of rotationally supported disks around massive protostars [46, 19, 65, 40, 118, 38, 82, 89, 77, e.g.,]. However, the internal physical structure and evolution of these disks, including the role of dust growth, remain poorly understood.

However, the internal physical structure and evolution of these disks, including the role of dust growth, remain poorly understood.

In this context, the recent polarimetric observation has suggested that dust grains may grow within massive protostellar disks [39]. Dust growth can significantly modify the disk opacity, thereby strongly affecting the disk emission properties at (sub)millimeter wavelengths [123]. Such opacity variations introduce systematic uncertainties in disk masses and temperatures inferred from (sub)millimeter observations [112, e.g.,], highlighting the importance of understanding dust growth processes in massive protostellar disks for the proper interpretation of observations.

Dust growth may also influence the physical evolution of massive protostellar disks themselves. Because these disks are sufficiently optically thick to thermal radiation, their cooling is primarily regulated by dust thermal emission. In this regime, lower opacity allows thermal radiation to escape more efficiently from the disk interior, thereby enhancing the cooling efficiency. Dust growth therefore reduces the infrared opacity and lowers the disk temperature [122]. This may enhance gravitational instability of the massive protostellar disk. Since gravitational instability is highly sensitive to the thermal state and cooling efficiency of the disk [37, 23, 60, e.g.,], dust growth may substantially alter the development of gravitational instability and the subsequent evolution of massive protostellar disks.

Such effects are particularly important because massive protostellar disks are thought to maintain their high accretion rates through gravitational instability. Massive protostellar disks are expected to achieve their high mass accretion rates of ∼10−4​M⊙​yr−1\sim 10^{-4}\>M_{\odot}\>\mathrm{yr}^{-1} via efficient angular momentum transport induced by gravitational instability. Consequently, nonaxisymmetric spiral structures and disk fragmentation leading to the formation of multiple systems have been suggested from both theoretical and observational perspectives [52, 7, 9, 79, e.g.,]. Furthermore, numerical simulations have demonstrated that the infall of fragments onto the central protostar can trigger episodic accretion bursts in massive protostars [69, 67, 33, e.g.,]. Such processes have been proposed as a possible origin of the luminosity outbursts observed in several massive protostars [17, 126, 43, 97, 15, 20, 94, e.g.,].

Dust growth in massive protostellar disks has been investigated theoretically by R. Yamamuro et al. [122], R. Yamamuro et al. [123] using steady, axisymmetric disk models. These studies showed that dust grains can grow efficiently in gravitationally unstable massive protostellar disks and that the resulting opacity evolution can modify the disk thermal structure and gravitational stability. However, massive protostellar disks are expected to be time-dependent and nonaxisymmetric, because gravitational instability produces spiral arms, clumps, and episodic accretion. In such disks, dust growth and gravitational instability should influence each other: dust growth changes the opacity and cooling rate of the disk, while the evolving disk structure controls the local density, temperature, and collision timescale that regulate dust growth. It therefore remains unclear whether the dust-growth framework developed for steady disks remains applicable to dynamically evolving gravitationally unstable disks. It is also unclear how dust-growth-induced opacity evolution feeds back on disk fragmentation and accretion variability.

To this end, we perform self-consistent two-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations that follow the coupled evolution of gas and dust. This paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we describe the numerical methods and simulation setup. In Section III, we present the main results of the coevolution of the disk, central star, and dust in nonaxisymmetric massive protostellar disks. In Section IV, we compare the differences in disk evolution with and without dust growth. In Section V, we compare the dust growth in this study with predictions from a 1D steady disk model and show the implications of dust growth for disk gravitational instability.

papers.title: Deterministic Shift Equivalence Testing for Sparse Polynomials
papers.abstract: We study the shift equivalence testing problem for high-degree sparse multivariate polynomials. Given explicit spar se representations of two polynomials $f,g\in\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, with exponents encoded in binary, sparsities $s$ and $t$, and total degree at most $d$, the task is to decide whether there is a vector $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Q}^n$ such that $f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{a})\equiv g(\mathbf{x})$. Furthermore, one needs to output such a vector if it exists. Dvir, Oliveira, and Shpilka (ICALP 2014) studied shift equivalence for low-degree arithmetic circuits. Their framew ork does not apply directly to sparse polynomials, which are not closed under shifts, and they left open whether shift equivalence of sparse polynomials admits an efficient deterministic algorithm. We answer this question positively over $\mathbb{Q}$. If the input coefficients have bit-size at most $τ$, we sh ow that a rational shift of polynomial bit-size exists whenever the polynomials are shift equivalent. Moreover, our alg orithm outputs such a shift and has a running time of $\operatorname{poly}(n,s,t,τ,\log d)$ in the bit model. The ar ithmetic and structural parts of our result also hold over any field of characteristic zero or characteristic larger th an $d$.

The symbol ≡\equiv emphasizes that the equality is an identity of formal polynomials, not merely an equality of functions. Over ℚ\mathbb{Q} these two notions coincide. The same is true, and the Taylor expansions used below remain valid, over any field of characteristic zero or characteristic larger than the degree under consideration. Note that shift equivalence is indeed an equivalence relation. It is reflexive, since ff can be transformed into itself by the zero shift. papers.title: Atomic identification via the Prandtl-Tomlinson stick-slip mechanism
papers.abstract: Distinguishing atomic species is an ongoing challenge in the field of scanning probe microscopy. Typically, atomic force microscopy makes use of electrostatic interactions to perform atomic identification. Here we perform lateral force microscopy (LFM) measurements with a CO terminated tip of a partially oxidized Cu(110) surface and show clear differences between the metal and oxygen sites over a large z-range. This allows for atomic identification on a typical metal oxide. Density functional theory based calculations show that the tip-sample interaction is dominated by short-ranged orbital interactions and that the electrostatic contribution is negligible. At small tip-sample distances, LFM can probe the Prandtl-Tomlinson stick-slip mechanism on the single-atom scale. It is visible as a striking asymmetry in the forward and backward scan directions, experimentally revealing this fundamental model for nanotribology on the single-atom scale.

papers.title: Avoiding abelian squares with three colours in the continuous setting
papers.abstract: An $n$-colouring of the real line is a Lebesgue measurable function $f \colon \mathbb{R} \to A$, where $A$ is a set of $n$ colours. An abelian square for $f$ is a finite interval $U\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ where every colour shows up in the left and in the right half of $U$ with exactly the same Lebesgue measure. It is known that every $2$-colouring contains an abelian square. On the other hand, Alon, Grytczuk, Laso{ń}, and Michałek (2009) proved that there exist $4$-colourings that avoid abelian squares, while the question for $3$-colourings remained open. We construct a $3$-colouring that avoids abelian squares, disproving a conjecture of Laso{ń} (2015). However, in contrast to the case of 4-colourings, the set of 3-colourings that avoid abelian squares is meagre. We show this using an argument based on the KKM lemma.

papers.title: P$^3$-VLM: A Point-based Alternative for Grounded 3D Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Examining existing benchmarks for grounding in 3D VLMs reveals a pervasive "semantic leakage" in the evaluation and prompting protocols: a heavy reliance on bounding boxes as spatial prompts or representation primitives. Because bounding boxes are highly informative of object categories, they introduce a shortcut for the models to neglect visual information during 3D VLM training. We demonstrate this with a "blind" LLM that, prompted only with the box coordinates, can perform surprisingly well. To further analyze this shortcut, we propose point-based grounding prompting - querying models with a single 3D point instead of a box. Under this protocol, the accuracy of the blind LLM drops from 36.4% to 18.0% on ScanNet's Nr3D, and similarly degrades for 3D VLMs (e.g. LL3DA). Building on this insight, we introduce P$^3$-VLM, a novel tri-pathway 3D VLM that supports point-based prompts and achieves 52.1% state-of-the-art accuracy on location-grounded captioning under this setting. To achieve this, we redesign the architecture while keeping it detector-free, scene-centric, and suitable for 3D GS inputs. P$^3$-VLM utilizes three complementary pathways (location-, task-, and context-aware), enabling strong reasoning about scenes without any bounding box dependencies. The key benefit of point-based learning is a consistent improvement across settings: P$^3$-VLM achieves state-of-the-art performance under point-based grounding while also improving robustness, OOD generalization, and performance on ungrounded scene-centric 3D VQA benchmarks, reflecting its reduced reliance on bounding-box shortcuts and resulting stronger visual-spatial reasoning.

papers.intro:
3D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold the promise of generalist scene understanding: given a 3D representation of an environment, such a model should be able to answer both grounded queries – those anchored to a specific location or object in the scene – and ungrounded queries about the scene at large [8, 24, 8, 20, 23]. Significant progress has been made in this direction, yet a fundamental question remains open: to what extent do current 3D VLMs actually observe the scene, rather than exploit contextual shortcuts?

3D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold the promise of generalist scene understanding: given a 3D representation of an environment, such a model should be able to answer both grounded queries – those anchored to a specific location or object in the scene – and ungrounded queries about the scene at large [8, 24, 8, 20, 23]. Significant progress has been made in this direction, yet a fundamental question remains open: to what extent do current 3D VLMs actually observe the scene, rather than exploit contextual shortcuts?

We investigate this question through grounded object understanding: identifying the correct object given a 3D spatial prompt. This requires jointly reasoning about geometry and semantics, including localizing the queried region, interpreting its visual content, and producing a semantically accurate response [11, 6, 19, 18]. We find that existing object- and scene-centric paradigms share a common issue of “semantic leakage” in evaluation protocols, arising from the widespread use of bounding boxes as either prompts or representation primitives. Because bounding boxes carry strong categorical cues through their size, shape, and aspect ratio, they enable shortcut solutions (e.g., a tall narrow box often corresponds to a door; beds have standardized measurements) that reduce the need for true visual-spatial reasoning. They also implicitly assume accurate object localization, which is usually unrealistic in real-world 3D applications.

These findings motivate both a new evaluation protocol and a new model design. We propose point-based grounding prompting, where queries are specified using only a single 3D point on the target object. Unlike bounding boxes, point prompts do not reveal object shape or extent, substantially reducing category-specific geometric cues and incentivizing models to rely on genuine visual-spatial understanding. This large margin demonstrates that its visual encoder is genuinely load-bearing. Moreover, by avoiding bounding-box shortcuts, P3-VLM is not only more robust but also exhibits stronger scene-level OOD generalization (see Fig. 2), while maintaining consistent gains on ungrounded scene understanding benchmarks such as ScanQA [3] and SQA3D [33]. papers.title: AutoSim: A Self-Improving User Simulator for Conversational Search Evaluation
papers.abstract: User simulators promise to evaluate conversational search systems at a scale human studies cannot reach, but only if their behavior is realistic enough to trust. We study AutoSim, a conversational-search user simulator whose relevance judgments rank a controlled pool of retrieval systems in agreement with NIST across three TREC iKAT years (Kendall's $τ$ of $0.66$, $0.91$, and $0.91$; all $p{\le}0.002$), an agreement that survives removing its persona. AutoSim self-improves against a held-out signal from real users, and we find that fine-tuning its weights makes it behave like real users, which in turn gives a more accurate estimate of how well a system serves them. Reaching that behavior takes more than prompting: when discriminating between real and simulated user sessions, no prompt we tried lowers a held-out real-versus-simulated classifier below AUC $0.85$, whereas fine-tuning the weights drives it to $0.45$, where neither the classifier nor a human reading full dialogues can tell it from a real user. That added realism is what makes the evaluation more accurate: where real users retrieve little, a prompted simulator over-estimates retrieval effectiveness by $+0.136$ nDCG and returns a relevant passage on $57\%$ of the turns where real users find none, enough to change a deployment decision. Only the weight-level simulator escapes this bias. We release the framework and code.

A simulator stands in for a population of users, so retrieval and response strategies can be compared reproducibly when tuning a ranker or a clarifying-question policy.

Because a simulator is fixed at design time as a set of personas, prompts, and decision rules, its behavior drifts from that of real users as the systems it evaluates change. papers.title: RAG-NIMBF: A Non-Invasive, Modular Benchmarking Framework for Automated RAG Configuration Analysis
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the dominant paradigm for grounding the outputs of large language models (LLM) in external knowledge. However, practitioners are faced with a vast configuration space comprising chunking, embedding, retrieval, reranking, prompting and generation models, and there is limited guidance on how these components interact. We present RAG-NIMBF, a modular benchmarking framework that attaches to existing RAG pipelines as a non-invasive evaluation layer. It evaluates the configuration space through controlled ablation with end-to-end experiment tracking. The evaluation combines LLM-based answer quality scores, retrieval correctness measures, and runtime indicators. This study validates the framework across multiple generation models on the SQuAD dataset. This process reveals non-obvious interactions and demonstrates how the experiments are tracked. The findings indicate that the retrieval balance of relevance and diversity substantially enhances the relevance and coverage of retrieved context in comparison to a conventional similarity search, with MMR raising nDCG@5 by +4 to +11 percentage points across the swept models. More detailed prompt instructions meaningfully increase how faithfully generated answers stick to the retrieved evidence, especially for capable and reasoning models (+10 to +13pp on Qwen3.6-27B, GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3.5-think, but negligible on the 20B generator). Overall, RAG-NIMBF transforms the configuration space of RAG into reproducible, comparable experiments. By attaching to existing production pipelines in a non-invasive way, it enables practitioners to systematically evaluate and improve deployed systems without disrupting existing workflows. This replaces ad hoc choices with evidence-based decisions.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [18] has emerged as the standard architecture for building knowledge-grounded question-answering systems. Rather than relying solely on parametric knowledge stored in model weights, RAG pipelines retrieve relevant documents from an external corpus and condition answer generation on the retrieved context. This approach reduces hallucination [32] and enables domain-specific applications without costly fine-tuning.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [18] has emerged as the standard architecture for building knowledge-grounded question-answering systems. Rather than relying solely on parametric knowledge stored in model weights, RAG pipelines retrieve relevant documents from an external corpus and condition answer generation on the retrieved context. This approach reduces hallucination [32] and enables domain-specific applications without costly fine-tuning.

A production RAG pipeline involves multiple interacting components: 1. A chunking strategy splits source documents into retrievable segments. 2. An embedding model maps chunks and queries to a shared vector space. 3. A retrieval method selects the most relevant chunks. 4. An optional reranker re-orders them. 5. A prompt template frames the generation task. 6. A generation model produces the final answer [9]. Each component offers multiple design choices resulting in a large combinatorial configuration space. Even small changes in chunk size, retrieval strategy, or prompt wording can shift faithfulness scores by more than ten percentage points [6]. However, practitioners often select configurations based on intuition, vendor claims, or community defaults rather than systematic evaluations against their own data [8, 31], and such defaults are highly sensitive to corpus and model [1, 28]. For smaller organisations, building RAG on consumer-grade hardware rather than dedicated GPU clusters is the only economically viable path [33], so this study covers models that run on such hardware. Although several evaluation frameworks exist [8, 31, 30], their primary focus is on scoring a given pipeline rather than treating the configuration itself as the object of study. Systematic sweeps, component-interaction analysis, and reproducibility tracking are typically out of scope, and none of them are compatible with existing RAG pipelines.

These issues are addressed by RAG-NIMBF (RAG-Non-Invasive Modular Benchmarking Framework), a framework which is designed around three core principles: 1. Non-invasive integration: The framework wraps existing RAG components without modifying model or retriever internals. It connects to Ollama and OpenAI compatible endpoints (vLLM, TGI, …) through provider routing, requiring only model identifier strings and access data. 2. Systematic configuration exploration: A declarative environment configuration specifies parameter ranges for all components. The framework generates the cartesian product and benchmarks every combination, producing and tracking structured results suitable for direct comparison. 3. papers.title: MuPACE: Learning to Pace Muon for LoRA Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Learning rate schedules are typically fixed before training begins, yet when fine-tuning large language models with low-rank adapters (LoRA), the appropriate scale varies substantially with the model, task, and adapter configuration. Practitioners re-tune a schedule for every new problem, yet a tuned schedule still cannot react to the training dynamics it encounters. We instead amortize learning rate selection across LoRA fine-tuning problems. We leave the base optimizer, Muon, untouched, so that its normalized update fixes the direction, and meta-learn only the global step size. Our method MuPACE is a small recurrent policy, meta-trained across a distribution of fine-tuning runs, that conditions on the observed trajectory and emits bounded adjustments to an interpretable analytic schedule. On 64 fine-tuning problems, MuPACE outperforms standard fixed schedules at a strong shared default on 64-78% of problems and is on par with the same schedules with per-task tuned peaks. Meta-trained only on models with up to 16 layers, MuPACE transfers one-shot to unseen tasks on models as deep as 64 layers, such as Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, where a single run remains competitive with swept schedules.

papers.title: Two $\operatorname{ReLU}$ Layers is All You Need
papers.abstract: We prove that every $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network can be exactly simulated by a $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network with two hidden layers. We present two proofs: one that is based on fillings in homological algebra and a direct combinatorial proof.

papers.title: Real-Time Ground Normal Vector Estimation for Spherical Mobile 3D Mapping using LiDAR-Inertial Odometry
papers.abstract: Accurate ground plane normal estimation is essential for odometry in spherical mobile mapping systems (SMMS), which face challenges from rapid rotations and limited ground coverage. We propose two RANSAC-based approaches: single-scan estimation with normal vector scoring and multi-step validation, and LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO)-based estimation using a global 3D map. Evaluated across diverse real-world datasets against terrestrial laser scanner ground truth, results show that LIO-based estimation significantly outperforms single-scan methods in accuracy and robustness. Integrating ground normal estimates into the motion model improves pose estimation, supporting autonomous navigation in challenging and hazardous environments.

papers.intro:
Gathering information about the environment has always been a foundational desire of the human species. Though, the method of doing so has changed significantly over time. Nowadays, there is no longer the need to take unnecessary risks to explore unknown and potentially hazardous environments. Instead, unmanned autonomous robotic systems are applied for this purpose. While this trend in exploration innovation improves safety for humans and enables the acquisition of large datasets in a short amount of time, there is no generally applicable approach, valid for all the different kinds of environments. On Earth alone, the exploration of different environments requires heavy adaption of the robotic systems that are used, like wheeled robots for planar environments, legged robots for rough outdoor terrain, and unmanned aerial vehicles for places too hard to traverse. Going beyond Earth to outer space introduces even more challenging environments. These also include our Moon, which is of major interest for current and upcoming space missions. Next to the harsh lunar surface, there exist lunar caves or lava tubes, originating from volcanic activity on the Moon [1]. These underground structures are of high interest for scientific missions that try to learn more about the evolution of Luna [2], our solar system’s history [3], and exploring potential human habitats for crewed Moon base in the near future [4].

While there already exist satellite imagery [5] and radar-based analysis [6] of lunar caves by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Mission, onsite autonomous robotic exploration offers a lot more possibilities to gather information about these unique environments, just recently shown by Calvo et al. [7]. Having high resolution 3D maps of these caves would enable a huge step to further understanding their characteristics, which is why Borrmann et al. proposed the Descent And Exploration in Deep Autonomy of Lava Underground Structures project for this very purpose in 2021 [8]. It allows traversal of the challenging lunar cave terrain thanks to its protective outer shell and rolling motion. The rotation-based locomotion of the SMMS inherently offers a large Field of View during motion and consequently enables building 3D point clouds that cover the entire surrounding environment. For reliable navigation and mapping by the SMMS, knowledge of the current ground plane the system is traversing on is crucial. Therefore, this thesis focuses on the problem of computing a reliable and real-time estimate of the ground plane normal vector, as well as integrating it into an existing pose estimation approach. To achieve successful and reliable SLAM in real-time, the current pose estimate of the robot must be computed as accurately as possible onboard the system. The lunar environment with a lack of a Global Navigation Satellite System, and rough, non-planar terrain makes this increasingly hard. While there exist multiple approaches to estimate the current pose, most of them require information about the plane the system is moving on to provide reliable results. The SMMS filters IMU data to calculate pose data and, by default, assumes a flat ground plane. With this assumption, the resulting trajectory will not include any information about the movement in the upwards or downwards direction over time, resulting in a pose estimation process restricted to five of the six possible Degrees of Freedom with static height of the system. Additionally, the process of mapping the surrounding environment and computing a global 3D point cloud using LIO further depends on these pose estimates, which is the basis for reliable SLAM on the robot. However, the sphere’s kinematic motion model introduces additional challenges to the ground normal estimation. Its fast rotations and orientation-dependent ground coverage by the LiDAR sensor make straightforward single-scan-based ground normal computation prone to outliers. Thus, a more robust approach is needed to achieve the full potential of the SMMS for exploring and mapping challenging terrain like lunar caves. This work proposes a novel method to extract the normal vector of the current ground plane underneath a spherical robot. This approach uses a global 3D map as input for the ground normal estimation to assure an adequate amount of points and ground coverage for the normal computation. An existing approach for estimating the ground normal vector, based on single LiDAR scans, is extended with a scoring system and additional validation techniques to improve robustness. Both processes are evaluated for their accuracy and runtime using different in and outdoor datasets. Furthermore, the impact of feeding the ground normal vector into an IMU-based pose estimator with motion-acceleration compensation is evaluated, in order to assess its impact compared to the prior approach assuming a flat ground plane. Finally, the proposed ground normal extraction method allows future algorithms on the SMMS to go beyond the planar ground assumption, enabling the system to traverse more complex cave-like terrain and further improve the mapping of the surrounding environment.
