papers.title: Enhanced orbital-angular-momentum dimensionality and spatial-spectral decoupling in thin-film SPDC
papers.abstract: Thin-film spontaneous parametric down-conversion, due to the relaxed phase-matching condition, generates photon pairs that are extremely broadband in frequency and angle and highly entangled in time/frequency and position/momentum. Here we show that it also provides a very broad orbital angular momentum (OAM) spectrum, which, in contrast to the case of bulk crystals, is decoupled from the frequency spectrum. To demonstrate it experimentally, we generate photon pairs in a $7~μ\mathrm{m}$-thick lithium niobate film and compare them with those from a $500~μ\mathrm{m}$-thick periodically poled lithium niobate crystal under identical pump conditions. The thin-film source exhibits a substantially broader OAM spectrum, with the azimuthal Schmidt number almost 9 times larger than that of the bulk source. On this highly entangled state, we perform quantum-state tomography in selected two- and four-dimensional OAM subspaces, demonstrating high-purity maximally entangled states. These results highlight thin nonlinear films as a promising platform for high-dimensional quantum-state generation with weak spatial--spectral coupling.

papers.intro:
Thin-film nonlinear films have recently emerged as versatile platforms for the generation of entangled photons through spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) [11]. In films with thickness comparable to or smaller than the nonlinear coherence length of SPDC, the phase matching is satisfied automatically [18, 22, 23]. As a result, unlike bulk crystals, thin films can generate photon pairs under nonzero wavevector mismatch. This enables SPDC with large spectral and angular bandwidth and provides substantially greater flexibility in the choice of nonlinear material and operating wavelength. At the same time, the micro- or nanometer-scale thickness of such nonlinear media facilitates their direct integration with planar photonic platforms and heterostructures, providing a route toward compact on-chip quantum-light sources [9, 4].

The giant angular bandwidth of thin-film SPDC provides access to a large number of spatial modes, forming high-dimensional photonic Hilbert spaces. This makes thin-film SPDC particularly attractive for spatial-mode encoding, including orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) entanglement and high-dimensional quantum information processing [17, 2]. In a dd-dimensional space, a single photon can encode up to log2​d\log_{2}d bits of classical information using dd orthogonal states, exceeding the one-bit capacity of a two-dimensional encoding [7, 20].

Simultaneous access to spatial and spectral modes provides an additional resource for quantum-state engineering. In particular, OAM and frequency can be exploited jointly for multidimensional encoding, multiplexing, and the generation of hyperentangled states [6, 5]. For these applications, however, the spatial and spectral degrees of freedom should ideally remain independently addressable. In conventional SPDC, this is not the case [3, 19]: the spatial and spectral degrees of freedom are generally coupled because both depend on the longitudinal phase matching. In thin films, the longitudinal phase-matching constraint is strongly relaxed, which leads to factorable, albeit extremely broad, frequency and angular spectra.

In this work, we experimentally demonstrate the substantially increased spatial dimensionality enabled by thin-film nonlinear sources. We directly compare the spiral (OAM) bandwidths of photon pairs generated in a 7​μ​m7~\mu\mathrm{m}-thick lithium niobate film and a 500​μ​m500~\mu\mathrm{m}-thick phase-matched lithium niobate crystal under identical pump conditions. We show that the thin-film source features a considerably broader OAM spectrum. Further, using the thin-film source, we perform quantum-state tomography of the generated two-photon states in three two-dimensional OAM subspaces and one four-dimensional subspace, revealing high-purity states with high fidelity to the corresponding maximally entangled target states. We further investigate spatial–spectral coupling of the generated OAM states. Numerical simulations show that the thin-film source preserves a nearly unchanged spiral spectrum over a broad spectral range, whereas the bulk crystal exhibits a pronounced frequency-dependent variation of the OAM distribution. Frequency-resolved OAM measurements provide the first experimental indication of spatial–spectral decoupling in the thin-film source. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of thin-film nonlinear crystals for broadband, high-dimensional quantum-state generation with reduced coupling between the spatial and spectral degrees of freedom, opening opportunities for spatial–spectral hyperentanglement.

papers.title: pyFDN: A Python Toolbox for Feedback Delay Network Design, Analysis, and Optimization
papers.abstract: Feedback delay networks (FDNs) provide a compact representation of recursive audio systems for artificial reverberation and decorrelation. Their practical use spans structured matrix design, acoustic decay shaping, numerical simulation, and modal analysis, increasingly combined with differentiable optimization. We present pyFDN, an open-source Python toolbox that brings these operations into a common workflow. The library combines numerical design and analysis routines with block-based time-domain processing and integration with FLAMO for frequency-domain differentiable processing. Explicit network builds and JSON presets connect design, optimization, rendering, and reuse. This paper describes the software architecture, representative capabilities, and reproducibility mechanisms of version 0.5.0, providing a reference for research and teaching that use the toolbox.

papers.title: Velocity Optimization via Thermal Imaging Enhances Autonomous Tumor Resection
papers.abstract: Objective: To demonstrate and evaluate THERMO, a thermal-velocity optimization algorithm for autonomous electrosurgery, in ex vivo porcine tissue using the UR10e-based ASTR system. Methods: Thermography for Electrosurgical Rate Modulation via Optimization (ThERMO), a closed-loop algorithm that uses real-time thermal imaging data to minimize thermal injury while ensuring accurate cut margins, was tested on ex vivo porcine tissue. Histological analysis was performed to detect thermal injury extent at a cellular level, and 3D photogrammetric measurement was used to verify margin accuracy. ThERMO's performance was compared against two previously used fixed velocity methods. Results: ThERMO outperformed both fixed velocity comparison methods without requiring data-driven training or iterative tuning, reducing thermal injury by up to 52%, improving cut accuracy by up to 59%, and maintaining task completion speed. Conclusions: Closed-loop thermal feedback via ThERMO improves autonomous robotic electrosurgery by simultaneously reducing thermal injury and improving margin accuracy, reinforcing its value over fixed velocity approaches for tumor resection applications. Significance: This work advances autonomous robotic tumor resection by demonstrating that real-time closed-loop thermal feedback control can substantially reduce collateral tissue damage and improve surgical margin accuracy.

papers.intro:
Oral cavity cancer (OCC) is cancer of the mouth, tongue, lips, and cheeks. Approximately 377,000 new OCC cases are diagnosed each year globally, leading to 178,000 deaths. Tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and human papillomavirus (HPV) are risk factors for developing OCC. Over 90% of OCC cases are squamous cell carcinoma, or cancer of the cells that line the outer layer of the tongue, cheeks, gums, and throat [1]. For treatment of pre-metastatic oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), surgical intervention is often the most effective treatment [2].

Tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and human papillomavirus (HPV) are risk factors for developing OCC. Over 90% of OCC cases are squamous cell carcinoma, or cancer of the cells that line the outer layer of the tongue, cheeks, gums, and throat [1]. For treatment of pre-metastatic oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), surgical intervention is often the most effective treatment [2].

The standard surgical approach is the partial glossectomy procedure, where the portion of the tongue consisting of the OSCC tumor is removed. Cancer recurrence rates are minimized if the surgical margins (the region between the tumor and the cut boundary) reach 5 mm5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} [3]. The term negative margin indicates that no cancer cells were found in the margin, while positive margin indicates the opposite. Though positive margins increase recurrence risk, excess negative margins indicate excess healthy tissue removal and worsen post-operative recovery and quality of life [4, 5]. Therefore, it is critical to ensure accurate surgical margins during tumor resection.

Electrosurgery is a common technique for removing tumor tissue, wherein a surgical tool conducts electricity to generate heat in tissue, thereby causing it to denature. The heat-induced tissue denaturation reduces mechanical cutting effort while controlling bleeding. Monopolar electrosurgery directly heats the tissue by passing current from the tool tip through the body to an alternate-site grounding pad. Excess application of electrosurgery, however, may cause trauma to the lingual nerve in the tongue and permanently impair tongue sensory function. Insufficient application, by contrast, reduces cut accuracy by causing tissue snagging, which negatively impacts surgical margins and outcomes. As such, electrosurgery requires surgeons to diligently monitor tissue conditions to prevent adverse outcomes.

Monitoring and safely controlling electrosurgery becomes increasingly difficult in the tight constraints of the oral cavity. Consequently, robotics has provided advances in ergonomics and visualization during oral surgeries [6, 7]. Systems like the da Vinci Single Port (Intuitive Surgical Inc., Sunnyvale, California, USA) have made trans-oral robotic surgery (TORS) possible by reducing tool size while maintaining high-quality stereoscopic vision. The application of robotics to head and neck surgery offers the possibility of procedural enhancements with sensing, feedback, and automation.

In the few early demonstrations of autonomous tumor resection has been an active research field, a discrepancy exists between the surgeon’s technique and the robot’s. While experienced surgeons adjust their cutting speed based on visual feedback of cut accuracy and thermal injury, current autonomous electrosurgical robots do not.

Autonomous surgical debridement of bone tissue was first demonstrated in human cadavers by Sefati et al. [9]. They used a hybrid continuum robot on a UR10 robot to perform osteolytic debridement in the pelvis using a surgeon-approved preoperative plan. Autonomous cutting of hard tissue like bone does not face many of the challenges of cutting soft tissue. Autonomous surgical cutting has typically run in an open-loop fashion, using a velocity predetermined via trial-and-error tuning or simulation. Studies have shown that autonomous robotic electrosurgery of this form causes more cellular injury than manual electrosurgery, indicating that the fine adjustments surgeons make during surgery have a substantial impact on excess heat injury [10]. In past demonstrations of autonomous tumor resection, researchers have prioritized cutting accuracy over thermal injury and manually selected low cutting speeds. For instance, Opfermann et al. first demonstrated a visual servoing approach for electrosurgical cutting on the Smart Tissue Autonomous Robot (STAR) [11, 12]. Saeidi et al. similarly showed that STAR could perform tissue-cutting tasks using a predetermined cut speed [13]. Ge et al. introduced the Autonomous System for Tumor Resection (ASTR) system for fully autonomous tumor resection and demonstrated successful cutting at 2 mm/s2\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}\text{/}\mathrm{s} [14]. Ge et al. later proposed that for faster velocities that excessively deform tissue, simulation-based trajectory augmentation could reduce spatial error [15]. However, soft tissue simulation is both challenging and not patient-specific, potentially limiting robustness, optimality, and safety without additional feedback mechanisms.

Bao and Mazumder showed that thermal imaging can control the denaturation zone using a novel computer-controllable electrosurgical unit (ESU) [22]. Surgeons, however, typically employ a fixed power level, and most ESUs are not capable of real-time power modulation. El-Kebir et al. instead used thermal sensing to train a data-driven non-linear autoregressive exogenous input (NLARX) model to determine when a static surgical tool should move to the next waypoint [23]. It is still unclear, however, if these data-driven models generalize from laboratory settings to the complex surgical environment. Some researchers instead have developed methods to estimate soft tissue parameters online, including by use of thermography, Bayesian and Gaussian Estimation, and finite element models [24, 25, 26, 27, 28].

papers.title: Ask to Learn: Query-Based Collaborative Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning is fundamentally limited by the coverage of the available data, while collecting additional trajectories through online exploration may be costly, unsafe, or infeasible. We study whether this limitation can be overcome without directly interacting with the underlying environment. Motivated by practical settings such as collaborator-mediated simulation, where a collaborator can provide information complementary to the offline data, we introduce query-based collaborative reinforcement learning to study how to acquire this information efficiently. The learner starts with a fixed offline dataset and adaptively queries state-time pairs; the collaborator samples an action according to a fixed, possibly suboptimal policy, and the simulator returns the corresponding reward and next state. For finite-horizon tabular problems, we derive an instance-dependent information-theoretic lower bound on the additional queries required to identify an $ε$-optimal policy and develop a local quadratic approximation. Guided by this characterization, we develop an adaptive query-allocation algorithm whose query complexity nearly matches the local benchmark under suitable conditions. Experiments on multiple synthetic and semi-synthetic environments demonstrate the empirical efficiency of the proposed method.

papers.title: Efficient Perturbation-Based SC Decoding for Long Polar Codes
papers.abstract: Soft information perturbations can significantly improve the successive cancellation (SC) decoding performance of polar codes. This is an effective method for realizing low-latency yet high performance for long polar codes, since each perturbation-based SC (PSC) decoding can be performed in parallel. However, little theoretical insight has been revealed so far regarding its work rationale. This paper provides the theoretical analysis of the soft information perturbation. It reveals that PSC decoding improves the SC decoding performance through correcting the erroneous bit estimations, especially the first erroneous bit (FEB). It further validates that perturbing the soft information does not degrade the error-correction capability of SC decoding. Such revelations lead to the design of optimal perturbations that maximizes the FEB correction probability, resulting in an enhanced PSC decoding performance. Based on this, a novel hybrid PSC (HPSC) decoding is proposed. By introducing the random and biased perturbations, the HPSC decoding can better divert from the initial erroneous estimation and converge to the intended one. Our simulation results demonstrate that with the optimal perturbation, the HPSC decoding can achieve a similar performance as the cyclic redundancy check (CRC) aided SC list (CA-SCL) decoding, while avoiding path sorting and expansion.

papers.intro:
Polar codes, invented by Arıkan [1], are the first theoretically proven capacity-achieving codes, where the proof was conducted over symmetric binary-input discrete memoryless channels (B-DMCs) by the use of successive cancellation (SC) decoding. However, in the short-to-moderate codeword length regime, SC decoding suffers from poor performance, since there exist a substantial portion of subchannels without a polarized capacity. Subsequently, its rate profiling becomes less effective. The SC list (SCL) decoding [2, 3] was later proposed to improve the performance. It preserves multiple decoding paths over the decoding tree that also represents the codebook. By utilizing an outer cyclic redundancy check (CRC) code to identify the intended decoding path, the CRC aided SCL (CA-SCL) decoding [4] can further improve the SCL decoding performance. However, the above mentioned SCL decoding algorithms [2, 3, 4, 5, 6] require path expansion and sorting operations when estimating each information bit, leading to substantial memory and computation costs. More importantly, the successive estimation of the above mentioned decoding inevitably leads to the latency challenge, especially for long polar codes.

Addressing the above mentioned challenges, the SC-flip (SCF) decoding was proposed in [7]. It freezes the possibly erroneous bit to the opposite of its SC decoding estimation. Afterwards, an additional SC decoding attempt is performed to re-estimate the information bits. The SCF decoding yields an enhanced SC decoding performance with a reduced memory cost. This method works well if the real first erroneous bit (FEB) is flipped. However, constructing a flipping set (FS) that includes the real FEB remains challenging. In [7, 8, 9, 10, 11], numerous metrics were proposed for the formation of the FS, including the ones based on the magnitude of decoding a posteriori log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) [7], and the error probability of bit estimation [8]. In [12], the thresholded SCF (TSCF) decoding was proposed. By utilizing the LLR-threshold, it can further reduce the searching space for possible erroneous positions. Based on the constructed FS [8], the dynamic SCF (DSCF) decoding was proposed [13]. By utilizing the multi-level flipping strategy, it can correct multiple erroneous bits within a single decoding attempt. However, despite the above mentioned SCF-based decoding algorithms performing well, efficiency of the bit-flipping vanishes rapidly as the codeword length increases, especially when the codeword length exceeds 4096. Moreover, performance gain of the SCF decoding is still exchanged by additional decoding attempts that bring substantial complexity and latency costs. They are becoming prohibitive for long polar codes.

papers.title: ICIBS: Increasing the Context for Ice Boundary Segmentation
papers.abstract: Mountain glaciers and ice sheets are undergoing rapid loss of ice mass. To assess their current volume and ice-thickness distribution, and to accurately forecast their future, ground-penetrating radar systems are employed to measure ice thickness. These instruments produce radio-echo sounding data that reveal the internal structure of the ice and its boundaries at the surface and beneath the ice body. However, delineating these interfaces is time-consuming as the surveyed area can span several hundred kilometers. To accelerate the labelling process, automated methods have emerged, but they often struggle to delineate the ice bottom, particularly in temperate glaciers. The high water content inherent in temperate ice increases both scattering and attenuation of the radar signal, resulting in weak and ambiguous reflections at the ice bottom and generally noisier data. As a result, the visual features corresponding to the ice bottom become ambiguous. To address this issue, we propose several extensions to deep learning models that incorporate additional contextual information into the prediction. Specifically, we integrate modifications that incorporate additional spatial and geo-spatial contextual information into the network. With these enhancements, we achieve a new state-of-the-art performance on the IceAnatomy benchmark dataset, with mean errors of 10.9 m for the FAU subset and 43.4 m for the CReSIS subset in a single combined system. We also demonstrate that our method generalises well to previously unseen data, outperforming the baseline by 49.6 % on new campaign data from Patagonia. The model code and the new dataset are available at https://github.com/ki7077/ICIBS/tree/main and https://zenodo.org/records/23392580.

papers.intro:
Estimates indicate that 49–83 % of mountain glaciers will disappear by 2100 [1], which will have a strong impact on local environments, ecosystems, and communities [2, 3]. These projections highlight the need for robust baseline assessments of glacier thicknesses at specific points in time. However, among the more than 200,000 glaciers located outside Greenland and the Antarctic Ice Sheet, less than 5,000 have concrete ice thickness measurements [4, 5]. To address this data scarcity, scientists conduct field campaigns using ground-penetrating radar systems to measure ice thickness in previously unobserved glaciers [6]. The systems operate by transmitting electromagnetic waves into the ice and recording the returning signals, producing radargrams or image-like maps of subsurface reflection amplitudes via inversion techniques [7, 8]. These radargrams enable the interpretation of internal glacier structures along with the delineation of ice boundaries, respectively, the ice thickness, which are essential variables for predicting the future glacier evolution. However, radar surveys accumulate vast amounts of data, making manual analysis increasingly impractical [9].

To address this issue, algorithms and deep learning models have been developed to automatically delineate the ice boundaries [10]. These approaches have achieved promising results, particularly for cold glaciers, where the recorded radar reflection amplitudes remain largely undistorted. In contrast, the results for temperate and polythermal glaciers are often worse, as water attenuates and scatters the signal, complicating echo interpretation [11]. Likewise, thick glaciers can attenuate the received signal, further complicating the distinction between internal features. In such cases, accurate delineation of the ice bottom requires frequent manual interpretation. However, that raises the question of why human annotators are better at interpreting radar data.

papers.title: A bright X-ray flaring event from the intermediate supergiant fast X-ray transient IGR J00370+6122 observed with NuSTAR
papers.abstract: We present an analysis of a long NuSTAR observation of the intermediate supergiant fast X-ray transient (SFXT) IGR J00370+6122, obtained around the peak of its orbital modulation. The observation has a net exposure ~93 ks. During the observation, the source displayed a bright flaring event that was resolved into numerous short flares with durations of 10-1000 s. The 3-70 keV luminosity spanned a dynamic range of ~200, from ~1E34 to ~1.8E36 erg/s; the maximum was reached for only ~40 s in total. The spectrum is well described by an absorbed double-Comptonisation model, with parameters consistent with those found in other X-ray pulsars accreting at similarly low luminosities. This is the first detection of a double-hump continuum in IGR J00370+6122, which extends this spectral state to the class of intermediate SFXTs. We searched for the previously reported ~346 s and ~674 s periodicities and find no significant signal at either period, which makes their interpretation as the neutron star spin period less likely. Using ~21 yr of Swift/BAT monitoring, we refine the orbital period of the system to P_orb=15.6654 +/- 0.0008 d. Finally, we discuss the observed flaring activity in the framework of quasi-spherical settling accretion, which is expected at the observed luminosities.

papers.intro:
High-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) consist of an OB-type donor star and a compact object, either a neutron star (NS) or, more rarely, a black hole, that accretes matter from its companion and produces X-ray emission (Kretschmar et al., 2019, for a review, see e.g.). Within this class, supergiant X-ray binaries (SGXBs) host a compact object that orbits an OB supergiant donor and accretes from its powerful, radiatively driven stellar wind. Classical persistent SGXBs (e.g. Vela X−-1 and 4U 1700−-377) are characterised by continuous X-ray emission with moderate variability, typically about one order of magnitude, which is generally attributed to intrinsic clumpiness and inhomogeneities in the wind from the donor star (Fürst et al., 2010, e.g.).

The discovery rate of SGXBs increased substantially following the 2002 launch of the International Gamma-Ray Astrophysics Laboratory (INTEGRAL; Winkler et al. 2003). Its hard X-ray monitoring capabilities revealed a previously unrecognised subclass of highly variable sources, subsequently classified as supergiant fast X-ray transients (Negueruela et al., 2006; Sguera et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2004, SFXTs;). Unlike classical SGXBs, SFXTs spend most of their time in a faint, quiescent state (LX∼1032−1033L_{\rm X}\sim 10^{32}-10^{33} erg s-1), interrupted by rare, bright outbursts lasting a few 10410^{4} s, during which the luminosity typically reaches LX∼1036−1037L_{\rm X}\sim 10^{36}-10^{37} erg s-1 (Romano, 2015; Sidoli, 2017, e.g.); a few exceptional cases reach up to ∼1038\sim 10^{38} erg s-1 (e.g. IGR J17544−-2619; Romano et al. 2015). These outbursts are composed of multiple short flares with durations of ∼1000\sim 1000 s. On short timescales (<104<10^{4} s), SFXTs display dynamic ranges in luminosity of ∼103−105\sim 10^{3}-10^{5}, much larger than those of classical SGXBs, which makes them one of the most extreme classes of variable HMXBs known. To date, several dozen SFXTs and SFXT candidates have been identified, although orbital and spin periods have been measured for only a subset of these sources (Romano, 2015; Sidoli, 2017, e.g.).

The physical mechanism responsible for the extreme variability of SFXTs remains debated, and more than one mechanism likely contributes across the class. Proposed explanations include (i) clumpiness of the supergiant wind, whereby accretion of individual dense clumps produces sudden X-ray flares (in’t Zand, 2005, e.g.); (ii) centrifugal and magnetic gating mechanisms, in which the NS spin and its strong magnetic field can temporarily inhibit accretion (Grebenev and Sunyaev, 2007; Bozzo et al., 2008, e.g.); and (iii) quasi-spherical settling accretion, in which a hot, quasi-static shell forms above the magnetosphere and regulates the plasma entry rate through Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities. In this scenario, moderate flares arise when local fluctuations in the wind density or velocity shift the cooling regime near the magnetosphere, while brighter flares occur when the NS captures a magnetised wind structure. This triggers magnetic reconnection, which induces the unstable collapse of the shell onto the NS surface (Shakura et al., 2014).

papers.title: Variable-Resolution Scattering Reveals Ensemble Properties
papers.abstract: SAXS/SANS determine the size and structure of particles and macromolecules in solution. However, the conventional low-angle determination of the radius of gyration, Rg, cannot separately resolve its scattering-weighted mean and the width of its distribution. Because the apparent Rg includes a contribution from ensemble variance, the distribution width is required even to recover the mean Rg. Here, we introduce TENOR-SAXS, a method for estimating the scattering-weighted width of an Rg distribution by applying two anisotropic digital smearings to a single 2D scattering image. Comparing the smeared images provides curvature information unavailable from the conventional radial profile. The resulting observables require no explicit model of the native instrumental point-spread function and show only weak sensitivity over the range of native resolutions typical of SAXS measurements examined here. Analytical expressions are derived in the low-angle and narrow-distribution limits for ensembles described by a known or independently constrained single-particle form factor. For verification, we simulated scattering by particles with several form factors and ensembles with different size distributions, all agree well with the analytical theory. To leading order, the principal observable depends on the scattering-weighted mean and variance rather than on the distribution's functional form or higher moments. For simulated data corresponding to feasible synchrotron exposure times for biological samples, the distribution width and, expressed as a fraction of its mean, was recovered with a typical discrepancy of ~0.1, while the scattering-weighted mean Rg was recovered with ~2% relative discrepancy. TENOR-SAXS thus provides a framework for estimating ensemble width from existing 2D scattering data without explicit instrumental desmearing and for correcting the variance contribution to the apparent radius
papers.intro:
Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) is a widely used technique for characterizing nanostructures, providing ensemble-averaged information on particle size, shape, and conformational flexibility. Small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) shares similar analysis techniques, although its resolution and noise characteristics differ from those of SAXS [jeffries2021primer]. Since the early developments of Guinier and co-workers [guinier1955, glatter1982], SAXS has become central in nanoscopic characterization, in particular for samples measured in solution. A relevant example includes the study of nanoscale biological substances (e.g., proteins, lipids, nucleic acids and their complexes), where it complements high-resolution crystallography and NMR by accessing macromolecular length-scale and states in solution, including flexible and heterogeneous systems [svergun2003, jacques2010, mohammed2024]. In soft condensed matter and materials science, SAXS is similarly applied to polymers, nanoparticles, colloids, and porous media, enabling quantitative description of morphology and hierarchical structure [feigin1987, pauw2013].

The distribution of nano-particle sizes has fundamental effects in many cases in materials science and pharmaceuticals [schoepe2007, garcia2009, pastoriza2011, danaei2018]. This motivates the development of SAXS methods to observe and characterize the polydispersity of a nanoscopic ensemble. SAXS is fundamentally limited, since the measured intensity represents an average over all scatterers in the illuminated volume. Samples such as intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) populate heterogeneous conformational ensembles, which may be represented in part by a distribution of radii of gyration, P⁡(Rg)P(R_{g}), rather than by a single characteristic structure [ahmed2020, gomes2020, song2021, koren_intramolecular_2023]. Integrative studies further demonstrate that ensembles with similar SAXS-derived mean RgR_{g} values may nevertheless differ substantially in end-to-end distances, internal-distance scaling, shape, and conformational fluctuations [gomes2020]. Thus, a mean RgR_{g} obtained by conventional SAXS analysis can mask structurally and functionally relevant heterogeneity and, in a polydisperse ensemble, may also be shifted by the underlying RgR_{g} distribution. Approaches to recover ensemble heterogeneity include the ensemble optimization method [bernado2007, tria2015], Bayesian inference [hummer2015, antonov2016, chatzimagas2023], molecular form factor [riback2017] and related modeling frameworks. Recently, Tomchuk et al. introduced a new analysis protocol to extract polydispersity directly from SAXS [tomchuk2023] by extracting observable values from the data. However, the quantitative interpretation of this analysis is sensitive to the assumed functional form of the particle-size distribution, which is generally unknown, and is derived for spherical particles.

Instrumental effects provide an additional complication. Deliberate manipulation of the effective SAXS point-spread function has itself been used to extract information, by modifying the incoming beam shape and translating the detector in sub-pixel steps to retrieve an angularly super-resolved pattern [gutman2020]. Beam divergence and detector resolution broaden the measured scattering profile through convolution with the point-spread function (PSF, or resolution function). This broadening mimics the effect of particle-size polydispersity, so that accurate recovery of ensemble variance from a single scattering profile requires knowledge of the PSF. However, PSF characterization is often incomplete and may vary with beamline configuration [pedersen1990, vad2010, rennie2013]. Although deconvolution approaches are sometimes used in principle to correct for instrumental broadening, deconvolution itself requires accurate knowledge of the PSF and is typically ill-posed; as a result, it propagates PSF uncertainty directly into the inferred variance and can introduce systematic bias [tikhonov1977, bertero1998, svergun1988, vad2011, glatter1974].

In this work, we introduce a Technique for Ensemble Observation by Resolution variation in SAXS (TENOR-SAXS), which avoids explicit deconvolution and reduces sensitivity to the native instrumental PSF by comparing controlled changes in effective resolution. The method leverages changes in digital filtering resolution to construct observables whose dependence on the variance of RgR_{g} is analytically defined and is only weakly sensitive to the shape of the examined size-distribution families when expressed in terms of scattering-weighted variance. Scattering patterns acquired at different effective resolutions, either experimentally (e.g. via slit or collimation adjustments) or by applying digital smearing, are compared to separate instrumental and structural contributions to profile broadening, see Fig. 1 for a visual conceptualization of the method. In this way, the ensemble’s polydispersity is characterized without requiring explicit knowledge of the PSF and without the systematic bias associated with deconvolution-based approaches.

papers.title: Convergent Performance, Divergent Mechanisms in LoRA-Adapted Vision Foundation Models for Brain MRI
papers.abstract: Adapting Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) to medical imaging via LoRA has become standard practice, yet model selection is guided almost entirely by downstream task metrics, treating backbones with similar performance as interchangeable. We investigate whether equal performance implies equal internal representational shift. We analyse four ViT-B/16 backbones, DINOv3, SigLIP2, MerMED-FM, and BiomedCLIP, pre-trained with different objectives (self-distillation vs. contrastive vision-language) and on different data domains (natural vs. medical images). We adapt each to brain tumour segmentation and evaluate on six datasets covering both segmentation and Alzheimer's disease classification. Using attention divergence, weight-change analysis, and activation patching, we find that the four models converge to similar segmentation performance (mean Dice 78-81%) through markedly different internal dynamics, yet diverge in cross-task transfer: segmentation adaptation improves Alzheimer's disease classification for DINOv3 but degrades it for the other three backbones. We reveal a dissociation between modification magnitude and causal importance: the most heavily modified layers are not the causally relevant ones, with early-to-mid layers identified as sufficient for segmentation recovery. Restricting LoRA to these layers matches or approaches full-layer segmentation while reducing classification degradation in the three affected backbones, providing a mechanistically grounded strategy that is more parameter-efficient and more robust than standard full-layer adaptation.

papers.intro:
Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), which are pretrained on large-scale image datasets, provide powerful visual feature encoders applicable to diverse downstream computer vision tasks [1]. Adapting them via Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has become standard practice, with methods like LoRA [2] achieving competitive results across diverse data domains [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9] at a fraction of full fine-tuning costs. In medical imaging tasks, such as brain tumour segmentation, LoRA-adapted foundation models now rival fully supervised baselines [10, 11]. Given the numerous publicly available VFMs backbones [12, 13, 14, 15], choosing which backbone best serves the downstream task becomes a key design decision. Currently, model selection is guided almost entirely by downstream task metrics [16]; i.e., two backbones that reach the same segmentation Dice score are treated as interchangeable. In this paper, we investigate an intriguing mechanistic question: whether equal performance implies equal internal representation shift, as differences in how models reshape their representations may expose hidden generalisability risks and point to different backbone-selection or fine-tuning strategies.

In model deployment, a single backbone often serves multiple downstream tasks. A model whose representations degrade on one task while improving on another poses a deployment risk that task-specific evaluation cannot detect. Understanding how models adapt, not only how well they perform, is therefore necessary for informed backbone selection. Mechanistic interpretability tools developed for natural language and vision models [17] offer a principled way to characterise this representational shift and to identify which layers drive task performance.

All four models are adapted via LoRA to brain tumour segmentation on multi-parametric MRI and evaluated across six datasets spanning three segmentation tasks (BraTS-GLI [18, 19, 20], BraTS-Africa [21], BraTS-PED [22]) and three classification tasks (OASIS-1 [23], ADNI binary, ADNI multi-class [24]). We analyse the adaptation process through the lens of four complementary mechanistic tools: attention Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence [25], LoRA weight-change ratios [2], off-brain attention fraction, and layer-wise activation patching [26]. Guided by the mechanistic diagnosis, we further propose and validate an early-layer LoRA strategy that restricts adaptation to the layers identified as causally important.

Our main findings are as follows. (i) Although the four backbones converge to similar segmentation performance after LoRA adaptation, they diverge substantially in cross-task classification transfer. papers.title: Continuous-Time Policy Gradient from Discrete Data: Convergence Analysis and Model-Free Algorithms
papers.abstract: Continuous-time reinforcement learning seeks an optimal policy under unknown dynamics driven by stochastic differential equations using observations collected at discrete times. We develop a policy gradient framework that combines rigorous convergence analysis with learning from discrete data. We first establish a performance difference lemma and derive policy gradient formulas for randomized and parametrized policies. We then prove exponential convergence of an entropy-regularized policy flow to the regularized optimum. For discrete parametrized updates, we derive a convergence bound that explicitly separates the contributions of critic error, policy-regression error, and the learning step size. To enable learning under unknown dynamics, we integrate this framework with PhiBE, which constructs a continuous-time surrogate generator from discrete transition data. The resulting on-policy and off-policy model-free actor-critic algorithms preserve the continuous-time structure of the control problem. Numerical experiments on an entropy-regularized linear-quadratic regulator and a nonlinear wheeled robot demonstrate the performance and stability of the proposed methods with both known and data-driven dynamics.

Reinforcement learning (RL) in continuous time provides a natural framework for sequential decision making in systems governed by differential equations, with applications in robotics [21], autonomous systems [32], manufacturing [30], and finance [24]. In many of these settings, the system evolves continuously while data are recorded only at discrete times through sensors or simulations. We consider controlled stochastic systems modeled by stochastic differential equations (SDEs), with decisions represented by randomized feedback policies. Thus, the dynamics and objective remain continuous in time, while learning relies on discrete observations.

Value-based methods face several difficulties in continuous-time RL. Under a fixed policy, the value function is characterized by a PDE involving the infinitesimal generator of the controlled diffusion rather than by a Bellman recursion [38, 7]. Moreover, the usual discrete-time state-action value function loses its action-dependent information in the continuous-time limit, as the QQ-function converges to the state value function when the action duration tends to zero [12]. Even after policy evaluation, extracting a policy requires additional computation: a greedy construction requires optimization over the action space at every state [20], while a softmax construction requires approximating its normalization constant [36]. Thus, continuous-time value-based methods require suitable formulations of policy evaluation and advantage estimation, followed by a separate policy-extraction step.

Policy gradient methods avoid this separate policy-extraction step by optimizing a parametrized policy directly [33]. Direct policy parametrization also makes it possible to control the size of each update: trust-region and proximal methods restrict the change between consecutive policies through a KL constraint or a clipped surrogate objective [27, 28]. Policy gradient methods still require policy evaluation, since the gradient depends on an advantage function, but the resulting estimate is used to update the policy directly rather than to recover it through an additional maximization problem.

For controlled diffusions, [10] characterized policy evaluation through martingale identities and developed methods based on martingale losses or orthogonality conditions. This approach was extended to parametrized policy gradients and actor–critic algorithms in [11], and to the little-qq function in [12], which represents an instantaneous action-dependent return rate and is jointly characterized with the value function through on- and off-policy martingale conditions. Closest to our theoretical analysis, [41] uses discounted occupation measures to derive performance-difference and local-approximation formulas, together with a parametric policy-gradient representation. We first characterize the directional derivative of the performance functional along general admissible policy perturbations, controlling the perturbed occupation measure through SDE stability estimates, and then establish the corresponding parametric score formula. At the algorithmic level, we develop model-free on- and off-policy actor–critic methods based on PhiBE [49, 47]. In contrast to the neural actor–critic solver for elliptic HJB equations in [43], our methods require neither known drift nor known diffusion coefficients. While the online actor updates in [11], the sampled advantage estimator in [41], and the control-randomization actor updates in [6] use differences of value-function estimates, our construction preserves the differential structure of both policy evaluation and advantage estimation: it retains the first- and second-order spatial derivatives of the critic and replaces the unknown generator by a PhiBE operator that uses discrete-time data.

papers.title: TracePrism: Extending Semantic Trace Topics to Iterative, Encoding-Aware Trace Partitioning
papers.abstract: Process mining typically explains an event log with a single model, clustering, or classifier fitted to all cases, although real logs often mix cases that follow different sub-processes. Trace clustering separates sub-populations, but it fixes one notion of trace similarity for the whole analysis. We propose TracePrism, which treats process discovery as iterative partitioning with three characteristics. The trace encoding is adaptive: it is chosen for each working set of remaining traces from a library of encodings, with suggestions scored for that set. The partitioning is iterative: the analyst forms a candidate group based on a rule, a dominant topic, a cluster over topic weights, or a region of an embedding, accepts it if it is coherent in both process structure and outcome, and continues with the remaining traces. Decisions are revisable and recorded: a group can be reopened under a different working set or encoding, and the findings repository keeps both the earlier decision and its revision. We implement TracePrism as an open-source prototype and demonstrate it in usage scenarios on three real-world event logs. The scenarios also revealed behavior that we had not anticipated, such as process drift.

papers.intro:
Process mining reconstructs the behavior of a business process from event data that information systems record during execution [1]. An event log is a collection of traces, each an ordered sequence of events belonging to one case, for example one loan application, one hospital stay, or one traffic fine. Process discovery derives a model from the log, most often a graph of frequent transitions such as a directly-follows graph (DFG), in which nodes are activities and edges connect an activity to the activity that directly follows it [2].

Process discovery derives a model from the log, most often a graph of frequent transitions such as a directly-follows graph (DFG), in which nodes are activities and edges connect an activity to the activity that directly follows it [2].

A DFG is a single aggregate: every edge is computed over the whole case population. Real logs routinely mix cases governed by different policies, channels, or periods of the same procedure. Consider traffic fines that are paid without incident, fines for which notification fails and the case escalates to collection, and fines that take much longer and end differently again. A DFG of all three shows every activity and most transitions, but it merges three regimes into one picture that corresponds to no actual case. Filtering by variant, frequency, or case attribute helps only if the analyst already knows which partition to use. Finding that partition is the problem we address, specifically the discovery of several models of coherent sub-populations of cases instead of one model of the whole log.

Trace clustering is the usual response [3, 4, 5]. It represents cases under a chosen notion of similarity, partitions them into groups, and analyzes each group separately. The representation is typically selected once for the whole analysis. It then determines what similarity means: distinctions that the representation does not express cannot drive the partition. This is restrictive when sub-populations differ in different aspects of behavior. One group may be characterized by a local sequence of activities, another by timing, and another by case attributes. A representation that exposes one of them may obscure another. In addition, a group that looked plausible may become questionable once the analyst has examined it in context. This calls for revising the representation under which groups were found, and not only their number or boundaries.

The intended users are process analysts and process owners who examine the event log of a process that they want to understand or improve, with an outcome of interest in mind, such as payment, admission, or escalation. Their questions have the form: which kinds of cases exist, how do they proceed, and how do they end? An answer is a set of named sub-processes, each with a description and a known outcome profile.

Another question is when a candidate group is worth retaining. Two properties are important. The members of a group must look alike under an inspectable description of the trace, which we call structural coherence, and they must behave alike with respect to an outcome of interest, which we call outcome coherence. Neither is sufficient alone. Structural coherence alone can accept a group with a shared pattern but no consistent outcome, which does not help an analyst who asks what distinguishes good outcomes from bad ones. Outcome coherence alone can accept a group with similar outcomes but no process description that explains why they belong together. A system should report both to the analyst and not combine them into one score, since no fixed weighting of structural tightness against outcome purity holds across domains. Trace clustering does not in general require outcome coherence, and outcome-oriented predictive process monitoring [6] does not require structural coherence. Either can yield groups that are coherent in both senses, but neither uses the two as an acceptance criterion. Where no outcome label exists, any case-level partition of interest, such as a duration tier, a conformance verdict, or a cost band, can play a role instead.

Some methods iterate. Closest to our work is the interactive outcome explanation of Völzer et al. [7]. The analyst accepts a rule over case predicates, removes the cases it covers from further search, and continues with the rest, revising the attribute vocabulary along the way. Their acceptance criteria resemble ours: an explanation must be precise with respect to the outcome and meaningful to the analyst. In none of these approaches are the representation of a trace and the notion of similarity revised as the analysis proceeds. Section II discusses these differences in more detail.

In earlier work, we proposed Semantic Trace Topics [12], a text-inspired encoding that represents each trace as a document of tokens describing activities, local sequence, and timing. Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) of the resulting trace-token matrix yields topics, which are interpretable, combinable components of process behavior, each tied to the traces that predominantly express it. That paper evaluated the encoding in a single pass over one working set and one encoding. It left open how to choose among encodings and the topic count, how a topic-based decomposition relates to other ways of forming groups, and what to do once an initial decomposition has been interpreted. We also build on SmartIterator [13], which supports an informed choice of parameters for a single grouping step from a whole sweep of results instead of one result. TracePrism carries this principle from the group count to the working set and the encoding.

papers.title: Tree Lattices and the Neumann-Zagier conjecture
papers.abstract: A tree with integer weights on its vertices presents an integral lattice called a tree lattice. We prove that if a tree lattice is positive definite, then one of the vertex elements is irreducible, i.e. determines a facet of its Voronoi polyhedron. As a corollary, we settle a 1985 conjecture of Neumann and Zagier: if a tree lattice is isometric to the lattice of integer points in Euclidean space, then the tree contains a vertex of weight one.

papers.title: Persistent Photo-Enhancement of Molecular Orbital Excitations in the Kondo Insulator FeSb$_2$
papers.abstract: When insulators are excited by photons with above-gap energies, photo-doped carriers are transiently generated. Typically, orbital excitations weaken and broaden due to increased screening by these transient carriers, followed by a few-ps recovery via phonon thermalization. Here we report the observation of anomalous dynamics of many-body molecular orbital excitations in the narrow-gap Kondo insulator FeSb$_2$. In the pumped X-ray absorption spectra following excitation with 1~$μ$m photons, we observe a transient transfer of absorption intensity from the delocalized states at the main absorption peak to the localized molecular orbital states at the pre-edge. At the resonance of the low-energy molecular orbital excitations, the pumped resonant inelastic X-ray spectra show an approximately 30\% intensity increase at a pump fluence of 11 mJ/cm$^2$ concomitant with the emergence of an energy gain feature. While the energy gain feature disappears after about 1-2~ps, the increased molecular orbital excitation intensities partially persist for at least 50~ps with no discernible energy shift. These observations require the invocation of a many-body excitation picture beyond single particle population changes.

papers.title: Toward Agentic AI for the 6G Physical Layer: From Algorithm Discovery to Verified Baseband Silicon
papers.abstract: 6G will be designed faster than it can be built: AI-driven search already proposes physical-layer algorithms at machine speed, while carrying a single one onto embedded baseband silicon remains specialist work. That silicon imposes hard memory and numeric limits, but also exposes cost structures a GPU lacks, and a design flow that never runs on the target sees neither. We present an agentic workflow in which an LLM coding agent implements algorithms on a commercial baseband SoC, optimizes them down to agent-written vector assembly, and validates them on silicon. The agent is guided by a knowledge base of measured platform facts, checked at every step against evaluators it is instructed never to edit, and metered per phase. We showcase the workflow on an AI-discovered orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) detector portfolio on the open 6G4All platform. It yields twelve kernels that run cycle-exactly on silicon, their optimized versions at 18k-405k cycles (30-660 $μ$s) per frame. It also yields a new detector shaped by the chip's measured costs that needs 13.9% fewer cycles than the port of the discovered detector while matching its error rate, with a measured edge our evaluation cannot statistically resolve, a structure that a hardware-blind search objective had no reason to find. What is not specific to OTFS is the workflow: an LLM agent exploring an implementation space under real hardware limits, with the cost of every choice measured rather than assumed.

papers.intro:
Whatever 6G turns out to be (new waveforms, integrated sensing, AI-native receivers), each of its features will in the end be a signal-processing algorithm that has to run inside the cycle, memory and power envelope of baseband silicon. How fast those features reach real radios will therefore be limited less by algorithm ideas than by the path from idea to silicon. Candidate algorithms already arrive faster than they can be deployed: large language model (LLM)-driven evolutionary search explores physical-layer solution spaces wholesale, and the framework of Aït Aoudia et al. [1] explored 1114 distinct orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) equalizer architectures and produced a detector that outperforms published baselines, in simulation and on graphics processing units (GPUs). Carrying any one of those ideas onto an embedded baseband processor remains specialist work. Such parts earn their power efficiency by omitting what a general-purpose core provides: the digital signal processor (DSP) used here has no scalar floating-point unit at all, so scalar float arithmetic falls back on software emulation and costs orders of magnitude more than the same work on the vector array. Respecting that asymmetry is not an optimization detail; it decides whether an algorithm fits at all. Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) has reached the physical layer at the level of intent and configuration, in simulation [2]; this paper turns it toward implementation on the silicon itself: we demonstrate, on the open 6G4All platform [3], that an appropriately instrumented environment lets an LLM coding agent do that specialist work end to end (implement, optimize at assembly level, validate on silicon) at measured cost. If new algorithms can reach real baseband hardware this cheaply, the hardware stops being where 6G research ends and becomes part of the loop that proposes it.

papers.title: HRoPE: Homography Relative Positional Encoding
papers.abstract: Geometric Relative Positional Encoding has become the primary mechanism for injecting spatial inductive biases into multi-view transformers. Existing designs condition attention on camera-level frustums or ray-marched depth, associating cross-view tokens through the sensor geometry. Such sensor-centric formulations, however, describe only where a token is observed from, leaving the rich surface geometry of the scene region depicted by the token. In this paper, we advocate a shift toward surface-aware positional encoding that explicitly grounds patch tokens in the geometry of physical surfaces. We introduce HRoPE, which represents the local geometry of each patch as a slanted 3D plane, following the slanted support-window assumption of classical multi-view stereo. We inject token-level, plane-induced homographies into attention as relative transformations. This equips the transformer with a geometric prior for rectifying perspective distortions and aligning patch features across viewpoints. Our encoding requires no ground-truth geometry: the plane parameters can be predicted end-to-end under a view-synthesis objective alone, or derived from foundation models. Extensive experiments on RealEstate10K, CO3Dv2, and DL3DV show that our best variant of HRoPE consistently outperforms the evaluated geometric positional encodings for novel view synthesis. Extensive ablations and analysis show the effectiveness of the proposed encoding. Please refer to our project page at: https://gaohchen.github.io/HRoPE

papers.intro:
The Transformer has become the de facto architecture for recent feed-forward 3D vision (Wang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025). By tokenizing images from multiple viewpoints and exchanging information via attention, these models exhibit strong capabilities in jointly resolving appearance, visibility, and scene geometry. Attention, however, is permutation-equivariant: it operates on unordered sets and is inherently agnostic to the camera poses, metric scales, and epipolar constraints that couple multi-view observations. Consequently, geometric priors must be explicitly injected, either by conditioning token representations directly (e.g., via camera tokens (Wang et al., 2025) or ray maps (Jin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024a)) or by imposing epipolar constraints on attention (He et al., 2020; Charatan et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024). Positional encoding (PE) introduces geometric structure directly into attention by modulating pairwise token comparisons.

Positional encoding (PE) introduces geometric structure directly into attention by modulating pairwise token comparisons.

While existing PE designs exhibit increasing geometric fidelity by using priors from images, cameras, and rays, they invariably anchor positional information to the sensor. RoPE extensions (Su et al., 2024) encode 2D intra-view offsets, leaving inter-view transformations implicit (Weinzaepfel et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). GTA (Miyato et al., 2024) and CaPE (Kong et al., 2024) inject relative camera extrinsics to achieve invariance to global rigid motions, while PRoPE (Li et al., 2025) generalizes this to the full projection matrix. Ray-based formulations like RayRoPE (Wu et al., 2026) and URoPE (Xie et al., 2026) integrate depth by localizing patches along viewing rays and re-projecting into the query frame. Across this progression, geometry is parameterized via sensor-centric abstractions: an image coordinate, a camera frustum, or a point of ray termination, leaving the rich local surface structure of the underlying scene unmodeled (see Fig. 1, left and middle).

This limitation is fundamental because multi-view matching does not compare isolated points; it compares local neighborhoods whose appearances are related through surface-induced deformations. A patch in one view and its corresponding patch in another are connected by a warp determined by the underlying surface geometry, and reliable correspondence requires compensating for this warp before comparing visual features. Given the pixel location and camera geometry, depth locates the patch center, while surface orientation additionally determines how its surrounding neighborhood deforms across views. By providing only view or positional information, existing PEs implicitly impose a fronto-parallel assumption on the attention computation mechanism. Although large neural models can learn to compensate for this bias given sufficient training data, doing so compromises efficiency and generalization. We argue that surface orientation is the missing degree of freedom: current PEs capture the zeroth-order position of a patch but neglect the first-order local orientation that dictates its cross-view appearance transformation.

To this end, we present HRoPE, a Homography Relative Positional Encoding that embeds orientation-aware rectification directly into the attention mechanism (Fig. 1, right). Inspired by the slanted support windows of classical multi-view stereo (Bleyer et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2021a), HRoPE anchors a local tangent plane to each patch token. We use the plane normal and distance, together with the camera poses, to define the homography governing cross-view neighborhood deformations. Concretely, we apply a per-patch 3×33\times 3 transformation block-diagonally to the queries, keys, and values, and incorporate a closed-form inverse into the key projection so that the resulting attention logits depend exclusively on the relative homography between tokens. As we show in Sec. 3.2 and Appendix A.2, this mechanism acts as an in-attention analogue of computing a matching score only after both neighborhoods have been rectified onto a shared tangent plane. Consequently, whereas prior geometric PEs merely encode where a token is located, HRoPE explicitly models how its underlying surface transforms across views. This formulation offers two compelling advantages. First, HRoPE strictly generalizes point- and ray-based PEs: when a predicted normal aligns with the viewing direction, the induced transformation naturally reduces to the fronto-parallel case. Second, the per-patch transformation parameters can be regressed from patch features by a lightweight head trained jointly with the view-synthesis model, using the view-synthesis objective alone. The head can optionally use pretrained features from DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) or VGGT (Wang et al., 2025), without changing the encoding formulation or training objective.

papers.title: The Shape of the DPO Hyperparameter Landscape: What to Measure, How It Moves with Scale, and When Not to Transfer It
papers.abstract: Direct preference optimisation (DPO) is widely used for language model post-training, but its performance depends strongly on the choice of its hyperparameters, such as the learning rate and the reference-policy regularisation parameter $β$. To better understand the DPO hyperparameter landscape, we conduct extensive experiments using a dense hyperparameter grid across different model scales from the same family. This allows us to analyse how the optimal DPO hyperparameters evolve with model size and the number of update steps, with intermediate checkpoints providing an inexpensive signal to accelerate the hyperparameter optimisation process. Furthermore, by evaluating our models on both static and dynamic benchmarks, we identify which benchmarks provide the strongest signal for hyperparameter selection. Finally, we investigate how different state-of-the-art hyperparameter optimisation strategies perform in this setting. Our experiments show that the optimal learning rate varies with model size and that hyperparameters are not transferable across training datasets. We also find that validation loss is a poor proxy for hyperparameter optimisation, as hyperparameters that minimize validation loss only weakly correlate with optimal hyperparameters for downstream benchmarks. Therefore, DPO hyperparameters need to be tuned specifically for the target model, dataset, and evaluation objective. We also show that short candidate training runs can substantially reduce the cost of this selection. We release all our training configurations and evaluation results to support reproducible analysis of selection quality and training cost.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly advanced in both capability and scale, but pretrained models are not necessarily well-suited for interaction with users: they may fail to reliably follow instructions, answer questions, or respond appropriately to user intent. Post-training is therefore a critical step in transforming a pretrained model into a useful assistant (Ouyang et al., 2022). Common post-training recipes consist of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which teaches a model to follow instructions using demonstration data, followed by preference optimisation that adapts model behaviour toward preferred responses.

Direct preference optimisation (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023) optimises directly from preference pairs relative to a fixed SFT reference policy, without a separate reward-model training stage. Its learning rate controls the size of the update, while β\beta controls the strength of the reference-adjusted preference signal in the DPO objective and therefore the objective’s trade-off between fitting preference pairs and remaining close to the reference policy. Both hyperparameters may therefore have effects that depend on the reference checkpoint and preference data. Prior work has already shown sensitivity to β\beta and the characteristics of preference pairs (Wu et al., 2024). This raises the question: how reliably can a DPO configuration selected in one setting be applied to another?

Post-training recipes commonly report configurations that perform well for a particular model, dataset, and reference checkpoint, often using a fixed suite of static capability benchmarks to guide those choices (Tunstall et al., 2024; Ivison et al., 2023; Lambert et al., 2025; Team Olmo, 2025; Allal et al., 2025). These configurations are then generally reused across related models or experiments, implicitly assuming both that the configuration transfers and that the static evaluation signal used to select it remains informative. Whether either assumption holds across model scale has received substantially less systematic investigation. Getting this wrong is not a minor efficiency loss. In our primary sweep, the gap between the best and the worst configuration within a single model size reaches roughly 295 Elo points at a 4B parameter scale (Figure 1). Under the fitted Bradley–Terry model used to construct these scores, this corresponds to an estimated 84.5%84.5\% probability that the best configuration wins a pairwise comparison with the worst. By comparison, the DPO improvement over its SFT checkpoint is 176 Elo points, corresponding to a 73.3%73.3\% win probability. The worst configurations in the grid also land below the SFT checkpoint. A poor configuration can therefore erase the entire benefit of the stage and leave a model worse than its SFT checkpoint.

Our contributions are as follows: • Evaluation signals for DPO tuning. We show that validation loss is an unreliable selection signal and that chat benchmarks produce more consistent configuration rankings than static benchmarks, with limited sensitivity to the choice of the judge model used. • Transfer across scale and training data. We show that DPO configurations do not reliably transfer across model sizes or training preference datasets. Preferred learning rates exhibit an overall decrease with Qwen3 model scale, but configuration rankings can vary sharply even between neighbouring models. • Compute-efficient hyperparameter selection. Partial model training runs can provide useful ranking information within roughly 2020–30%30\% of training. We also show that under sufficient budgets, adaptive HPO methods can outperform random search. • An offline benchmark for DPO hyperparameter selection. We release checkpoint-level Qwen3 and Llama trajectories with training costs and scores on eleven benchmarks, along with code to reconstruct the surrogate environments and HPO experiments. This enables reproducible research on selection signals, early-selection policies, transfer, and compute allocation without repeating these expensive DPO runs.

papers.title: Stabilizing Filters for Graph Signal Generation
papers.abstract: Generating graph signals is an important task in machine learning, and incorporating the underlying graph into a generative model enables structurally-informed distribution modeling. However, said graph is often noisy or imperfectly estimated, and structural errors can affect the generative process and the resulting signal distribution. While recent work has established stability guarantees for graph neural ordinary differential equations, the robustness of graph-aware reference dynamics, as used in topological Schrödinger bridge models, remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate the structural stability of continuous-time generative models whose dynamics combine a graph filter with a learned graph neural network. We first derive a Wasserstein stability bound that quantifies the effect of graph perturbations on the generated signal distributions. Informed by this analysis, we then propose a principled framework for designing graph filters that balance structural stability with induced signal smoothing. We characterize the optimal filter design and provide an explicit family of polynomial filters with provable stability guarantees. Experiments on synthetic graphs and real-world fMRI signals support our theoretical findings, illustrating the enhanced structural stability of the proposed filters while preserving generative performance.
papers.intro:
Finding a map transporting a given data distribution to another is a fundamental problem underlying generative modeling, with numerous applications in machine learning and signal processing; see e.g., [2, 3]. Recent advances in continuous-time generative modeling [4, 5, 6] have achieved remarkable success generating realistic images, audio and video. However, their application to irregular, non-Euclidean domains that can be naturally represented using graphs is still fairly underdeveloped. While considerable research has focused on generating graph topologies [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12], far less attention has been paid to generating graph signals [13, 14, 15, 16, 17]. These signals are ubiquitous in real-world networked systems, such as neural time courses over structural brain connectomes [18], vehicular flows on transportation networks [19], and resource (e.g., power) allocations in wireless networks [20]. Learning to faithfully generate graph signals has broad applicability, ranging from synthetic data augmentation and implicit priors to realistic system simulations across various timely domains.

Graph-aware reference dynamics. Among the many stochastic processes that match a given pair of endpoint distributions, the dynamic Schrödinger bridge problem provides a principled solution that favors the process closest to a prescribed reference dynamics [21, 22, 23]. In the classical formulation, the reference is typically chosen as a standard Wiener process. Among the many stochastic processes that match a given pair of endpoint distributions, the dynamic Schrödinger bridge problem provides a principled solution that favors the process closest to a prescribed reference dynamics [21, 22, 23]. In practice, however, the observed graph is only an imperfect reflection of the true complex system [24, Ch. 7]. For instance, correlation networks inferred from nodal measurements can vary significantly with the sample size [25], leading to noisy graph representations [26, 27]. Consequently, unavoidable graph perturbations can skew the entire generative trajectory and the final distribution of the generated signals. This motivates the study of structural stability, which quantifies the sensitivity of generative model outputs to perturbations in the graph parameterizing the generative dynamics.

Paper outline. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the necessary background on graph signal processing (GSP), the structural stability of graph operators, and generative modeling with topological Schrödinger bridges; as needed to formally state the problem. Section III formulates the continuous-time generative dynamics, and derives Wasserstein stability bounds under structural perturbations. Leveraging these theoretical insights, Section IV introduces our principled filter design framework to delineate relevant stability-smoothness tradeoffs. To this end, we formulate a semi-infinite linear program and derive explicit optimal polynomial filter constructions. Section V numerically corroborates the efficacy of our optimal filter design relative to the heat diffusion baseline, both in a synthetic test case and a study involving fMRI brain signals. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper by summarizing our findings, discussing the impact of the chosen perturbation model on the optimal design, and contextualizing the practical upshot of our bounds. All technical details and proofs are deferred to the appendices.

papers.title: DeclineCraft: A RAG Abstention Benchmark for Jointly Measuring Combined Retrieval and Parametric Knowledge
papers.abstract: Reliable retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires recognizing when neither retrieved documents nor parametric knowledge supports an answer. We introduce DeclineCraft, a dynamic abstention benchmark whose unanswerable questions target Minecraft feature additions after a corpus cut-off, with audits of possible parametric exposure. Later cut-offs support evaluation of future models. Across 27 LLMs, we measure Correct Abstention Rate (CAR; how often models acknowledge insufficient knowledge on unanswerable questions), Answerable Attempt Rate and Answer Accuracy. We find that (1) single-shot retrieval significantly raises CAR in 38 of 40 configurations (model and thinking setting) versus no retrieval. (2) Iterative RAG, in which the model self-assesses its context and can request up to two further retrieval rounds, significantly lowers CAR versus single-shot RAG in 30 of 40 configurations (mean 46.4%), with little change in Answer Accuracy (68.5% to 69.3%). Adding query rewriting and reranking to hybrid (dense & sparse) retrieval lowers CAR for all 12 models tested. (3) Larger models answer more accurately (Spearman $ρ= +0.60$ with total parameters), but neither model size nor release date shows a significant association with CAR. (4) Without retrieval, enabling thinking on the same weights lowers CAR significantly for 8 of 13 models (by 14% points on average), and the responses shift from acknowledged uncertainty to premise denial.

papers.intro:
A player fleeing skeletons in Minecraft Java Edition asks an assistant whether copper horse armor would let a horse survive three arrows. Answering requires combining the rules for arrow damage, horse health points, and the protection supplied by this particular armor in a specific game edition. Suppose copper horse armor was introduced after both the model’s training and its retrieval corpus. Passages about horses, skeletons and other armor types may be relevant, yet the key fact about the horse’s armor is missing. The assistant must acknowledge this knowledge gap. For instance, when asked for the armor’s protection, Qwen3 32B with thinking enabled instead declares: “Since ‘copper horse armor’ is not a recognized item in the game, it would provide 0 armor points. If you meant golden horse armor, it provides 7 armor points.” (Table 1). This response treats a presupposition it cannot verify as false (Kim et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2023), a premise denial, then substitutes a different item for the one the user asked about.

For RAG systems, recognizing such a knowledge gap must remain part of the decision to answer as retrieval and thinking proceed. This matters most when the answers are consumed by AI agents, which may not notice that a premise denial is unsupported by the model’s available knowledge. A human user, by contrast, may know that a new law was just passed, or that copper horse armor was added to Minecraft, when posing their query. Evaluation must therefore distinguish an admission of missing knowledge from a premise denial that the model cannot verify.

Distinguishing abstention from premise denial matters for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) wherever documentation and the world it describes can change (Barnett et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024). RAG systems can combine retrieved documents with parametric knowledge, the information stored in a model’s weights (Lewis et al., 2020). Unless explicitly asked about a historical version, a system should allow for questions about a time after both the corpus cut-off and the model’s knowledge cut-off. An item absent from an earlier version may exist when the user asks about it; absence from the available sources does not establish present-day nonexistence. A reliable system should therefore abstain when these sources together cannot support an answer, identifying the knowledge gap, without categorically rejecting a premise it cannot verify.

Evaluating this behavior is challenging: an answer missing from retrieved passages may still be available in the model’s weights. Context-grounded benchmarks instruct models to answer only from supplied documents (Song et al., 2025; Ming et al., 2025; Muhamed et al., 2026). UAEval4RAG’s out-of-database questions include facts from newer news absent from its database, under a database-grounded answering protocol (Peng et al., 2025). AbstentionBench evaluates, without retrieval, questions whose answers changed after the models’ knowledge cut-offs (Kirichenko et al., 2025). Our study combines a time-partitioned corpus, whose later part postdates the models’ knowledge cut-offs, with related but insufficient retrieved evidence, and scores premise denial separately from acknowledged uncertainty.

The interacting game mechanics of Minecraft and its feature additions over time create facts that can only be learned from new wiki pages: e.g., knowing how existing armor works does not establish the protection of a newly introduced material against a pre-existing weapon. We construct a retrieval corpus (CpreC_{\text{pre}}) from wiki pages as they stood at a corpus cut-off and generate unanswerable questions from pages created later (CpostC_{\text{post}}). Answerable questions use the same generation pipeline as unanswerable ones, with their target facts drawn from the earlier corpus (Figure 1). We audit our unanswerable questions against the earlier documentation. To assess possible parametric exposure, we use published knowledge cut-offs and a leakage audit. The leakage audit tests whether models answer the unanswerable questions correctly without retrieval. The temporal design establishes a knowledge gap when the required facts postdate both parametric knowledge and the RAG corpus. The benchmark is dynamic: it can be regenerated with a later corpus cut-off as new game content becomes available.
