papers.title: infomeasure-rs: A High-Performance Rust Library for Information-Theoretic Measures and Estimators
papers.abstract: Information theory has become a standard tool across the natural and social sciences, yet practical use is limited by estimator choice, fragmented software, reproducibility, and computational cost. We present infomeasure-rs, an open-source Rust library that brings a broad set of information-theoretic measures and estimators into one self-contained, type-safe package. It covers entropy, mutual information, conditional mutual information, transfer entropy, conditional transfer entropy, cross-entropy, and the Kullback-Leibler and Jensen-Shannon divergences, with discrete (plug-in and bias-corrected), kernel, ordinal, and nearest-neighbour estimators, including the Rényi and Tsallis families, and exposes local and global values and significance testing through a consistent trait interface. It ships as a single portable binary with no runtime dependency and is continuously validated against a reference implementation. On a single central processing unit (CPU) core, and even without its GPU or parallel paths, it is the fastest of the packages we compared across languages, matching the closest packages only for plug-in discrete entropy and substantially faster for mutual information, the conditional and transfer measures, and the kernel, ordinal, and generalised-entropy estimators. The optional GPU and multi-threaded paths accelerate selected continuous estimators further. The library is open source and, to our knowledge, the most complete information-theory package for Rust.

papers.intro:
Information theory, the mathematical study of information and its processing [1], has become a cornerstone of modern data analysis, with applications ranging from neuroscience [2, 3] and complex systems [4] to finance [5]. Applying it in practice, however, is rarely as simple as choosing a measure and computing it. Four barriers recur [6]. First, information-theoretic quantities are functionals of probability distributions that are unknown in practice and must be estimated from finite samples. The choice of estimator strongly affects the result, and limited guidelines exist for selecting it [7, 8]. Second, the software landscape is fragmented: individual packages tend to concentrate on a subset of measures or estimators, which makes systematic comparison cumbersome. Third, implementation-level differences between packages hinder reproducibility. Fourth, the estimators are computationally intensive, so large data sets are prohibitive unless the implementation is carefully optimised.

Third, implementation-level differences between packages hinder reproducibility. Fourth, the estimators are computationally intensive, so large data sets are prohibitive unless the implementation is carefully optimised.

The Python package infomeasure was introduced to lower these barriers by unifying a broad set of measures and estimators under one consistent interface [6]. After a year since its introduction, it is used in research across several fields, including neuroscience [9, 10, 11, 12], transport-delay analysis [13, 14], energy and industrial monitoring [15, 16], biology and biophysics [17, 18], security and privacy [19], the study of complex systems [20], and methodological work on information estimation [21, 22, 23, 24, 25]. This highlights the importance that such unifying implementations have in the scientific community, as they lower the implementation cost and enhance reproducibility. For the most demanding workloads the Python runtime is the limiting factor, and a compiled implementation removes it while keeping the numerical results identical. The same compiled library can serve as a backend for the Python package, so existing users gain the speed without changing their workflow.

papers.title: Control of Isolated Four-Quadrant Single-Stage Three-/Single-Phase X-Rectifier for EV On-Board Chargers
papers.abstract: The single-stage isolated eXtended-functionality rectifier (X-Rectifier) electric vehicle (EV) on-board charger (OBC) employs 650V GaN monolithic bidirectional power transistors (M-BDS) in the input stage, provides sinusoidal input currents and four-quadrant operation in three-phase and split/single phase grids without power derating, operates from asymmetrical three-phase mains, provides reactive power if needed, and supports extremely asymmetric phase loading in standalone vehicle-to-load (V2L) mode. This paper presents a new improved phase-modular control method for the X-Rectifier that enables tracking of arbitrary and independent phase current references regardless of the instantaneous grid voltage (i.e., enables four-quadrant operation). The method supports grid-tied (i.e., grid-to-vehicle, G2V, or vehicle-to grid, V2G) and grid-forming (i.e., V2L) operation. Further, aiming towards a practical realization of the X-Rectifier, the paper addresses implementation aspects of the M-BDS half-bridges, like commutation logic around the grid-voltage zero crossing, fault handling, and soft-switching behaviour. Finally, a realized 5.5 kVA hardware demonstrator of the X-Rectifier is used to validate the proposed control method experimentally for all operating modes, including grid-tied three- and single-phase four-quadrant operation (G2V, V2G, and full reactive power modes). Further, robust V2L operation is verified with real-world loads, i.e., in three-phase mode with asymmetrical loading of the phases including a woodworking power tool, and in single-phase mode with a high-power vacuum cleaner with high inrush current and hence momentary overload of the X-Rectifier demonstrator.
papers.intro:
\IEEEPARstart The IEA’s current global electric vehicle (EV) outlook anticipates a fivefold growth of the global electric car fleet between 2025 and 2035, reaching more than 450 million vehicles [17]. All passenger EVs feature an on-board charger (OBC), originally to enable battery charging from the available grid connections at home or at work. Typical power levels are between 3.3 kW and 22 kW [38]. During driving the OBC sits idle performing no function and hence the weight and volume should be minimised, i.e., the converter’s power density should be maximized. For safety purposes, galvanic isolation between the EV battery and the grid is necessary, and sinusoidal input currents drawn from the grid ensure compliance with standards. Finally, the output dc voltage must cover the wide voltage range of the EV battery (e.g., 250 V to 450 V for a 400 V nominal battery, depending on its state of charge).

Finally, the output dc voltage must cover the wide voltage range of the EV battery (e.g., 250 V to 450 V for a 400 V nominal battery, depending on its state of charge).

Next-generation OBCs should provide extended functionality as visualized in Fig. 1. In grid-tied operation, conventional grid-to-vehicle (G2V) mode must provide nominal power delivery from both, a three-phase (Fig. 1i) and a single-/split-phase mains (Fig. 1ii), i.e., no derating for single-phase operation is allowed. The EV battery can serve as an energy storage device, and hence the OBC must offer full four-quadrant operation for vehicle-to-grid (V2G) modes and grid-support functions. Similarly, the EV battery can serve as a standalone power source, e.g., for supplying electric power tools on a construction site [38]. Such vehicle-to-load (V2L) modes are attractive to users and increase the utility of a vehicle, but these are also the modes in which very strong imbalances in the loading of the phases can occur, and generally loads with arbitrary characteristic can be connected, which again implies the need for a robust four-quadrant control.

Matrix-type topologies do not require any dc capacitor on the primary side. Instead, switches with bidirectional voltage blocking capability (bidirectional switches, BDSs) facilitate direct power conversion between the three-phase low-frequency (LF) ac mains and a single-phase HF voltage applied to the primary side of the HF transformer; both dual active bridge (DAB)-type [36] and series resonant converter (SRC)-type [32] modes of operation are possible. papers.title: Steady-state cooperative emission of interlayer excitons in atomically thin light-emitting diodes
papers.abstract: When an ensemble of emitters is confined within an optical wavelength, its radiation can become correlated, leading to cooperative emission. In two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) electron-hole bilayers, strong light-matter coupling enables the formation of interlayer excitons (IXs), long-lived dipolar excitations that provide an ideal setting for emergent collective phenomena. Here, we engineer an atomically thin light-emitting diode (LED) that generates electroluminescence (EL) from electrically injected IXs that are confined near the sample edges by an edge-enhanced fringing electric field. By measuring Hanbury-Brown-Twiss photon-photon correlations, we find pronounced signatures of collective decay in the form of large photon bunching followed by finite delay antibunching and bunching revivals. These emitter correlation signatures disappear when free charge carriers are doped to form a degenerate Fermi sea but are enhanced by the introduction of localized electrons. The results are consistent with a many-body quantum master equation that models the steady-state superradiant photon statistics of incoherently injected IXs. Our work establishes steady-state cooperative emission in a 2D TMD LED as a platform for studying strong light-matter interactions in electrically driven, non-equilibrium phases of Bose-Fermi mixtures.

papers.title: Observation Assimilation Transformer: Probabilistic Weather Analysis from Sparse Station Observations
papers.abstract: We present the Observation Assimilation Transformer (OAT), a geometry-aware neural process that corrects and refines a prior numerical weather prediction (NWP) field into a high-resolution posterior field by assimilating sparse observations. OAT is an encoder-decoder transformer that considers a set of observed locations and their NWP prior to condition predictions at a set of arbitrary unobserved query locations. Its sparse attention mechanism makes it scalable to thousands of station observations and depends on relative positions between locations, never on the absolute coordinates. The model allows for partially missing observations, predictions at arbitrary continuous locations without grid projection, and outputs are parametric distributions. A station-randomized training algorithm is developed with continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) loss. We test OAT on two datasets - one at regional scale with hundreds of stations, and one at continental scale with thousands of stations. On these datasets OAT outperforms several baselines and shows well calibrated predictions. In an illustrative case study, OAT's downscaling capabilities are demonstrated by downscaling ERA5 (~31km) to COSMO (1km), where OAT achieves lower mean absolute error (MAE) and CRPS for temperature and precipitation on test stations compared to COSMO.

papers.intro:
Numerical weather prediction (NWP) models solve the governing equations of the atmospheric motions on high-performance computing (HPC) systems (Bauer et al., 2015), but their utility is fundamentally limited by the spatial resolution at which these equations can be practically solved. Their spatial and temporal discretization introduces errors and systematic biases through imperfect modelling of processes occurring at scales smaller than the model grid. Additionally, in the presence of complex topography, the spatial resolution of the NWP grid may be insufficient to accurately represent the underlying terrain over which the equations are solved. While increasing the horizontal spatial resolution can reduce some of these errors, doing so comes at a substantial increase of computational cost. Fully data-driven alternatives to NWP models are currently achieving remarkable results at a fraction of the inference cost, often matching or surpassing NWP models on specific metrics. However their trustworthiness and ability to model extreme events is still, at the time of writing, an open question (Bonavita, 2024). A natural approach to address these limitations, is to reconcile NWP output with observations, which, despite being affected by measurement errors, are the best available estimate of the true atmospheric state.

A natural approach to address these limitations, is to reconcile NWP output with observations, which, despite being affected by measurement errors, are the best available estimate of the true atmospheric state.

Statistical postprocessing (Rasp and Lerch, 2018) addresses the issue by learning a distribution that corrects systematic errors of raw NWP ensemble forecasts at station locations, conditioned on an NWP ensemble, geographic location and a set of predictors features derived from topography. Observations serve as training target, and if the learned model does not rely on station-specific embeddings, it can be transferred to arbitrary locations, under the assumption that topographic features alone are sufficient to describe the local processes. However, statistical postprocessing treats prediction locations independently, where neighboring stations are not used to inform predictions at nearby or related locations. Furthermore, observations are only used as training targets, meaning the model can be applied before any observation is available but fails to assimilate the actual realization of the target process at inference time. Statistical downscaling (Rampal et al., 2024; Mardani et al., 2025) addresses a complementary limitation; rather than correcting errors at station locations, it learns a mapping from a coarse resolution field, to fine-scale predictions by targeting high-resolution gridded references. This may or may not include coupled past observations (Vaughan et al., 2022; Bruinsma et al., 2023; Sousa et al., 2026). However, like statistical postprocessing, downscaling typically does not assimilate observations at inference time. In contrast, data assimilation (Carrassi et al., 2018) explicitly combines model forecasts with newly available observations to refine the estimated atmospheric state at any given time, and is an integral part of the NWP pipeline. These approaches are complementary; statistical postprocessing focuses on correcting biases, statistical downscaling primarily enhances spatial resolution and data assimilation incorporates observations at inference time.

(2024a). • Scalability to thousands of stations via kNN-sparsified attention. • Embedding partial observations via a neural gating mechanism. • A randomized training algorithm using station observations as target.

papers.title: Spin-wave circulation in unbounded ferromagnetic film
papers.abstract: A key challenge in spin-wave computing is steering spin waves through circuits without wave distortion or reflections. This often results in 1D propagation scenarios, which hinder applicability in 2D magnonic circuits. We demonstrate experimentally a novel approach using a hard magnetic spherical microparticle to guide spin-waves onto a closed path in a plain thin YIG film. The particle stray field induces a radially symmetrical magnetization landscape, which allows spin-waves to loop around. In parallel, we conducted micromagnetic simulations reproducing the experimental conditions, which confirm the circulation of spin-waves over several loops around the particle. This work demonstrates the possibility to steer spin-waves onto a circular path using inhomogeneous magnetic landscape, as well as advancing scalable spin-wave-based information processing technologies.

papers.title: Topology-Adaptive Seismic Response Prediction of Interconnected Structural Systems Using Reduced Order Model Embedded Graph Neural Network
papers.abstract: Electrical substation equipment is commonly interconnected by busbars and flexible conductors. Such interconnected infrastructures exhibit complex dynamic interactions, where the response of each component is influenced by local structural properties, mechanical coupling, system topology, and transient excitation. High-fidelity FE models can capture some of these effects, but their computational cost limits their use for real-time prediction. Purely data-driven models offer faster inference, yet they struggle to generalize, requiring additional simulations and retraining for each new configuration. This work presents a ROM embedded Graph Neural Network (ROMeGNN) for topology-aware seismic digital twins of interconnected structural systems. The system is represented as a graph, where structural components are treated as nodes and mechanical interconnections as edges. Each high-fidelity component model is first reduced to a reduced-order modal representation, which forms a differentiable dynamics operator within the GNN. Rather than learning the full response directly, the GNN estimates topology-dependent interaction forces that enter the differentiable ROM solver as coupling inputs for modal state advancement. This hybrid formulation preserves the known component-level physics and uses data-driven message passing to learn complex inter-component forces across varying system layouts. The framework is demonstrated on interconnected electrical substation equipment subjected to randomized seismic inputs. It delivers rapid predictions of response quantities relevant to seismic damage assessment while remaining applicable across varying layouts, component combinations, and excitation scenarios. These results highlight the potential of embedding physics within graph learning architectures for real-time, interpretable, topology-adaptive seismic digital twins of interconnected engineering systems.

papers.intro:
Electric power systems play a crucial role in modern society, providing the backbone for essential functions ranging from residential utility to industrial production. Among the key elements of these systems, electrical substations stand out as vital infrastructure to adjust power voltage and control power flow, ensuring efficient power transformation and distribution to end users across various geographic areas [1]. However, substation electrical equipment is particularly vulnerable to seismic excitation because of the widespread use of brittle porcelain materials, low inherent damping, and slender structural configurations [2, 3]. Damage to such equipment can interrupt power delivery, trigger cascading failures, and cause substantial economic and societal losses [4].

Electric power systems play a crucial role in modern society, providing the backbone for essential functions ranging from residential utility to industrial production. Among the key elements of these systems, electrical substations stand out as vital infrastructure to adjust power voltage and control power flow, ensuring efficient power transformation and distribution to end users across various geographic areas [1]. However, substation electrical equipment is particularly vulnerable to seismic excitation because of the widespread use of brittle porcelain materials, low inherent damping, and slender structural configurations [2, 3]. Damage to such equipment can interrupt power delivery, trigger cascading failures, and cause substantial economic and societal losses [4].

Given the critical importance of substations to power-system reliability, extensive experimental studies have been conducted to evaluate and improve the seismic performance of substation electrical equipment [5, 6, 7, 8]. Shaking-table tests are widely used because they provide direct and reliable evidence of equipment dynamic behaviour, failure mechanisms, and seismic capacity. However, due to limitations in table size, payload capacity, and testing cost, most tests have focused on individual equipment [6, 7, 8] or, at most, three connected components [9]. This individual component-level focus does not fully represent practical substations, where electrical equipment rarely behaves as isolated units. Adjacent devices are commonly interconnected through rigid busbars or flexible conductors, as illustrated in Figure 1. These interconnections can transmit interaction forces during earthquakes, causing the response of each component to depend not only on its own structural properties but also on neighboring equipment, connection characteristics, system topology, and transient ground motion. Field investigations and experimental studies have shown that such connection-induced interaction forces may contribute significantly to seismic damage, especially under strong excitation [9, 10].

These interconnections can transmit interaction forces during earthquakes, causing the response of each component to depend not only on its own structural properties but also on neighboring equipment, connection characteristics, system topology, and transient ground motion. Field investigations and experimental studies have shown that such connection-induced interaction forces may contribute significantly to seismic damage, especially under strong excitation [9, 10].

High-fidelity finite element (FE) modeling remains a powerful tool for analyzing the seismic behavior of interconnected power infrastructures [11, 12, 13]. Such models can represent geometric details and component flexibility, and compute local response quantities (e.g., stress at the bottom cross-section of the equipment) relevant to damage assessment. However, their computational cost becomes prohibitive when repeated simulations are required for uncertainty quantification, digital twin updating, seismic retrofitting optimization, or real-time scenario evaluation. This challenge is further amplified for interconnected electrical equipment, where the interaction dynamics are difficult to model explicitly. Rigid busbars with sliding end connections [14] and flexible conductors attached through clamp fittings [15, 10] may introduce nonlinear coupling effects, localized sliding behavior, uncertain boundary conditions, and installation-dependent connection properties. In practice, these coupling mechanisms are rarely known with sufficient accuracy, and representing them using ideal spring-dampers or rigid links may introduce modeling errors, limiting purely simulation-based approaches in both efficiency and predictive reliability.

Reduced-order models (ROMs) provide an alternative route for efficient physics-based simulation. By projecting high-fidelity structural dynamics onto a low-dimensional modal or reduced basis, ROMs can substantially reduce computational costs while preserving essential structural dynamics [16, 17, 18]. Projection-based model reduction has been widely studied for large-scale dynamical systems and many-query simulations [19, 20]. In SHM and digital twin contexts, ROMs have been used to accelerate simulation-based training, online inference, and structural state estimation [21, 22, 23]. Nevertheless, conventional ROMs are usually constructed for a prescribed structural system or a fixed set of parameters. When the system topology changes, such as when different equipment components are connected in different layouts, the reduced operators and coupling terms may need to be reassembled or redefined. Moreover, if inter-component forces are nonlinear or only partially known, a purely physics-based ROM may still require explicit constitutive assumptions for the coupling behavior.

Structural health monitoring (SHM) and data-driven modeling have provided new opportunities for rapid condition assessment and response prediction of engineering structures [24]. With the increasing availability of sensor data, simulation data, and data science tools, machine learning methods have been widely explored for damage detection, response reconstruction, and structural state estimation [25]. Classical SHM frameworks rely on measured response features and statistical pattern recognition to infer structural condition [26, 27], while recent deep learning methods have extended these ideas to high-dimensional time-series data, image-based inspection, and vibration-based diagnostics [28, 29, 30]. For post-earthquake assessment of substation equipment, however, directly instrumenting every device is often impractical because of cost, insulation constraints, and electromagnetic interference. In contrast, ground motion records are easier to monitor at the substation level and can be shared across equipment. This makes ground-motion-driven response prediction an attractive alternative for rapid assessment of interconnected electrical equipment [12, 31]. Despite these advances, many data-driven models are trained for a fixed structural configuration and learn a direct mapping from excitation or sensor measurements to response or damage indicators [12, 26, 27]. Such models may perform well within the training distribution but often struggle when the system topology, number of components, component types, or connection properties change. For topology-adaptive digital twins, this limitation is critical because retraining a separate model for every possible configuration would require extremely high computational costs and defeat the purpose of rapid deployment.

papers.title: On the stability of displacement energy in toric manifolds
papers.abstract: We present a quantitative exploration of the behaviour of displacement energy of Lagrangians under stabilization. In particular, we completely characterize the displacement behaviour of toric fibres in Fano 4-manifolds. Our approach relates the geometry of the moment polytope's caustic to the structure of the (bulk-deformed) superpotential and to the presence of symmetric probes.

papers.title: Local crystallization in three-dimensional quantization
papers.abstract: A long-standing conjecture on the quantization problem due to Gersho, which remains open in dimensions higher than two, posits that optimal quantizers crystallize into a lattice structure; in dimension three, the natural candidate is the body-centered cubic (BCC) lattice, known to be optimal among other lattices. In this paper, we establish the asymptotic local optimality of the BCC lattice under small periodic perturbations, extending its known stability beyond the class of lattice configurations. Our approach connects the discrete geometry of Voronoi tessellations with a continuum variational problem, showing that the rescaled quadratic quantization energies converge to a continuum functional describing locally deformed BCC lattices. A central ingredient is a geometric and algebraic framework that combines the stability of the BCC Voronoi structure, a discrete calculus on its adjacency graph and an analysis of the lattice symmetries via representation theory, allowing us to establish the positivity of the second variation at the BCC configuration and thereby prove the local minimality of the BCC lattice for the limiting energy.

papers.intro:
This paper is devoted to the study of the three-dimensional quantization problem, with the aim of understanding the local optimality and stability of the body-centered cubic (BCC) lattice beyond the class of lattice configurations. The quantization problem, whose precise formulation we recall below, seeks to approximate a given probability distribution by a prescribed number of representative points with minimal average error, a question that arises in many areas of mathematics and its applications, ranging from signal processing and data compression to approximation theory and optimal location problems.

This paper is devoted to the study of the three-dimensional quantization problem, with the aim of understanding the local optimality and stability of the body-centered cubic (BCC) lattice beyond the class of lattice configurations. The quantization problem, whose precise formulation we recall below, seeks to approximate a given probability distribution by a prescribed number of representative points with minimal average error, a question that arises in many areas of mathematics and its applications, ranging from signal processing and data compression to approximation theory and optimal location problems.

The structure of the problem depends strongly on the dimension, and the extent of our understanding differs substantially between the one-, two-, and three-dimensional settings. The three-dimensional case, which is the natural one to describe configurations in physical space, remains significantly less understood than its lower-dimensional counterparts.

The three-dimensional case, which is the natural one to describe configurations in physical space, remains significantly less understood than its lower-dimensional counterparts.

For a uniform distribution, the problem becomes a geometric question about how points should be arranged in space, with equally spaced points being optimal in one dimension and regular triangular patterns achieving asymptotic optimality in two dimensions. In three dimensions, the conjectured optimal arrangement is the body-centered cubic (BCC) lattice, which can be constructed by placing points at the vertices and centers of the cubes in a regular cubic tiling. The BCC lattice is known to be optimal among lattices, but it remains an open question whether this optimality carries over to arbitrary non-lattice configurations.

The BCC lattice is known to be optimal among lattices, but it remains an open question whether this optimality carries over to arbitrary non-lattice configurations.

We address this question from a local perspective by studying the stability of the BCC lattice under small periodic deformations of space. This local setting allows us to exhibit the discrete quantization problem, under appropriate rescaling, as a graph discretization of a continuous variational problem, from which we obtain the convergence of the quantization error to an integral functional which depends on the gradient of the deformation. In the absence of a tractable closed-form formula for the limiting functional, we exploit the representation theory of the BCC symmetry group to compute the second variation at the unperturbed configuration and thus conclude that the BCC lattice is a strict local minimizer of the limiting energy.

papers.title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95-100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D, PUN achieves 10.7-60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29-32.15 times faster.

papers.intro:
Planning (Latombe, 1991) is one of the most fundamental problems in robotics. Given a robot’s configuration space (LaValle, 2006), planning computes a path from the current configuration to a goal that is optimal under a given cost function. Real robots do not execute a commanded motion exactly (Thrun, 2002). These errors accumulate along a motion, so a route planned with a few centimetres of clearance can be executed into a wall. Sampling-based planners such as PRM (Kavraki et al., 1996) and RRT (LaValle and Kuffner, 2001), and graph search such as A⋆ (Hart et al., 1968), plan for a nominal system that executes commands exactly and leave the noise to a tracking controller. Sampling-based methods such as MPPI (Williams et al., 2017a) and PI2-CMA (Stulp and Sigaud, 2012) optimize control sequences or policy parameters using sampled trajectory costs. Optimal feedback under execution noise can be derived from a value function, which gives the minimum expected cost of reaching the goal from each configuration and satisfies the nonlinear Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation (Fleming and Soner, 2006). Solving this equation on a grid scales exponentially with the dimension of the configuration space (Bellman, 1957; Han et al., 2018).

Conventional mesh-based numerical methods can solve the screened Poisson equation efficiently in two and three dimensions. However, a robot with dd degrees of freedom (DoF) induces a dd-dimensional configuration space, making volumetric discretizations and numerical PDE solution increasingly expensive. Planning must also accommodate complex and previously unseen obstacle geometries, for which constructing a new mesh and solving the PDE from scratch can be costly. Mesh-free Monte Carlo methods (Muller, 1956; Sawhney and Crane, 2020; Sawhney et al., 2023; Jambon et al., 2026) support PDE solution on complex geometries, motivating their use for planning in higher-dimensional configuration spaces.

Among these, Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) (Muller, 1956) estimates the solution at a point by jumping repeatedly to a uniformly sampled point on the largest ball fitting in free space, until it reaches a boundary of known value, which requires every reachable boundary to be Dirichlet. Walk-on-Stars (WoSt) (Sawhney et al., 2023) accommodates reflecting obstacles by replacing that ball with a star-shaped region that may contain part of the obstacle boundary, keeping every boundary point visible from the center so that one ray continues the walk instead of branching at each contact. The screened kernels for Walk-on-Stars have been derived only in two and three dimensions (Sawhney et al., 2023). Moreover, directly planning with Monte Carlo estimates is unreliable: trajectories depend on local value gradients, and even modest estimator noise can corrupt or reverse the estimated direction, leading to planning failure.

Neural operators (Kovachki et al., 2023) can amortize expensive PDE solves by learning mappings from input geometries directly to solution fields. Moreover, prior work has shown that fully converged labels are unnecessary when training from Monte Carlo simulations: neural operators can recover accurate predictions from noisy, partially converged estimates (Viswanath et al., 2026). We propose Planning Under Noise (PUN), shown in Fig. 2, an operator-learning framework that maps environment geometry to value fields that account for control noise. Boundary conditions can be understood through a heat analogy. With unit desirability at the goal and zero desirability on obstacle boundaries, the goal acts like a hot source, while the obstacle walls act like cold sinks. The zero-Dirichlet condition fixes the field to zero along each obstacle surface, making the entire obstacle boundary a heat sink. In a long or narrow passage, heat spreading from the goal therefore leaks into the walls along the route. The farther the goal’s influence must travel, the more it is attenuated, leaving a weak signal in distant parts of free space that discretization, sampling, or learning errors can obscure. Narrow passages make this particularly pronounced because the absorbing walls remain close on both sides. This attenuation is visible in Fig. 1(c), where the weak goal signal provides insufficient directional guidance for starting points far from the goal, making it difficult to navigate toward the target. Moreover, the screened Poisson equation already includes decay throughout free space through its screening term; absorbing obstacle boundaries introduce an additional source of attenuation. We therefore keep a Dirichlet condition at the goal but impose homogeneous Neumann (zero-flux) conditions on obstacle boundaries. The walls now act like insulation: they prevent heat from escaping through the boundary without forcing the desirability itself to vanish there. Heat can spread along a corridor without continually draining into its walls, allowing the goal’s influence to reach farther into free space. Screening still causes decay, but the additional loss through obstacles is removed. This is precisely the effect illustrated in Fig. 1(d): compared with the absorbing Dirichlet field in Fig. 1(c), the mixed-boundary field extends the goal’s influence much farther through the environment, preserving a stronger signal for planning along long routes. The Neumann condition also makes the value gradient parallel to smooth obstacle boundaries; therefore, gradient-based planning directs motion along walls rather than into them. This permits guidance along walls in narrow passages without the strong repulsion induced by zero-Dirichlet conditions. Under our regularity assumptions, the value field and control remain bounded at obstacles, whereas zero-Dirichlet desirability makes both diverge there (Appendix C.4).

papers.title: Can Native Safety Travel? Reusing Safety Pretraining Across Models via On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Safety pretraining has emerged as a promising paradigm for embedding safety deeply into a model during pretraining, yielding robustness to subsequent fine-tuning that conventional safety post-training often lacks. We refer to this safety acquired during model pretraining as native safety. Yet native safety is expensive to acquire, confined to the model in which it was pretrained, and often accompanied by lower general utility. In this work, we rethink the practical value of safety-pretrained models and introduce, for the first time, the native safety reuse problem: Can native safety be transferred from a specialized, potentially smaller, safety-pretrained "teacher" to standard-pretrained "students," enabling them to inherit its robustness while preserving their general utility? We show that native safety can "travel" through on-policy distillation. A standard-pretrained student generates responses to safety-pretraining prompts, while a small safety-pretrained teacher supervises the student's token-level predictions along its own generated trajectories; cross-tokenizer alignment further enables transfer across model families. The resulting students exhibit substantially greater safety robustness than their safety-post-trained counterparts while retaining higher general utility than the teacher: subsequent fine-tuning raises the average attack success rate (ASR) of the 1.7B student by only 5.00%, compared with 11.58% for safety post-training, and its average utility of 48.20% far exceeds the aligned teacher's 27.42%. Unlike conventional large-to-small knowledge distillation, our framework enables selective, small-to-large safety transfer: it reuses the robust safety expertise of a smaller pretrained teacher without inheriting its utility limitations. These findings establish native safety as a reusable model property rather than one permanently tied to the originally pretrained model.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in open-ended and high-stakes settings, making their safety a priority. The prevailing approach is safety alignment through post-training, which uses supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, reinforcement learning, or related techniques to shape the behavior of a pretrained model (Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023; Bianchi et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2023b; Shen et al., 2023). Although safety post-training can substantially reduce harmful compliance at the resulting checkpoint, this protection is often fragile. Aligned models remain vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks (Zou et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2025). More alarmingly, their safety can deteriorate during subsequent fine-tuning even when the downstream data are entirely benign and unrelated to harmful behavior (Qi et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2025). Thus, ordinary model adaptation can inadvertently undo safety previously acquired through post-training.

From the perspective of downstream adaptation, the difficulty of preserving post-training safety has been viewed as a fine-tuning-induced misalignment problem (Siddiqui et al., 2026a). However, it also exposes a fundamental limitation of safety post-training itself: the learned safety may remain shallow (Qi et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2024; Tice et al., 2026). Post-training updates an already pretrained model using a comparatively small alignment dataset and limited optimization budget, often inducing only modest changes to its weights (Siddiqui et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2019). Consequently, the model may learn safe behavior at the surface level without deeply integrating safety into its underlying representations (Qi et al., 2025). Subsequent safety-irrelevant updates can then overwrite this behavior when improving performance on the intended downstream task, such as mathematical reasoning.

(Q) Can native safety “travel”—that is, be transferred from a safety-pretrained model and reused by larger, more capable standard models?

We refer to (Q) as the native safety reuse problem. Solving it can improve the value and scalability of safety pretraining: rather than treating native safety as a model-specific property that must be relearned through costly pretraining, we could acquire it once and reuse it across architectures and modalities. papers.title: LVMem: Image-Augmented Memory for Long-Horizon Question Answering
papers.abstract: Reliable language-guided perception is essential for embodied agents, where questions about objects, events, and their locations must be answered from long observation histories. Unlike conventional visual question answering, realistic robotic settings require reasoning over extended temporal horizons and persistent scene memory. We build upon the view-based memory paradigm and propose an efficient framework for long-horizon spatio-temporal question answering. While existing view-based systems typically store either text captions or visual embeddings, we extend the ReMEmbR-style memory with image paths that link each stored description to its original visual content. To make the stored annotations more informative, we replace uniform sampling during memory construction with an optical-flow-based frame selection strategy (PSFR) and store an object-centric descriptive scene representation instead of plain captions. We further equip a VLM-based agent with an adaptive retrieval tool that returns the image associated with the most relevant caption, allowing the agent to decide when visual inspection is needed. On the OC-NaVQA benchmark, LVMem outperforms ReMEmbR on binary and positional metrics with both backbones and matches or exceeds a 4D scene graph DAAAM baseline on binary accuracy, while operating on a lightweight view-based memory that requires no explicit graph construction.

Embodied agents that operate over hours or days accumulate vast streams of visual experience. A warehouse robot, for example, may be asked: “Which shelf had the damaged box?” or “What did the loading dock look like when you passed it?”. Answering such queries goes beyond retrieving a text snippet: the agent must recall what it actually saw, where, and when. This demands a memory that preserves visual evidence across long horizons, remains spatially and temporally consistent, and can be queried efficiently as it grows.

We formalize the problem of long-horizon spatio-temporal question answering as follows. Given a continuous stream of RGB observations with associated poses and timestamps, and a natural language query about objects, events, or states in the environment, the goal is to produce an accurate answer. This requires building a memory representation from the observation stream and reasoning jointly over visual appearance, spatial locations, and temporal ordering.

Given a continuous stream of RGB observations with associated poses and timestamps, and a natural language query about objects, events, or states in the environment, the goal is to produce an accurate answer. This requires building a memory representation from the observation stream and reasoning jointly over visual appearance, spatial locations, and temporal ordering.

This challenge becomes especially difficult in realistic robotic scenarios, where the environment evolves over time and the robot must reason over extended temporal horizons. A robot may observe the same object from multiple viewpoints, encounter changes in object locations, and need to combine information collected at different moments in time. Multimodal large language models have demonstrated strong capabilities in visual reasoning and language understanding [1, 2], but they still struggle with long video sequences [3, 4], persistent scene memory [5], and efficient retrieval of relevant information from large observation histories.

Structured scene representations offer a promising direction for addressing these limitations. In particular, scene graphs provide a compact and interpretable representation of objects, their attributes and interactions [6], and have been extended to dynamic 4D settings where nodes correspond to entities, edges encode semantic and spatial relations, and temporal information captures scene evolution [7, 8]. Recent approaches such as DAAAM [9] have explored 4D scene graphs for robotics, yet they rely on explicit geometric reconstruction and per-object description generation. Such representations are attractive for robotics because they support persistent memory and enable reasoning across long horizons. However, constructing and maintaining explicit 4D scene graphs in large-scale environments remains computationally demanding.

Our contribution can be summarized as follows: • We introduce LVMem, a view-based framework for long-horizon spatio-temporal question answering over recorded robot observations. LVMem represents observations as object-centric scene descriptions and links each to its source image, timestamp, and pose, equipping a VLM agent with a selectively invoked visual retrieval tool. This enables the agent to inspect visual details omitted from the stored descriptions while retaining text-, position-, and time-based access to memory, without explicit 3D reconstruction. • We propose motion-guided memory construction under a fixed frame budget by integration of the existing Patchwise Sparse-Flow Retention (PSFR) method into segment-level scene description generation and evaluate it against uniform sampling with identical segment lengths and frame counts. With six frames per 10-second segment, PSFR improves binary accuracy by 8.96 percentage points and reduces mean positional error from 89.98 m to 68.16 m, demonstrating the importance of frame selection for downstream memory-based question answering. • Through comparisons with ReMEmbR and DAAAM methods and ablations on OC-NaVQA, we examine how frame selection, visual retrieval, text retrieval depth, and scene description configuration affect answer quality. LVMem improves binary and free-form text accuracy over ReMEmbR by 10.95 and 15.15 percentage points with Qwen3.5-9B, and by 19.90 and 5.05 points with GPT-5-Mini, respectively. Our ablations further show that visual augmentation depends on retrieval context: additional images can improve descriptive answers while degrading positional estimates or destabilizing temporal predictions.

papers.title: Steering Vision-Language Models for Visual-Contextual Privacy in Location Disclosure
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer sensitive information such as geolocation from subtle visual cues, creating privacy risks when responses disclose more detail than the visual context warrants. We study visual-contextual privacy in geolocation disclosure, where a VLM should reveal location information only at the granularity appropriate to the visual context depicted in the image. We first show that this contextually appropriate granularity is recoverable from pre-generation hidden states, even when generated responses are misaligned, with disclosure levels exhibiting an ordered structure along a common hidden-state direction. Motivated by this, we propose an inference-time route-and-steer framework: an ordinal granularity router maps visual-contextual privacy representations to a disclosure route, and a disclosure-level-conditioned steering module applies route-specific hidden-state interventions during decoding. Across four VLM backbones, our method improves visual-context-aware disclosure alignment, better balances over- and under-disclosure, and incurs only modest changes on general capability benchmarks. It further transfers to another dataset with a distinct data distribution and privacy-risk taxonomy.

papers.intro:
Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly capable of extracting, inferring, and reasoning about information embedded in visual inputs (Yang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Beyond recognizing explicitly visible attributes, they can combine subtle visual cues with linguistic knowledge to infer latent personal information, such as the location depicted in an image. While these capabilities improve visual understanding and assistance, they also create new privacy risks: seemingly innocuous images may reveal sensitive information that individuals did not intend to share.

Beyond recognizing explicitly visible attributes, they can combine subtle visual cues with linguistic knowledge to infer latent personal information, such as the location depicted in an image. While these capabilities improve visual understanding and assistance, they also create new privacy risks: seemingly innocuous images may reveal sensitive information that individuals did not intend to share.

Prior work has begun to characterize and mitigate privacy risks in multimodal settings, ranging from privacy attribute recognition (Samson et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026a) to reasoning-level inference (Tömekçe et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). However, they predominantly treat privacy as a static property of information, such as personally identifiable information (PII). This framing reduces privacy protection to an access-control question: whether a particular type of information should be disclosed or withheld. In practice, however, the appropriateness of disclosure depends on the visual context depicted in the image.

Under contextual integrity theory (Nissenbaum, 2004), privacy is not framed as a fixed property of an information type, but the appropriateness of an information flow within a given context. In our setting, this context is the visual content depicted in the image. Consider the same location-inference request applied to two images: a private residential scene and a public landmark (Figure 1). A precise answer may be appropriate for the landmark image, but the same level of specificity for the residential scene may reveal location cues its owner never intended to disclose. Treating both cases identically either risks privacy leakage in the private scene or suppresses useful assistance for the public landmark. We therefore consider a VLM provider serving image-based location queries, including privacy-seeking requests about others, with the goal of enforcing visual-context-dependent disclosure norms (Mireshghallah et al., 2026).

Recent work has moved toward visual contextual privacy. In particular, emerging benchmarks (Yang et al., 2026; Wang and Zhang, 2026) evaluate whether VLM responses conform to context-dependent privacy norms. However, effective mechanisms for enforcing contextual privacy in VLMs remain underexplored. Existing approaches primarily rely on prompting (Yang et al., 2026) or fine-tuning (Franchi et al., 2026). Prompt-based method relies on ground-truth demonstration from similar image content (Yang et al., 2026), making it sensitive to demonstration quality and availability. Training-based intervention is costly to adapt: supporting even a modest number of disclosure policies can require a separate fine-tuned model per policy (Mendes et al., 2024).

Different from these methods targeting visual-context-aware disclosure behavior end-to-end, we analyze visual contextual disclosure alignment in terms of two roles: deciding what disclosure granularity is appropriate for the image context, and controlling generation so that the response realizes that granularity. This separation is motivated by our finding that pre-generation hidden states already contain recoverable information about the appropriate disclosure level, even when the final response does not faithfully reflect that level (Section 3.1). Moreover, disclosure levels are ordered by their projection onto a common direction in representation space (Section 3.2). Building on these observations, we introduce an inference-time route-and-steer framework. A router projects contextual privacy representations onto a disclosure-granularity coordinate and maps the resulting score to a target route (Section 4.1), while a steering module applies route-specific hidden-state interventions during decoding to align the generated response with the routed granularity (Section 4.2). We propose a modular framework that maps contextual privacy representations to a disclosure route and applies route-specific hidden-state interventions during decoding. • Improved contextual disclosure alignment. Across multiple VLM backbones, our method improves contextual disclosure alignment, better balances over- and under-disclosure, incurs modest alignment tax, and generalizes to DoxBench.

papers.title: SRE: Accelerating Zero-Knowledge Proofs via Scalar Redundancy Elimination in Multi-Scalar Multiplication
papers.abstract: Multi-Scalar Multiplication (MSM) is a fundamental cryptographic operation used in Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) across a wide range of applications. Its computation involves intensive elliptic curve point additions (PADD). MSM plays a critical role in cryptographic primitives such as polynomial commitments and zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs), where it often becomes the runtime bottleneck. Consequently, optimizing MSM is an active area of research focused on reducing computational complexity and accelerating performance. The current state-of-the-art algorithm for large-scale MSM is Pippenger's bucket method, which consists of three main steps: point merging, bucket aggregation, and window aggregation. Among these, the point merging step is the primary performance bottleneck. Our work targets this major computational bottleneck. To reduce operations for practical applications, we propose a novel Scalar Redundancy Elimination (SRE) algorithm with three approaches: a vanilla array-based approach, a list-based greedy approach, and a list-based exhaustive approach, all incorporating an early stopping technique. Depending on the use case, these strategies can be integrated into our modified MSM algorithm, which is based on Pippenger's bucket method. As a result, our proposed MSM algorithm, enhanced with the SRE technique, incurs less than $3\%$ additional search time, while reducing the number of operations by $25\%$, leading to a $30\%$ speedup in runtime compared to the standard Pippenger's bucket method. This translates to a $10 \sim 20\%$ runtime reduction in various ZKP systems that rely heavily on MSM.

papers.intro:
Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) [20] have played a transformative role in modern cryptography, enabling numerous applications since their introduction. Unlike their original formulations, contemporary ZKPs are typically built on Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), with prominent examples including Zero-Knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge (zk-SNARKs). However, generating such proofs requires significant computation to preserve the property of zero-knowledge. Key cryptographic operations include the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) and Multi-Scalar Multiplication (MSM) on elliptic curves (ECs), with MSM alone accounting for more than 70% of the total runtime [30]. Consequently, this work focuses on optimizing MSM to reduce computation time and accelerate zk-SNARKs for practical cryptographic applications.

ECC is one of the most widely used approaches for public-key cryptography. It is based on computations on ECs defined over finite fields. One of its main advantages is the use of smaller key sizes compared to RSA, which has been in use for decades. Due to its numerous benefits, ECC has been widely adopted in various applications, for example, traditional digital signatures, polynomial commitments, and ZKPs mentioned earlier, to name a few. However, computations on ECs still demand significant computing resources due to the large bitwidth operands and the complexity of the underlying cryptographic operations. Among these, MSM on ECs is one of the most computationally intensive tasks. It is a fundamental operation in certain ZKP protocols and accounts for the majority of computation time during the setup phase. As a result, this computational bottleneck hinders the widespread deployment of such applications in practice.

Joint efforts from both the hardware and software communities have contributed to analyzing [44] and optimizing computations, from low-level modular arithmetic [29, 33, 49], to EC operations [10], and up to cryptographic accelerators specifically designed for ZKPs [49, 53, 1, 42, 41, 52, 50, 30, 32, 54], to make them suitable for real-world applications. However, progress from cryptographic operation perspective has been limited due to the maturity of established approaches. However, operational improvement remains critical, as computational complexity is still a key bottleneck in these applications. In this work, we focus on MSM, which is one of the primary performance bottlenecks in ZKPs. We provide a comprehensive overview of the current methods used in various scenarios along with their respective advantages and limitations.

Pippenger’s bucket method is widely used in state-of-the-art implementations and frameworks for large-scale MSM, such as those employed in ZKP systems [21, 19]. The algorithm merges EC points based on their corresponding scalars. These scalars are split into multiple windows, and matches are identified across these windows to reduce redundant operations that would otherwise occur in a naive computation. We will discuss this algorithm in detail in Section 3. Pippenger’s bucket method can be broken down into three main steps: point merging, bucket aggregation, and window aggregation. Among these, point merging accounts for approximately 90% of the total MSM runtime [32]. To optimize computation time more effectively in ZKP schemes, it is therefore crucial to focus on the point merging step, guided by the well-known Amdahl’s Law [2]. A key insight is that the algorithm can be further improved by identifying and eliminating additional redundancy across multiple windows of scalars, rather than just one. This enhancement allows for greater efficiency beyond what is achieved by the standard Pippenger’s bucket method. The actual runtime breakdown of zk-SNARK applications is shown in Figure 1, using Groth16 [21] and Plonk [19] as examples with a problem size of 2162^{16} under the BN254 EC. The breakdown includes operations such as NTT, MSM, point subtraction (Sub), and others. The results highlight that MSM, and in particular the point merging step, is the primary bottleneck in these cryptographic primitives.

These approaches offer tradeoffs between search time and the amount of redundancy identified. The early stopping technique aims to determine an optimal threshold, the ratio of matched bits to the total scalar length, beyond which the search yields diminishing returns in redundancy while consuming more time. Our experimental results, evaluated by various parameters, show that an additional 3% search cost yields a 25% reduction in operations, resulting in a general 30% runtime speedup over the original Pippenger’s method. This demonstrates the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach in practical scenarios.

papers.title: A $\wedge$-like metallicity profile in the disk of the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy
papers.abstract: Unveiling the properties of the progenitors that formed the tidal structures of the Milky Way (MW) is essential for exploring the MW's assembly history. Such studies further afford a unique opportunity to dissect the formation and evolution of dwarf galaxies by contrasting surviving and disrupted systems. However, reconstructing the intrinsic structure of progenitors solely from the positions and velocities of their tidal debris remains a formidable challenge. Here, we decode the chemo-kinematic signatures embedded in the stellar streams of the Sagittarius (Sgr) dwarf galaxy through N-body simulations. Our simulation reproduces a vertical metallicity gradient in the Sgr streams. We show that this feature is naturally explained if the stream originated from a disk component with a $\wedge$-like metallicity profile. Remarkably, similar metallicity profiles are identified in MaNGA survey data for a few (3/217) field dwarf galaxies, suggesting this feature is rare but not unique to Sgr. The vertical metallicity gradient of stellar streams preserves extra detailed galactic fossil records, enabling quantitative reconstruction of the peculiar structure of the satellite galaxy. The similar metallicity profiles of Sgr and MW raise the question of a possible special coevolution.

papers.title: ZKPU: Zero-Knowledge Processing Unit for Heterogeneous Workloads
papers.abstract: Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) have become a fundamental building block for privacy-preserving computation, blockchain systems, and verifiable machine learning. Modern ZKP protocols span two distinct families: curve-based protocols, which rely on large finite-field arithmetic, and hash-based protocols, which operate over native 64-bit fields. Existing hardware accelerators are specialized for one protocol family because they are built on operand-scanning Montgomery multiplication, resulting in fixed-width datapaths, poor utilization across heterogeneous operand widths, and limited scalability. This paper presents \emph{ZKPU}, a Zero-Knowledge Processing Unit for heterogeneous ZKP workloads. ZKPU introduces a new compute paradigm by co-designing finely integrated product scanning (FIPS) Montgomery multiplication with a reconfigurable Twin Systolic Fabric (TSF), enabling modular multiplication at arbitrary widths in 64-bit increments. Combined with a fine-grained Deque buffer, on-chip twiddle-factor generator, and memory-efficient MSM preprocessing strategy, ZKPU provides a unified architecture for both curve-based and hash-based protocols. Evaluation using Groth16 and Plonky2 shows that ZKPU achieves up to $144\times$ speedup for NTT, $13.6\times$ for MSM, and approximately $7.2\times$ end-to-end application speedup over state-of-the-art accelerators, while being the first architecture to efficiently support both protocol families on a single reconfigurable hardware platform.

Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) [12] enable a prover to convince a verifier that a statement is true without revealing any information beyond its validity, and have become a fundamental building block for blockchain systems [4, 24, 15], verifiable computation [28], and machine-learning verification[40, 20, 7], etc [6]. Practical ZKP protocols broadly fall into two families. Curve-based protocols, such as Groth16 [14] and PLONK [10], rely on elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC) to generate succinct proofs with fast verification. Their prover execution is dominated by arithmetic-intensive kernels, primarily number-theoretic transforms (NTTs) and multi-scalar multiplication (MSM), over 256∼768256\sim 768-bit prime fields. In contrast, hash-based protocols, including Plonky2 [33] and Starky [39], rely on ZKP-friendly hash functions such as Poseidon [13], eliminating the need for trusted setup while providing post-quantum security. papers.title: Collective Hall quantization in 3D Chern vector systems
papers.abstract: Understanding the three-dimensional (3D) quantum Hall effect, characterized by a Chern vector rather than a single Chern number, has been a central pursuit in topological physics. While quantized Hall transport is established for the special case with one nonzero Chern component, recent realizations of more general Chern-vector states raise a fundamental question: how does such topology protect quantized transport? Here, we predict a distinct 3D quantized Hall effect protected by $\mathbf{C}=(0,m,n)$. For samples with dimensions $L_y$ and $L_z$, global topology enforces collective quantization of $mL_y+nL_z$, despite the fragility of individual edge modes to disorder. This reveals a novel transport regime in which robust quantization emerges as a holistic property of a unified chiral network,rather than of its constituent modes. Crucially, this collective response manifests as a quantized Hall conductance $G_{xy}=\pm(mL_y+nL_z)e^2/h$, with a distinctive dependence on both Chern-vector components and sample dimensions. We propose candidate materials to facilitate experimental observation.

Recently, interest has expanded to three-dimensional (3D) systems where various Hall responses have been proposed and experimentally verified [44, 45, 23, 31, 34, 18, 43, 42, 27, 19, 9, 41, 29, 15, 36, 40]. Consequently, standard frameworks, such as the layer-based TKNN formula [30, 8], fail to capture the transport physics, raising a fundamental question: Can any quantized transport signature survive when local edge-state protection is compromised by global network complexity?

papers.title: HypTI: Hyperbolic Geometry-Aware Multimodal Feature Fusion Framework for Dementia Detection Based on Tabular-Image Data
papers.abstract: AI-assisted dementia detection usually requires multimodal fusion of diverse data, such as clinical tabular assessments and neuroimaging data. However, most existing approaches perform feature fusion in Euclidean space. This overlooks the geometric structure of representation, including hierarchical organization in clinical assessments and multi-scale anatomical patterns in neuroimaging data. Recent studies have proved hyperbolic space provides a natural geometry for modelling hierarchical and multi-scale structures due to its exponentially expanding space. Motivated by these, we propose HypTI, a hyperbolic geometry-aware multimodal fusion framework for dementia detection based on clinical tabular assessments and MRI scans. HypTI extends hyperbolic representation learning to an underexplored tabular-MRI setting, jointly modelling clinical tabular, MRI scans, and cross-modal interactions in hyperbolic space. Specifically, clinical tabular variables are represented through learnable Lorentz prototypes to capture hierarchical relationships among assessments, while MRI scans are encoded using ROI-guided multi-scale representation learning to capture anatomical patterns across brain regions and spatial scales in Lorentz space. The multimodal representations are integrated through an adaptive fusion module generates subject-specific scale and shift coefficients to dynamically modulate and integrate the multimodal embeddings, enabling effective patient-level tabular-image representation learning for dementia detection. Experiments on OASIS-3 dataset show that the proposed framework achieves strong performance compared with representative approaches.

Dementia syndrome detection requires integrating heterogeneous complementary evidence from clinical assessments and neuroimaging. Clinical tabular variables describe risk factors, cognitive impairments, functional decline, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and clinical staging, whereas T1-weighted MRI provides structural evidence of neurodegeneration and regional brain atrophy[35]. Therefore, dementia classification is not only an image recognition problem, but also requires multimodal integration of clinical assessments and neuroanatomical evidence[34].

Dementia syndrome detection requires integrating heterogeneous complementary evidence from clinical assessments and neuroimaging. Clinical tabular variables describe risk factors, cognitive impairments, functional decline, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and clinical staging, whereas T1-weighted MRI provides structural evidence of neurodegeneration and regional brain atrophy[35]. Therefore, dementia classification is not only an image recognition problem, but also requires multimodal integration of clinical assessments and neuroanatomical evidence[34].

However, learning effective representations from clinical tabular data and MRI remains challenging. The two modalities exhibit substantial differences in their data structure and semantic granularity[1]. Clinical tabular variables follow a hierarchical organization consistent with dementia assessment workflows. Broad clinical domains are divided into subdomains and quantified through standardized assessments in a NACC Uniform Data Set (UDS)-style structure, collectively characterizing disease severity[22]. Structural MRI is a high-dimensional 3D signal whose disease-related patterns appear across multiple anatomical scales, ranging from local patch-level tissue changes to region-level atrophy and broader brain-wide structural alterations[26]. In addition, the brain is organized hierarchically across multiple spatial scales[3]. Voxel-level measurements can be aggregated into anatomical regions, which are in turn embedded within larger structural and functional systems, while neurodegenerative changes often follow non-random spatial patterns across the hierarchy[30]. Such hierarchical structures are not naturally aligned with flat Euclidean geometry, whose representational capacity grows only polynomially with distance from the origin[23]. Most existing multimodal dementia models perform feature fusion in Euclidean space using concatenation-, convolution-, kernel-, or attention-based mechanisms[33, 16, 25]. However, such approaches largely overlook the hierarchical and multi-scale geometric structure underlying clinical tabular and neuroimaging representations. Hyperbolic geometry provides a natural alternative for modelling hierarchical and branching structures, as it can compactly organize representations with different levels of specificity within a shared embedding space[23, 24]. Recent advances have extended hyperbolic representation learning to neural networks, graph learning, and vision models[13, 7, 11]. However, hyperbolic methods have focused on brain connectivity graphs[19, 33], while joint hyperbolic fusion of clinical tabular data and structural MRI remains largely unexplored.

papers.title: Speculative Imbalance Positions by Non-Physical Traders: Impacts on Electricity System Balancing in Great Britain
papers.abstract: The electricity system in Great Britain (GB) allows participants to deliberately produce or consume a different volume to their traded position and has incentivised this practice with a single imbalance price since 2015. In particular, non-physical traders (NPTs) often take an open position to imbalance without any intention to produce or consume power. However, new government proposals could restrict this practice due to concerns over supply-demand balancing feasibility and costs. This article presents the first empirical analysis of speculative imbalance positioning (SIP) by NPTs in the GB electricity system through its effects on imbalance volumes, balancing costs, the imbalance price, and associated settlement costs over the period 2021-2024. Our research uses party-level imbalance data in each settlement period to run counterfactual simulations of the electricity balancing mechanism without the aggregate NPT imbalance. Our results indicate that SIP by NPTs reduced the total net balancing volume required by 3.1-3.9 TWh (16-20%), reduced system imbalance standard deviation by 48-65 MWh (13-17%), reduced balancing costs by £347-396m (5.9-6.7%), and reduced supplier imbalance costs by £193-325m (65-75%) over the analysis period. These results suggest that consumer bills would have been higher without SIP by NPTs, since the extra costs would likely have been passed on to consumers through levies, although the potential for effects in the wholesale (primarily late-stage intraday) markets complicates this picture.

Trading parties in the GB electricity system are financially accountable for differences between their contracted and physical positions. In GB, along with other markets such as the Irish Single Electricity Market, the Netherlands, Denmark, and France, parties are allowed to take speculative positions on the imbalance price. This research assesses whether speculative imbalance positioning (SIP) by non-physical traders (NPTs) benefits the GB electricity system.

One key reason to permit SIP is to incentivise ‘helpful’ imbalances (Ofgem, 2015), as explained in the following example. Suppose an NPT buys energy ahead of time, consumes no energy, but the system has a net upward balancing energy requirement anyway. This energy purchase likely induced an increase in generation, which reduces the net balancing energy requirement compared with the counterfactual of no purchase. The trade is profitable if the price at which the NPT’s imbalance is settled (i.e. at which they sell their excess energy) exceeds the purchase cost. If the imbalance price is tied to the marginal cost of energy balancing, profitable imbalance arbitrage will also reduce the system imbalance (Bunn and Kermer, 2021). However, whether this idealised scenario plays out in practice is an empirical matter. For example, if the settlement price (SP) does not reflect the marginal cost of buying balancing power, NPTs may be incentivised to take positions which exacerbate the system imbalance. Despite this trading strategy being common in GB (Elexon, 2019a), no study has quantified its effects on the GB system.

In this research, we focus on the effects of SIP (by NPTs only) on balancing and imbalance settlement volumes and costs. Reducing these is one of the key aims of permitting SIP (see Section 2), and of significant public interest given the recent rise in balancing costs. Combining extensive publicly available data in new ways, we run counterfactual simulations of the GB balancing mechanism as the basis of our analysis. Over the period 2021–2024, our modelling suggests that SIP reduced the total volume of energy balancing actions required by 3.1–3.9 TWh (16–20%), and reduced consumer bills through lower balancing costs to NESO (between £347–396m, or 5.9–6.7%) and a reduction in imbalance charges to suppliers (between £193–£325m, or 65–75%). While SIP also plays an important role in changing overall system emissions and short-term market price formation, estimating these effects either requires non-public information or ex-ante market modelling, which is outside the scope of this paper.

papers.title: From Code Generator to Engineering Companion: A Plant-aware Agent for PLC Programming
papers.abstract: Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) coding remains a manual, IDE-centric task that demands constant context switching between documentation, project files, and code editors. Recent work has demonstrated that retrieval-augmented large language models can generate vendor-compliant Structured Text at high compilation rates, yet these systems treat code generation as a one-shot pipeline: the engineer submits a query and receives code, with no persistent knowledge of the specific plant. We present a plant-aware conversational copilot that extends this paradigm in three directions: plant-specific context ingestion, a chat-first interaction model for explanation and debugging, and a graduated tool-access ladder from chat to deployment. The system is designed for real plant infrastructure and keeps the engineer in control of each step that produces real-world effects.

Prior work [1] demonstrated that a retrieval-augmented coding assistant for Mitsubishi Electric’s GX Works3 environment can generate vendor-compliant ST code at high compilation rates using only a structured knowledge base of function-block definitions and documentation excerpts, without exposing proprietary code to cloud providers.

The gap we address is not code generation per se, but the engineering interaction model. A copilot that knows the plant-specific I/O list, labels, and existing program fragments can generate code that is immediately appropriate for the target namespace. Moreover, in our setting we find that agents often only write correct code when they know the real-world setup of the plant. papers.title: CPVB-RG: Cross-Prior Visual Bridging for Prior-Aware Chest X-Ray Report Generation
papers.abstract: Radiologists interpret follow-up chest X-rays by comparing current and prior examinations to identify new, resolved or progressing findings. Most report generation systems either omit this longitudinal context or fuse prior features without distinguishing interval changes from anatomy that remains stable over time. We propose CPVB-RG, a prior-aware framework that combines current and prior radiographs with available clinical text. Its Cross-Prior Visual Bridge (CPVB) contains Progression-Guided Focus Attention (PGFA) and two Cross-Attention units. PGFA is designed to contrast progression-difference attention with shared-spatial attention, aiming to reduce invariant responses whilst retaining coarse spatial correspondence between examinations. The Cross-Attention units then connect the resulting longitudinal visual evidence with clinical semantics. CPVB-RG is trained in two stages, using prior-guided image-text alignment followed by autoregressive report generation with a lightweight language decoder. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR and IU X-Ray show consistent improvements across language and clinical metrics. On MIMIC-CXR, CPVB-RG achieves 0.2847 F1RadGraph and 0.6692 VLScore, with statistically significant gains over the closest decoder-matched prior-aware baseline. These results support the effectiveness of the proposed difference-aware and spatially guided fusion design for prior-aware chest X-ray report generation.
