Chest X-rays are among the most commonly used imaging examinations for assessing thoracic disease [50, 16]. Automatic report generation could reduce repetitive reporting effort, but a follow-up report is not simply a textual description of the current image. Findings are often subtle and spatially localised, and their interpretation depends on whether they are new, stable or changing relative to an earlier examination [17, 43]. Report-generation models must therefore identify interval changes while filtering responses from anatomy that remains unchanged.

papers.title: Fast and scalable multi-GPU sliced FFT solvers for asymptotically compatible discretizations of 3D nonlocal diffusion problems
papers.abstract: Large-scale 3D peridynamic transient diffusion simulations are constrained by the computational cost and memory requirements of nonlocal interactions. We propose a fast and scalable multi-GPU sliced FFT algorithm based on the recently developed asymptotically compatible finite difference (ACFD) scheme. By exploiting the discrete operator's structure and finite interaction range, the algorithm combines FFT acceleration with local inter-GPU communication. It preserves the ACFD scheme while avoiding the global data redistribution required by full 3D FFTs. We build a matrix-free GPU conjugate gradient (CG) solver, use multigrid preconditioning to reduce iteration counts, and introduce a human-audited configuration agent for efficient cross-level configuration. Strong-scaling tests show that sliced FFT-CG achieves 93.2% parallel efficiency on eight GPUs, compared with 28.2% for full FFT-CG on the same problem and hardware. The framework supports approximately 10.29 billion degrees of freedom on eight RTX 4090 GPUs with 24 GB of memory each. The insulated penny-shaped cutout benchmark demonstrates transient simulation with approximately 8.58 billion degrees of freedom. Three-dimensional star-shaped interface evolution further demonstrates convergence toward the local solution in a nonlinear phase-field problem. These results demonstrate that sliced FFT provides a scalable multi-GPU approach for fast computation of 3D peridynamic diffusion.

Peridynamics (PD) formulates continuum interactions over finite distances through integral equations, providing a unified nonlocal description of problems with spatial discontinuities, such as material fracture [1, 2]. Originally developed for solid mechanics, this framework has been extended to heat and mass transport, with PD diffusion models replacing local diffusion operators by neighborhood integrals [3, 4, 5]. These models have been applied to transient heat conduction in domains containing cracks or cutouts and to mass transport during corrosion damage evolution [6, 7, 8]. However, evaluating a volume integral at every spatial node generates extensive neighborhood interactions, making 3D simulations computationally expensive.

Exploiting the massive thread parallelism of GPUs to accelerate neighborhood evaluation is an important route to improving the efficiency of peridynamic simulations. OpenCL implementations [16, 17], CUDA parallelism at both particle and bond levels [18], and memory optimization [19] have reduced runtimes and increased attainable problem sizes. For example, PeriPy achieves speedups of 1.4–10 over an existing OpenCL implementation in the reported tests [17]. Wang et al. further simulate heat conduction with moving sources using approximately 76 million particles on three GPUs [20]. These advances primarily arise from parallel execution and storage optimization of neighborhood calculations, whose core remains the evaluation of particle or bond interactions. Thus, although GPUs execute these calculations faster, they still face substantial arithmetic work that grows with the number of neighbors per node.

Combining the low arithmetic complexity of FFTs with the parallel computing capacity of multiple GPUs is a natural choice for further improving solver efficiency. Previous studies have pursued this approach by developing distributed multi-GPU FFT methods, but simply distributing the computational workload across more GPUs has not automatically yielded proportional speedups [27, 28, 29]. The key obstacle is that full 3D FFTs require global data redistribution when performing transforms along different directions: as the GPU count increases, the local computational workload per GPU decreases, whereas inter-GPU data exchange and synchronization costs are difficult to reduce proportionally, severely limiting strong scalability [23, 24, 25, 30, 31]. In their strong-scaling analysis, Ayala et al. further point out that network saturation reduces the average bandwidth available to each process, ultimately causing linear strong scaling to break down [25]. To mitigate this problem, researchers have adopted different domain decomposition schemes, communication optimizations, and strategies for overlapping computation and communication [23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29]. However, these optimizations retain the global data redistribution required by the full 3D transform, leaving the communication bottleneck unresolved. For example, for a fixed 102431024^{3} transform, AccFFT, which uses pencil decomposition and communication overlap, achieves only 26% strong-scaling efficiency when the GPU count increases from 128 to 4,096 [27]; after adopting slab decomposition and asynchronous communication optimizations, Verma et al. report that, for a double-precision transform of the same size, the fraction of total runtime spent on communication rises sharply from 51% to 98% as the number of A100 GPUs increases from 8 to 128 [29]. Ayala et al. also explicitly identify the current need to develop algorithms that reduce communication to achieve further speedups while maintaining good scalability [23]. Thus, simply combining FFTs with GPU computing does not yield the efficient solver sought here. The key challenge is how to preserve the original discrete operator and the computational advantages of FFTs while avoiding the global data redistribution introduced by full 3D FFTs, and to translate the finite interaction range of the nonlocal operator into a local communication structure suited to multi-GPU parallelism.

papers.title: Linear Axiomatization of Linear Differential Equations
papers.abstract: This article presents an axiomatization of linear differential equations that is complete for topologically open properties with compact initial conditions and time horizons by proving them deductively via a sound reduction to formulas of linear real arithmetic. Indeed, linearity is preserved: linear differential invariants are complete for open properties of linear differential equations and reduce with a linear number of Lie derivatives (per atom) to linear real arithmetic. In particular, this article shows that the linear fragment of differential dynamic logic (dL), a modal extension of standard first-order logic over the reals satisfies these completeness properties. By establishing completeness within decidable linear real arithmetic, the need for proving sophisticated nonlinear formulas of real arithmetic is circumvented. Furthermore, this article establishes generalizations to the nonlinear fragment of dL that enable the practical certification of reachability computations, validating the output of external computations in dL with machine-checkable proofs.

papers.title: Composite Variable Strategies for Continuous Endpoints
papers.abstract: Composite endpoints are common in clinical trials for binary, time-to-event or recurrent outcomes. Recently, there has been interest in estimands for continuous endpoints that employ a composite variable strategy for handling intercurrent events, whereby a value on the continuous scale is defined as the outcome. In this paper we describe these continuous composite endpoints where participants who experience the intercurrent event are assigned a pre-specified value on the outcome scale (which we call the failure value) instead of a measurement. We describe these endpoints and the difficulty of choosing the failure value when the mean is the chosen summary statistic. The large impact of the choice of failure value on the variance of the distribution of the endpoint is quantified as a function of the probability of the event and the standardised difference of the failure value from the mean of the unaffected values. Strategies for choosing failure values are discussed, emphasising the need to balance the clinical relevance and interpretability of the estimand with the need to reliably estimate it. Two potential solutions to situations where there is no relevant and viable choice of failure value are proposed; using failure values based on distributional characteristics to generate clinical relevance and using alternative summary measures to avoid the need to select specific values.

papers.title: Trail-Weighted Influence Scores for Approximate Outcome Prediction in Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: We study trail-weighted pruning of evidence for Bayesian-network prediction. A traversal enumerates the active trails from each evidence node to the outcome, scores each trail by the product of its edge strengths, and drops evidence whose score falls below a threshold. For collider-free networks (chains and forks) over binary variables, we show that the trail score equals the exact correlation between a trail's endpoints, that a chain and a fork with equal edge strengths have identical joint distributions, and that the pruned posterior is within a computable sum of per-trail terms of the exact posterior when each dropped trail lies in its own branch of the outcome node. We prove this bound, check it exhaustively on all small trees, and show that it fails when dropped trails share a branch. In simulations on random trees, thresholding trail scores gives 1.4 to 13 times lower error than random pruning of the same size. We also apply the score, as an unproven heuristic, to seven bnlearn networks with colliders and loops. Keeping the top half of the active evidence by trail score gives lower error than random pruning on all seven, but it is not clearly better than a mutual-information ranking, and scoring costs more than the inference it saves on six of the seven, so we show no speedup. Models trained on trail, graph and information features and tested on networks they never saw do not beat the trail score or mutual information, but trail features carry most of what they use and clearly outperform generic graph features. A bound for general networks is left to future work.

Predicting an outcome YY from partial evidence EE in a Bayesian network requires the posterior P⁡(Y∣E)P(Y\mid E), which is NP-hard to compute exactly in general (Cooper, 1990). A user also wants to know which evidence actually drove the prediction, and ideally to compute the answer from that evidence alone.

Standard relevance pruning uses d-separation. Evidence that is d-separated from YY by other observed nodes can be removed with no error (Geiger, Verma and Pearl, 1990; Shachter, 1998). This is exact but coarse: every evidence node with an active trail to YY is kept, even when that trail is a long chain of weak dependencies whose effect on YY is negligible.

This is exact but coarse: every evidence node with an active trail to YY is kept, even when that trail is a long chain of weak dependencies whose effect on YY is negligible.

We rank the remaining evidence by trail strength. A traversal from YY enumerates the active trails, each trail is scored by composing the strengths of its edges, and evidence whose best trail scores below a threshold is discarded. The score needs no inference, and it names the trail responsible for each piece of evidence. Earlier approximations delete weak links from the network (Kjærulff, 1994; Choi, Chan and Darwiche, 2005). We instead prune the evidence set and leave the network intact.

This paper makes six contributions. The first four concern collider-free networks (chains and forks) over binary variables, and the last two are empirical: 1. Exact trail scores. The product of edge strengths along a trail equals the exact correlation between its endpoints, and mutual information is a monotone function of it. 2. Chain–fork equivalence. A chain and a fork with equal edge strengths have identical joint distributions, so every trail score treats them identically, which illustrates Markov equivalence. 3. On seven bnlearn networks, with colliders and loops handled heuristically, trail pruning beats random pruning on every network and hop distance on four of seven, is not clearly better than a mutual-information ranking, and shows no speedup. 6. A test of learned calibration. Models trained on trail, graph and information features and tested on unseen networks do not beat the trail score or mutual information. Trail features add clear predictive value over generic graph features and make up 64% of the model’s attributions. A bound for colliders and loopy networks is outside this paper and is described under future work.

papers.title: Real In, Real Out: What If We Only Use Real Data for Scene Text Editing?
papers.abstract: Aiming to modify textual content while preserving the original style, Scene Text Editing (STE) has significant practical value in many applications. STE typically requires paired images before and after editing for training. However, recent approaches rely heavily on synthetic paired data and complex disentanglement strategies. They struggle to faithfully capture the diversity and complexity of natural scenes, often producing artifacts or hallucinations. In this work, we challenge the common practice and investigate whether STE can be driven by turning each real sample into its own paired supervision. Concretely, we explore multiple ways to disrupt the original image (e.g., Crop, Shuffle, Mask) to construct self-paired training data, and build a strong baseline (TextRIRO}) upon a conditional diffusion architecture. Our experiments show that combining character-column shuffling with image cropping (Shuffle&Crop) effectively destroys text semantics while preserving key style cues, enabling the model to learn editing behaviors directly from the real text image. With this concise yet real-oriented design, TextRIRO achieves promising performance in both accuracy and visual realism across real-world benchmarks, substantially mitigating the synthetic-to-real domain gap. Furthermore, we leverage TextRIRO to build TextRIRO-3M, a large-scale realistic dataset for long-text recognition by concatenating edited and original images. Experimental results show that training recognition models with TextRIRO-3M significantly improves recognition accuracy, demonstrating that TextRIRO provides highly useful training resources for downstream tasks. Overall, TextRIRO lifts STE to realistic, reliable, and widely applicable new levels. Code is available at https://github.com/YesianRohn/TextRIRO.

Scene Text Editing (STE) aims to extract the style of the given text and replace it with a new string, while maintaining both visual realism and style consistency [36]. STE is typically formulated as a generative task, and its applications grow with the advancement of generative models. It addresses practical needs such as replacing text in images for artistic creation and also facilitates various downstream scene text tasks. Notably, STE shows significant potential in generating data [39] for scene text recognition (STR) [6, 48, 11, 10], as it can generate samples with the same style but different content from existing images.

However, it is hardly possible to get different texts with the same background style in real-world scenarios. To address this, previous methods [36, 38, 29, 20, 43] rely heavily on synthetic data, as shown in Fig. 1(a). On the one hand, two-stage explicit disentanglement methods [36, 38, 29] use rendering tools to synthesize paired images with identical style but different text over a background image, followed by foreground-background separation and fusion. But they fail to separate text from the background, resulting in incomplete removal of the source text, as shown in cases (1) and (2) in Fig. 1(e). On the other hand, implicit disentanglement approaches [20, 43] leverage various pre-trained models to extract features for directly generating target images, which is less controllable, resulting in hallucinations such as case (3), with misspelled or missing characters. Recent efforts [26, 22, 9] have explored semi-supervised learning with real data by erasing itself and writing back or paired training using pseudo-labeled data, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b). Nevertheless, synthetic data still remains dominant. As evident from the editing results in Fig. 1(e), this branch of methods easily leads to case (4): even when the target text is generated, it often appears mismatched in style or contains visible artifacts. Furthermore, inpainting-based STE paradigms (Fig. 1(c)) mask the text region and attempt to restore it using surrounding context [15, 2, 39, 4]. We therefore ask the simplest possible version of the question: What if we only use real data for scene text editing, with neither synthetic triplets nor expensive paired collection?

What if we only use real data for scene text editing, with neither synthetic triplets nor expensive paired collection?

The core challenge is to extract stable style guidance from the source text image while suppressing the side effect from semantic text content. Our key insight is that scene text style mainly lies in low-level cues such as color, texture, and illumination, while semantic text is a high-level sequential structure. Based on this, we explore multiple self-paired real-data schemes that force the model to focus on style rather than semantics. Specifically, we experiment with (i) shuffling and recombining the text region either column-wise or block-wise (Shuffle), (ii) cropping local sub-regions (Crop), and (iii) masking parts of the original image (Mask). Empirically, we find that combining column-wise Shuffle with Crop (Shuffle&Crop) achieves the best performance.

To realize the idea, we propose TextRIRO, a conditional diffusion model that takes only Real data as Input and produces Realistic Output for scene Text editing. During training, TextRIRO applies “Shuffle&Crop” to a real text image to separate its style and semantics, and then reconstructs the original image. By removing the reliance on synthetic data, it overcomes the bottleneck of high-quality generation during inference. For style features, we process them into multi-scale representations and then inject them into the conditional U-Net using the ControlNet-like process [45] for efficient integration. For text encoding, we use an STR pre-trained encoder [16] to extract character-level features, which improves text understanding and enables robust STE transfer.

TextRIRO removes the need for explicit or implicit disentanglement and avoids using the synthetic domain as the main training support. On real benchmarks for STE, it produces more realistic results with markedly reduced “synthetic flavor.” It also achieves higher accuracy on equal-length editing and variable-length editing tasks. These results show that self-paired training on real data effectively moves STE toward realistic generation. We further ask whether STE can help STR data generation [39, 40, 42]. We find that TextRIRO already outperforms existing STE methods, but the editing accuracy still limits direct use as training data. We then use STE as data expansion by concatenating the original image with its edited counterpart. This preserves style but adds content, which yields high-quality, scene-consistent samples for long-text recognition. Starting from the labeled real dataset U14M-Filter [16, 7], we build a 3M-scale dataset, TextRIRO-3M. On Union14M-Benchmark [16], training an STR model on mixed TextRIRO-3M and real data improves overall accuracy by 1.91% over a real-only baseline, and improves the Multi-words subset by 3.28%. These gains indicate that current STR training data are not saturated and STE-based synthetic data substantially boost STR.

papers.title: CyberHull: Deterministic Malicious URL Isolation via Convex Hull
papers.abstract: The emergence of increasingly sophisticated and evasion-resistant phishing attack strategies represents a significant threat to modern cybersecurity, particularly in cyber-physical systems and internet-based networks. Traditional probabilistic methods and certain machine learning approaches often struggle to detect novel attacks and may lack interpretability or portability. To address these challenges, we introduce CyberHull, a resource-efficient and deterministic framework for identifying malicious URLs through mathematically defined convex hull boundaries across multiple orthogonal feature domains, including structural content entropy, hyperlink graph topology, and semantic token distribution. CyberHull constructs compact convex hulls, referred to as vaults, using the QuickHull algorithm, with a training complexity of O(n log n) under suitable assumptions. URL classification is performed through point-in-polyhedron tests that impose relatively low computational overhead on standard CPUs. Experimental results demonstrate that CyberHull achieves 92 percent detection accuracy, substantially outperforming a baseline linear approach based on Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which achieves 32 percent accuracy. Furthermore, CyberHull offers a computationally efficient alternative to resource-intensive deep learning approaches for malicious URL detection.

papers.intro:
The phishing site can be described as a website that mimics the websites of well-known organizations. It is intended to trick users into surrendering their login information and other sensitive data. The use of such websites as a launching pad for cyber attacks means that phishing pages have become more and more sophisticated. The use of advanced phishing frameworks is an emerging and serious threat to the worldwide network systems.

Today’s cyber attackers have moved beyond simple fake domain names. Instead, they use automated phishing generation pipelines that can produce adaptive malicious URLs with advanced evasion techniques such as highly obfuscated HTML structures [1], randomized routing mechanisms [2], and irregular entropy distributions in web content [3]. Industry reports from recent years illustrate the scale and impact of these threats. The Anti-Phishing Working Group (APWG) has reported more than one million phishing campaigns each quarter [4] . The FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) reports billions of dollars in annual losses due to phishing and business-email-compromise incidents [5]. By design, these adversaries mimic legitimate site behavior while constantly changing observable signatures, severely degrading the effectiveness of traditional blacklist and signature-based detection systems [6]. This has resulted in the emergence of novel, previously unseen phishing campaigns that threaten the operational integrity of large-scale Internet infrastructures and critical cyber-physical systems.

To deal with such challenges, cybersecurity professionals have introduced different analytical methods [7], but all of them involve essential weaknesses. Traditional statistical and probabilistic algorithms are usually ineffective since they operate under fixed constraints regarding past data distribution patterns [8]; these systems are prone to quickly deteriorate in case if the attack causes changes to the nature of the signature left by the adversary. Graph-theoretic and heuristic methods, in turn, try to understand the network connections [9] and structure of the content [10], but they are costly and can easily be interfered with by "noise," such as injecting innocent keywords and dead links by the attacker. The proposed framework uses convex geometric representations to give mathematically provable safe regions that represent predictable benign web traffic, enabling deterministic isolation of anomalous requests that stray outside the learned spatial boundaries.

To this end, ℂ\mathbb{C}yberℍ\mathbb{H}ull maps high-variance web attributes such as aggregate content entropy, semantic keyword distributions and hyperlink topology ratios into a multi-dimensional coordinate space. The framework then constructs several independent geometric “Vaults” for cross-space verification using QuickHull [13]-based convex boundary generation. Thus, even if a sophisticated phishing payload succeeds in mimicking one structural property of legitimate traffic, it is mathematically bound to violate the orthogonal constraints of another Vault during spatial containment verification [6]. This multi-tier geometric verification strategy also enhances interpretability by substituting opaque probabilistic decision boundaries with mathematically explainable spatial constraints. Experiments on benchmark phishing datasets demonstrate that the proposed multi-tier geometric framework achieves 92% detection accuracy with significantly lower computational overhead compared to deep learning alternatives. However, applying the framework in practice poses several challenges, including the computational cost of mapping high-dimensional spaces and the need to periodically re-calibrate convex boundaries to account for the evolving topology of legitimate web infrastructures over time.

papers.title: Photometric variability of blue supergiants: Constraints on stellar masses and evolutionary stages
papers.abstract: Blue supergiants (BSGs) are crucial to understanding the evolution of massive stars. Although distinguishing between pre- and post-red supergiant (RSG) phases is challenging, stellar pulsations provide valuable constraints on their masses and evolutionary status. This study analyzes TESS light curves of six BSGs with high L/M to identify periodicities. We performed theoretical modeling of the radial unstable modes to characterize the strange modes. We aim to estimate asteroseismic masses, compare them with spectroscopic and evolutionary mass estimates, and assess the evolutionary stage of the stars. We employed the Lomb-Scargle periodogram and the weighted wavelet Z-transform to address quasiperiodic behavior and time-varying signals. A linear nonadiabatic stability analysis was performed to test for radial perturbations, generating eigenfrequencies that enable stellar mass estimation. In addition, we characterized the stochastic low-frequency variability (SLFV). We derive a first guess at the asteroseismic masses. We find that HD 74371 and HD 79186 are evolving blueward following the RSG phase, while the evolutionary stage of HD 115842 cannot be uniquely determined with the available mass estimates. We also find that HD 52382 and HD 99953 are likely in the post-RSG phase; however, their low masses are difficult to reconcile with the available evolutionary models. The extreme supergiant HD 80077 shows the largest mass discrepancy in the sample, suggesting a more complex evolutionary history. The SLFV properties do not provide a clear diagnostic of the evolutionary stage. These results highlight the potential of asteroseismology as a complementary tool for constraining the evolutionary status of BSGs. However, the mass discrepancies found for some objects indicate that additional observational and theoretical efforts are required.

papers.intro:
There are still important open questions about massive stars that profoundly impact our understanding of their future evolution. These questions involve the formation process of massive stars (Tan et al. 2014), the amount of mass lost via stellar winds (Venero et al. 2024), the interplay between mass loss and stellar pulsations (Kraus et al. 2015; Cidale et al. 2023), the long-standing mass-discrepancy problem (Herrero et al. 1992; Crowther et al. 2006; Searle et al. 2008; Aidelman et al. 2012), the fraction of binary mergers (Langer 2022), among others. Massive stars of more than 88 M☉ remain as early B- or O-type stars in the main sequence (MS) for most of their lifetimes. Beyond this phase, the transition to red supergiants (RSGs) occurs gradually over several 10410^{4} years at an almost constant stellar luminosity while hydrogen-shell burning becomes the dominant energy source. During this evolution, stars pass through the blue supergiant (BSG) phase. In general, stars with initial masses between 20−4520-45 M⊙ undergo a "blue-loop" phase (Ekström et al. 2012), evolving back toward the BSG region during core helium burning. In contrast, stars with initial masses below 2020 M⊙ may undergo blue loops before returning to the red region of the Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram (Sánchez Arias et al. 2023). However, the mass limit separating these evolutionary paths depends on the mixing processes and mass-loss rate, two critical ingredients in stellar evolution, which are often uncertainly modeled. This makes it observationally challenging to identify whether BSGs are in a pre- or post-RSG phase since it cannot be understood from the location of the star on the HR diagram alone. Distinguishing between the two pathways might be plausible by studying the pulsation modes of BSG stars (Saio et al. 2013b), through photometric and spectroscopic analyses (Saio et al. 2006; Kraus et al. 2012; Kraus et al. 2015; Sánchez Arias et al. 2023). Specifically, this distinction relies on the fact that significant mass loss after going through the RSG stage significantly increases the luminosity-to-mass ratio (L/ML/M) than during the first crossing. Saio et al. (2013a) showed that radial pulsations are excited in the BSG region only in models that were previously RSGs, while, at a given effective temperature, these models also exhibit a much richer spectrum of non-radial pulsation modes than their pre-RSG counterparts. These pulsations cause either slight variations or slight changes in the broadening of line profiles (Simón-Díaz et al. 2010; Aerts et al. 2009; Aerts et al. 2010; Bowman 2023; de Burgos et al. 2023).

Typical oscillation modes observed in BSGs are p and g modes excited by the κ\kappa mechanism at the Fe bump of opacity (Pamyatnykh 1999, see, e.g.,) and stochastic excitations caused by different mechanisms (Mathis et al. 2014; Aerts and Rogers 2015). For stars with L/ML/M (in solar units) exceeding 10410^{4}, the stellar envelopes are characterized by short thermal timescales and are dominated by radiation pressure (Gautschy and Glatzel 1990b; Glatzel and Kraus 2024). In this regime, the standard spectrum of acoustic modes is crossed by additional modes, the so-called strange modes, that cannot be explained by classical κ\kappa and ϵ\epsilon mechanisms (Gautschy and Glatzel 1990b; Glatzel 1994; Yadav and Glatzel 2016). These strange mode instabilities persist over the entire range of effective temperatures from red to BSGs and have been associated with variable mass-loss phenomena (Glatzel et al. 1999; Kraus et al. 2015; Haucke et al. 2018; Cidale et al. 2023; Glatzel and Kraus 2024), with direct consequences for their evolutionary trajectory and final fate.

In this study, we aim to identify the oscillation modes and analyze the frequencies of selected southern BSGs as a means for constraining their properties. Nowadays, satellite data enable studies of light curves of massive stars over long time intervals with a temporal resolution of a few minutes, allowing for the detection of "micro" oscillations. A good example is the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) space mission (Ricker et al. 2015). The availability of high-precision TESS photometric data provides an excellent opportunity to investigate six BSGs (HD~52382, HD~74371, HD~79186, HD~80077, HD~99953, and HD~115842) selected from the sample of Haucke et al. (2018). All exhibit L/M>104L/M>10^{4}, in solar units, making them promising candidates for strange-mode pulsations. We also aim to compare the observed frequencies with the predictions from linear, nonadiabatic pulsation models. This comparison allows us to estimate the asteroseismic masses of the stars, which can then be contrasted with those derived from evolutionary models or spectroscopic techniques, thereby providing insights into the mass discrepancy problem.

papers.title: TOI-3686: A Hot Jupiter and Sub-Neptune In A 2:1 Mean-Motion Resonance
papers.abstract: Hot Jupiters are typically thought to be "lonely", but a small and growing subset of them have been found to have nearby planets in the same system. We present the discovery of a new member of this class of systems, TOI-3686. TOI-3686 c is a hot Jupiter with $P_\mathrm{orb} = 5.078$ days detected by NASA's TESS mission that shows peak-to-peak transit timing variations (TTVs) of 40 minutes, amongst the largest ever observed for a hot Jupiter. A subsequent search of the TESS data revealed the transits of a second planet, TOI-3686 b, a sub-Neptune with $P_\mathrm{orb} = 2.54$~days and peak-to-peak TTVs of 10 hours, $\sim 16\%$ of its orbital period. We characterized the system through photodynamical modeling of photometry from TESS and ground-based facilities, as well as radial velocity measurements from the NEID and MAROON-X spectrographs. We find that the two planets in the TOI-3686 system are deep in a 2:1 mean-motion resonance, making this the only hot Jupiter system currently known to be in a truly resonant configuration, which may be related to its $\lesssim1$~Gyr system age. Systems like TOI-3686 likely formed through a dynamically quiescent pathway and were captured into resonance after migration through a disk, and may represent the high-mass end of processes that occur in compact systems of smaller planets.

papers.intro:
Most hot Jupiters—giant planets with orbital periods of less than ten days—appear to be isolated, without nearby planetary companions [80, 130, 64, 125]. This observation has been interpreted as evidence that hot Jupiters form farther out in the protoplanetary disk and arrive at their current close-in orbits via a dynamically disruptive, high-eccentricity migration pathway. In this picture, a wide-orbiting giant planet is excited onto a highly eccentric orbit through mechanisms like planet-planet scattering [111, 141] or secular interactions [144, 45, 145], before undergoing orbit circularization due to tidal interactions with the host star [44]. Since any interior planets would likely be disrupted during the high-eccentricity phase [15], such hot Jupiters would end up isolated.

papers.title: Resolving the extended interstellar medium of infrared galaxies II. Fine-structure line emission
papers.abstract: We investigate how star formation and active galactic nuclei (AGNs) shape the ionized and neutral interstellar medium in 67 nearby luminous and ultraluminous infrared galaxies from the Great Observatories All-sky LIRG Survey (GOALS). Combining mid-infrared (MIR) spectral mapping from the Spitzer Infrared Spectrograph with far-infrared (FIR) spectroscopy from the Herschel Photodetector Array Camera and Spectrometer, we measure fine-structure emission lines in aperture grids extending to projected galactocentric distances of about 14 kpc. We compare the measurements with CLOUDY photoionization models to constrain the ionization parameter, hydrogen density, stellar age, and metallicity. In starburst-dominated galaxies, the combined MIR+FIR fits yield a decreasing ionization parameter with radius, approximately constant hydrogen densities, uniformly young stellar populations, and flat metallicity profiles. MIR-only fits instead yield an increasing ionization parameter with radius, highlighting the importance of FIR diagnostics, particularly the [C II] emission associated with photodissociation regions, in constraining the multiphase gas. In the strongest AGN-dominated system, the nucleus and inner extended regions show elevated [Ne III]/[Ne II] and suppressed [C II]/[O I] ratios, while the outermost regions, at projected distances of about 6 kpc and beyond, show values typical of star-forming regions. This suggests that the AGN may affect gas excitation out to about 5 kpc. Our results demonstrate the importance of combining MIR and FIR diagnostics to recover radial trends that can be hidden in galaxy-integrated measurements. Together with Paper I, they provide a benchmark for spatially resolved studies of gas and dust in starbursts and AGN-hosting galaxies.

papers.intro:
Infrared (IR) spectroscopy, particularly at mid- and far-infrared wavelengths (MIR and FIR, respectively), plays a central role in the study of the interstellar medium (ISM) in galaxies by providing access to gas and dust components that are heavily obscured at optical and ultraviolet wavelengths. A significant fraction of the physical processes associated with star formation and nuclear activity in massive galaxies takes place in dust-embedded environments, where extinction substantially limits the diagnostic power of traditional tracers. Infrared observations, by contrast, are only weakly affected by dust attenuation and therefore offer direct probes of the physical conditions in obscured regions of the ISM (Spinoglio and Malkan, 1992). IR fine-structure emission lines enable a powerful set of diagnostics with which we can investigate the multiphase structure of the ISM. Their line ratios are well known to be sensitive to key physical parameters such as the hardness of the radiation field, the ionization parameter, the gas density, and the metallicity (Decarli and Díaz-Santos, 2025, e.g.). MIR lines trace photoionized gas in H II regions and are widely used to constrain the properties of the ionizing stellar population, while FIR lines dominate the cooling of neutral gas in photodissociation regions (PDRs), which are the interface zones between ionized and molecular gas (Tielens and Hollenbach, 1985; Wolfire et al., 1990).

Infrared observations, by contrast, are only weakly affected by dust attenuation and therefore offer direct probes of the physical conditions in obscured regions of the ISM (Spinoglio and Malkan, 1992). IR fine-structure emission lines enable a powerful set of diagnostics with which we can investigate the multiphase structure of the ISM. Their line ratios are well known to be sensitive to key physical parameters such as the hardness of the radiation field, the ionization parameter, the gas density, and the metallicity (Decarli and Díaz-Santos, 2025, e.g.). MIR lines trace photoionized gas in H II regions and are widely used to constrain the properties of the ionizing stellar population, while FIR lines dominate the cooling of neutral gas in photodissociation regions (PDRs), which are the interface zones between ionized and molecular gas (Tielens and Hollenbach, 1985; Wolfire et al., 1990).

During the past two decades, the Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) on board the Spitzer Space Telescope (Spitzer hereafter; Werner et al. (2004)) enabled uniform spectroscopic observations of large and diverse galaxy samples. Measurements of fine-structure emission lines such as [Ne ii]13 and [Ne iii]15 provided constraints on the properties of the ionizing stellar population, the hardness of the radiation field (Ho and Keto, 2007), and the relative contributions of star formation and activity from active galactic nuclei (AGNs) (Tommasin et al., 2008; Tommasin et al., 2010), while density-sensitive ratios including [S iii]33/[S iii]19 allowed us to obtain extinction-independent estimates of electron densities in ionized gas. At longer wavelengths, the Herschel Space Observatory (Herschel hereafter; Pilbratt et al. (2010)) extended these diagnostics into the FIR with improved sensitivity. Spectroscopy with the Photodetector Array Camera and Spectrometer (PACS) and the Spectral and Photometric Imaging Receiver (SPIRE) on board Herschel provided access to the dominant cooling lines of the neutral ISM, [Cii]158 and [Oi]63, which trace the cold neutral gas (Tielens and Hollenbach, 1985; Spinoglio et al., 2015). Large Herschel surveys revealed variations in the FIR line emission with global galaxy properties, demonstrating the sensitivity of these diagnostics to changes in ionization parameter, gas density, and dust–gas coupling (Graciá-Carpio et al., 2011; Farrah et al., 2013; Díaz-Santos et al., 2013; Díaz-Santos et al., 2014; Rosenberg et al., 2015).

While many IR spectroscopic studies have focused on nuclear and/or galaxy-integrated measurements, spatially resolved observations have shown that the ISM properties change significantly on kiloparsec scales. MIR spectral mapping with Spitzer revealed extended ionized gas and star formation in disks and circumnuclear regions, traced by low-ionization lines, and spatial variations in the radiation hardness (Armus et al., 2004; Armus et al., 2006; Pereira-Santaella et al., 2010; Díaz-Santos et al., 2011). FIR observations further showed that several FIR lines exhibit deficits with increasing dust temperature, most notably [Cii]158, [Nii]122, and [Nii]205. (2016); Herrera-Camus et al. (2018)). However, the majority of these combined Spitzer+Herschel studies relied on galaxy-integrated measurements for entire galaxies. Spatially resolved analyses that combine these datasets have remained challenging because their sensitivities and spatial resolutions are different.

This work is the second of a two-part series of papers that investigates the ISM in a subsample of the Great Observatories All-sky LIRG Survey (GOALS) galaxies (Armus et al., 2009). The first paper (Paper I; Lofaro et al. (2026)) focused on the resolved measurements of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), while this work examines the spatial structure and physical properties of the ISM in the subsample. Our analysis targets regions located well beyond the nuclear zones and extends to galactocentric distances that exceed the spatial coverage typically probed by a single pointing of any James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) integral-field unit (IFU). We focus on how AGN activity and star formation shape the ionized and neutral gas in different galactic environments. By combining spatially resolved MIR maps from Spitzer with IFU measurements from Herschel, we present a joint spatially resolved analysis of LIRGs on kiloparsec scales.

papers.title: Resolving the extended interstellar medium of infrared galaxies I. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon emission
papers.abstract: We investigate spatial variations in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) properties and photoelectric heating efficiency in 67 nearby luminous infrared galaxies from the Great Observatories All-sky LIRG Survey (GOALS). Using mid-infrared spectroscopy from Spitzer and far-infrared cooling-line maps from Herschel, we extract spectra in concentric annuli and matched aperture grids out to about 14 kpc. PAH features are measured with the CAFE spectral decomposition tool. We trace photoelectric heating efficiency by combining PAH emission with cooling lines after isolating the neutral-gas contribution. In starburst galaxies, the PAH 11.3/7.7 ratio rises out to about 5 kpc while 6.2/7.7 remains nearly constant, indicating predominantly large, neutral PAHs. Between 5 and 8 kpc, 11.3/7.7 continues to rise while inferred PAH sizes decrease. Beyond 8 kpc, 11.3/7.7 falls and 6.2/7.7 rises, indicating smaller, more ionized PAHs. These trends are consistent with PAH photodestruction near the central starburst. Strong active galactic nucleus (AGN) systems show more neutral PAHs and harder radiation fields in their nuclear and inner regions. Beyond about 5 kpc, PAHs become more ionized and approach the starburst locus as the radiation field weakens. Strong AGNs influence average PAH charge states at 6-14 kpc as effectively as moderate AGNs at 1-6 kpc. Photoelectric heating efficiency increases with radius in both starburst and AGN-hosting galaxies as the radiation field weakens. In starbursts, higher efficiency is associated with more neutral PAHs, while AGN-dominated systems show the opposite relation. These results provide quantitative, spatially resolved constraints on the extent of AGN effects on dust properties in a population of luminous infrared galaxies.

Luminous infrared galaxies span the full evolutionary merger sequence, from isolated galaxies to advanced mergers. They are particularly significant among the star-forming galaxy population as they exhibit elevated star formation rates (SFRs) and specific SFRs (sSFRs), resulting from the concentration of large quantities of gas and dust toward their nuclei (Sanders and Mirabel, 1996), which, in interacting systems, is driven by the loss of angular momentum during the dynamical interaction (Hopkins et al., 2008). This phase profoundly impacts the evolution of merging galaxies, triggering a morphological transformation into an elliptical galaxy after the suppression of star formation and black hole growth due to feedback from the dominant energy source(s) (e.g., Hopkins et al. 2008). Therefore, LIRGs represent a critical phase in galaxy evolution studies, and potentially highlight gaps in our understanding of the transitional processes that shape galaxy morphology and activity.

While LIRGs are uncommon in the local Universe and ULIRGs even rarer, their numbers increase dramatically (by a factor of ∼\mathchar 12824100) at z∼\mathchar 128241 (Le Floc’h et al., 2005; Magnelli et al., 2009). At this redshift, LIRGs dominate the star formation activity and the IR background, whereas at z∼\mathchar 128242, the so-called cosmic noon, ULIRGs become predominant (Le Floc’h et al., 2005; Pérez-González et al., 2005; Caputi et al., 2007; Berta et al., 2011; Magnelli et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2011). This dramatic evolution highlights the importance of understanding the mechanisms that give birth to the LIRG phase. Nearby LIRGs serve as an essential link between normal star-forming galaxies, such as the Milky Way, and the most extreme systems dominated by AGNs (Sanders and Mirabel 1996).

Among the many infrared tracers of the interstellar medium (ISM) in LIRGs, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are of particular importance. PAHs are small carbonaceous grains that efficiently absorb ultraviolet (UV) photons and re-emit the energy through a series of prominent vibrational features between roughly 3 and 17 μ\mathchar 28950m (Leger and Puget, 1984; Allamandola et al., 1985; Allamandola et al., 1989; Draine and Li, 2001). In addition to their role as tracers of star formation, PAHs play a fundamental role in regulating the thermal balance of the ISM (Galliano et al., 2008; Tielens, 2008). PAH emission probes photoelectric heating in photodissociation regions (PDRs), predominantly composed of cold neutral gas (Wolfire et al., 2003), which are the interfaces between ionized gas in Hii regions and the molecular gas in H2 clouds (Wolfire et al., 1990). When a UV photon is absorbed by a PAH grain, part of its energy can be used to eject an electron via the photoelectric effect. The resulting photoelectron transfers kinetic energy to the surrounding gas through collisions, primarily with H and H2. This heating increases the gas temperature and enables the collisional excitation of C+ and O, which subsequently radiate and act as the dominant cooling channels of the ISM (Tielens and Hollenbach 1985; Hollenbach and Tielens 1997; Kaufman et al. 1999 and references therein). Therefore, the efficiency of photoelectric heating depends sensitively on the physical properties of the dust grains, particularly their size distribution and charge state (Bakes and Tielens, 1994).

papers.title: Characterizing supersolid phase transitions in trapped quantum gases with tilted dipoles at finite temperature
papers.abstract: Motivated by a recent experimental work arXiv:2608.20327, we theoretically investigate the nature of phase transitions in a trapped dipolar quantum gas upon tuning the contact interaction strength and dipole orientation. Using extended Gross-Pitaevskii simulations including thermal and quantum effects, we map the phase diagram comprising unmodulated superfluids, triangular droplet arrays, and stripe states. We further characterize the order of the transitions separating them through imaginary-time hysteresis analysis. The unmodulated-to-modulated transition evolves from discontinuous to continuous with increasing dipole tilt before becoming discontinuous again at large tilts. The degree of continuity is further affected by particle number, temperature, and confinement. While continuous behavior generally correlates with the emergence of stripe states, this correspondence is not systematic, and finite-size effects also influence the continuity of the transition. The triangular-to-stripe transition is found to be discontinuous at small contact interaction strengths and becomes increasingly continuous upon approaching the unmodulated-to-modulated phase boundary. Our results reveal a tunable transition order in finite dipolar quantum gases and provide guidance for its experimental investigation.

papers.intro:
The theory of phase transitions describes how distinct macroscopic phases emerge as external parameters are varied [20]. Within the Landau paradigm, a phase transition is characterized by an order parameter, and, in the thermodynamic limit, it is associated with a nonanalyticity of the free energy. The nature of this nonanalyticity determines the order of the transition and governs the system’s behavior in its vicinity. While more general types of phase transitions exist, conventional symmetry-breaking transitions are commonly classified as first- or second-order. A first-order transition is characterized by a discontinuity in the first derivative of the free energy. This typically entails a discontinuous change of the order parameter at the transition, the metastability of the competing phases in the vicinity of the transition, and hysteresis upon its dynamical crossing. In contrast, second-order transitions exhibit higher-order nonanalyticities of the free energy, are characterized by a continuous evolution of the order parameter, and are associated with critical scaling behaviors defining broad universality classes.

In contrast, second-order transitions exhibit higher-order nonanalyticities of the free energy, are characterized by a continuous evolution of the order parameter, and are associated with critical scaling behaviors defining broad universality classes.

Phase transitions become notably rich when several orders compete within the same system. Supersolids provide an ideal setting in this respect, combining superfluidity and crystalline orders with potentially different spatial arrangements [22, 21, 10]. Such a rich landscape is especially well realized and controlled in dipolar quantum gases [16, 17, 15, 48, 11, 47, 34, 4, 8, 24, 13]. Supersolid states have been realized in magnetic-gas experiments in the form of one- and two-dimensional droplet arrangements with dipoles polarized along the tight confinement axis [34, 8, 48, 11, 15, 16, 17, 4] as well as, most recently, two-dimensional droplet and stripe states with tilted dipoles [24, 13]. In the latter case, transitions between unmodulated superfluids, triangular supersolids, stripe supersolids, and the corresponding insulating states were explored in a single system upon tuning dipole tilt and interaction strength [13].

Supersolids provide an ideal setting in this respect, combining superfluidity and crystalline orders with potentially different spatial arrangements [22, 21, 10]. Such a rich landscape is especially well realized and controlled in dipolar quantum gases [16, 17, 15, 48, 11, 47, 34, 4, 8, 24, 13]. Supersolid states have been realized in magnetic-gas experiments in the form of one- and two-dimensional droplet arrangements with dipoles polarized along the tight confinement axis [34, 8, 48, 11, 15, 16, 17, 4] as well as, most recently, two-dimensional droplet and stripe states with tilted dipoles [24, 13]. In the latter case, transitions between unmodulated superfluids, triangular supersolids, stripe supersolids, and the corresponding insulating states were explored in a single system upon tuning dipole tilt and interaction strength [13].

These experimental advances have been accompanied by extensive theoretical efforts to understand the stability, structure, and phase diagrams of dipolar supersolids. Their description largely relies on the extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation (eGPE), an effective mean-field approach incorporating beyond-mean-field corrections from quantum fluctuations, which are essential for stabilizing droplets and supersolid states [49, 50, 3, 44, 14]. This framework has been used extensively to map the zero-temperature phase diagrams of dipolar gases [2, 38, 54, 36, 4, 37, 55, 32, 41]. More recently, thermal fluctuations have also been included in finite-temperature extensions of the eGPE [40, 23] and their impact on the phase diagram has been studied [9, 42, 53, 47, 43]. Depending on contact and dipolar interaction strengths, dipole orientation, density, confinement, and temperature, the gas can evolve between unmodulated superfluid and density-modulated states with a rich variety of crystalline structures, varying from triangular to stripe and labyrinthine states, or even honeycomb for increasing densities [33, 54, 34, 25, 8, 37, 23].

The nature of the phase transitions connecting these different states has also attracted significant theoretical interest. Studies in infinite systems have shown that the order of the unmodulated-to-modulated transition can vary depending on the gas parameters and geometry. For one-dimensional crystals, it can be continuous or discontinuous depending on the gas density [7]. For two-dimensional crystalline structures, triangular arrangements generally favor a first-order transition, whereas stripes, which are effectively one-dimensional modulations, may yield continuous transitions [33, 54, 37, 39, 4, 32]. Further studies have investigated the influence of finite size and trapping on the continuity of the transition [4, 36, 46], and of finite temperature on the phase boundaries [42, 53]. The triangular-to-stripe transition has also been investigated in the thermodynamic limit [54, 37, 32]. It is generally first-order but has been predicted to become second-order with increasing dipole tilt, depending on the density [32]. However, the combined influence of dipole tilt, temperature, particle number, and confinement on the character of the different transitions remains largely unexplored.

The nature of the phase transitions connecting these different states has also attracted significant theoretical interest. Studies in infinite systems have shown that the order of the unmodulated-to-modulated transition can vary depending on the gas parameters and geometry. For one-dimensional crystals, it can be continuous or discontinuous depending on the gas density [7]. For two-dimensional crystalline structures, triangular arrangements generally favor a first-order transition, whereas stripes, which are effectively one-dimensional modulations, may yield continuous transitions [33, 54, 37, 39, 4, 32]. Further studies have investigated the influence of finite size and trapping on the continuity of the transition [4, 36, 46], and of finite temperature on the phase boundaries [42, 53]. The triangular-to-stripe transition has also been investigated in the thermodynamic limit [54, 37, 32]. It is generally first-order but has been predicted to become second-order with increasing dipole tilt, depending on the density [32]. However, the combined influence of dipole tilt, temperature, particle number, and confinement on the character of the different transitions remains largely unexplored.

In this work, motivated by the experimental exploration of Ref. [13], we investigate how the nature of the phase transitions in a trapped dipolar gas evolves with dipole tilt and contact interaction strength, for varying trap parameters, temperature, and atom number. In particular, we consider parameter ranges consistent with the experimental values of Ref. [13]. In Sec. II, we introduce the system and the extended Gross-Pitaevskii framework used to model it, including quantum and finite-temperature corrections. In Sec. III, we explore the phase diagram of our trapped gas of magnetic atoms. We investigate the unmodulated-to-modulated and triangular-to-stripe transitions via hysteresis between opposite imaginary-time propagation directions in Sec. III.1 and III.2, respectively. Finally, in Sec. III.3, we discuss the distinct unmodulated-to-modulated transition behavior found at large tilt angles. Sec. IV summarizes the results and gives directions for further studies.

papers.title: Agentic Verified Optimization of Real-World Software
papers.abstract: Program optimization aims to improve performance while preserving behavior. Coding agents can already make programs faster by changing algorithms, data structures, and execution strategies. However, existing equivalence checks mostly rely on tests, which agents have been shown to exploit, passing the tests without preserving the intended behavior. We propose agentic verified optimization, in which an agent produces a faster implementation together with a machine-checked proof of equivalence to the existing one. Because the existing implementation serves as the specification, the task avoids the specification-writing bottleneck of verified code generation, and recent advances in theorem proving make the proofs attainable. We formulate the task at the function and repository levels in Lean 4, where programs can be both executed and reasoned about. Few real-world applications are written in Lean, so we develop Aqueduct, an agentic framework that migrates C, C++, Go, and Rust programs into native Lean, validates each port by differential testing against its original. On the 189 reference implementations in Verina, agents produce faster proved rewrites for 156, including algorithmic changes such as replacing exponential recursion with dynamic programming. On 17 migrated applications, their 92 proved rewrites speed up 47 of 51 application scenarios. These application-level gains are smaller than the function-level ones, making the choice of functions to optimize an important problem. Current agents can thus already carry out verified optimization on both standalone functions and applications migrated from real programs. We discuss the remaining challenges and the steps toward verified optimization in production.

papers.intro:
Coding agents are increasingly used to write and modify software [6, 30, 82]. They are now also asked to make code faster [26, 18, 74]. This goal continues a long line of work on automatic optimization. Before language models, superoptimizers searched instruction sequences [47, 62], learned models guided search over programs [5], and reinforcement learning discovered faster algorithms [46]. Language models and coding agents have since taken on the task, as PIE [65] rewrites programs for speed, KernelBench [53] studies efficient GPU kernel generation, and Jitskit [40] synthesizes systems specialized to a workload. These optimizations range from local changes that eliminate redundant computation to new data representations and algorithms. Whatever the strategy, a faster replacement must preserve the behavior of the program it replaces.

Agents can already find substantial performance gains, but existing work checks behavior preservation with tests, which, as Dijkstra [16] observed, can show the presence of errors but not their absence. This limitation matters more when the tests also define an agent’s reward. Agents then learn to pass the tests rather than preserve the behavior, a pattern studied as reward hacking [67] and observed in coding agents that special-case the tested inputs [92]. In optimization, reward hacking yields speedups from programs that do not preserve behavior. Jitskit [40] describes an apparent 6×6\times improvement that came from regenerating test values rather than storing them, and an audit found correctness failures in 39.5% of the GPU kernels that an optimization harness had accepted [63]. A proof of equivalence avoids this problem because it covers every input, the criterion used in translation validation [55, 50] and regression verification [24, 10]. With a proof as the check, an agent can change algorithms and data representations freely without weakening correctness.

We study agentic verified optimization, in which an agent produces a faster implementation f′f^{\prime} of a reference function ff together with a machine-checked equivalence proof. The proof establishes ∀x,f⁡(x)=f′​(x)\forall x,\,f(x)=f^{\prime}(x), with the reference implementation ff as the specification for correctness. This avoids the specification-writing problem in verified code generation, where writing specifications that capture the intended behavior remains difficult, even manually [19, 86, 45]. This task can also be viewed as the refinement step that formal methods have long advocated, in which a simple implementation is proved correct and then refined into a fast one that inherits its guarantees. By hand, it is costly and has been reserved for critical domains such as cryptography [21]. Agents are a natural fit for this work. In verified code generation, proofs can push agents toward simple implementations [84]. Agentic verified optimization keeps the simple, proved version and then allow agent to search complicated, optimized version with the same correctness guarantee. The task in turn helps improve agents. Every function in an existing codebase is an instance with its specification in place, and because correctness is fixed while speedup is a continuous measure rather than a pass rate, the task is open-ended and does not saturate as agents improve.

The task couples implementation and proof search. For example, replacing recursive enumeration with dynamic programming can remove repeated work, but its proof needs an invariant connecting table entries to the original recursion. An implementation may be equivalent and fast yet difficult for the agent to prove within a limited search budget. Conversely, a readily proved rewrite may offer little improvement. The agent must decide whether to improve a candidate further, invest in its proof, or pursue another implementation. Verified optimization therefore tests how agents coordinate program reasoning, performance analysis, and proof construction.

papers.title: Temporal Evidence Allocation For Longitudinal Clinical Retrieval: A Position And Technical Report
papers.abstract: Electronic health records are written to support care, not retrieval. Across years of oncology notes, the primary diagnosis is restated in report after report, while the events that shape a patient's course, such as a recurrence or a change in therapy, may be recorded only once. A retriever that ranks passages by similarity to the query keeps returning the repeated material and can miss these transitions, that is, it exhibits temporal redundancy across historical narratives. We argue that longitudinal clinical retrieval should be treated as allocating a limited evidence budget across time, not just ranking by relevance. We separate the task into three objectives: temporal evidence allocation, candidate reconstruction, and clinical validation. In Study A (13 clinical queries over 20 patient records, with two-stage reconstruction), the Temporal-15 configuration reaches a milestone slot recall of 0.538, compared with 0.388 for the Global-50 baseline. However, it also retrieves far more evidence (496 versus 50 indexed units per query), so the gain cannot be credited to allocation alone. When evidence is held fixed, removing prompted precedence rules raises schema-order reversals from 0.010 to 0.080. A five-patient, single-query pilot with fixed budgets finds that wider temporal coverage does not reliably yield more dated milestones. Together, these results suggest that how much a record says about a period is a poor guide to how useful that period is as evidence. Because no expert reference timelines are available, our measurements describe retrieval behavior rather than clinical accuracy. This position and technical report presents the retrieval analysis behind the Onco-CONSTRUE framework and sets out a research agenda for budget-constrained longitudinal clinical retrieval.

papers.title: Auditing Where Concept Bottleneck Accuracy Comes From on CUB
papers.abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) promise predictions that humans can inspect and correct through concepts such as "curved beak". Yet on CUB-200-2011, their standard benchmark, progress is measured like that of ordinary classifiers: by task and concept accuracy. Neither reveals whether the label is predicted from the exposed concept scores, or whether a concept is supported by visual evidence of that concept rather than by co-occurring features such as cues to the species as a whole. We audit where the accuracy of CBMs and Concept Embedding Models (CEMs) on CUB comes from. The CUB annotations are too noisy to explain it: class-level training labels agree with per-image annotations on only ~82% of image--concept pairs, and classifiers trained on per-image annotations reach only ~37% species accuracy. Leakage probes show that CEM predictions cannot be reconstructed from their concept scores; the missing class information sits in internal embeddings. We identify four design axes through which class information can enter concept scores---receptive field, shared versus concept-specific representations, norm-dependent scoring, and task supervision. An ablation shows that most of it enters through non-local features: restricting a ResNet50 backbone to local BagNet patches lowers the accuracy recoverable from concept scores from 72% to 43%, close to what ground-truth annotations support, while joint training raises it again at the cost of concept accuracy. Localization and occlusion show that locality makes grounding measurable but does not guarantee it: under class-level labels, local concept scores use the head as a proxy for body, wing, and tail concepts, and CEM concept scores barely respond to occluding their supporting part. Task and concept accuracy should thus support, not drive, the evaluation of CBMs, and given the noisy annotations, CUB accuracy gaps should not be overinterpreted.

papers.intro:
Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) [15; 23] are designed to make predictions through human-understandable concepts, such as “has red wing” or “long beak”. Their appeal rests on two promises beyond predictive accuracy: interpretability – a decision can be inspected through the concepts that produced it – and intervenability – a decision can be corrected by correcting those concepts.

Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) [15; 23] are designed to make predictions through human-understandable concepts, such as “has red wing” or “long beak”. Their appeal rests on two promises beyond predictive accuracy: interpretability – a decision can be inspected through the concepts that produced it – and intervenability – a decision can be corrected by correcting those concepts.

The CUB-200-2011 dataset [26] is the standard visual benchmark for this paradigm. As a result, progress in CBMs is often summarized by higher classification accuracy on CUB, whether reported at the class (species) level or at the instance level – the same metric used to evaluate ordinary classifiers. This creates a tension: neither of these accuracy numbers confirms the interpretability promise above – that predictions are actually mediated by concepts a human can recognize in the image, e.g., actually seeing a curved beak, not merely a pattern that correlates with the label.

The interpretability promise can fail in two distinct ways. First, the label predictor could rely on information that the concepts do not express: either by bypassing the exposed concept scores – the model’s concept interface – altogether (e.g., through the internal concept embedding in CEMs), or through structured variation encoded within the concept scores themselves, as soft concept scores are known to do [17; 10]. Second, even when the label predictor uses only the concept scores, those scores could be predicted from image features that co-occur with the concept in the training data but that a human would not perceive as evidence for it – e.g., predicting “curved beak” from cues to the species as a whole. Such a concept score is predictive, but not visually grounded in the sense a human inspecting the image would expect.

This second failure mode also undermines intervenability. The label predictor learns what a concept score means from the model’s own scores: if the score for “curved beak” in fact tracks species cues elsewhere in the image, the label predictor learns to read it as species evidence. A human who corrects this score after inspecting the beak then feeds the label predictor a value whose meaning differs from the one it was trained on, so the effect of the correction on the prediction no longer reflects the human’s judgment about the beak. We do not evaluate interventions directly; instead, we test their precondition, namely whether concept scores are driven by the evidence a human would inspect.

As a first check, we therefore estimate how much task information the CUB concept annotations themselves provide, by training classifiers on ground-truth instance-level concept vectors. The resulting concept-only reference accuracy is only ≈\approx37%. Because the annotations are noisy – a single Amazon Mechanical Turk annotator per image – this value marks a reference band rather than a strict upper bound on faithful concept reasoning – yet even allowing for this noise, it is far below the 70%+ accuracies reported by widely used CBM and CEM models, which suggests that concept annotations alone do not explain those numbers.

For the second, we ask how class information enters the concept scores themselves. We identify four design choices through which this can happen – the receptive field of the features, shared versus concept-specific representations, norm-dependent scoring, and task supervision of the concept scores – and sweep receptive field, head sharing, and task supervision systematically within one model template, measuring how much class information a probe recovers from the frozen concept scores of each configuration. The receptive field turns out to be the main lever, and the configuration in which all four choices are constrained carries roughly as much class information as the ground-truth concept annotations. Because this configuration computes each concept score from a local image patch, it also makes grounding measurable: spatial localization tests whether its concept scores peak on the image regions a human would use to recognize the concept. Our contributions are fourfold: (i) We show that the CUB concept annotations alone cannot account for the accuracies reported by CBM/CEM models: classifiers trained directly on ground-truth concept vectors reach only ≈\approx37% task accuracy – far below the 70%+ typically reported – and this gap partly reflects a structural mismatch between the class-level concept labels used for training (identical for every image of a species) and the instance-level concept evidence actually visible in each image; (ii) We identify four design axes – receptive field, shared concept representations, norm-dependent scoring, and task supervision – through which CBMs and CEMs can place class information in their concept scores that is not backed by visual evidence for the annotated concepts; (iii) We audit where CBM and CEM accuracy on CUB comes from: leakage probes show that CEM predictions partly bypass the exposed concept scores, and a systematic ablation over these axes shows that non-local features and task supervision are the main sources of class information in concept scores, while closing all four pathways brings this information down to the level of the concept annotations; (iv) We show that locality makes grounding measurable but does not guarantee it: under class-level supervision, local concept scores use the head as a proxy for body, wing, and tail concepts, and CEM concept scores barely respond when the evidence that should support them is occluded.

papers.title: Sum-over-poles framework for quantum embedding to approach the real-frequency axis
papers.abstract: We introduce a real-frequency framework for the quantum embedding of solids, based on sum-over-poles (SOP) representations. We partition the lattice into periodically repeated interacting fragments and derive an embedded Dyson equation for the fragment, to be solved self-consistently. The resulting scheme generalizes the algorithmic-inversion method of our previous work to interacting Hamiltonians and is closely related to dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), especially when an extended impurity problem is introduced. By exploiting the compact pole expansion of the embedding potential, we carry out the self-consistent procedure close to the real axis, which avoids ill-posed analytic continuation. In addition, the SOP representation allows us to introduce a pole-and-residue dynamics, which we use to reach the self-consistent solution. After deriving the method, we benchmark it against exact-diagonalization implementations of DMFT on the one-dimensional Hubbard ring at half filling. The framework offers a natural route to real-space dynamical quantum embedding, for periodic systems as well as for strongly correlated defects in materials.

Understanding the physics of interacting electrons remains one of the central challenges in condensed-matter theory. Many of the most striking phenomena in correlated materials - metal-insulator transitions [21], quasiparticle renormalization [32], Kondo screening [35], unconventional superconductivity [6]- arise from a subtle interplay of itinerancy and local interactions that cannot be captured within static or mean-field descriptions of the electronic structure. While first-principles frameworks such as density-functional theory [23] often provide reliable band structures, their inherent lack of dynamical correlations limits their predictive power when treating strongly correlated materials.

While first-principles frameworks such as density-functional theory [23] often provide reliable band structures, their inherent lack of dynamical correlations limits their predictive power when treating strongly correlated materials.

Quantum embedding approaches provide a powerful and systematically improvable route to bridge this gap. In a nutshell, these approaches are based on the identification of a ”fragment” of the whole system, which is ideally solved exactly, while the rest of the system and the interaction between the two parts are treated within some suitable approximation. For some molecular system of impurities, the natural choice of the fragment is the active part of a larger system, while the rest of the system is weakly correlated. For a periodic solid, as we show below, an embedding scheme arises by partitioning the system in periodically repeated fragments coupled via a dynamical embedding potential vemb​(ω)v_{\text{emb}}(\omega).

papers.title: What is a Good Projection?: Correctness and Separation Results of End-Point Projections
papers.abstract: \emph{Multiparty session types} (MPST) is a type discipline for ensuring distributed programs are implemented correctly \emph{by construction}. MPST starts by specifying a choreographic protocol as a \emph{global type} and \emph{projects} it onto each participant, generating \emph{local types} with a guarantee of type soundness and deadlock-freedom. A central issue of MPST is that its type soundness is fragile, as it must be proven each time with respect to a chosen projection algorithm under specific semantics with a specific program correctness goal. To overcome this problem, we propose general criteria for a \emph{good projection} -- a set of requirements for projection algorithms by which type soundness, deadlock-freedom and liveness of distributed programs are \emph{automatically} derived. Using the criteria, we prove that 8 distinct projections in the literature are good under both synchronous and asynchronous semantics, and that 4 are incorrect, failing type soundness. We extend the good projection criteria to mixed choice global types and asynchronous communication optimisations, proposing new ``good projection'' algorithms. We apply properties of good projections to prove \emph{separation} and \emph{expressiveness} results over the projection algorithms and MPST typing systems. Having a generalised typing system that is robust with respect to the good projection criteria, we provide an implementation with mixed choice global types that is \emph{modular} with respect to a chosen projection algorithm and desired program properties. Our separation results help programmers make informed trade-offs between complexity and expressiveness when choosing projection algorithms, and our theory ensures their chosen algorithms are correctly applied.

papers.title: Combining Exponential and Polynomial Convergence Rates for Accelerated Extremum Seeking: A High-Order Lie Bracket Approach
papers.abstract: In this paper, we leverage the recently developed general higher-order Lie bracket approximation theory and framework for control-affine systems to show that we can design extremum seeking (ES) systems that combine flows based on: (i) first-order Lie bracket approximation, which provide an exponential convergence rate for quadratic objective functions and polynomial convergence rate for non-quadratic objective functions; and (ii) higher-order Lie bracket approximation, which provide exponential convergence rate near the minimizer even if the objective function is non-quadratic (i.e., flatter and possesses vanishing Hessian at the minimizer). Such combination provides an accelerated ES design that benefits from the polynomial decay rate farther away from the minimizer and exponential decay rate near the minimizer even for complicated nature of objective functions. We provide numerical simulations to demonstrate the results, including multi-variable and nonpolynomial flat-bottomed objective functions.

papers.title: Revolutionizing 6G Wireless Networks with RISs: Enhancements in Sensing and Communications
papers.abstract: Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) have emerged as one of the most promising technologies for the next-generation wireless networks, offering advantages such as cost efficiency, low power consumption, flexible deployment, and large effective aperture. Extensive studies have demonstrated the capabilities of RISs to enhance communication performance, including coverage extension, sum-rate improvement, interference suppression, security enhancement, etc. As 6G networks continue to evolve, wireless sensing is expected to play a pivotal role alongside communication. Undoubtedly, RISs possess great potential to enable seamless integration of sensing and communication by supporting both passive and active sensing paradigms. This paper explores how RISs can revolutionize wireless networks by enhancing both communication and sensing capabilities. Specifically, we highlight the fundamental principles, potential applications, and future trends of RIS-assisted integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), anticipating that RIS-enabled ISAC will become a key enabler in the upcoming 6G era.
