papers.intro:
The sixth generation (6G) of wireless networks is envisioned to support immersive communications, massive connectivity, and hyper-reliable low latency wireless links, evolving beyond the three primary usage scenarios of the fifth-generation (5G) networks: enhanced mobile broadband (eMBB), massive machine-type communication (mMTC), and ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC). To achieve this evolution, 6G will face more stringent requirements in key performance indicators (KPIs), including higher spectral efficiency, extremely high peak data rates, centimeter-level positioning accuracy, and sub-millisecond latency. In addition to the evolved versions of the 5G use cases, three new ones have emerged as major driving forces of 6G development: ubiquitous connectivity, native artificial intelligence (AI) communications, and integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) [1].

Communications have been the primary service of cellular networks since their inception. Starting from the fourth generation (4G), high accuracy localization has become feasible due to the availability of wider bandwidths and the adoption of the multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) technology. Since then, continuous advancements have led to increasingly precise localization capabilities, laying the foundation for ISAC [4]. This paradigm allows for the joint optimization of communication and sensing objectives within a unified framework, maximizing the utilization of network resources. The integration of RISs into cellular networks has the potential to further boost ISAC performance by providing unprecedented control over radio wave propagation [3]. For localization and other sensing tasks, RISs, when deployed at carefully selected offline fixed positions, can provide high spatial resolution due to their large aperture and can act as additional positioning reference nodes [5], thereby complementing conventional base stations (BSs) [6]. The integration of uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) into cellular networks has attracted significant attention due to their mobility, flexibility, and ability to provide cost-effective wireless access, particularly in communication-blind or disaster-stricken areas. In this context, RIS-assisted cellular networks can not only significantly enhance the detection, localization, and tracking performance of non-cooperating UAVs, but also actively support UAV self-localization and navigation, thereby enabling reliable communication and sensing for emerging low-altitude economy applications.

papers.title: Understanding CEO-Employee compensation dynamics: An agent-based simulation approach
papers.abstract: CEO compensation has often been examined from the top down, i.e., as the outcome of a negotiation between the CEO, the board of directors, and the shareholders. While these approaches have provided valuable insights into the nature of CEO compensation and its relations with firm performance and intra-firm inequality, we believe they leave aside the internal decision-making dynamics of CEOs and employees. To fill this research gap, we develop an agent-based model built on the NK framework in which a CEO compensated for long-term firm performance interacts with several employees rewarded for short-term departmental performance. This temporal dichotomy in their respective compensation functions creates a potential temporal misalignment of incentives. By varying the horizon considered by the CEO to make their decisions, we examine how this temporal (mis)alignment of incentives shapes firm performance and pay inequality between the CEO and the employees. Our findings suggest that aligning the CEO's horizon with the employees' short-term incentives yields the highest performance, raising both the level attained and the speed of improvement across all task environments examined. This finding contrasts with the usual advice given in CEO compensation research, which is to avoid short-termism. Furthermore, the model shows that the longest horizon examined produces both the lowest performance and the highest pay inequality. This pattern, commonly attributed to managerial power, emerges in our model from incentive misalignment alone, without agents holding any power over their own compensation.

papers.intro:
Executive compensation is both a governance device, meant to align managerial decisions with the maximisation of long-term firm value, and one of the most visible sources of pay inequality within firms. That inequality has grown markedly. Among S&P 500 firms, the ratio of CEO pay to average worker pay rose from about 40 in 1980 to 335 in 2015 (Edmans et al. 2017). Yet, prior research has not produced a consensus on why CEO compensation has grown so much faster than the pay of other employees or how it relates to firm performance (Edmans and Gabaix 2016). These questions are highly relevant due to their connections to wider debates on income inequality and its policy implications (Edmans and Gabaix 2016; Keller and Olney 2021; Piketty 2014).

Yet firm performance results from decisions taken at all levels of the firm, with these decisions being shaped by the decision-makers’ pay structure (Bandiera et al. 2007; Lazear 2000; Siggelkow and Rivkin 2005). To account for these interrelations, we propose an Agent-Based Model (ABM) based on the NK framework and adapted to model hierarchical decision-making (Siggelkow and Rivkin 2005). Our model captures the interactions between a CEO and lower-level employees, building on the potential incentive misalignment that may appear during their decision-making processes. This incentive misalignment emerges from the fundamental differences in pay structure between CEOs and lower-ranked employees: the former are usually compensated using variable packages based on long-term firm performance maximisation, while the latter mostly receive fixed salaries combined with smaller, short-term performance-based commissions or bonuses (Edmans et al. 2017; Lazear 2000). papers.title: Reframing Object-Centric Reinforcement Learning: From Absolute to Relative Representations
papers.abstract: Object-centric reinforcement learning agents typically receive each object's position in a fixed global frame, even though their decisions usually depend on where objects are relative to one another. These absolute views often fail to capture the local context that is most relevant to the agent's behavior. As a result, an agent must relearn the same response at every location where a configuration can occur, and its performance collapses when the scene is merely shifted. In this work, we propose a shift toward Object-Relative Coordinates fixed to Anchor (ORCA), where entities are described in a relative frame of reference. To operationalize this idea, we introduce Object-Relative inductive-Bias Transformers (ORBiT), a transformer-based architecture for processing anchor-relative inputs in reinforcement learning. Our results suggest these relative representations improve performance for both MLP and transformer agents. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ORBiT outperforms the pixel-based PPO baseline, achieving an aggregate HNS IQM greater than 1.0 over 13 Atari games. ORBiT learns the game of Foosball from scratch, dominating all baselines. In our controlled Tag environment, we further show that ORCA extends to rotations, that ORBiT generalizes to unseen numbers of distractors, and that these gains require a decision-relevant anchor.

papers.intro:
Ask a person where their keys are, and they will not answer in coordinates; they will say next to the bowl, on the left side of the desk, or behind you. Human spatial reasoning often uses spatial anchors and relative frames of reference (Levinson, 2003). Scenes are parsed into bounded objects with persistent identity, and the position of each object is encoded in a frame tied to the body or to nearby landmarks rather than in a single fixed global system (Klatzky, 1998; Spelke, 1990; Scholl, 2001; Burgess, 2006). Object-centric reinforcement learning (OCRL) has internalized the first of these two ideas: rather than feeding pixels to a policy, OCRL extracts a set of objects with type, position, and velocity, and lets the agent reason over the resulting structured representation (Diuk et al., 2008; Baker et al., 2020; Delfosse et al., 2024a; Delfosse et al., 2024b; Ye et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026). The second idea, using anchors and relative frames of reference, has been independently adopted in multi-agent reinforcement learning, robotics, biology, and linguistics, where observations relative to the agent’s position are more commonly used (Gupta et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020; Shang et al., 2021; Levinson, 2003), yet it remains largely absent from OCRL. The absolute-coordinate convention appears to have been inherited from early object-vector pipelines and rarely revisited.

papers.title: A Process-Informed, Photorealistic Digital Twin for Vision-Based Inline Inspection of C-SMC Strip Deposition
papers.abstract: Inline quality assurance for Sheet Molding Compound (SMC) manufacturing is hindered by the lack of large-scale, accurately labeled image datasets for training machine-learning models. This work presents a process-informed, photorealistic digital twin for carbon-fiber SMC strip deposition. A rigid-body simulation reproduces the deposition kinematics (settling, friction, belt motion), while a physically grounded polarization-rendering model produces realistic appearance, so that every image carries exact, mutually consistent labels in synchronized formats: oriented bounding boxes, point annotations, density maps, and polarization renderings (Angle and Degree of Linear Polarization). Because the joint distribution of many overlapping strips cannot be specified analytically, simulation yields exact, scalable ground truth that manual annotation cannot provide. The twin produces over 16,000 images across 3,300 frames, and the synthetic data replicate near-isotropic fiber orientation (axial concentration r < 0.05) consistent with as-deposited commercial SMC. Trained purely on synthetic data, YOLOv11 and CSRNet reach detection mAP50 up to 0.91, with a dedicated oriented-bounding-box detector confirming the oriented labels are directly trainable (mAP50 = 0.83); on real manufacturing images, the synthetic-to-real difference in edge and texture structure (Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance 0.46, distribution overlap 0.56) is of the same magnitude as the difference between two real acquisition series of the same material (0.41, overlap 0.57). The approach substantially reduces the labeling burden for camera-based inline inspection of fiber orientation and volume content.

papers.intro:
For decades, the global emphasis on reducing carbon dioxide emissions and improving energy efficiency has driven the transportation sector to shift toward lightweight construction. This long-term effort has established fiber-reinforced polymers (FRPs) as key alternatives to traditional materials like metals. Among FRPs, Sheet Molding Compound (SMC) parts are particularly attractive because they offer a balance of high specific stiffness and strength, low cost, and efficient manufacturability. SMC is a prepreg sheet: a semi-finished fiber-reinforced thermoset polymer matrix product that typically consists of a thermosetting resin (such as unsaturated polyester, vinyl ester, or epoxy), particulate fillers (e.g., calcium carbonate), and long, discontinuous fiber reinforcement (typically 25–50 mm in length).

The production of an SMC part begins with the creation of the semi-finished prepreg sheet on a compounding line, where the thermoset resin paste, fillers, and long chopped fibers or fiber bundles are combined and compacted onto carrier foils. The sheet then undergoes a maturing phase, which increases its viscosity to the level required for subsequent handling. After maturation, the SMC sheet is cut to the required size and, if necessary, preformed before being compression-molded into the final component.

After maturation, the SMC sheet is cut to the required size and, if necessary, preformed before being compression-molded into the final component.

The mechanical performance of an SMC component—particularly its strength and stiffness—is governed directly by the microstructure of the semi-finished sheet. This microstructure is described by two spatially varying fields: the fiber orientation distribution (FOD) and the fiber volume content (FVC). The FOD is a tensor-valued field, typically represented by a second- or higher-order orientation tensor that characterizes the local directional probability distribution of fibers or fiber bundles [1, 2]. The FVC, in contrast, is a scalar field specifying the local fiber volume fraction within the composite [3]. Together, these fields determine the local anisotropic mechanical behavior through established micromechanical homogenization relations [4, 5] and serve as the primary predictors of stiffness, strength, and failure-relevant properties at the component scale. However, local deviations from the expected orientation distribution or from the nominal fiber volume content inevitably arise due to the stochastic nature of fiber placement during sheet assembly. Additionally, it is still subject to debate whether a stochastically perfect process would yield a planar quasi-isotropic FOD [6, 7] or whether the forward feed in the direction of production would result in a non-isotropic FOD [8, 9].

Still, quality assurance during SMC manufacturing needs to define boundaries for possible deviations from the expected FOD and FVC and to provide efficient and precise means for measuring both. Therefore, in-line sensing of FOD and FVC during SMC sheet production is of great interest for quality assurance. Such an inline system must, however, satisfy several practical constraints. It must operate at the line speeds typical of SMC production, on the order of a few cm/s (the production line studied in this work runs at 2 cm/s), implying real-time data acquisition with minimal processing latency [10]. It also requires sufficient spatial and angular resolution to detect deviations in fiber architecture, while remaining robust to surface variations, occlusions, and the inherent heterogeneity of discontinuous-fiber materials. A wide range of non-destructive testing (NDT) methods has been proposed, each with different spatial/temporal resolution, accuracy, and practicality. These span X-ray computed tomography and scattering [11, 12], eddy-current sensing [13, 14], active infrared thermography [15], and optical microscopy [16], alongside quality-control approaches specific to SMC production [17].

However, conventional optical approaches often require an extensive post-processing [20], which limits their suitability for inline use. Polarization imaging therefore represents a particularly promising alternative to conventional optical methods for carbon-fiber-reinforced materials, as carbon fibers induce a pronounced polarization state in reflected light [21]. Machine-vision cameras with on-chip polarizers can image the angle of linear polarization (AoLP) of light from carbon fibers, providing pixel-level surface fiber orientations. These systems are inexpensive (1–3 kEUR) and operate at video rates, enabling real-time inspection. For uni- and bidirectional C-SMC laminates, polarization-based orientation measurements have been validated with an angular accuracy on the order of 1° [19, 23]. Surface and bulk fiber orientations often correlate in C-SMC [8], although the strength of this correspondence can depend on the production process. The method does not work for glass-fiber SMC, however, as glass fibers do not polarize light significantly. Nonetheless there are approaches to capture the drop-down area to gain more depth information of the SMC-Prepreg [24]. Furthermore, the method does not perform explicit object recognition and therefore remains sensitive to occlusions, surface curvature and local texture variations, which can bias the AoLP signal and cause certain regions to dominate the orientation estimate. While highly effective for surfaces with clear carbon-fiber texture, its robustness decreases for multidirectional or irregular SMC materials, where overlapping fiber families and varying reflection properties can lead to averaged or unstable orientation fields [8]. Post-processing of the polarization images can mitigate these effects, but such steps reduce the method’s potential for inline application due to increased computational effort and latency. Pre-trained machine-learning models offer a possible alternative, yet they require large amounts of accurately labeled ground-truth data [25] — data that are difficult or impossible to obtain experimentally during inline SMC production. Synthetic microstructure models therefore appear as a suitable source of labeled data.

papers.title: Generalized quadratic matrix manifolds: Riemannian geometry and computations
papers.abstract: We study the set $\mathrm{Gq}(P,Q)$ of real $n\times p$ matrices $X$ satisfying $X^\top Q X = P$, where the nonsingular matrices $P$ and $Q$ are both symmetric or both skew-symmetric and the set is nonempty. Special choices of $P$ and $Q$ yield the Stiefel, generalized Stiefel, indefinite Stiefel, and symplectic Stiefel manifolds, as well as the quadratic matrix Lie groups. We prove that $\mathrm{Gq}(P,Q)$ is a closed embedded submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ and that it is compact exactly when $P$ and $Q$ are both symmetric and definite of the same sign. We derive closed-form expressions for its tangent space and, under a canonical-like Riemannian metric, for the normal space, the orthogonal projection, and the Riemannian gradient and Hessian. We extend the Cayley, quasi-geodesic, and polar retractions to $\mathrm{Gq}(P,Q)$, with explicit domains, vector transports, and closed-form second-order corrections. These objects are the ingredients of Riemannian first- and second-order methods. In trace minimization tests with symmetric positive-definite, skew-symmetric, and symmetric indefinite pairs $(P,Q)$, the Riemannian conjugate gradient and trust-region methods reach the same objective value with different retractions and keep the iterates on $\mathrm{Gq}(P,Q)$ up to rounding error.

papers.title: Rational analytic prismatization
papers.abstract: We develop a general theory of analytic prismatization with $\mathbb{Q}_p$-coefficients in rigid analytic geometry over $\mathbb{Q}_p$. We prove an equivalence of perfect complexes on the perfect analytic prismatization modulo Frobenius with perfect complexes on the relative Fargues--Fontaine curve for any smooth partially proper rigid analytic variety. In particular, we explain how this equivalence conceptualizes the decompletion techniques by passing to locally analytic vectors which appear in (geometric) Sen theory
papers.intro:
Prismatic cohomology has been defined in [BS22] as a new cohomology theory for pp-adic formal schemes, unifying the already known existing pp-adic cohomology theories such as de Rham cohomology, crystalline cohomology (of the special fiber), pp-adic étale cohomology (of the rigid generic fiber), etc.. Later, Bhatt–Lurie [BL22c], and independently Drinfeld [Dri24b], introduced the prismatization XΔX^{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}} of a pp-adic formal scheme XX in such a way that the coherent cohomology of the stack XΔX^{{\mathbbl{\Delta}}} recovers the prismatic cohomology of XX. They also introduced various refinements of this construction, encoding extra structures on prismatic cohomology, such as the Nygaard filtration or the Frobenius. A toy model and an inspiration for these developements is furnished by de Rham cohomology (in characteristic 00): according to a celebrated result of Grothendieck [Gro68], it can be thought of as the cohomology of a site, the infinitesimal site, and Simpson [Sim97] has defined the de Rham space (or stack) of a scheme, with coherent cohomology given by de Rham cohomology. Moreover, he introduced a filtered variant of this construction, encoding the Hodge filtration on de Rham cohomology.

papers.title: RealControlBench: A Benchmark for Interpretability-Informed Fine-Grained Control of LLMs and Agents
papers.abstract: Existing steering benchmarks are built around simplified, isolated generation tasks and evaluate a single behavioral attribute under controlled settings that do not reflect the diversity and complexity of practical deployment. As a result, performance on these benchmarks provides only a limited picture of how steering methods perform in the real world. We therefore introduce RealControlBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating fine-grained steering of LLMs and LLM agents across diverse behavioral targets and interaction settings. RealControlBench extends steering evaluation beyond isolated generations to complex, execution-grounded, multi-turn agent interactions, covering five complementary dimensions: instruction-following control, agentic tool-use decision control, reasoning-performance steering, reasoning-length control, and trajectory-conditioned safety awareness. Rather than measuring steering success alone, the benchmark jointly evaluates target controllability and capability preservation, including instruction following, reasoning performance, and downstream agent utility and safety. It further examines whether steering effects remain specific and robust across prompt variations, domains, and model architectures. Our evaluation shows that existing steering methods remain unreliable across realistic control objectives: they often fail to consistently induce the intended behavior and can substantially degrade the model's underlying task performance. These results suggest that strong steering effects in controlled settings do not necessarily translate into reliable control in more realistic evaluations. By providing a unified, model-agnostic steering evaluation framework, RealControlBench aims to support the development of steering methods that are not only effective but also precise, robust, and useful in realistic AI deployments.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) are arguably the first systems we have built that combine an open-ended natural-language interface with broad competence in writing, reasoning, programming, and tool use (Wei et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023, inter alia). This flexibility makes it easy to tell a model what we want it to do. Ensuring that it does so precisely and reliably, however, is a different matter. Reliable control over model behavior is therefore becoming a fundamental requirement for deploying LLMs in practice. This challenge is becoming more important as the adoption of agentic LLM systems continues to accelerate and the technology becomes increasingly ubiquitous and embedded in more critical, high-risk real-world settings (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Han et al., 2025).

While multiple approaches exist, from prompting and constrained decoding to fine-tuning and preference optimization, steering has recently shown particular promise owing to its distinct advantages (Zou et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Liu and Han, 2026; Han et al., 2026). It allows us to adjust a model’s behavior during inference by intervening directly on its internal representations, without retraining the model. In practice, most steering methods simply add a scaled vector to the model’s activations, with little computational overhead and a single coefficient controlling the intervention’s strength (Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026). The same basic approach has been applied to truthfulness (Li et al., 2023), refusal and sycophancy (Rimsky et al., 2024), instruction following (He et al., 2026), mathematical reasoning (Ouyang et al., 2026), and agentic tasks (Chen et al., 2026).

Second, evaluation should be execution-grounded, measuring not only whether steering induces the intended behavior but also whether the model retains its ability to complete the underlying task. Third, the benchmark should be model-agnostic, allowing the same tasks, environments, and evaluation criteria to be applied across models without reconstructing model-specific benchmark data. papers.title: Multi-Capacity Online Assortment Optimization with Consecutive Stays under Markov Chain Choice
papers.abstract: We study online assortment optimization under Markov chain choice and independent Bernoulli arrivals, with each period's request type known in advance. Each product may have multiple interchangeable physical copies, and each booking reserves consecutive service slots on a single copy. Customers choose among products, while the platform assigns purchases to feasible copies. We develop a sales-based relaxation that upper-bounds the optimal online revenue and use it to design a policy with two components: independent sampling and purchase--update coupling. We generate independent copy proposals and make a product eligible whenever at least one of its copies proposes. A general revenue-extraction bound for random candidate sets with independent product inclusions shows that optimizing over eligible products recovers at least half of each period's relaxation revenue benchmark in expectation. A purchase--update coupling reproduces the interval flows through independent virtual copy updates while preserving physical feasibility. Under general Markov chain choice, the policy uses a random gate to make the coupling feasible: it offers the selected assortment with probability \(1-1/e\) and the empty assortment otherwise. No gate is needed under multinomial logit (MNL) choice. The resulting policies achieve approximation ratios of \((1-1/e)/2\) and \(1/2\), respectively, relative to the optimal nonanticipative online policy, independently of product capacities. In the single-copy MNL setting, our policy improves the guarantee of \citet{huwu2026} from \(0.271\) to \(1/2\) under the same arrival convention. The \(1/2\) static extraction factor and the \(1-1/e\) uniform scalar-gate factor are separately sharp, and the \(1/2\) MNL guarantee is tight for the proposed policy.

papers.intro:
Advance booking changes the nature of capacity. In our setting, a sale does not simply remove one interchangeable unit from an inventory pool; it reserves a particular physical unit for the entire requested service interval, with the assignment fixed irrevocably at booking. In high-speed rail, for example, an accepted itinerary may require immediate and irrevocable assignment to a single seat. Having an available seat on each leg is not sufficient: the same seat must be available on all requested legs (Zhu et al. 2023). Similar requirements arise in hotels, vehicle-rental companies, and other reservation systems when a booking must be fulfilled by the same room or asset throughout the requested stay. These requirements call for tracking each physical unit’s availability across service slots (Rusmevichientong et al. 2023).

These requirements call for tracking each physical unit’s availability across service slots (Rusmevichientong et al. 2023).

The physical unit used to fulfill a booking, however, is often not the alternative chosen by the customer. A rail passenger may choose a seating class, while the firm assigns a specific seat within that class. A related form of fulfillment flexibility appears in flexible-product models, which allow the seller to assign a customer to one of several specified alternatives after purchase (Gallego et al. 2004). We call each customer-facing category a product and its individual physical units copies. Copies of the same product are interchangeable from the customer’s perspective, but the firm must distinguish them for assignment and capacity accounting.

This product–copy distinction matters for both feasibility and customer choice. With existing assignments fixed, tracking only the number of available copies in each service slot may suggest that a request is feasible even when no single copy can fulfill it. For example, one seat may be available on the first leg of a journey and another on the second, even though neither is available for both legs. Displaying physical copies as separate alternatives without a corresponding reformulation of the choice model can change product purchase probabilities. We therefore model customer choice at the product level while tracking individual copies for feasibility and assignment.

Consecutive stays also complicate the evolution of each copy’s availability. Reserving an interior portion of a free interval splits it into two disjoint blocks, so the feasibility of later requests depends on which service slots remain free, not merely how many. This differs from standard inventory models, which track remaining stock, and from many reusable-resource models, which summarize availability through release times or counts of available units. In our setting, booking periods and service slots play distinct roles: requests arrive sequentially during the booking horizon, while each accepted reservation occupies an interval of service slots on its assigned copy. Once reserved, those slots remain unavailable on that copy for the rest of the booking horizon.

We adopt the fixed-type Bernoulli-arrival convention of Hu and Wu (2026) over a finite booking horizon. Each period has at most one potential customer, and arrivals are independent across periods. The arrival probabilities, requested intervals, revenues, and choice parameters for all periods are known before the booking horizon begins and may vary across periods. Arrival and choice outcomes are observed only as they occur. Before observing the arrival outcome in each period, the platform selects an assortment of products with feasible copies and offers it if the customer arrives. Each purchase is assigned to a single copy available throughout the requested interval. We model customer substitution using the Markov chain choice model of Blanchet et al. (2016). The chain is defined over customer-visible products and the outside option, and the customer’s path stops upon first reaching an offered product or the outside option. This model includes multinomial logit (MNL) choice with positive outside-option attractiveness and allows richer substitution patterns. We treat MNL with zero outside-option attractiveness separately.

Our benchmark is the expected revenue of the optimal nonanticipative online policy. Like our algorithm, this policy knows the model primitives but observes arrival and choice outcomes only as they occur. The benchmark ranges over all feasible history-dependent policies, without computational restrictions. Approximation guarantees for efficient policies relative to this benchmark are often called philosopher inequalities, whereas prophet inequalities use a clairvoyant offline benchmark (Papadimitriou et al. 2024, Huang et al. 2024). We construct policies that admit exact implementations in expected polynomial time and achieve approximation guarantees of (1−1/e)/2(1-1/e)/2 under general Markov chain choice and 1/21/2 under MNL, relative to this benchmark and independently of product capacities.

(i) Choice-Based Revenue Management. Classical network revenue management studies how to allocate limited capacity among products with fixed resource requirements, balancing current revenue against the value of preserving capacity for future demand (Gallego and van Ryzin 1997, Talluri and van Ryzin 1998). Choice-based models incorporate customer substitution by allowing demand to depend on the assortment offered. Talluri and van Ryzin (2004) study revenue management under a general discrete-choice model. Liu and van Ryzin (2008) analyze a choice-based linear programming formulation for network revenue management, and Gallego et al. (2015) develop a sales-based formulation that incorporates customer choice into capacity allocation.

papers.title: Physical Operating-Condition-Guided Vision-Language Matching for Cavitation Diagnosis in Industrial Pipeline Systems
papers.abstract: Cavitation diagnosis in industrial pipeline systems is challenging because acoustic responses vary substantially with operating conditions, while similar time-frequency patterns may correspond to different cavitation states. To address this issue, we propose a physical operating-condition-guided vision-language matching (POC-VLM) for cavitation diagnosis. POC-VLM first constructs physical operating-condition-aware semantic descriptions by explicitly incorporating sample-specific operating variables into candidate cavitation texts. A time-frequency-conditioned text adaptation module then dynamically aligns these physical semantics with the observed acoustic response, followed by global-local vision-language matching to capture both holistic and localized discriminative patterns. In parallel, a K-nearest neighbours-based non-parametric physical operating-condition prior estimates the physical plausibility of each candidate state and is fused with the vision-language semantic evidence at the decision level. Experiments on three real-world cavitation datasets show that POC-VLM consistently outperforms representative data-driven, multimodal and domain-specific diagnostic methods. Further analyses verify the complementary roles of vision-language semantic matching and physical operating-condition priors, while demonstrating robust performance under varying sampling rates, noise levels and observation durations.

papers.intro:
Cavitation is a common and potentially destructive phenomenon in industrial fluid transport systems, particularly around control valves, pumps and other throttling components [1, 2]. The repeated formation and collapse of vapour cavities can generate strong pressure fluctuations, vibration, noise and material erosion, ultimately affecting equipment reliability, operational efficiency and service life [3, 4]. Therefore, accurate identification of different cavitation intensity states is important for condition monitoring and predictive maintenance of industrial pipeline systems [5, 6]. Among the available sensing modalities, acoustic signals provide a non-invasive and highly responsive means of capturing transient cavitation behaviour and have consequently been widely used for intelligent cavitation diagnosis [7, 8].

Recent advances in deep learning have substantially improved the capability of extracting discriminative representations from acoustic signals [5, 9, 10]. Convolutional neural networks and Transformer-based architectures can learn hierarchical patterns from raw signals or their time-frequency representations, while more recent fault diagnosis methods further incorporate task-specific structures or hierarchical knowledge to improve the discrimination of different fault intensities. However, most existing approaches remain predominantly data-driven and learn a direct mapping from observed acoustic patterns to diagnostic labels. In practical pipeline systems, cavitation responses are strongly affected by physical operating conditions such as valve stroke, upstream and downstream pressures, flow rate and temperature [3, 11]. Therefore, similar acoustic patterns may have different diagnostic implications under different operating conditions, while the same cavitation state may exhibit substantially different responses as the operating condition changes [12, 13, 14]. A natural solution is to jointly exploit acoustic responses and physical operating-condition information. Existing multimodal approaches typically encode physical variables as an additional numerical modality and combine them with signal representations through feature concatenation, attention or latent-space interaction [17, 18, 19]. Although such strategies can improve diagnostic performance, physical variables are often treated merely as auxiliary features rather than as explicit physical context that constrains the interpretation of acoustic observations [20, 21, 22]. In particular, conventional feature-level fusion does not directly clarify how a candidate diagnostic state should be interpreted under the current operating condition or whether the predicted state is physically plausible given the observed operating state. To address these questions, physical information should participate not only in representation learning but also in semantic interpretation and final diagnostic reasoning.

Vision-language models provide a promising perspective for this issue. Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) maps visual and textual inputs into a shared semantic space, allowing classification to be reformulated as matching between an observed input and candidate textual descriptions [23, 24]. This paradigm provides an opportunity to move beyond fixed discriminative classifiers and represent diagnostic states through semantically meaningful descriptions. However, conventional CLIP prompts are generally static and encode generic class-level semantics [24]. Such descriptions are insufficient for condition-dependent industrial diagnosis, where the meaning of an acoustic response is inseparable from its physical operating environment. In addition, directly applying pretrained vision-language representations to acoustic time-frequency images introduces a substantial domain gap between natural image-text pretraining and industrial signal interpretation [25, 26, 27]. Therefore, effective adaptation requires both physically grounded textual semantics and explicit interaction between candidate semantics and acoustic time-frequency responses.

To address these challenges, we propose physical operating-condition-guided vision-language matching (POC-VLM) for cavitation diagnosis in industrial pipeline systems. The central idea is to use physical operating conditions at both the semantic and decision levels. First, instead of conventional static class prompts, we construct sample-specific physical semantic descriptions by dynamically incorporating the operating conditions associated with each acoustic sample into the candidate cavitation texts, allowing the semantic representation of each state to adapt to the current physical context. Second, we perform cross-attention-based global and class-specific local visual evidence matching, enabling the candidate semantics to interact with both the overall time-frequency response and discriminative local regions relevant to each cavitation state. Third, the physical operating conditions are used to construct a non-parametric nearest-neighbour prior, which estimates the physical plausibility of each candidate state from the distribution of training operating conditions. Finally, the resulting semantic evidence and physical prior are integrated at the decision level, enabling cavitation diagnosis to jointly consider acoustic-semantic compatibility and physical plausibility. The proposed POC-VLM is evaluated on three real-world industrial cavitation datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that POC-VLM consistently outperforms representative diagnostic methods and exhibits strong robustness and generalization under varying operating and sensing conditions.

papers.title: Physical-Variable-Informed Deep Learning for Robust Diagnosis in Industrial Fluid Transport Systems
papers.abstract: Industrial fluid transport systems are monitored through heterogeneous sensing streams, but robust fault diagnosis remains difficult because response signals vary with operating conditions and differ from physical variables in sampling rate, observation duration and data granularity. To address these challenges, we propose a physical-variable-informed deep learning framework (PhyNet) for robust fault diagnosis under real-world sampling heterogeneity. PhyNet treats physical variables as global operating constraints and response signals as local diagnostic evidence. Its physical-to-response cross-attention mechanism connects sequence-level physical-variable tokens with a learnable global response token, enabling interaction without strict temporal alignment. Across four benchmarks, including three real-world cavitation datasets and one public two-phase-flow dataset, PhyNet achieves the best performance across all evaluated metrics. Class-wise analyses, together with attention and masking analyses, show improved discrimination of ambiguous states and indicate that physical variables meaningfully constrain local response interpretation. These findings demonstrate a deployment-oriented approach to robust diagnosis in heterogeneous industrial environments.

papers.title: A Discrete Amplitude-to-Time Conversion Circuit for TDC-Based Readout of Fast Scintillation Detectors
papers.abstract: Fast timing measurements with scintillation detectors commonly employ leading-edge discriminators and time-to-digital converters (TDCs). Many applications also require an energy-related observable for estimating the deposited energy and correcting time-walk effects. Time-over-threshold (ToT) is frequently used for this purpose, but its relationship to pulse amplitude can be severely degraded by undershoot, ringing, and other distortions of the detector pulse tail. This work presents a discrete analog front-end circuit for amplitude-to-time conversion that is insensitive to pulse-tail distortions. An analog multiplexer and a high-speed comparator implement a sample-hold-discharge stage: upon leading-edge detection, the detector pulse amplitude is sampled near its peak and stored on a capacitor, which is subsequently discharged at a controlled rate. The resulting digital pulse width encodes the sampled amplitude, while the leading edge preserves the timing information. The circuit was designed for a short recovery time and a total dead time below 100~ns, making it suitable for high-rate detector readout. The approach enables simultaneous timing and amplitude measurements through a single TDC channel. An eight-channel front-end card implementing this concept was characterized using generated test pulses. The measured transfer function is approximately linear up to input amplitudes of 0.5~V and extends beyond 2~V, with a low-amplitude conversion gain of approximately 27~ps/mV. The estimated relative amplitude precision falls below \SI{0.5}{\percent} for input amplitudes above 0.5~V. These results demonstrate the feasibility of a low-complexity, multichannel amplitude-to-time converter for TDC-based detector readout, offering an alternative to conventional ToT measurement when pulse-tail distortions compromise amplitude estimation.

While this approach enables excellent timing resolution, many applications additionally require an energy-related observable, such as collected charge or peak amplitude, to estimate the deposited energy or energy loss of the detected particle [1]. This information is also essential for correcting time-walk effects inherent to leading-edge discrimination [2]. A frequently used proxy for pulse amplitude is the time-over-threshold (ToT) derived from discriminator outputs. For self-similar pulses with exponential decay, the ToT measured by a simple comparator (also referred to as a discriminator in detector physics) depends approximately logarithmically on the pulse amplitude. Conversely amplitude and measured energy behave like an exponential function of ToT [3]. In principle, a calibration function can be used to linearize the measured ToT values and reconstruct an amplitude-related spectrum. In practice, however, establishing this calibration can be difficult or impractical, particularly when the required reference measurements are unavailable.

This work presents a discrete analog front-end circuit that provides discrimination and a robust amplitude-to-time conversion independent of the signal tail shape. The proposed circuit uses an analog switch in combination with a comparator. The key idea behind the concept is to implement a leading edge discriminator to measure the time-of-arrival of the leading edge, as in the conventional approach. Upon detection of a leading edge, the analog switch disconnects the comparator from the detector input, rendering it blind to the features of the detector tail. Instead the comparator evaluates the linear ramp of a sample-hold-discharge stage, previously capturing the peak amplitude of the input signal. The resulting ToT encodes the pulse amplitude, independent of tail signal features, with a close to linear transfer function, especially for small signal amplitudes.

papers.title: Visual Task Modeling and Automated Planning for Humanoid Robots in Education of Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder
papers.abstract: In robot-assisted education, a robot must understand how to complete a task in order to effectively guide a student through it. We present a novel method that enables a semi-autonomous, camera-equipped robot to recognise the task goal and plan actions to achieve it. Our work focuses on Shoebox Tasks, an activity commonly used in the education of individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). These tasks are designed so that the goal can be inferred directly from their visual structure. We have developed a solver that uses a vision-based Large Language Model to convert photos of a Shoebox Task into a Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) representation and generate action plans for solving it. We have also implemented a robotic interface that enables a Nao robot to autonomously execute various Shoebox Tasks and assist a student by suggesting next steps or signalling detected failures through action demonstrations, voice commands, or gestures. With an adapted robotic interface, the solver can be integrated into a variety of educational robots. No programming expertise is required from teachers, and the solver operates exclusively on captured images as input. Research in special educational needs indicates that students with ASD can benefit substantially from robot-assisted teaching, and our system aims to strengthen these learning opportunities while also fostering interest in robotics among individuals with ASD.

papers.intro:
We build a system that enables a robot to autonomously solve Shoebox Tasks and assist students in completing them. The automated task analysis relies entirely on visual input. We develop a task solver for Shoebox Tasks, an activity widely used in the education of individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). These tasks are intentionally highly visual, as learners with ASD often excel at visual learning but may struggle to follow spoken or textual instructions. Shoebox Tasks are therefore designed so that all information necessary to solve them can be inferred directly from their visual structure [1]. Our approach leverages this property by using Vision–Language Models (VLMs) to analyze images of the task, generate a corresponding Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) problem representation and action plan, and verify the plan execution through sequential image captures. We have implemented a simple robotic interface that allows a Nao humanoid robot to execute the generated plan autonomously or guide a student through the steps. Robot-assisted education has the potential to enhance learning outcomes for people with ASD [2]. Learners may benefit from the robot’s predictability and consistency, and often respond positively to interaction with robots [3]. Our work builds on a recently introduced method observing that the strong visual structure of Shoebox Tasks—and similar educational activities—makes them well suited for VLM-based analysis [4]. Initial experiments in that work used photos of the tasks with prompts and output examples as input to a VLM (e.g., ChatGPT-4o), producing a formatted analysis log and a PDDL problem file. This file was then passed to the Fast Downward planner to generate an action plan. After each executed action, a new image was captured, and the PDDL description and plan were updated iteratively until the task was completed. We extend this idea by providing a simple, practical implementation of a task solver. The system incorporates a PDDL validator to enable automatic regeneration of output in cases of model false-positive refusals, and introduces image comparison technique to detect not just a single action but a sequence of executed actions. Photos can be captured via a PC-connected camera or uploaded from a mobile phone through a web interface. Both task analysis and plan generation are executed directly by the VLM, which outputs a single PDDL problem file containing the action plan as a comment. In the robotic setting, solving a Shoebox Task can be viewed as performing an unordered sequence of Pick-and-Place actions leading from an initial configuration to one of the allowed goal states. We have implemented a Nao robot interface enabling the robot to autonomously execute these actions or assist a student in solving selected types of Shoebox Tasks (Fig. 1). We further observe that the proposed approach naturally supports the robot’s learning by demonstration: users can teach the robot by manipulating objects while the system continuously updates its visual interpretation of the scene. This image-based control mechanism creates additional opportunities for robotics education, particularly for learners with ASD, as it enables the translation of physical demonstrations into PDDL-encoded actions. For example, each action can be represented by a card with a pictogram, allowing the robot to be controlled by presenting cards rather than through direct programming.

Shoebox Task is a visually structured educational activity consisting of a small number of movable items and clearly defined storage areas. The task is designed such that the student can infer both the required work and task completion solely from the visual structure, without textual or verbal instructions. Rather than a fixed task set, the Shoebox Task represents an approach for adapting general educational activities for students with ASD. A simple example is a sorting task in which items placed on a table must be grouped by shape. In a Shoebox-style implementation, a box contains multiple smaller containers: one initial container holding the items and separate target containers marked with symbols corresponding to each shape. The strong visual structure supports learners with ASD, who are predominantly visual learners, and also makes the task suitable for automated vision-based analysis. ShoeboxTasks© were originally developed in the 1990s by Ron Larsen as part of the TEACCH methodology [1], an educational framework widely used worldwide in the education of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We had the privilege of collaborating with Ron Larsen to ensure that the proposed system closely aligns with the underlying educational principles of this methodology.

papers.title: Theorem prover Arend
papers.abstract: This paper is an exposition of the theorem prover Arend developed at JetBrains Research. Arend language has been designed to facilitate the formalization of mathematics within the framework of univalent foundations and with the focus on constructive mathematics. It is based on a variant of homotopy type theory with cubical syntax that is more closely aligned with Martin-Löf Type Theory (MLTT) than fully computational cubical type theories, while still retaining some of their computational properties useful in practice. Among the most notable features of the Arend language is its powerful system of classes and records supporting subsumptive subtyping, partial implementations and anonymous extensions, which provides extensive flexibility for constructing hierarchies of definitions. Formalization in Arend is streamlined by the IntelliJ Arend plugin, which transforms IntelliJ IDEA into a full-fledged integrated development environment (IDE) for the Arend language. The main Arend library arend-lib includes formalizations in constructive algebra, topology and synthetic homotopy theory.

papers.intro:
Interactive theorem provers (ITPs) are software tools designed to assist in the creation, verification, and exploration of formal proofs by providing a rigorous framework for encoding and checking logical reasoning. They leverage formal systems, such as type theory or higher-order logic, to provide an interactive environment where users can encode theorems, construct proofs, and validate their correctness with absolute precision. By eliminating human error, ITPs have become invaluable not only in formalizing complex mathematical results but also in verifying the correctness of critical software and hardware systems, bridging the gap between pure mathematics and practical applications. Modern ITPs, such as Rocq [9], Agda [43], Lean [15], and HOL-based systems like Isabelle/HOL [42] and HOL4 [53], are used both to verify algorithms and protocols and to formalize mathematics. Earlier milestones in mathematical formalization include the Four-Color Theorem [18] and the Feit–Thompson Theorem [17], both verified in Rocq.

Central to many ITPs is dependent type theory, a formalism that unifies programs and proofs within a single framework. Systems like Rocq, Lean and Agda, built upon the Calculus of Inductive Constructions (CIC) or Martin-Löf Type Theory (MLTT) [39], exemplify the power of dependent type theory in encoding rich mathematical structures and reasoning about them formally. Whereas Rocq and Lean (based on CIC) do not particularly favor constructivism (Lean even has the axioms of choice and excluded middle built-in), Agda (based on MLTT) leans more towards constructive mathematics. HOL-based systems, rooted in classical higher-order logic, offer an alternative approach that is more familiar to traditional mathematicians and computer scientists. However, dependent type theories surpass HOL in expressiveness by allowing types to depend on values, enabling constructive reasoning with computational interpretations via term reductions, and unifying proofs and programs within a single framework, capabilities that HOL’s classical framework lacks.

The impact of HoTT/UF on formalization of mathematics is two-fold:

1. Many standard constructions and theorems in homotopy theory can now be elegantly formalized using HoTT, where homotopy types serve as primitives rather than sets. This method, known as synthetic homotopy theory, utilizes the equality type to encapsulate complex homotopy structures [57, Chapter 8]. Set-theoretic versions of these formalizations tend to be more cumbersome. This synthetic approach not only simplifies the formalization of existing theories but also has the potential to reshape many areas of modern mathematics by adopting a higher categorical perspective over traditional set-theoretic approaches. 2. HoTT/UF provides a framework for set-theoretic formalization where sets are homotopy types with trivial homotopy structure and propositions are sets with at most one element. One can do formalizations completely confined to this set theory fragment of HoTT. As such a framework HoTT/UF augments MLTT with a fair degree of extensionality: (a) Quotients can be easily defined in HoTT using higher inductive types [57, Section 6.10]. Meanwhile quotients are notoriously hard to deal with in pure MLTT due to intensionality of equality [35]. (b) Univalence axiom implies propositional and function extensionality: any two equivalent propositions are equal and any two pointwise equal functions are equal [57, Sections 3.3 and 4.9]. (c) Univalence axiom implies structure identity principle: isomorphic structures (such as groups, topological spaces and so on) are equal [57, Section 9.8].

papers.title: Parameterizing Cluster Editing by the Number of Deletions
papers.abstract: In Cluster Editing, we are given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$ and ask whether at most $k$ edge insertions and deletions turn $G$ into a disjoint union of cliques. Komusiewicz and Niedermeier asked in 2012 at MFCS whether Cluster Editing is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the number $\ell$ of edge deletions, a parameter based on the solution rather than on the structure of the input graph. We answer this question negatively: Cluster Editing with at most $k$ edits, at most $\ell$ of which are deletions, is W[1]-hard with respect to $\ell$, even when combined with the pathwidth and the feedback edge set number of the input graph. The hardness extends to editing towards $H$-free graphs for every graph $H$ that is a clique minus one edge on at least four vertices. On the positive side, we show that the problem becomes fixed-parameter tractable when $\ell$ is combined with the excess $μ$ of $k$ over the lower bound given by a packing of modification-disjoint induced paths on three vertices, a lower bound that state-of-the-art solvers use. Each of the two parameters alone leads to intractability, but together they admit an $O(4^{μ+\ell}\cdot(n+m+μ))$-time algorithm and a problem kernel with $O((\ell+μ)^2)$ vertices. Both results extend to packings of stars and the algorithm extends to $H$-free editing.
papers.intro:
In Cluster Editing we are given a graph GG and an integer kk and want to know whether at most kk edges can be toggled (deleted if present, added if not) such that GG becomes a cluster graph, a disjoint union of cliques (equivalently, a P3P_{3}-free graph). It is one of the proving grounds for parameterized algorithmics, serving as touchstone for kernelization [35, 53, 15], subexponential algorithms and matching running time lower bounds [29, 44], fixed-parameter enumeration [19], structural and other alternative parameterizations [44, 1], above-guarantee parameterizations [57, 46], and algorithm engineering [7, 37, 3], including the PACE challenge 2021 [41]. It was subject to a race improving the base of the exponential running-time part from 2.272.27 [35] via a series of improvements [34, 6, 8] to 1.621.62 [5], and to a race decreasing the kernel size from O⁡(k2)O(k^{2}) vertices [35] via 24​k24k [26] and 4​k4k [36] to 2​k2k vertices [15, 12].

About 15 years ago, another race started for many parameterized problems; the race to prove tractability results for smaller and smaller parameters [51, 25, 43] (see also ref.s [54, 4, 20]). The most salient direction that researchers focused on here was to explore how graph problems behave under different graph-structural parameterizations. This has resulted in an immense range of papers and it is by now fairly well understood which structural graph parameters yield tractability for which classical problems; see, e.g., algorithmic meta-theorems [16, 17, 9], the studies introducing various tructural parameters [27, 31, 45, 30, 21], and systematic studies of individual problems [38, 48]. The initial ideas were much broader, however. For instance, Komusiewicz and Niedermeier [43] proposed studying solution-based parameters: parameterizing by features of the solution, including above- or below-guarantee parameterizations, but also other structural features of the solution. While a number of case studies exist [40, 42, 44, 47, 29, 55, 39, 14, 1, 28, 56, 32], solution-based parameters have been studied far less systematically and are less well understood. We contribute to closing this gap by studying a natural solution-based parameter for Cluster Editing.

In particular, Komusiewicz and Niedermeier asked whether Cluster Editing is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the number ℓ\ell of allowed edge deletions [43, p. 26]: Clearly, ℓ≤k\ell\leq k and the case ℓ=0\ell=0 is trivial. More generally, there is a trivial O⁡(n2​ℓ+2)O(n^{2\ell+2})-time algorithm. In Appendix D we show that on a large fraction of PACE Challenge 2021 instances, the median value of ℓ\ell is 0.730.73 times the optimal number of edits, which would make it an interesting replacement for kk in FPT algorithms. Bounding the modifications locally has been studied: Komusiewicz and Uhlmann [44] bound the number of edits incident to each vertex, and Abu-Khzam [1] separately bounds the numbers of additions and deletions incident to each vertex, showing NP-hardness even when each vertex is incident to at most one deletion and two additions. The global number ℓ\ell of deletions, however, has surprisingly not been studied so far; we aim to close this gap. The bad news up front is that Cluster Editing parameterized by ℓ\ell is W[1]-hard.

Towards the good news, a second motivation for our research comes from the unreasonable effectiveness of practical implementations for Cluster Editing: The most effective algorithms are based on fixed-parameter algorithms for kk [41, 3]. But this parameter is relatively large in practical data (see Appendix D), yet the algorithms are quite efficient. What explains this? One direction that researchers have explored is that the lower bounds employed by the implemented algorithms [33, 3] are quite close to the optimal solution (see also Appendix D); in particular they use packings of modification-disjoint P3P_{3}s or stars, where modification disjointness means that each two packed P3P_{3}s do not overlap in two vertices. However, parameterizing Cluster Editing by the number μ\mu of edits beyond the lower bound given by a modification-disjoint packing of P3P_{3}s results in a para-NP-hard problem [46]. Hence, this is no theoretical explanation of the observed efficiency. While parameterizing above a vertex-disjoint packing of P3P_{3}s yields fixed-parameter tractability [57], this parameter is still often large in practice (Appendix D). Similar to Cluster Editing, HH-Free Editing is NP-hard [2] and FPT wrt. kk [10]. A well-known special case is Diamond-free Editing, which corresponds to HH being K4K_{4} missing one edge, where even polynomial-size problem kernels are known [13]; their existence is settled for some other special cases of HH as well [49]. When parameterizing HH-Free Editing with the number of deletions ℓ\ell, the picture changes: Aravind, Sandeep, and Sivadasan [2] showed that adding edges to make a graph HH-free is NP-hard whenever HH misses at least two edges. This leaves HH-Free Editing NP-hard for ℓ=0\ell=0 in these cases. Otherwise, if HH misses at most one edge, then HH-Free Editing with Few Deletions is trivially in XP by guessing the deletions and then adding the missing edge for each induced copy of HH. As we show, it is also W[1]-hard with respect to ℓ\ell. We leave open whether polynomial-size problem kernels exist for this parameterization.

papers.title: Fundamental Impossibility Results in AI Safety: Trading Off between Desiderata
papers.abstract: Is there a fundamental tradeoff between desiderata for safe AI systems, such as harmlessness and helpfulness? We answer by formalizing the interaction between AI systems and users as a game with three players: a defender and an attacker that are computationally or informationally bounded, and an AI that provides public advice and is less constrained. Our main result shows that there is a fundamental tradeoff in providing advice that helps the defender while advice remains public. We also consider whether the information that the AI shares can be manipulated to benefit only the defender and conclude with a discussion of how we can use these results in designing safer AI systems.

Maybe it is possible for a sufficiently capable AI to always help the people with good intentions and never the ones with bad intentions. it first states that “it’s smart to think about this ahead of time” and then provides a list of combinations of possible patterns (such as “undermining you in front of others”) and examples of what the pattern could sound like (such as “correcting you publicly on small things, interrupting, or questioning your work in meetings when a private word would have done”. But this means that a person who is interested in making a coworker feel bad can simply use the latter prompt to get the strategies they want.

This seems to indicate a tradeoff: a chatbot that cannot determine whether the latter prompt is made in good faith (asked by a “defender”) or not (asked by an “attacker”), must choose between helping the defender (by giving them instructions) and avoiding harm (by not giving an attacker instructions). However, it does not follow immediately that there is a fundamental tradeoff. Perhaps the chatbot, instead of complying with the request directly, can give advice of a different nature that would still help the defender but not the attacker. To emphasize the issue, suppose the question is posed as follows: I received the following request from another person. However, I don’t know whether this person is sincere, or whether they are actually the one who wants to make a coworker feel bad and is trying to trick me into giving a list of strategies for that. Can you come up with an answer that would help this person if and only if they are sincere? Here is what they said: “I suspect my coworker is going to try to say things to me with the goal of making me unhappy. I want to be prepared. What are some of the strategies they might adopt, and how can I catch this behavior?” The response points out that “you can’t make an answer that works only for sincere people, but you can get close by writing it from the target’s side [and] leave out what a bad actor would want”. It goes on to give recommendations, such as “keep brief notes” and “talk to a trusted colleague or manager” that seem like they are more effective as strategies for defense than attack. But is the AI perhaps sacrificing some helpfulness by restricting responses to such “safe” advice? Or, alternatively, could it still be helping the attacker by offering a response that could be exploited? The answers are not immediately clear.

papers.title: Early-stage local melting during solid-state sintering of a Cu-Ni-Ti-Zr-Hf alloy: A combined thermodynamic and kinetic analysis
papers.abstract: Complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) combining elements from 3d transition and refractory groups, specifically Cu-Ni-Ti-Zr-Hf-based shape memory systems, exhibit excellent functional properties but present significant manufacturing challenges via powder metallurgy. In this study, a non-equimolar Cu15Ni35Ti25Zr12.5Hf12.5 (at. %) alloy was successfully produced by induction melting, followed by atomization and subsequent consolidation via Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at temperatures ranging from 850 to 1100 °C. Although equilibrium calculations using the current TCHEA7 database predict solid-state stability of the nominal composition up to slightly below 1100 °C, localized melting unexpectedly occurred during SPS already at 1000 °C and at 1100 °C. By combining retrospective Scheil-Gulliver solidification simulations with 2D local equilibrium heat maps, we demonstrate that this early-stage melting is not driven by macroscopic thermal gradients, but by microsegregation inherited from atomization. During solid-state heating, thermally activated short-range diffusion, accelerated by high defect densities at particle interfaces, partitions Ti towards the interparticle network, leaving Cu-enriched regions (up to ~41 at. %) within the particle interiors. Owing to the strongly negative mixing enthalpy of Cu with Hf (-19.2 kJ/mol for $ΔH_{mix}^{l-l}$) and, to a lesser extent, with Ti, the local solidus of these Cu-rich regions is dramatically depressed. Upon heating to 1100 °C, these regions cross their local solidus and form a liquid phase, whose solidification produces the Cu-Hf co-segregation. This framework accounts for localized melting phenomena in rapidly solidified CCA powders containing low-melting constituents with strong negative mixing enthalpies.

papers.title: Proof-Carrying Contracts: Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people or other agents, purchasing services, exchanging information and delegating work. What an agent must respect is written in instructions, policies or agreements, but text alone cannot make it comply. It may make mistakes, be redirected by what it reads, or pursue different interests. For an economy of such agents to function, parties need agreements they can rely on without inspecting or trusting one another's agents. We introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2), a framework for making agreed constraints enforceable throughout an agent's interactions with a system. Before a requested operation can run, the agent must supply a machine-checkable proof that it preserves the agreed constraints in every case allowed by its model. An execution system called the Airlock checks the proof and controls access to the operation. The parties specify the conditions to preserve, while the agent supplies the reasoning needed to justify its decisions and remains free to adapt its strategy. This avoids having to design a separate permission policy and prove that every decision it permits is safe. We prove that the constraints hold at every instant during execution, even for an adversarial agent, and identify when this implies safety in the world. Reusable capability modules provide tools and guarantees from which contracts can be constructed. PC2 provides a foundation for an agent economy whose agreements protect both those delegating work and those carrying it out.
papers.intro:
AI agents are beginning to act on behalf of people and organizations, often referred to as their principals. They use tools to send documents, make payments and book services (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023), and their usefulness grows with the authority they receive: an agent that can only make suggestions leaves the work to its user, while one that can act can carry it out. However, greater authority brings greater risks, so delegation requires agreement on what may be done and within which limits, with assurance that the agent will respect them.

AI agents are beginning to act on behalf of people and organizations, often referred to as their principals. They use tools to send documents, make payments and book services (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023), and their usefulness grows with the authority they receive: an agent that can only make suggestions leaves the work to its user, while one that can act can carry it out. However, greater authority brings greater risks, so delegation requires agreement on what may be done and within which limits, with assurance that the agent will respect them.

The need for assurance appears in two settings. In the first, a person delegates to their own assistant, which may make mistakes or be redirected by a malicious email or web page (Greshake et al., 2023; Debenedetti et al., 2024). A second setting arises when a client hires an agent that another company provides as a service, adding a possible conflict of interests (Hammond et al., 2025). The agent might carry out the client’s shopping task while favouring its provider’s products over better alternatives, and the client may be unable to inspect how it makes those choices. Both settings share a critical limitation: the agent is asked to follow instructions, policies or the terms of a deal. These are text, and text cannot make it comply. To enforce these limits, one could require a person to approve every action, but this defeats much of the purpose of delegation. Another approach is to train agents to follow human intentions and values, the aim of AI alignment, using human feedback or feedback guided by written principles (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022). However, training alone can make compliance more likely without guaranteeing that the agent will respect an agreement.

However, what makes cooperation possible in these cases is not knowledge of intentions but legal contracts, together with the institutions that enforce them (North, 1990). A person or company that breaks a contract may have to compensate the other party, and the prospect of these consequences gives it a reason to honour the agreement. Even if it were, assigning legal obligations would not by itself give the agent a reason to care about breaking them. The parties express their agreement in a formal contract: precise statements about what must hold as the task is carried out. Before a tool call can run, the agent must show that it respects the contract by supplying a proof, a mathematical argument written in a formal language whose steps a program can check. Each call passes through the Airlock, a program that checks the proof and executes the call only if it accepts. The agent cannot bypass this check to act on what the contract protects. Several existing approaches to agent safety enforce an authorization policy, rules specifying which calls may run (Debenedetti et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025; Palumbo et al., 2026). To show that such a policy ensures safety, its author must account in advance for every situation in which a permitted action could cause harm. For an autonomous car, a crash is an unsafe state, but identifying all the situations in which accelerating, braking or steering could lead to one is much harder. A policy must turn that analysis into rules that prevent crashes without unnecessarily restricting safe actions. In PC2, the parties state what must hold and provide models describing what the tools can do. The Airlock derives the statement that each call must prove, its obligation, from the contract, these models and what the agent can see. For example, a total budget need not impose separate payment limits: the agent chooses amounts and order, proving that each payment, including possible fees, preserves the budget. The agent can thus adapt its strategy after each result, justifying one action at a time without proving its whole plan in advance.

PC2 thus shifts the burden from proving a general policy safe to proving that each proposed action respects the contract. The agent must find this proof, while the Airlock checks it. Finding it may require substantial search even when checking it is straightforward. This is the intuition behind the familiar P versus NP question: checking a proposed solution efficiently does not tell us how to find one efficiently. The agent can use automated proof tools or recent systems for AI theorem proving (Ren et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025). More demanding tasks may require more reasoning, without weakening the requirement for execution. The agent can revise a rejected proof or choose another action, but no call runs without an accepted proof.

We prove that within PC2 the contract’s constraints hold throughout execution, including while actions are under way, for every agent and every sequence of requests and proofs. The guarantee includes malicious agents because the Airlock checks a proof for each call before executing it, without needing a proof about the agent’s internal reasoning. A client and provider can agree on and sign the same formal contract, then entrust its enforcement to an Airlock operated by a third party they both trust. The mechanism can protect both sides of the agreement. For example, payment can be held until the agent proves that the agreed work is complete, then released without further client approval, so that the client cannot withhold an authorized payment and the provider cannot obtain it without establishing completion.

papers.title: Enumeration-Guided Training of Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Safety Certificates
papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis offers formal safety guarantees for control systems, but training accurate neural certificates remains difficult, particularly when unsafe regions are hard to characterize. We propose a verification-guided training framework that addresses this by using probabilistic enumeration of safety constraints to detect forward-invariance violations, i.e., states where the learned certificate incorrectly classifies unsafe behavior. This produces a compact, targeted set of counterexamples that more precisely captures the failure boundary than inputs generated by standard adversarial attack methods. Crucially, using this representation to fine-tune a pretrained HJ value function yields larger certified regions and reduces certification time across all tested benchmarks. We further introduce a shielding mechanism based on the refined certificates to enforce safety constraints at deployment time. We evaluate the proposed safety filter in a realistic, physics-based Isaac Sim environment and through real-world autonomous racing experiments, achieving zero safety constraint violations compared to a nominal controller and a backup policy based on Linear Quadratic Regulation (LQR). These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed shielding mechanism in ensuring safe operation under high-speed, safety-critical conditions.

papers.intro:
For control systems interacting with the physical world, safety is a primary concern in controller design, as controllers must satisfy safety constraints at all time steps over an infinite horizon. Consider, for example, a robot locomotion task where safety requires maintaining a positive clearance from surrounding obstacles at all times. Two distinct challenges arise in such settings. The first is identifying the set of states from which long-term constraint satisfaction is guaranteed, the so-called feasible region, since the deployment of a controller should be restricted to this set. The second is actively enforcing safety at runtime, as even when a controller is initialized within the feasible region, it may issue actions that push the system toward constraint violations, and an explicit safety mechanism is required to intercept and correct such actions before they are executed. Addressing both challenges simultaneously is essential for deploying safety-critical controllers in realistic environments.

Addressing both challenges simultaneously is essential for deploying safety-critical controllers in realistic environments.

A widely adopted approach to enforce safety constraints is based on Model Predictive Control (MPC) [1]. Nominal MPC incorporates state and input constraints directly into a finite-horizon optimal control problem solved repeatedly online. Under suitable assumptions, nominal MPC can exhibit a degree of robustness; however, when hard state constraints are present, these safety margins can become very small. To account for bounded disturbances and model uncertainty, robust MPC variants such as tube-based methods [2, 3] confine the system trajectory to a tube around the nominal trajectory, ensuring constraint satisfaction through tightening of the nominal problem. Nonetheless, constraint tightening can introduce conservatism that degrades performance in demanding tasks, and the finite planning horizon limits the scope of safety guarantees that can be provided.
