A more principled framework for characterizing safety over an infinite horizon is Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis [4], which offers a formal setting for computing feasible regions of control systems subject to safety constraints. HJ reachability defines the feasible region as the zero-sublevel set of a value function V⁡(x)V(x), representing the worst-case constraint violation along an optimally controlled trajectory originating from state xx. Compared with MPC-based approaches, HJ reachability provides direct global safety guarantees rather than relying on finite-horizon optimization and repeated replanning. This makes VV a natural candidate not only for certifying the feasible region, but also for constructing a runtime safety filter, namely a shield, that corrects unsafe control actions by substituting a verified backup policy whenever a nominal controller would violate the safe set boundary. However, this increased rigor comes at a high computational cost, as the underlying HJ partial differential equations suffer from the well-known curse of dimensionality, making exact solutions intractable for high-dimensional systems.

To address this limitation, several recent works have proposed neural HJ certificates, leveraging function approximation to scale reachability analysis to more complex systems [5, 6]. Nevertheless, learned certificates do not inherently guarantee that the resulting zero-sublevel set defines a sound feasible region and therefore require formal verification to confirm that safety guarantees are preserved. This limitation motivated the approach of Yang. et al. [7], which integrates neural value function learning within a training loop guided by adversarial search and formal verification. While this approach improves scalability and enables learning of provably safe certificates, it faces three critical challenges that we aim to address in this work. First, the adversarial procedure is empirical and relies on sparse, locally generated counterexamples as gradient-based attacks explore only a narrow neighborhood of the current iterate and may therefore miss failures located in other regions of the state space. As a result, the search may report no violation even when unsafe states remain in the fine-tuned certificate, not because these states are genuinely safe, but because the search did not reach them. This false negative prematurely triggers the formal verifier, which, being NP-hard [8], can incur substantial computational cost. The verifier then identifies the violation that the adversarial search missed, generates additional counterexamples, and initiates another fine-tuning cycle. This process can repeat over many iterations, leading to significant verification overhead before convergence. The inefficiency becomes particularly acute in high-dimensional systems, where the local coverage of adversarial search can be small relative to the global extent of the failure set. Second, even after a verified certificate has been obtained, the question of how to exploit it as a practical runtime safety filter for a learned controller operating in a complex environment remains unaddressed: translating the certified feasible region into an effective shielding mechanism requires additional design choices that the learning procedure alone does not resolve.

papers.title: Sparse RL Relaxation for LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent work has explored continuous representations in place of discrete tokens during Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, often referred to as soft CoT. This is motivated by the idea that a mixture of token embeddings can represent a superposition of multiple reasoning possibilities within a single step. However, it remains challenging to train large language models to realize this potential. Existing work has explored reinforcement learning (RL)-style training for soft CoT. However, these approaches treat soft tokens as actions in a Markov decision process rather than as differentiable intermediate computation steps. Thus, they do not propagate gradients across the soft tokens and miss out on the signal of how the choice of one soft token affects the next. In this paper, we propose a sparse relaxation method for RL (called SpaRLax), which leverages the differentiability of soft-CoT reasoning over time steps and makes training more stable and effective. We adopt an entmax sparsity method that adaptively determines the degree of softness, which truncates long-tail noise at confident steps while retaining multiple plausible candidates when uncertain. Across nine reasoning benchmarks, our method achieves the highest average performance compared with baseline methods. Further analyses validate the effective use of soft-token superposition in our approach, and also demonstrate the contribution of adaptive sparsity in our approach.
papers.intro:
Chain of Thoughts (Wei et al., 2022, CoT;) improves the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) by generating intermediate steps before the final answer. Despite its effectiveness, CoT produces a single discrete token at each step, collapsing the LLM’s output distribution to one token and discarding alternatives that may be useful later. This has motivated recent work on soft CoT, where intermediate reasoning tokens are represented by continuous embeddings (Hao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025b). Among these approaches, Zhang et al. (2025) construct each CoT token as a probability-weighted mixture of token embeddings, referred to as a soft token, allowing multiple candidate semantics to coexist at a reasoning step. Theoretical analyses (Zhu et al., 2025) further show that such continuous representation can represent multiple reasoning paths in superposition and can be more expressive than discrete CoT, suggesting soft CoT as a promising direction for improving LLM reasoning.

We propose a solution to this problem by using sparse relaxation, which concentrates probability mass on a few candidate tokens, while assigning exactly zero probability to low-scoring tokens. In particular, we apply entmax (Peters et al., 2019) on top of the Gumbel reparametrization trick when constructing the soft-token distribution, as entmax can naturally adapt the degree of softness by the uncertainty of each reasoning step.

papers.title: Stacking-Induced Tuning of a Flat-Band Surface State in NbIrTe4
papers.abstract: Ternary layered transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) offer high tunability and access to correlated and topological states. However, like the broader family of layered TMDCs, their properties are sensitive to stacking order and interlayer coupling. Here, we investigate the electronic structure and surface states of NbIrTe$_4$, a candidate Weyl semimetal in bulk, and predicted to be a quantum spin Hall insulator in monolayer form. Using scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM), angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), and density-functional theory (DFT), we attribute the strong resonance in tunnelling spectroscopy located approximately 8 meV below the Fermi level to a surface-derived flat band which shows sensitivity to the local stacking order at the surface. In regions where the top layer is laterally shifted, tunnelling spectroscopy instead shows a gap-like feature with intensity near the Fermi level shifted in energy. Combining DFT and quasiparticle interference (QPI) measurements, we find this dramatic change in the spectroscopy in the vicinity of the quasi-1D flat-band surface state becomes dispersive due to a change in the spatial distribution of the density of states in the top two layers. These findings establish NbIrTe$_4$ as a platform where surface band dispersion can be effectively tuned through local structural manipulation.

papers.intro:
Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) have long provided a versatile platform for exploring symmetry-broken and correlated phases [1, 2, 3]. Members of this material class frequently host electronic instabilities and nontrivial band topology, giving rise to a diverse phase diagram that includes charge-density waves (CDWs) [3, 4], superconductivity [5], and topological states such as type-II Weyl semimetals [6, 7]. Due to the weak interlayer van der Waals (vdW) coupling, a defining characteristic of TMDCs is the tunability of their electronic structure via stacking order and layer thickness [8, 9, 10, 11]. Within the bulk phases, different polymorphs consisting of different stacking orders exhibit different electronic properties [1, 12], while fabrication of monolayer, bilayer, and twisted stacking have demonstrated the incredible power of modifying interlayer coupling and stacking symmetry [13, 14, 15, 16].

Moving beyond binary TMDCs, ternary compounds of layered transition metal chalcogenides further expand the phase space for correlated and topological phenomena. The integration of an additional transition metal species introduces extra orbital degrees of freedom and reduced lattice symmetry, resulting in a complex and tunable electronic structure [17, 18, 19]. In the prototypical type-II Weyl semimetal TaIrTe4\text{TaIrTe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}}, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and transport measurements have revealed a nontrivial topology characterized by Weyl points and Fermi-arc surface states [20, 21, 22].

The sister compound NbIrTe4\text{NbIrTe}_{4} is isostructural to TaIrTe4\text{TaIrTe}_{4}, adopting the noncentrosymmetric orthorhombic space group P​m​n​21Pmn2_{1} [23, 24]. This distorted octahedral coordination leads to structural anisotropy and broken inversion symmetry, hosting a variety of exotic electronic phases. Notably, bulk NbIrTe4\text{NbIrTe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}} exhibits non-saturating magnetoresistance at ambient pressure [25, 26, 27], and pressure-induced superconductivity has also been reported [28, 29], highlighting the sensitivity of its electronic properties to subtle lattice modifications and structural tuning.

Prior studies have indicated that accessing such exotic states may not strictly require physical exfoliation as local variations in stacking order and the associated symmetry breaking can fundamentally alter the band topology, such as in the case of graphite, where altering the Bernal stacking decouples the surface layer and recovers monolayer-like Dirac-dispersion [34, 35, 36], while a recent THz STM study showed evidence of a topological phase transition coupled to shear of the topmost atomic layer of bulk WTe2\text{WTe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} [37]. In this work, we present a combined experimental and theoretical study of the surface electronic structure of NbIrTe4\text{NbIrTe}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}}. Using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), we identify a prominent surface state resonance just below the Fermi level. Complementary ARPES measurements reveal that this feature originates from a quasi-1D flat band along the Γ\Gamma–YY direction, giving rise to a sharp enhancement in the density of states. Notably, we find that this sharp spectral signature vanishes in regions where the top surface layer is laterally shifted, demonstrating the critical sensitivity of the electronic structure to the local stacking order. papers.title: Kinematically isolating intracluster light in AS1063: a distinct stellar population tracing the dark matter core
papers.abstract: We present a technique using integral-field spectroscopy to kinematically isolate intracluster light (ICL) from the brightest cluster galaxy (BCG), enabling insights into their contrasting stellar populations and the inner dark matter halo profile. Applying this technique to MUSE data of Abell S1063, we find that both components are old (~9 Gyr), but the ICL is more metal-poor than the BCG, implying distinct progenitor pathways. Within 100 kpc, the ICL comprises 55 per cent of the BCG+ICL stellar mass - substantially more than inferred from photometric decompositions. The BCG and ICL possess distinct velocity distributions, which remain nearly constant with radius, with an ICL velocity dispersion more than twice that of the BCG, and a line-of-sight velocity offset of 86 +- 18 km/s. Two-dimensional Sérsic fits yield an ICL centroid offset of 5.2 +- 1.5 kpc from the BCG. These phase-space offsets are indicative of the BCG oscillating in a broad potential minimum. Furthermore, the ICL surface-brightness profile matches that of strong-lensing estimates assuming a cored halo. Simulations indicate that the inner halo profile varies systematically for different dark matter models. Applied to larger samples, our method therefore offers a complementary route to testing the nature of dark matter, while simultaneously revealing the stellar origins of the ICL.

papers.intro:
Intracluster light (ICL) is a diffuse stellar component of galaxy clusters, composed of stars that have been stripped from their host galaxies through tidal interactions and mergers, and are instead bound to the gravitational potential of the cluster as a whole (Zwicky, 1951). As a record of disrupted galaxies, the ICL provides insights into the hierarchical assembly of clusters (Contini et al., 2014; Mihos et al., 2017), encodes the timing and nature of past dynamical interactions (Montes & Trujillo, 2018; DeMaio et al., 2020), and closely traces the underlying dark matter distribution on large scales, potentially serving as a luminous proxy for dark matter in optical observations (Montes & Trujillo, 2019; Alonso Asensio et al., 2020).

The central regions of clusters – where the ICL spatially overlaps with the brightest cluster galaxy (BCG) – are particularly important for understanding both cluster and BCG assembly. This region captures the buildup of both components through mergers and accretion (Murante et al., 2007; Burke et al., 2015), and provides a window into their stellar population differences, such as age and metallicity gradients (Montes & Trujillo, 2014; Edwards et al., 2020; Barbosa et al., 2021). Furthermore, detailed mapping of this transition region enables tests of dark matter models, as competing theories predict subtle differences in inner density profiles and dynamics (Newman et al., 2013; Schaller et al., 2015; Robertson et al., 2019; Andrade et al., 2022). Constraining the structure of the BCG–ICL interface is therefore essential for probing both baryonic and dark matter physics in cluster cores.

While the ICL and BCG can appear blended photometrically due to their continuous luminosity profiles, simulations show they occupy distinct dynamical states: ICL stars exhibit higher velocity dispersions and trace the cluster potential, whereas BCG stars are more centrally bound (Dolag et al., 2010; Remus et al., 2017; Marini et al., 2021). Pearce et al. (2026) explains the dichotomy as resulting from a strongly mass-dependent combination of dynamical friction, tidal stripping and violent relaxation. Observational evidence supports this separation through spectroscopy of integrated stellar light (Kelson et al., 2002; Bender et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2020) and discrete tracers such as planetary nebulae (Longobardi et al., 2015; Hartke et al., 2022), both of which reveal rising velocity dispersion profiles consistent with an extended ICL component. Kinematics thus provide a physically motivated framework for separating the BCG and ICL, especially in the central regions.

Photometric methods remain widely used for ICL identification due to their simplicity and applicability to imaging surveys. These include surface-brightness thresholds (Feldmeier et al., 2004; Burke et al., 2015, e.g.), multi-component profile fitting (Gonzalez et al., 2005; Kluge et al., 2021), and non-parametric techniques such as wavelet decomposition, which isolate large-scale diffuse emission (Ellien et al., 2019). However, comparisons with simulations – where the BCG and ICL can be defined kinematically – show that photometric methods often underestimate the ICL fraction and are sensitive to model assumptions, projection effects, and data depth (Rudick et al., 2011; Pillepich et al., 2018; Cañas et al., 2020). A recent study by Brough et al. (2024) applied a range of photometric techniques to mock observations from hydrodynamical simulations and found systematic biases across all methods. Multi-galaxy fitting yielded the most accurate results, while surface-brightness cuts and profile decompositions showed larger discrepancies. Empirical corrections were proposed to calibrate photometric ICL estimates to kinematic definitions. While some overlap exists between photometric and kinematic components in observed systems, they are not interchangeable, underscoring the limitations of relying solely on imaging data (Longobardi et al., 2015; Barbosa et al., 2021; Hartke et al., 2022).

A complementary – and potentially transformative – motivation for isolating the ICL is its use as a dynamical tracer of the inner halo, which could help to elucidate the nature of dark matter. While cold dark matter (CDM) is typically assumed by current simulations of galaxy formation, several alternative models – including warm, mixed, fuzzy, and self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) – can also match existing observations. A promising way to distinguish among these scenarios is to examine the inner regions of dark matter halos, since the additional physical processes in many alternative models alter the central structure of halos, producing ‘cored’ mass distributions, with shallow central density profiles compared to the sharply-peaked, ‘cuspy’, profiles formed in standard CDM (Harvey et al., 2019). Strong lensing is the current gold standard for measuring inner mass profiles (Gassis et al., 2025), but only in projection, and it is limited by our ability to model the detailed sub-structure of the mass distribution (Roche et al., 2024; Perera et al., 2025). X-rays are also useful, but they trace hot gas, which is complex to model and easily disturbed (Sanders et al., 2020; XRISM Collaboration et al., 2025).

The gravitational potential within a galaxy cluster is set primarily by dark matter, so stars on higher-energy orbits that populate the extended ICL can, in principle, map that potential. Gravitational lensing already indicates that, in cluster outskirts, the isophotes of the diffuse stellar light closely follow the total mass distribution (Montes & Trujillo, 2019). Spectroscopically isolating the ICL throughout the cluster core would enable constraints on the inner density profile and, uniquely, simultaneous measurements of BCG–halo offsets in both projected position and line-of-sight velocity. Since motion of the BCG is less constrained within a cored halo, the joint distribution of such phase-space offsets across a sample of clusters is a predicted discriminator among dark matter models (Harvey et al., 2019; Harvey et al., 2025), provided the BCG and ICL can be separated robustly. To date, that separation has remained the principal obstacle to using ICL as a probe of halo cores.

papers.title: Large Deviations in Stochastic Dynamics: A Hamiltonian Perspective
papers.abstract: These lecture notes present an introduction to large deviations in stochastic dynamical systems, adapted from a lecture series given at the Les Houches school ``Large Deviations: Theory and Applications'' in July 2024. The exposition develops the theory through a unified methodology: WKB analysis of backward Kolmogorov equations, which reveals the Hamiltonian structure underlying all large deviation principles considered here. We treat three asymptotic regimes systematically. First, the small-noise limit for stochastic differential equations and the large-volume limit for Markov jump processes, where the Large Deviation Principle emerges from the Law of Large Numbers through progressively finer characterizations of fluctuations. Second, the long-time limit combined with small noise, yielding the quasipotential formalism for metastability and transition rates in both equilibrium and nonequlibrium systems. Third, the long-time limit at finite noise, connecting to spectral methods via tilted generators and enabling reduction of multiscale systems. We survey computational approaches including minimum action methods, their geometric variants for quasipotential calculations, and neural network techniques. The Schlögl model of chemical bistability serves as a running example, illustrating both scalar and spatially extended settings. Appendices provide self-contained background on stochastic calculus and Markov jump processes.

papers.intro:
Rare events—nucleation of a new phase, switching between metastable states, extreme fluctuations of currents or densities—often have dramatic consequences for the behavior of stochastic systems. Yet because they occur with probabilities that are exponentially small on the natural time scales of the dynamics, they are inaccessible to direct simulation or standard perturbation theory. Large deviation theory provides the natural mathematical framework for analyzing such events: it characterizes exponentially rare fluctuations through variational principles that transform probabilistic questions into deterministic optimization problems. These notes, adapted from lectures given at the Les Houches school “Large Deviations: Theory and Applications” (July 2024), develop this theory for stochastic dynamical systems with an emphasis on the computational structures that emerge.

These notes, adapted from lectures given at the Les Houches school “Large Deviations: Theory and Applications” (July 2024), develop this theory for stochastic dynamical systems with an emphasis on the computational structures that emerge.

The unifying thread of these notes is methodological: in each setting we derive the Large Deviation Principle (LDP) from a multiscale expansion technique, namely the WKB (Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin) ansatz. We apply this formal asymptotic expansion to the appropriate backward equation to obtain the LDP. This approach is simple and transparent, revealing the Hamiltonian structure that underlies all large deviation problems in a unified way. This Hamiltonian structure reflects the Gärtner–Ellis theorem at the infinitesimal level: the Hamiltonian is a cumulant generating function, and the Lagrangian—obtained via Legendre transform—is the corresponding rate function. The WKB approach is also generic, applying with minimal modification across limits taken in noise, spatial discretization, and time. While these formal derivations are not rigorous, the resulting statements can be established rigorously using the theory of viscosity solutions or probabilistic methods; we refer to the foundational texts [21, 9, 43, 10, 19] for complete proofs.

papers.title: Core-Collapse Supernova Rates in the Dark Energy Survey
papers.abstract: Over its five-year campaign (2013-2017), the Dark Energy Survey (DES) supernova (SN) survey recorded 31,636 light curves. Using a custom-built, two-stage random forest classifier, we identified 2,445 likely core-collapse SNe (CC SNe) within the survey rate analysis footprint. With this sample, we measure the volumetric CC SN rate from redshift z = 0 to 1.3 in 11 redshift bins, representing the most detailed single-survey coverage to date across nine billion years of lookback time. Over this interval, the CC SN rates are well fit by a power law R_CC(z) = R_0 (1 + z)^α, with R_0 = 1.58 \pm 0.17 \times 10^{-4} \text{ yr}^{-1} \text{ Mpc}^{-3} and α= 2.85 \pm 0.25. The rate turnover, expected at cosmic noon, is not yet apparent. Because CC SNe trace recent star formation, we compare our measurements with recent cosmic star-formation history (CSFH) models. Our measurements are ~70 per cent higher than CSFH models using a Salpeter initial mass function (IMF) to predict CC SN rates. Replacing the Salpeter IMF with a Baldry and Glazebrook IMF and a CC SN progenitor mass range of 8-40 M_\odot bridges the gap. Alternatively, CSFHs may miss a hitherto unidentified population of low-luminosity galaxies. We further find that the local ratio of stripped-envelope (SE) SNe to all CC SNe is 31 \pm 5 per cent, remaining constant from z = 0 to 1.3. Combined with an IMF analysis accounting for the "missing progenitor problem" of hydrogen-rich SNe, our results favour a mixture of single massive stars and binaries as SE SN progenitors, with the redshift-invariant ratio favouring binary channels.

papers.title: Likelihood-Based Confidence Curves for Bounded Parameters
papers.abstract: When a parameter is bounded, the likelihood ratio statistic does not generally follow the chi-square limit distribution of Wilks' theorem. In fact, its asymptotic null distribution depends on the distance from the null value to the boundary, interpolating between the chi-bar-square law on the boundary and the chi-square law in the deep interior of the parameter space. We derive this distribution and use it to construct confidence curves, which are nested collections of two-sided confidence intervals or regions, for bounded parameters. We extend the existing result for the scalar parameter to a two-dimensional parameter with one or both components bounded. As the bivariate distributions are integrals of normal distributions, which are not reducible to standard statistical functions, we also give a simpler approximated distribution obtained by moment-matching. We illustrate the methods on a canonical analysis from high-energy physics, namely the Poisson signal-plus-background experiment.
papers.intro:
Classical inference often depends on Wilks’ theorem (Wilks, 1938): under standard regularity conditions the likelihood ratio statistic has an asymptotic chi-square null distribution, providing the reference distribution for tests and confidence intervals. One of these regularity conditions is not met when the hypothesised null value of the parameter lies on the boundary of the parameter space (Brazzale and Mameli, 2024, see, e.g.,). For the simple case of testing a one-dimensional parameter on the boundary, Chernoff (1954) showed that the limiting law is a mixture of a point mass in zero and a chi-square with one degree of freedom. This work was later extended to the multivariate case mainly by Shapiro (1985); Shapiro (1988), Self and Liang (1987) and Kopylev and Sinha (2011). Together, these results form a well-developed theory for testing on the boundary, that is, when the parameter value specified under the null hypothesis lies exactly on the boundary of the parameter space. In this setting, provided there is no nuisance parameter constrained at the boundary, the null distribution is corrected from a chi-square to a chi-bar-square (Kudô, 1963), and fixed-level tests are adjusted accordingly.

Confidence intervals, however, require more than the distribution at a single boundary point. A confidence set is obtained by inverting a family of tests across a range of null values. As the null candidate approaches the boundary from the inside of the parameter space, the distribution of the likelihood ratio statistic passes from the standard chi-square law to the boundary chi-bar-square through a certain transition regime. Accurate intervals therefore need the null distribution not only on the boundary, where the chi-bar-square correction applies, but throughout all of its neighbourhood. In this article, we study this near-boundary distribution.

In this analysis, a detector records a count that is assumed to be Poisson-distributed with mean μ+β\mu+\beta, where β>0\beta>0 is the background rate expected from pre-established physical phenomena and μ≥0\mu\geq 0 the signal rate of potential new physics. The task is to summarise what the data say about μ\mu—in particular, how large it could plausibly be—through an appropriate confidence interval.

There are two main likelihood-based approaches to this problem. The first ignores the boundary at the inference stage: the likelihood ratio statistic is built from the unrestricted maximiser μ~\tilde{\mu}, which may take values outside the parameter space of μ\mu provided that the likelihood is mathematically defined there, and the statistic retains its usual chi-square limiting distribution. Throughout this paper, we refer to this method as the naïve approach, and μ~\tilde{\mu} as the naïve estimator. In the context of the signal-plus-background experiment, this approach is discussed in Mandelkern (2002), and is also used in, for instance, Fraser et al. (2004) and in the experimental papers The BABAR Collaboration (2006) and The BESIII Collaboration (2026). This approach is considered in Feldman and Cousins (1998) and Cowan et al. Mandelkern (2002) observed that the naïve approach can return empty intervals at nominal levels as high as 68%68\% or even 95%95\%, which is an outcome that is unsatisfactory to report. In response, Fraser et al. (2004) argued against reducing the inferential information to a single fixed-level confidence interval; such an interval treats inference as a decision, accepting the parameter values that fall inside and rejecting those outside, rather than conveying how much evidence the data carry for each. They proposed reporting the entire pp-value function instead. We follow Schweder and Hjort (2002) and Xie and Singh (2013) in calling this pp-value function a confidence distribution, which encodes one-sided confidence statements at every parameter value; its two-sided form, the confidence curve, carries the whole nested family of two-sided intervals at all levels in a single object.

Here, we build confidence curves from likelihood ratio statistics based on the MLE, combining the confidence distribution viewpoint of Fraser et al. (2004) with the boundary-respecting approach of Feldman and Cousins (1998). Since a confidence curve, like a confidence interval, is obtained by inverting a test at every candidate value θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, the null distribution of the test statistic must be known (or approximated) at each such θ\theta. Feldman and Cousins (1998) obtain the required null distribution pointwise and numerically, through numerical integration for a one-dimensional parameter of interest or by Monte Carlo (MC) simulation for a multidimensional one. Schweder and Hjort (2016, Section 4.2) likewise obtain the null distribution by simulation. Cowan et al. (2011) and Wu and Neale (2012) instead derive it analytically, as a piecewise function of standard normal cumulative distribution functions (CDFs), for a single bounded parameter of interest. This distribution interpolates between the chi-bar-square on the boundary and the ordinary chi-square in the interior, with the transition governed by the standardised distance from the null value to the boundary.

papers.title: Certified Non-Degenerate Maximum-Likelihood Benchmarking of Quantum LDPC Decoders
papers.abstract: The measured logical error rate of a quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) code depends on the decoding algorithm. We develop a framework that certifies non-degenerate maximum-likelihood (ML) decoding outcomes on individual sampled shots under circuit-level noise, providing a common reference for comparing decoders and codes. Upper and lower bounds on the minimum correction cost in the true and competing logical classes establish success, failure, or an undecided outcome. Branch-and-bound search refines these intervals while retaining valid bounds under resource limits. Counting the outcomes bounds the empirical ML logical error rate, with interval width equal to the undecided fraction. Results for two bivariate bicycle codes show that best-first ordered statistics decoding (BF-OSD) tracks the non-degenerate ML benchmark closely while leaving some ML-correctable shots.

papers.intro:
The error rate performance of a QLDPC code under practical decoding schemes is typically assessed by Monte Carlo simulation. On the other hand, Monte Carlo simulation typically cannot establish the performance of the same code under a specified maximum-likelihood (ML) rule, whose evaluation is generally computationally demanding [1]. Belief propagation (BP) with ordered statistics decoding (OSD) is the current state-of-the-art for QLDPC decoding [2, 3], and refinements continue to improve measured logical error rates and efficiency [4]. However, a search that finds no better correction does not establish optimality unless it also bounds the unexplored candidates.

A certificate is a set of verified bounds that proves a decoding outcome for a sampled shot, even if some candidate corrections remain unexplored. The term cost refers to the likelihood of an error: a more likely error has a lower cost. We use such certificates to establish the outcome of non-degenerate ML decoding: selecting the most probable error pattern under the specified detector error model and returning its logical effect, that is, the effect onto the logical qubits, referred to here as class. Two different physical errors can perform the same logical operation, i.e. they are part of the same class. Non-degenerate ML differs from degenerate ML, which maximizes the total probability of a class. For each sampled shot, bounds establish whether the most probable correction belongs to the true class, or leave the outcome undecided. Shot aggregation yields lower and upper bounds on the empirical non-degenerate ML error rate. The bounds provide a reference for comparing decoders and identify decoder failures on which this ML rule would succeed.

papers.title: A Bochner Weitzenböck Decomposition for Cellular Sheaf Laplacians, Curvature and Neural Sheaf Diffusion
papers.abstract: We extend the Bochner-Weitzenböck decomposition to cellular sheaf Laplacians, splitting it into a positive semidefinite term, the Bochner sheaf Laplacian, and a block diagonal term, the Forman curvature. We show that the Bochner Laplacians form a class of cellular sheaves that extends both connection and matrix-weighted Laplacians, and generalizes signed graphs to $d$ dimensions. We give a holonomy characterization of their kernel, prove the related Cheeger inequalities, and attach to them a random walk that generalizes the Gremban expansion. For the Forman term, we prove a discrete Bochner theorem, which bounds the first cohomology of a cellular sheaf with nonnegative curvature, and we read the whole decomposition as an opinion-dynamics model. We then apply this machinery to Sheaf Neural Networks, whose learnt Laplacian is otherwise unobserved. The Bochner interpretation yields a node-level conviction score that acts as an operational importance measure under frozen-model interventions, while the Forman profile provides a local descriptor of the learnt operator.
papers.intro:
A sheaf prescribes how local data glue into global data, and turns the obstruction to gluing into a cohomological invariant [11, 49, 51, 47]. On a graph or a simplicial complex, a cellular sheaf [17, 65] attaches a vector space to each cell and a linear map to each incidence, so that the theory becomes finite linear algebra. In this form sheaves have been used for fusing sensor readings [64], for distributed coordination and optimization [36, 38], and in topological data analysis [16, 21, 20], wherever a relation on a graph needs more than a scalar weight. Their central operator is the sheaf Laplacian, which has the foundations of a spectral theory [39] and a signal processing theory [19], and which models opinion dynamics, the stalks carrying private opinions and the restriction maps the discourse between agents [40].

In machine learning, where topology has entered from geometric deep learning [13] to higher-order domains such as simplicial complexes and hypergraphs [63, 12], the most notable application of sheaves is the Sheaf Neural Network [37, 7]. A graph neural network diffuses node features along the edges, and fails on heterophilic graphs, where neighbours tend to carry different labels. A Sheaf Neural Network learns a sheaf over the graph and diffuses with its sheaf Laplacian, so that each node transforms its message differently for each neighbour, which restores separation power on heterophilic data. The sheaf is then an object produced by training. The limiting behaviour of sheaf diffusion is described by the Hodge decomposition, which identifies the kernel of the sheaf Laplacian with sheaf cohomology. Three questions that are standard for the graph Laplacian, however, remain open for a general sheaf Laplacian. The first is spectral: a general spectral theory of cellular sheaves is still far from complete [39, 19], and Cheeger-type bounds, classical for graphs [14], are available only in special cases, notably connection Laplacians [4, 68]. The second is probabilistic: it is not clear how to attach to a sheaf Laplacian a vector-valued random walk, a question left open in [39]. The third is combinatorial: cellular sheaves lack an analogue of Forman’s Bochner decomposition [25], a local curvature, cheaper to compute than the spectrum and easier to interpret.

On a graph this is an opinion dynamics model, in which the Bochner term drives the agents towards a common conviction, the norm a stalk carries, and the Forman block measures how loudly an agent speaks relative to its neighbours, its relative volume.

The available theory describes what they can represent: convergence of sheaf diffusion, and a universal approximation theorem by which a network can learn any sheaf on a graph. What is missing is a description of what the learning mechanism does: which region of the sheaf space a training pipeline reaches, and whether different pipelines are biased towards different regions. From the decomposition we derive two diagnostics of neural sheaf diffusion, one per term: the conviction and the Forman profile. The conviction is an operational score of node importance: on a frozen trained network, removing the highest-conviction nodes is the most damaging intervention at every budget and in every perturbation mode, while removing the lowest-conviction ones costs less than removing arbitrary nodes of the same graph. The Forman profile tracks, layer by layer, how a learning mechanism navigates the sheaf space, and each of the three mechanisms we test leaves its own signature: normalized general sheaf learning converges to local alignment with the normalized graph Laplacian, unnormalized learning aligns with neither reference, and joint diffusion [45] reverses the role of normalization. Evaluated without normalization, the profile of the same learnt maps stays far from that of the identity sheaf, so we read the alignment as an inductive bias towards one region of the sheaf space.

papers.title: LocaLeJEPA: Maximum Entropy Representations under Geometric Priors
papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) offer an appealing approach to self-supervised learning, but are typically prone to representation collapse. LeJEPA resolves this by introducing a theoretically grounded distribution-matching objective that drives the embedding towards an isotropic Gaussian. However, this approach is fundamentally tied to Euclidean assumptions, and its global target does not reflect domain-specific geometric priors, such as the use of non-Euclidean embedding geometries, e.g., equivariant CNNs or hyperbolic ViTs. We thus introduce LocaLeJEPA, a framework motivated by a manifold-theoretic reformulation of LeJEPA's entropy-maximization property. The accompanying LocaLeReg, a novel locally Euclidean distribution-matching regularizer, enables a stable and scalable implementation of the LocaLeJEPA framework. We then perform extensive experiments in the vision setting on models trained on ImageNet-1K. LocaLeJEPA significantly outperforms LeJEPA when paired with hyperbolic ViT-S/8 and equivariant ResNet-50 backbones, and also with ordinary Euclidean ViT-S/8 and ViT-L/14 backbones. This holds both in terms of linear and k-NN classification performance on ImageNet and on a series of downstream tasks tested. We view the LocaLeJEPA formalism as a principled approach to the JEPA paradigm that better respects intrinsic data geometry while also accommodating generalizations to exotic embedding geometries. Code available at https://github.com/alessioborgi/LocaLeJEPA.

papers.title: A Semi-Analytical Inference Framework for Structural Causal Models
papers.abstract: Structural Causal Models (SCMs) provide a principled framework for observational, interventional, and counterfactual reasoning, all of which rely on probabilistic inference. Existing frameworks either transform SCMs into alternative tractable representations or rely on approximate inference with expressive generative models. We instead perform inference using a message passing scheme directly on the SCM by representing structural mechanisms and probability densities in a common finite-dimensional function space. Forward propagation combines a numerical realization of the Law of the Unconscious Statistician, while propagated densities are recovered by spline projection from LOTUS moments. The same representation naturally yields backward message passing for conditioning, providing a unified framework for causal inference. Using tensor-product B-spline bases, the resulting algorithm expresses inference through numerical quadrature and linear algebra without explicitly constructing conditional distributions. Experiments on randomly generated continuous SCMs demonstrate accurate approximation of Monte Carlo reference solutions and systematic improvement with increasing basis resolution.
papers.intro:
The notion of causality has been central to philosophical discourse since antiquity. Structural Causal Models (SCMs) provide one of the most widely used mathematical frameworks for causal reasoning (Pearl 2009). Under the assumption that the modeled system is causally closed, uncertainty is confined to exogenous variables and endogenous variables are related deterministically (Peters et al. 2017). SCMs support three levels of reasoning, known as Pearl’s causal hierarchy: association, intervention, and counterfactuals (Pearl and Mackenzie 2018). Although these three query types differ in their semantics, each ultimately requires evaluating probability distributions induced by the SCM. Efficient probabilistic inference therefore forms the computational core of causal reasoning. Observational queries require probabilistic inference in the observational distribution, i.e. the pushforward distribution of the exogenous distribution under the hierarchical causal mechanism, interventional queries require inference after modifying the structural equations, and counterfactual reasoning combines conditioning with hypothetical interventions (Han et al. 2023; Pearl 2009). Specifically, counterfactual inference can be formulated using a twin SCM or, equivalently, an abduct-intervene-infer procedure (Pearl 2009).

Specifically, counterfactual inference can be formulated using a twin SCM or, equivalently, an abduct-intervene-infer procedure (Pearl 2009).

While much of the causal modeling literature focuses on causal discovery, identification, and effect estimation from data (Peters et al. 2017), comparatively less attention has been devoted to efficiently evaluating queries in a given SCM (Darwiche 2022; Wang and Kwiatkowska 2023; Zečević et al. 2021; Pawlowski et al. 2020). These directions are complementary: discovery and identification determine the causal model and identifiable effects, whereas causal inference assumes a given SCM and answers causal queries. This setting naturally arises when the model is provided by expert knowledge or a preceding learning stage.

Causal inference appears closely related to inference in Bayesian networks (BNs) (Koller and Friedman 2009), where algorithms such as variable elimination, belief propagation, and junction-tree message passing enable efficient exact and approximate inference (Pearl 1982; Zhang and Poole 1996; Wainwright and Jordan 2008). Since every acyclic SCM induces a BN, it is natural to ask whether these methods apply directly. However, BN inference requires explicit conditional distributions, whereas SCMs define them only implicitly through deterministic structural mechanisms and exogenous noise. Thus, inference depends both on the graph structure and the representation of the structural mechanisms.

However, BN inference requires explicit conditional distributions, whereas SCMs define them only implicitly through deterministic structural mechanisms and exogenous noise. Thus, inference depends both on the graph structure and the representation of the structural mechanisms.

Several approaches have addressed this challenge. One line of work compiles SCMs into alternative representations that support tractable inference, including tractable circuits and related representations (Darwiche 2022; Wang and Kwiatkowska 2023; Zečević et al. 2021). Another employs expressive structural mechanisms based on deep generative models (Pawlowski et al. 2020), where inference is typically performed approximately. Existing methods therefore either transform the SCM into a tractable representation or perform inference approximately using sampling or learned generative models.

We instantiate the framework using tensor-product B-spline bases, whose approximation properties, numerical stability, and efficient quadrature algorithms (de Boor 2001; Schumaker 2007; Cottrell et al. 2009) allow inference to be expressed through linear algebra and numerical quadrature while representing highly nonlinear mechanisms. Specifically, we model both densities and structural mechanisms using tensor-product B-splines. Restricting structural mechanisms is not itself new (Hoyer et al. 2008; Bühlmann et al. 2014; Morville and Park 2025; Zhang and Hyvärinen 2009). papers.title: Norm-optimal model order reduction in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of model order reduction (MOR) in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs). We prove generalizations of well-known necessary interpolatory conditions for norm-optimal reduced-order models, originally stated for rational functions in $H_2$ Hardy-Hilbert spaces. We construct an alternative to the iterative rational Krylov (IRKA) algorithm for RKHSs with differentiable kernels to obtain norm-optimal reduced-order models. Then, we introduce generalized Malmquist-Takenaka (GMT) functions that can be used to define orthonormal bases in an arbitrary RKHS. Using GMT functions, we propose unitary transformations between separable RKHSs. This allows us to extend our optimality conditions and subsequent algorithms to MOR problems posed in RKHSs with non-differentiable kernels. The potential and versatility of the proposed MOR framework is demonstrated in several numerical experiments. We perform norm-optimal MOR on various machine learning models such as support vector machines and deep ReLU networks. In addition, we show how the proposed MOR framework can be used to solve seemingly unrelated problems. In particular, we provide an example for fitting high degree polynomials to data and also obtain a FEM-like method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with an optimal kernel basis.

The study of model order reduction deals with the simplification of mathematical models referred to as full–order models. In model order reduction, full–order models and their simplified approximants usually have prescribed structure. The obtained approximant is called the reduced–order model. Traditionally, model order reduction techniques have been developed for reducing the complexity of dynamical systems [31, 30, 11, 5, 42]. Since many control engineering applications must operate in real time under limited hardware capacity, control schemes based on reduced–order models have proven particularly useful [49]. Well–known techniques exist for the reduction of models that describe linear time–invariant systems [31, 30, 58, 60, 42].

In order to address the model order reduction of linear time–invariant systems, several well–known methods have been developed that preserve the structure of the full order model, but provide theoretical guarantees on the performance of the reduced–order model. One such well–known method is balanced truncation [31], which operates on the state–space representation of linear time–invariant systems. It relies on a balanced realization of the system, which can be obtained by solving Lyapunov equations. Then, the least controllable and observable states in the balanced system are disregarded to obtain the reduced–order model. One important benefit of the balanced truncation method is the theoretical guarantee it provides on the H∞H_{\infty} error of the reduced–order model.

papers.title: Efficient Edge-aware Attention Network for Graph Generation
papers.abstract: Graph generative models commonly use graph-specific Transformer architectures to jointly update node and edge features. However, these architectures do not directly benefit from recent hardware-aware attention implementations, limiting their scalability. The adaptation is, however, non-trivial: edge and graph-level features must be injected into pairwise attention scores, graph masks must be respected, and dynamic edge updates remain a major source of quadratic memory usage. We propose an edge-aware attention layer for graph generation that incorporates structural information through head-wise score modulation, while updating edge representations with a lightweight residual mechanism that retains attention-score dependent edge updates. This layer can be effectively implemented using PyTorch's FlexAttention. We achieve similar generation quality to our baseline while reducing peak GPU memory by around 65% and substantially improving training and sampling throughput. These results suggest that the proposed architecture is a practical step toward scalable graph foundation models.

papers.intro:
Graph generation (Simonovsky & Komodakis, 2018; Martinkus et al., 2022; Jo et al., 2024) has advanced substantially with discrete diffusion and flow-based models. A particularly influential line of work, initiated by the diffusion model DiGress (Vignac et al., 2023), and then flow-based models such as CatFlow (Eijkelboom et al., 2024), DeFoG (Qin et al., 2025a), BWFlow (Jiang et al., 2026), and VBFN (Xiong et al., 2026), and diffusion models such as Cometh (Siraudin et al., 2025), relies on a specific transformer backbone to denoise categorical node and edge features. This architecture is inspired by the original Graph Transformer (Dwivedi & Bresson, 2021), which already updates edge states from attention scores and uses edge states to modulate self-attention. The main differences are that it computes attention between all nodes as opposed to restricting it to neighbors, maintains a graph-level feature vector and uses FiLM (Perez et al., 2018) modules to couple node, edge, and graph-level features. This dense, layered interaction is central to its success in graph generation, where the model must capture both local connectivity and global graph structure.

This architecture is inspired by the original Graph Transformer (Dwivedi & Bresson, 2021), which already updates edge states from attention scores and uses edge states to modulate self-attention. The main differences are that it computes attention between all nodes as opposed to restricting it to neighbors, maintains a graph-level feature vector and uses FiLM (Perez et al., 2018) modules to couple node, edge, and graph-level features. This dense, layered interaction is central to its success in graph generation, where the model must capture both local connectivity and global graph structure.

However, this expressivity comes with a computational cost. Since the model must maintain dense pairwise edge states, both attention computation and dynamic edge representations scale quadratically with the number of nodes, making training expensive and difficult under limited GPU resources. A large body of work addresses this bottleneck through sparse attention patterns (Shirzad et al., 2023); hybrid local-global designs (Rampášek et al., 2022); linear and operator-based alternatives (Deng et al., 2024; Sancak et al., 2025); or tokenization-based formulations that cast graphs as sequences of node and edge tokens and apply standard Transformers with minimal graph-specific modifications (Kim et al., 2022). These methods are effective, but typically modify or replace dense self-attention altogether. In graph generation specifically, SparseDiff (Qin et al., 2025b) exploits sparsity to enable training on larger graphs, although this increases sampling time.

papers.title: PCLA-Bridge: A Framework for Cross-Domain Deployment of CARLA Agents
papers.abstract: Most high-performing end-to-end autonomous driving agents (ADAs) are developed for the CARLA Leaderboard, tightly coupling them to CARLA's APIs, sensor layouts, coordinate systems, and internal clock. Reusing these models on real datasets, alternative simulators, or physical platforms necessitates substantial manual re-engineering. We present PCLA-Bridge, a deployable tool that runs unmodified CARLA Leaderboard agents from any sensor source to any control destination without an active CARLA server. With PCLA-Bridge handling dependency isolation, tensor marshalling, routing, and synthetic timing, integrators only need to provide a minimal interface. We validate the tool across two operational paradigms: offline replay on in-domain CARLA recordings and real-world nuScenes logs, and live closed-loop control across three diverse simulation engines: MetaDrive, AWSIM, and AlpaSim. We analyze the lightweight integration requirements for each platform, highlighting output translation (such as converting agent actions into target trajectory formats) and coordinate-frame transformations, showing that integration requires minimal glue code rather than structural changes. All eight evaluated agents execute across all three simulators without modification, confirming the reliability of PCLA-Bridge and establishing a foundation for systematic sim-to-real, cross-sim, and security testing.

papers.intro:
End-to-end autonomous driving agents (ADAs) are typically built and evaluated in a single simulator, most commonly the CARLA simulator [1]. Because these implementations assume a specific end-to-end environment, relying on native sensor tensors, routing, temporal synchronization, and coordinate conventions, a published agent becomes tightly coupled to its original execution harness. This coupling hinders code reuse, cross-environment evaluation, and any transition toward physical deployment. Currently, to run a published CARLA agent on real-world logs or within another simulator, researchers must manually re-engineer the agent.

While the PCLA framework [2] decoupled 41 Leaderboard agents from the Leaderboard codebase [3] to enable execution across diverse CARLA environments, those agents remained bound to the simulator itself. This paper offers a tool that removes that dependency. PCLA-Bridge executes unmodified agents without a CARLA server, allowing any data source to drive the agent and any control target to consume its outputs. While an earlier extended abstract introduced this concept using offline replay [4], this paper describes a fully functional tool featuring live, closed-loop operation and documents the practical requirements for integrating new data sources.

papers.title: Dynamical stability of Magnetic Supramassive Neutron Stars
papers.abstract: We investigate the dynamical stability of strongly magnetized supramassive neutron stars close to the mass-shedding limit using fully general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations in three spatial dimensions. Equilibrium configurations are constructed using a microphysical equation of state and considering poloidal magnetic fields up to maximum strengths ${\sim} 10^{17}\,\mathrm{G}$. The initially unstable magnetic fields reorganize into mixed poloidal--toroidal configurations on Alfvén timescales shorter than the stellar rotation period. The subsequent dynamical evolution is governed by timescales set by the Lehnert number. For stars with masses sufficiently lower than the maximum mass, magnetic stresses redistribute angular momentum and drive the development of differential rotation, leading to a new quasi-stationary configuration that remains dynamically stable over several rotation periods. Magnetically-driven winds develop from the outer layers around the equatorial plane and remain baryon-matter dominated with magnetization ${\lesssim}0.2$. Over the simulated timescale, winds carry a total rest mass of order ${\sim}10^{-3}\mathrm{M}_\odot$ at outflow rates of up to a few $M_\odot/\mathrm{s}$. For stars close to (or beyond) the maximum-mass turning point along the stellar equilibrium sequence, strong magnetic fields trigger gravitational collapse by redistributing angular momentum away from the stellar core. The resulting black hole remnants are characterized by angular velocities up to ${\sim}49\%$ larger and angular momentum ${\lesssim}8\%$ smaller than those of the initial equilibrium stars. Our results show that extreme magnetic-field instabilities can significantly alter the structure of supramassive neutron stars, with possible implications for magnetars and long-lived binary neutron-star merger remnants.

papers.intro:
Neutron stars are rapidly rotating compact objects that can host extreme magnetic fields, with intensities reaching ∼1012{\sim}10^{12}–101510^{15} G in standard pulsars and magnetars [45, 36, 70]. These magnetic fields are thought to originate during the core collapse of massive stars and/or in the proto-neutron star phase, possibly through a combination of fossil fields, convective dynamos, and magnetothermal processes. Despite decades of observations across the electromagnetic spectrum, including radio, X-ray, and gamma-ray emission (such as soft gamma-ray repeaters, anomalous X-ray pulsars, and giant flares [33, 46, 44]) the internal structure and magnetic configuration of neutron stars remain poorly constrained.

Binary neutron star mergers (BNSM) provide an additional channel for the formation of strongly magnetized neutron stars. In particular, mergers with sufficiently low total mass, Mbin≲1.2−1.35​M⊙M_{\rm bin}\lesssim 1.2-1.35{\rm M_{\odot}}, can produce long-lived remnants endowed with magnetic fields as large as ∼1016{\sim}10^{16}–101710^{17} G, see e.g. [54, 29, 37]. Angular momentum redistribution driven by magnetic and viscous effects may drive the remnants’ rotation toward uniform rotation on secular timescales [55, 58], although the precise mechanisms remain uncertain. Strong magnetic fields may significantly delay collapse, potentially sustaining the remnant for timescales of up to years even in the presence of only moderate rotation [65].

Supramassive neutron stars (SMNSs) are uniformly rotating equilibrium configurations with masses exceeding the maximum mass of nonrotating (Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff, TOV) solutions for a given equation of state (EOS) [17, 16, 1]. Rotation provides additional support against gravity, allowing masses up to ∼20%{\sim}20\% larger than the TOV limit, i.e., M≳1.2​MmaxTOVM\gtrsim 1.2\,M^{\rm TOV}_{\rm max}. Studies of equilibrium sequences at fixed baryonic mass show that SMNSs evolve toward instability as they lose angular momentum, spinning up toward collapse on secular timescales [17]. Configurations at the mass-shedding limit are dynamically unstable to quasi-radial perturbations and are expected to undergo gravitational collapse to a black hole [57]. Finite-temperature effects can temporarily increase the maximum supported baryonic mass along stable branches, but their impact diminishes at high central densities near the maximum mass. Near this limit, SMNSs are less compact and possess more extended envelopes, reaching the mass-shedding threshold at lower angular velocities compared to colder configurations [35]. All of these results have been established in general relativity in the absence of magnetic fields.

However, the structure and stability of such configurations depend sensitively on the magnetic field geometry.

It is well established that purely poloidal or purely toroidal magnetic fields are unstable. Poloidal fields are subject to varicose instabilities, while toroidal fields suffer from the Tayler instability [66, 67, 42, 43, 73, 7]. Stable configurations are therefore expected to involve mixed field geometries, often described as twisted-torus structures [5, 6]. Time-dependent studies, both in Newtonian gravity and in general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD), have explored the nonlinear development of these instabilities and the possible emergence of stable equilibria [38, 14, 40, 15, 64, 63, 68, 12, 19, 10, 41]. Rapid rotation can partially suppress poloidal-field instabilities on Alfvén timescales [52], while purely toroidal fields remain unstable if the magnetic energy becomes sufficiently large compared to the rotational energy [38, 39]. On longer timescales, magnetic field evolution is governed by processes such as ambipolar diffusion, which can lead to gradual magnetic energy dissipation [65]. Determining the long-term stability of magnetized neutron stars remains a computationally challenging open problem.

Section II describes the formalism and computational framework utilized. III.2. Finally, in conclusion we discuss in Sec. IV the implications of our results for astrophysical pulsars and BNSM remnants.

papers.title: Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR Technical Report
papers.abstract: We present Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR, a family of audio-language models that builds upon its predecesor Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR with improved speech recognition and expanded capabilities in speaker-diarized transcription and general audio understanding. The family retains support for 30 languages and 16 Chinese dialects, together with instruction-controlled capabilities including historical-context conditioning, hierarchical hotword customization, and native transcription polishing. Speaker-diarized ASR produces structured outputs containing speaker labels, timestamps, and recognized text, maintaining consistent speaker labels across turns and the representation of overlapping speech. The general audio understanding capabilities cover audio-, speech-, and music-captioning, temporal grounding and sound event detection, as well as audio question answering and multiple-choice reasoning. These tasks broaden the application scope from recognizing spoken words to interpreting speakers, acoustic events, and their temporal relations. To accommodate different deployment requirements, the family includes variants for asynchronous file transcription, low-latency streaming, interactive voice input, and non-streaming recognition, with speaker-diarized transcription and general audio understanding available in certain variants. Evaluations span conventional ASR, multilingual and dialectal speech, speaker-diarized transcription, and general audio understanding, demonstrating the capabilities of the Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR family across transcription and broader audio analysis tasks.

papers.intro:
Automatic speech recognition (ASR) provides the linguistic foundation for voice interfaces, meeting transcription, and conversational systems. However, a transcript alone only captures partial information in an audio recording. Multi-party conversations require identifying who spoke and when, while interpreting speech, environmental sounds, and music requires information that may not be recoverable from words alone. Practical audio systems must therefore address three complementary questions: what was said [1, 2], who said it and when [3], and what the audio conveys beyond its transcript [4, 5]. These requirements motivate extending accurate speech recognition toward structured transcription and general audio understanding.

Recent audio-language models have made substantial progress toward this broader scope. Qwen3-ASR demonstrates the potential of building multilingual speech recognition upon an audio-capable language model [6]. In parallel, Qwen3-Omni integrates audio perception into a broader multimodal framework [7], while MOSS-Audio [8] explicitly supports captioning, timestamped transcription, and time-aware audio understanding. More recently, FireRedAudio [9] combines recognition and audio understanding with speech generation in a general-purpose audio-language model. Together, these developments establish audio-conditioned language modeling as a useful framework for tasks that range from lexical recognition to descriptions and answers grounded in acoustic input.

Speaker-diarized transcription introduces a distinct structural requirement. Beyond recognizing individual utterances, a system must associate words with consistent speaker labels and temporal boundaries, including during rapid turn-taking and overlapping speech. Recent systems such as MOSS Transcribe Diarize [10] and VibeVoice-ASR [3] jointly model transcription, speaker diarization, and timestamp prediction, offering an alternative to assembling these outputs through separate processing stages. This direction is particularly relevant to meetings and interviews, where a lexically accurate transcript can still misrepresent a conversation if speaker assignments or temporal relations are incorrect.

Benchmarks such as MMAU [4] evaluate understanding and reasoning across speech, sound, and music, while MMSU [5] examines fine-grained spoken-language understanding involving semantic, paralinguistic, and phonological information. These complementary perspectives motivate evaluating audio models beyond transcription error rates alone.

papers.title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics
papers.abstract: Model order reduction has the potential to enable real-time patient-specific assessment of cardiovascular flows. However, it still faces significant challenges stemming from the geometric variability of vascular anatomies. Building upon the SynthAorta dataset (Bosnjak et al., IEEE Trans. Med. Imag. 45(1), 2026) of physiological aortic geometries, we generate an extensive dataset of physiologically consistent computational fluid dynamics solutions through an automatic boundary-condition adjustment procedure. A common reference geometry allows all patient-specific anatomies to be represented by displacement fields, providing point-to-point correspondence without the need for geometric registration. Based on this dataset, we develop Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogate models to predict velocity and pressure fields at peak systole. We further investigate two strategies to enhance data efficiency and prediction accuracy: active learning and differentiable physical consistency constraints based on the finite element residual. The results show that active learning is strongly regime-dependent: while it offers little benefit over random sampling during early training, it improves performance during fine-tuning through gradient- and subspace-based acquisition strategies. Similarly, physical consistency constraints prove to be substantially more effective as a fine-tuning objective than as a regularizer applied throughout training. Finally, out-of-distribution studies demonstrate that the primary limitation of surrogate models lies in the geometric support of the underlying parametrization rather than in the neural network architectures themselves. The proposed framework combines synthetic dataset generation, geometry-aware surrogate modeling, physics-informed optimization, and active learning into a scalable workflow for inter-patient hemodynamic prediction.

papers.intro:
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD), applied to blood flow modeling and simulation, can support non-invasive diagnosis and assessment of cardiovascular diseases, as well as treatment planning and patient monitoring (see, e.g., [1, 2]). The development of numerical solvers, together with the constantly growing potential of computing resources, allows tackling applications of extremely high complexity. However, especially in the case of aortic blood flow, where fluid dynamics is characterized by highly nonlinear regimes, strongly dependent on patient geometry, the physical and geometrical complexity still requires considerable computational resources for physiological patient-specific simulations. This aspect is particularly relevant for outer-loop applications concerning, e.g., inverse problems, optimization, or uncertainty quantification, in which a large number of (forward) simulations is required at each iteration step. Reduced-order models and scientific machine learning (ML) can address this challenge by considering approximate dynamics on lower-dimensional spaces. These techniques rely on existing simulation (training) data to define high-fidelity reduced representations of target applications, and their capabilities are strongly dependent on data availability.

These techniques rely on existing simulation (training) data to define high-fidelity reduced representations of target applications, and their capabilities are strongly dependent on data availability.

Compared with other applications of model order reduction, biomedical applications are still constrained by limited data availability and substantial inter-patient variability in both anatomy and physiological conditions, concerning anatomical shape, cardiac output, peripheral pressure, and mechanical parameters, among others. Since full-order CFD simulations are computationally expensive, the predictive accuracy of inter-patient surrogate models is essential for clinically relevant applications.

This work addresses different challenges concerning inter-patient variability in the context of surrogate models of aortic blood flow. We study the approximation properties and the performance of ML surrogate models trained on synthetic data, i.e., data generated through high-fidelity numerical blood flow simulations (full-order models) on a dataset of variable patient anatomies sharing a common reference shape. In particular, we investigate the accuracy in terms of relevant biomarkers, namely, peak velocity, pressure, and wall shear stress (WSS), when predicting these quantities across shapes.

Handling the geometrical variability in the context of scientific ML requires tailored strategies for developing reduced spaces and deep learning architectures that can scale better during training and also generalize accurately to unseen geometries. Previous studies explored the use of the reduced basis method combined with domain decomposition strategies to attach archetypal subdomains [3], and combined with registration techniques to transport a reduced basis computed on a template shape onto patient geometries [4]. Recent works focusing on ML models have addressed the development of graph neural networks (GNNs) approximating the averaged quantities of interest (QoIs) from measurement data on the vessel centerline [5], the learning of equivalent one-dimensional (1D) models from measurement data, to be applied to variable three-dimensional (3D) anatomies [6], common GNN architectures applied to the 3D mesh [7], shape-informed GNNs, combined with registration strategies and trained on registered simulation data [8], and GNNs trained on image data of carotid arteries, which leverage first principles as soft constraints and equivariant layers [9]. In this work, we focus on graph- and transformer-based architectures [10], as they have proven effective for large-scale applications, and apply them to a database of physiological aortic geometries [11] generated from parametric deformations.

In this work, we focus on graph- and transformer-based architectures [10], as they have proven effective for large-scale applications, and apply them to a database of physiological aortic geometries [11] generated from parametric deformations.

The accuracy of surrogate models and their capability of generalizing to different patients strongly depend on the variability of the available training data. This aspect is particularly important in the context of blood flow in large vessels, where geometrical details and patient-specific boundary conditions strongly influence the fluid dynamics. Flexible registration techniques and parameter-dependent shape databases, such as the one considered in this work, provide useful tools to increase the size of the training set with additional simulations. Typical methods to perform data augmentation, increasing the number of different anatomical shapes, include steady-state free precession (SSFP) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to directly acquire them from patients, statistical shape models [5], parametric deformations [11], and generative models [12]. Although the availability of large datasets keeps increasing, the cost of generating high-fidelity CFD solutions remains high. The exploration of the space of all possible anatomical shapes must thus be optimized to reduce the computational costs. In this regard, active learning (AL) [13] and reinforcement learning provide promising strategies to select the most informative samples to be added to the training dataset. We test different strategies for the selection of additional training samples, comparing label-dependent (supervised) techniques, i.e., techniques requiring the full CFD solution computed on the candidate geometries, with label-free (unsupervised) ones, which only rely on surrogate approximations and are therefore suitable for practical applications.

A further aspect investigated in this work concerns the introduction of physically consistent soft constraints in the training loss, besides purely data-dependent residuals computed from the solutions on the different shapes. The enforcement of these constraints has been tested extensively in the literature. Among others, physics-informed neural networks [14] and neural emulators [15] use ML models as ansatz spaces while minimizing equation-based loss terms or residuals of numerical schemes via automatic differentiation. We are interested instead in physics constraints used as regularizers for surrogate models, with the aim of modeling a whole joint distribution of input parameters and output solutions, where the parameters represent complex boundary conditions or different computational domains. The efficiency of such regularizers with respect to state-of-the-art ML methods is not often benchmarked, making it difficult to discern whether purely data-informed or physics-informed losses yield the highest gain in generalization error relative to computational cost.

papers.title: Nanophotonic Extreme Ultraviolet Polarimeter
papers.abstract: Nanophotonic engineering has revolutionized how we manipulate the polarization of visible light. Here, we extend such control to extreme ultraviolet radiation, the spectral region of attosecond science and semiconductor lithography, where transmissive optical elements are lacking. We implement channel waveguides that restrict incident 41-nm-wavelength light to a few modes with defined spatial profiles and propagation constants. By designing the propagation-length-dependent interference of two eigenmodes, we achieve polarization-dependent forward scattering, which we exploit to create a transmissive nanophotonic analyzer that resolves the polarization axis and spectrum of extreme ultraviolet light from a single measurement. With a 0.9°-sensitivity for polarization rotations in a 1-second measurement and single-shot capability, the device opens new experimental opportunities in ultrafast magneto-optic spectroscopy and at accelerator-based light sources.

papers.title: Detection and Statistics of large-scale Sector Boundary Crossings in the Solar Wind: The SBCross Catalog
papers.abstract: Heliospheric sector boundary crossings (SBCs), composed of the Heliospheric Current Sheet (HCS), Heliospheric Plasma Sheet (HPS), and surrounding plasma halo, represent fundamental structures in the solar wind that influence interplanetary dynamics and space weather. We present the \textsc{SBCross} catalog, an automated, publicly available database containing 1,076 SBC events derived from in-situ observations spanning more than 30 years (1995--2026), covering Solar Cycles 23 and 24 alongside the rising and maximum phases of Solar Cycle 25. By combining interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) and 255~eV suprathermal electron pitch angle distributions (PAD) data, our algorithm reliably captures large-scale polarity transitions, with $76\%$ of detected SBCs exhibiting clear HPS signatures ($β> 1$, $n_{\mathrm{peak}} > 10\mathrm{\,cm^{-3}}$). Across the catalog, we find an average occurrence rate of $\approx 2.6$ events per Carrington rotation, a median event duration of $\approx 9.0$\,hours, and a median physical thickness of $\approx 7.4 \times 10^6$\,km. Furthermore, approximately $\approx 15\%$ of detected SBCs interact with interplanetary coronal mass ejections (CMEs) on average, with this proportion rising up to $33\%$ during solar maximum. These CME-associated events exhibit systematically longer durations (median of $10.0$\,hours), $54\%$ larger physical thicknesses, and higher average solar wind velocities. Notably, all high-velocity SBC events ($> 600\mathrm{\,km\,s^{-1}}$) are exclusively driven by CME interactions, demonstrating local plasma pile-up and structural entanglement resulting from fast CMEs overtaking the ambient slow background. The \textsc{SBCross} catalog serves as an updated successor to the classic SBC list by L. Svalgaard, delivering a standardized, open-access resource for the heliophysics community to systematically investigate sector boundary transitions.

papers.intro:
The heliosphere is continuously being replenished by the solar wind, a magnetized plasma stream expanding outward from the solar corona into interplanetary space [39]. Embedded within this global outflow is the Heliospheric Current Sheet [49, 54, 46, HCS; e.g.,], which represents the fundamental boundary separating regions of opposite magnetic polarity. Enclosing the HCS is the Heliospheric Plasma Sheet [6, HPS;], a region characterized by enhanced proton density, elevated plasma β\beta, a depressed helium-to-hydrogen ratio (He/H\mathrm{He/H}), and reduced magnetic field strength and temperature [17, 5, 56]. Observational manifestations of transitioning across these large-scale structures in in-situ data are defined as sector boundary crossings (SBCs). Crucially, SBCs are identified by directional reversals in the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) accompanied by abrupt shifts in the suprathermal electron heat flux [12, 21, 10]. Consequently, pitch angle distributions (PADs) of suprathermal electrons are frequently used to trace these magnetic polarity transitions [11, 18, e.g.,].

The location where the suprathermal electron strahl flips alignment from parallel to antiparallel (or vice versa) relative to the magnetic field is traditionally termed the ”true” sector boundary [20, 22]. While the true sector boundary is often synonymous with the HCS [3], N. U. Crooker et al. [9] demonstrated that the two features can become spatially or temporally misaligned due to interchange reconnection. Furthermore, a single sector boundary transition may contain multiple embedded HCS crossings [13, 28].
