The structure of the region where the large-scale IMF configuration flips can be understood as a multi-layer hierarchy. At the core lie one or multiple thin HCSs [13], high-β\beta current layers lasting from minutes to hours that maintain dynamic pressure balance with their surroundings. Within this localized view, the characteristic drop in magnetic field magnitude across the crossing is compensated primarily by a sharp rise in plasma density [56]. Individual HCSs exhibit typical thicknesses ranging from 600​km600\mathrm{\,km} to 1.1×106​km1.1\times 10^{6}\mathrm{\,km}, with an average scale on the order of 104​km10^{4}\mathrm{\,km} [56, 29, 4].

The structure of the region where the large-scale IMF configuration flips can be understood as a multi-layer hierarchy. At the core lie one or multiple thin HCSs [13], high-β\beta current layers lasting from minutes to hours that maintain dynamic pressure balance with their surroundings. Within this localized view, the characteristic drop in magnetic field magnitude across the crossing is compensated primarily by a sharp rise in plasma density [56]. Individual HCSs exhibit typical thicknesses ranging from 600​km600\mathrm{\,km} to 1.1×106​km1.1\times 10^{6}\mathrm{\,km}, with an average scale on the order of 104​km10^{4}\mathrm{\,km} [56, 29, 4].

Surrounding the thin HCS is the broader HPS, whose spatial extent spans from 3.2×105​km3.2\times 10^{5}\mathrm{\,km} to 4.7×106​km4.7\times 10^{6}\mathrm{\,km} [56, 29, 45, 57]. High-resolution analyses around the HPS reveal that this central plasma enhancement is itself nested within a broader, lower-density halo spanning several degrees in heliospheric latitude [2, 27]. Superposed epoch studies centered on HCS events demonstrate that these nested structures represent the interplanetary extension of coronal helmet streamers, where dense streamer stalks (∼1∘​–​2∘\sim 1^{\circ}\text{--}2^{\circ} wide) are embedded within wider coronal plasma outflows (∼15∘​–​20∘\sim 15^{\circ}\text{--}20^{\circ}) [5, 17, 2].

The spatial alignment of the HCS and the surrounding dense HPS plays a critical role in modulating the propagation dynamics and geoeffectiveness of Interplanetary Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs). When fast, transient CMEs erupt from the solar corona, their path through interplanetary space is fundamentally shaped by these large-scale ambient structures. A fast CME overtaking a slow-moving HPS leads to a dynamic collision; the high-density plasma of the sheet resists the expansion of the CME, leading to a plasma pile-up and strong structural deformation of the CME’s shock front [34, 30]. This structural distortion and compression can amplify the ambient plasma density and plasma β\beta at the interface boundary. Crucially, when the magnetic flux rope of an CME interacts with the HCS/HPS structure, the localized magnetic field is compressed, amplifying any southward magnetic field component (BzB_{z}) within the interaction region [34, 52]. When these heavily compressed, high-density structures interact with Earth’s magnetosphere, they deliver a spike in dynamic pressure along with possibly long periods of strong southward BzB_{z} [14]. In this study, we present a comprehensive statistical analysis of SBCs and provide a catalog spanning over 30 years of observations (1995–2026), covering entirely Solar Cycles 23 and 24, as well as the rising and maximum phases of Solar Cycle 25. The study details the distinctive physical properties of SBCs and the surrounding plasma environment derived from a systematic combination of IMF and PAD data. A major focus is the identification and analysis of SBC events that directly interact with interplanetary CMEs. As discussed above, the plasma environment during SBCs can distort the local plasma topology, causing significant variations in CME geoeffectiveness, altering shock propagation dynamics, and creating substantial statistical scatter in their downstream profiles compared to isolated, non-interacting events [40, 51]. By linking our SBC events to an existing in-situ CME catalog, this study offers a reliable statistical baseline for exploring how these large-scale background structures influence, shape, and accelerate severe space weather in the near-Earth environment.

papers.title: Spherical harmonics and infinitesimal projective transformations
papers.abstract: Consider the space of $C^\infty$-functions on the two-dimensional sphere $S^2$ and its decomposition $\oplus\mathcal H_m$ into a direct sum of minimal rotation-invariant spaces. We consider elements of $\oplus\mathcal H_m$ as functions of two variables, a nonnegative integer variable $m$ and a complex variable $u$ (a restriction of such function to a set $m=k$ is a polynomial in $u$ of degree $\le 2k$). The group $\mathrm{GL}\,(3,{\mathbb R})$ of all matrices of order 3 acts on $S^2$, so its Lie algebra acts in $C^\infty(S^2)$ by differentiations along vector fields. We construct operators in $\mathcal W^\infty$ corresponding such differentiations and obtain a collection of differential-difference operators in $\mathcal W^\infty$. The expressions include shifts $m\mapsto m\pm 2$ and derivatives of order 4 in $u$.

papers.title: Modular Bayesian Inference for Partially Misspecified Mixtures with Uncertain Class Labels
papers.abstract: Scientific inference often involves observations from multiple latent populations whose class memberships are uncertain and must be inferred from available data. While full Bayesian mixture modelling provides a principled approach to joint uncertainty quantification in this setting, often the model is misspecified or less trustworthy for populations that are not the target of the inference, which can distort posterior inference for the parameters of interest. We propose a modular Bayesian framework that safeguards against such biases. We decouple classification from downstream inference using fixed class probabilities, for example from a classifier trained on a subset of labelled data. We then protect inference on the parameters of interest by preventing the likelihood contributions of less trustworthy populations from influencing them. A key benefit of this principled modularization is that it greatly simplifies inference, reducing a fully joint mixture analysis to sampling label allocations, fitting the protected downstream model for each sample, and averaging the resulting posteriors. We establish calibration conditions on these class probabilities under which the proposed procedure preserves the inferential target of the analysis with known labels, and demonstrate the method in synthetic experiments and in cosmological analysis of photometric supernova samples.

papers.intro:
In many applications, populations of scientific interest are embedded in a larger mixture of latent classes, some of which may be of lesser interest and/or less reliably modelled. In these settings, class memberships are often uncertain and must be inferred from the data [28, 15]. Fully Bayesian mixture models provide a principled framework for joint uncertainty quantification across class assignments and model parameters, but misspecification of the less well understood population(s) can propagate through the mixture, altering the inferred class probabilities and distorting inference of the parameters of scientific interest.

In many applications, populations of scientific interest are embedded in a larger mixture of latent classes, some of which may be of lesser interest and/or less reliably modelled. In these settings, class memberships are often uncertain and must be inferred from the data [28, 15]. Fully Bayesian mixture models provide a principled framework for joint uncertainty quantification across class assignments and model parameters, but misspecification of the less well understood population(s) can propagate through the mixture, altering the inferred class probabilities and distorting inference of the parameters of scientific interest.

A prominent example is type Ia supernova (SN Ia) cosmology, where an empirical standardization procedure is used to derive precise distances and constrain the expansion history of the Universe [37, 33]. This relies on the purity of the sample, which has hitherto been achieved through costly spectroscopic follow-up for type confirmation. However, current and upcoming surveys will deliver vast samples of astronomical transients observed only through broadband photometry with only scarce (∼1%{\sim}1\,\%) follow-up [43], so future cosmological analyses must propagate the uncertainty of typing purely from photometry. Moreover, the contaminating non-Ia population comprises heterogeneous transient classes whose rates and brightness evolution are hard to model reliably [43, 31]. Existing analyses commonly combine type “probabilities” from machine-learning models [30, 36, e.g.] with a simple analytic likelihood for the non-Ia objects [23, 43, 1], so misspecification can propagate into cosmological inference. Recent simulation-based inference (SBI) approaches [21, 20, 5] add a further complication, as they require numerous realistic forward simulations of the non-Ia population, which can be extremely demanding.

The underlying problem is not specific to SN Ia cosmology. Stars observed in the same region of the sky may either belong to a stellar cluster of interest or to the surrounding field, with uncertain membership that must be propagated into inference on cluster properties of interest [17, 18]. The surrounding field population is typically much more heterogeneous and considerably harder to model reliably. Similar problems arise in galaxy-cluster cosmology [44, 10]. In gravitational-wave astronomy, candidate events may be astrophysical signals or detector artefacts that are difficult to characterize, with scientific interest focused on the astrophysical population [16]. In ecology, uncertain identification of similar species can propagate into inference on species-specific abundance and population dynamics [9]. In seismology, uncertain classification of earthquakes into different tectonic regimes can affect inference on aftershock and seismicity parameters [38]. In single-cell genomics, uncertain cell-type assignments can affect cell-type-specific inference, particularly when some populations are less well characterized [47, 45, 41]. These settings motivate methods that propagate classification uncertainty while limiting sensitivity to less reliable component models.

A range of Bayesian approaches have been developed to reduce sensitivity to model misspecification [32]. Generalized Bayesian inference replaces the usual log-likelihood contribution by a loss chosen for the inferential target, allowing parameters of interest to be updated without specifying and trusting a complete generative model [4]. Restricted-likelihood methods retain a probabilistic model but update the prior using the sampling distribution of carefully chosen summary statistics, such as robust estimators, thereby reducing sensitivity to aspects of the data that the model describes poorly [24]. Robust mixture models instead modify the component distributions themselves, e.g., by replacing Gaussian components with heavy-tailed Student-tt distributions so that atypical observations have less influence on the inferred mixture structure [40].

Generalized Bayesian inference replaces the usual log-likelihood contribution by a loss chosen for the inferential target, allowing parameters of interest to be updated without specifying and trusting a complete generative model [4]. Restricted-likelihood methods retain a probabilistic model but update the prior using the sampling distribution of carefully chosen summary statistics, such as robust estimators, thereby reducing sensitivity to aspects of the data that the model describes poorly [24]. Robust mixture models instead modify the component distributions themselves, e.g., by replacing Gaussian components with heavy-tailed Student-tt distributions so that atypical observations have less influence on the inferred mixture structure [40].

When misspecification is localized to particular parts of a joint model, modular Bayesian inference provides an alternative to modifying the model globally by restricting the flow of information between model components [3, 25]. The basic motivation is to keep a “good” or trusted module separate from a suspect module so that the latter does not contaminate inference in the former [3]. However, the notion of a “module” is not associated with a single universally adopted formal definition [32]. Liu and Goudie [25] provide a graph-based formalization in which modules are constructed from a partition of the observable variables and the graphical structure of the joint model. In their framework, a self-contained Bayesian module includes the variables required for a well-defined Bayesian analysis for a specified set of observables without requiring information external to the module. Modules may overlap through shared parameters or latent quantities.

A principal form of modular inference is cut inference, which protects a trusted module by removing feedback from a suspect module. Information and uncertainty inferred in the trusted module may still be propagated forward when analysing the suspect module, while information from the suspect module is prevented from updating the protected quantities [34, 19, 25]. Modular Bayesian inference has received considerable recent methodological attention. Semi-modular methods allow feedback to be attenuated rather than fully removed [7], while variational approaches provide alternative computational strategies for cut inference [46]. Recent work has also extended modular inference to likelihood-free and generalized-Bayesian settings [8, 12], and studied robustness, uncertainty quantification, and efficiency under misspecification [39, 13].

papers.title: J-PLUS: Identifying Outlier Spectral Energy Distributions in the Fourth Data Release Using Unsupervised Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The selection of candidates belonging to rare or underrepresented stellar populations, as well as novel objects, is essential for spectroscopic follow-up. In this work, we demonstrate how combining broad- and narrow-band photometric information with machine-learning techniques enables this selection. Using photometric data in twelve filters from the Javalambre Photometric Local Universe Survey (J-PLUS) as input, we applied an anomaly detection technique based on autoencoders to identify spectral energy distributions (SEDs) that deviate from the dominant pattern in the J-PLUS objects sample. Subsequently, we applied the t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) algorithm to the J-PLUS colors of the outlier SEDs population. Combining information from the SIMBAD database and other astronomical surveys to classify the outliers identified by the autoencoder, we are able to characterize over-densities in the t-SNE map. Our study specifically focuses on well-defined islands in the t-SNE space, corresponding to specific populations. We identified a large sample of white dwarfs and low-mass stars, including a small subset of polluted white dwarfs, and report potential candidates for spectroscopic follow-up, including 19 carbon-rich stars, 11 cataclysmic variables and 170 white-dwarfs-main-sequence binaries, all previously unreported in the literature.

papers.intro:
The selection of reliable stellar population candidates, either from low-resolution spectroscopy or multi-band photometric surveys, is a fundamental task in astronomy. This is especially relevant for potential high-resolution spectroscopic follow-up using either ground- or space-based facilities. Also, identifying rare or underrepresented stellar populations is essential for uncovering new astrophysical phenomena and constraining models of stellar and galactic evolution. Traditionally, candidate selection has relied on color-magnitude and color-color diagrams, in which common stellar and extragalactic populations occupy characteristic loci determined by their spectral energy distributions [27, 67]. Broad-band surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey [80, SDSS;] demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach. For example, Smolčić et al. [64] mapped the distribution of main-sequence stars, quasars, and white dwarfs in the (g−r)(g-r) versus (u−g)(u-g) plane, while Szkody et al. [68] showed that cataclysmic variables occupy distinct regions of color-color space owing to their accretion-dominated spectral energy distributions. Nevertheless, many rare populations overlap the loci of common sources or exhibit only subtle deviations in individual color projections, limiting the effectiveness of manually defined color cuts.

A significant advance toward systematic anomaly detection in photometric surveys was made by Covey et al. [21]. They modeled the stellar locus in seven-dimensional color space using SDSS and 2MASS photometry and introduced the seven-dimensional color distance (7DCD): a metric that quantifies an object’s separation from the stellar locus. By exploiting the joint distribution of multiple colors, the 7DCD enabled the identification of photometric outliers that are not readily apparent in individual color-color diagrams. The resulting outlier sample was enriched in unusual populations, including white dwarf-M dwarf binaries, quasars, and M giant-carbon star candidates, demonstrating the potential of multidimensional photometric information for discovering rare sources.

More recently, the increasing volume and complexity of astronomical surveys have motivated the development of machine learning approaches for anomaly detection. Rather than relying exclusively on manually defined selection criteria or explicit parametric descriptions of the data distribution, these methods learn patterns directly from observations and identify deviations in high-dimensional parameter spaces. Examples include one-class support vector machines applied to WISE photometric catalogs [65], unsupervised approaches for detecting anomalous light curves [30], and deep representation learning methods based on autoencoders for identifying spectroscopic outliers in DESI data [41] and low-resolution SDSS spectra [62].

The autoencoder is trained to compress and reconstruct the twelve-dimensional photometry of typical stars; then, objects with the highest reconstruction error are flagged as candidate outliers. This approach was previously demonstrated on S-PLUS data by Quispe-Huaynasi et al. [56], and we follow here the methodology described in that paper. In this paper, we extend that analysis to J-PLUS, exploiting the fact that the two surveys share an identical filter system but cover different sky regions. Thus, the autoencoder may reveal distinct populations of interest in the J-PLUS footprint.

To inspect the candidate outliers, we project the high-residual objects into two dimensions using t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE), which reveals clustering structure among the anomalies and guides visual inspection. We then cross-match these candidates with external astronomical databases to assess their nature and select promising targets for high-resolution spectroscopic follow-up. It is worth emphasizing that objects classified as outliers are not necessarily intrinsically peculiar or rare in an astronomical sense, although some may indeed be; instead, they correspond to objects that are underrepresented or absent in the training distribution.

papers.title: Kadison duality for biaffinely convex sets
papers.abstract: Classical Kadison duality establishes a categorical equivalence between compact convex sets and Archimedean order unit spaces of affine functions. This paper develops a Kadison-type duality for sets with coordinate-wise convex structure in product domains $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^m$. While slice-wise convex (biconvex) sets appear to be the natural geometric domain, separate convexity along coordinates is insufficient to ensure separation by biaffine polynomials. In classical convexity, every closed convex set is determined by affine functionals because any exterior point can be separated by a hyperplane. In contrast, biaffine polynomials can only probe a biconvex set $K$ up to its biaffine hull biconv$(K)$, the envelope formed by the intersection of all regions cut out by valid biaffine inequalities on $K$. To resolve this obstruction, the geometric setting is restricted to biaffinely convex sets, those that coincide with their biaffine hull ($K =$ biconv$(K)$) and therefore admit strict biaffine separation. On the algebraic side, we introduce the dual objects, which we call biaffine order unit spaces. These are finite-dimensional Archimedean order unit spaces defined on tensor products $E_1 \otimes E_2$ whose order units factor and whose positive cones are governed entirely by unentangled, rank-1 tensor evaluations. We prove a duality between the category of compact non-degenerate biaffinely convex sets with coordinate-wise affine maps and the category of abstract biaffine order unit spaces with tensor-factorized unital positive linear maps. In particular, every such biaffinely convex set is isomorphic to the coordinate state space of its biaffine polynomials, and conversely, every biaffine order unit space is order-isomorphic to the space of biaffine polynomials on its coordinate state space.

papers.intro:
Convexity is a foundational geometric concept that underpins vast areas of mathematics, from optimization and linear programming to functional analysis and probability theory. A subset of a vector space is convex if it contains the line segment connecting any two of its points, or equivalently, if it is closed under convex combinations of its points. In modern analysis, the structural power of convexity lies predominantly in its dual relationship with affine functions defined upon the set. The cornerstone of this perspective is the classical Kadison duality theorem [Alf71], which establishes a canonical equivalence between compact convex sets and function systems. The latter are Archimedean order unit spaces, concretely realized as spaces of continuous affine functions. A compact convex set KK is completely characterized by the order-theoretic and metric properties of its canonical function system, while conversely, any abstract function system is geometrically recovered through its state space of normalized positive linear functionals.

Building upon this classical foundation, several generalized convexity notions have been developed to capture richer algebraic and geometric behaviors [MM96, Nai04]. In the noncommutative, matrix convexity plays a central role [Wit84, EW97, WW99, HM12, HM14, HKM17, Zal17, HL21, DK25]. There, scalar sets are replaced by graded families of matrix tuples closed under direct sums and compressions. In direct analogy to Kadison duality, Webster–Winkler duality demonstrates that matrix convex sets are dual to operator systems [WW99], providing indispensable geometric tools for operator spaces, C∗C^{*}-algebras, and noncommutative function theory [Pau02, DM05, Arv08, DK15]. More recently, these notions have been extended to coordinate-dependent settings through Γ\Gamma-convexity, including noncommutative partial convexity [HHLM08, DHM17, JKMMP21, JKMMP22, KMŠ26], where sets exhibit convexity only with respect to designated coordinate blocks.

papers.title: Moments of Random Permanents and Hafnians: A Replica Approach
papers.abstract: Using contour-integral representations of the permanent and of the Hafnian, we turn the computation of their moments for random matrices into a replica calculation, analogous to that of the moments of the partition function of a mean-field spin glass. For the $2k$-th moment of $N\times N$ matrices with independent entries, the dominant saddle point is replica symmetric for $k>2$, and we obtain in closed form the exponential growth rate, the prefactor and the first $1/N$ correction, in agreement with exact enumerations. The growth rate depends only on whether the entries are real or complex; higher cumulants affect only the prefactor and the $1/N$ term. At $k=2$ the replica-symmetric solution becomes unstable, separating a power-law bulk of the distribution from a large-deviation tail, which we compute. The results apply to boson sampling with single photons and with squeezed light.

papers.title: The T-matrix method for modeling the optical properties of grains in exoplanetary atmospheres
papers.abstract: Observations of exoplanetary atmospheres have revealed a rather complex co-existence between the gaseous and condensed phases, ranging from atmospheres apparently covered in clouds to clear ones, across a myriad of intermediate regimes. The interaction between solids and stellar radiation is of fundamental importance when forward or retrieval models are compared to observations. The simplest approach is to assume spherical particles, whose scattering and absorption properties are readily computed with Mie theory. More advanced computational methods, however, can also treat non-spherical condensates. Among these, the transition matrix approach has proven to provide a rigorous and efficient calculation of the extinction by non-spherical particles over a broad range of sizes and refractive indices. We here focus on the absorption and scattering cross sections of forsterite, spinel and silicon monoxide from the near to the far infrared range for particles of different sizes, with shapes ranging from compact ensembles of spheres to porous aggregates. We find that, depending on the size and the configuration chosen, the differences in extinction can be as high as a factor of 2-3, with structured grains being more efficient absorbers in the near infrared for sizes greater than 1 $μ$m. In a fiducial transmission spectrum we show that in the $λ= 1-5\,μ$m range the amount of spherical material needed to match the contribution of the structured grains can be a factor 2 higher. Such calculations, available for the community through a Zenodo repository, prove to be useful for interpreting recent and future observations of exoplanetary atmospheres.

papers.intro:
Recent years have seen remarkable progress in characterizing exoplanet atmospheres, particularly through the detection of major volatile and metal-bearing species such as CO2\text{CO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}, H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}, CO, and metal oxides, primarily in the highly irradiated atmospheres of hot Jupiters, warm Neptunes, and temperate gas giants [50, 11, 4, 14]. However, these early observations often encountered an observational challenge: flat, muted, or even featureless transmission spectra caused by high-altitude atmospheric aerosols, generally classified as condensation clouds and photochemically produced hazes [24, 45, 17]. GJ 1214b became a reference target for these issues, as high-precision transmission spectroscopy yielded a remarkably flat spectrum across the optical and near-infrared regimes [25]. Recently, JWST observations have begun to break this observational barrier, revealing key water vapor absorption features in emission and pointing to a highly reflective, metal-rich atmosphere with a high Bond albedo [22]. Furthermore, near-infrared transmission spectroscopy has successfully detected signatures of CO2\text{CO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} and CH4\text{CH}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}}, suggesting a heavily enriched, super-solar metallicity. JWST observations have also revealed photochemically produced SO2\text{SO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} in the hot Saturn WASP-39b [52] and large-scale, weather-like temporal variations in WASP-121b [10]. These observations have begun to resolve the spatial and temporal dynamics of exoplanetary atmospheres, establishing that clouds are not static, uniform decks but active components of global meteorological cycles. Recent transit observations of the tidally locked hot Jupiter WASP-94A b have revealed that the cooler morning limb is heavily blanketed by high-altitude magnesium silicate MgSiO3\text{MgSiO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}} clouds that obscure gaseous signatures, while the hotter evening limb is clear and displays strong water vapor absorption [35]. This represents the first direct, spatially resolved detection of a planet-wide cloud cycle in action on a hot Jupiter. Additionally, JWST has provided further direct evidence for exotic aerosol compositions across cooler temperature regimes, such as salt clouds (e.g., KCl and ZnS) on the cold planet GJ 504b, which cover the atmosphere’s deeper layers and weaken molecular features [3].

papers.title: $L^{p}$-parabolicity of Riemannian manifolds
papers.abstract: We describe the $L^p$-parabolicity of a Riemannian manifold in terms of a unified theory of nonlinear $L^p$-capacities, for the whole range $1\leq p\leq \infty$. For example, the \(L^{1}\)-parabolicity is equivalent to the usual notion of parabolicity/recurrence, while \(L^{2}\)-parabolicity is equivalent to biparabolicity. For any $1\leq p\leq \infty,$ the $L^p$-parabolicity turns out to be equivalent to the $L^q$-Liouville property for positive superharmonic functions, where $p$ and $q$ are Hölder conjugate exponents. We also provide a new capacitary characterization of the $L^1$-Liouville property. Finally we obtain an almost optimal volume growth condition for the $L^p$-parabolicity for $1<p\leq 2$ as well as a sharp volume condition for all $1<p<\infty$ for manifolds of non-negative Ricci curvature and for model manifolds.

papers.title: Classical-to-Quantum Transition in Blackbody Radiation Thermodynamics: Planck's Law without Statistical Assumptions
papers.abstract: Inspired by Fermi's model of radiation-matter interaction, we investigate the classical dynamics of a closed, finite-energy system, in which matter is coupled to an electromagnetic field. We find that energy is progressively transferred to increasingly high-frequency field modes, so that the effective temperature of both matter and radiation approaches zero in the long-time limit - in sharp contradiction with the finite-temperature equilibrium assumed by classical blackbody thermodynamics. Requiring consistency with the Stefan-Boltzmann and Wien laws identifies a characteristic time $t_L$, at which both laws are simultaneously satisfied. Strikingly, classical spectra obtained for different energies and cavity sizes collapse onto the universal Planck distribution at $t_L$. We conjecture that quantum dynamical localization arrests the classical energy cascade at $t_L$, and that the Planck distribution emerges as a dynamical consequence of this arrest - without invoking any a priori statistical assumption.

papers.title: Beyond Two Tracks: Speaker-Anchored Full-Duplex Dialogue Recovery
papers.abstract: Spoken interaction is moving from alternating turns to full-duplex conversation, where an agent listens while speaking. Learning this coordination requires natural dialogue with persistent speaker-resolved tracks, a data requirement that remains difficult to satisfy at scale. Generative recovery offers a route from ordinary recordings, but recovering two voices is not enough: their track assignments can drift as the conversation unfolds. We address this missing link with speaker-anchored routing before diffusion: a 1.84M-parameter module matches the separator's coarse streams to fixed enrollment identities and orders them before a frozen generator reconstructs the speech, without retraining the generator or altering the reconstructed audio. On 25-minute remote conversations, routing cuts wrong-track time from 43.9% to 4.1%, below the 6.2% of matched-enrollment waveform re-identification, with its largest advantage when one participant holds the floor (17.8% versus 28.6%), and raises fixed-track activity F1 from 0.46 to 0.84 while per-chunk reconstruction quality is unchanged. The same router transfers to unseen face-to-face and telephone recordings, and a margin-gated verification step brings their wrong-track time to 0.9-1.7% while embedding 20-36% of the output, where full re-identification embeds all of it. Recovered voices thus become the participant-consistent tracks that full-duplex dialogue modeling needs. Audio examples: https://elpsykongloo.github.io/beyond-two-tracks/

papers.intro:
Speech interaction is moving beyond “listen, then answer.” A conversational agent should keep listening while it speaks, respond to an interruption, and distinguish a brief acknowledgment from a request to take the floor. Full-duplex spoken dialogue brings these behaviors into a continuous interaction rather than a sequence of isolated turns [1, 2]. This changes what a model must learn: not just the content of a response, but how two participants coordinate speech and silence on a shared timeline. Full-duplex models now span parallel-stream generation [3, 4], listening-while-speaking agents [5, 6], language-model-based duplex systems [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13], and multi-turn evaluation [14, 15].

papers.title: Euler Time-Discretization of Funnel-Controlled Dynamics
papers.abstract: We analyze explicit and implicit Euler discretizations of the continuous-time closed-loop dynamics generated by a funnel controller for a fully actuated nonlinear full-state system of relative degree one with scalar positive input gain. A quantitative continuous-time funnel margin provides the compactness and regularity bounds needed for the error analysis. For explicit Euler, a computable upper step-size threshold guarantees a global nodewise distance from the funnel boundary. We show that first-order convergence holds on finite time horizons and, under a~dissipativity condition (a~one-sided Lipschitz bound on the plant dominated by the funnel damping), uniformly in time. For implicit Euler, an admissible update exists for every step size and every trajectory initialized in the funnel retains a step-size-independent nodal margin. Under dissipativity, the admissible root is unique for every step size, the discrete flow is contractive, and the first-order error bound is uniform in time.

papers.title: The Spectrum of the Discrete Mathieu Operator with Nonreal Coupling
papers.abstract: We study the discrete Mathieu operator with nonreal coupling in the large-period limit, using complex WKB methods for analytic finite-difference equations. We obtain quantization formulas in different regions of the complex energy plane. Away from the corners of the image of the classical symbol, these formulas involve cosines of classical action integrals with small analytic corrections to the actions. Near each corner, we derive a uniform quantization formula involving the reciprocal Gamma function. The quantization formulas constrain spectral accumulation to curves determined by the competing exponential terms. Numerical computations illustrate the resulting spectral geometry.

papers.title: A general class of shared gamma frailty models for risk prediction, with application to breast cancer screening adherence
papers.abstract: We introduce a new class of mixed models for longitudinal or clustered binary data. The formulation is inspired by the shared frailty multivariate survival model for clustered data, and it allows for closed forms for all the relevant quantities, which allows for an efficient and fast computational solution of the associated inferential and prediction problems. We focus on an easily interpretable specification of the model, discuss the associated individual risk prediction, and compare our results to the traditional GLMM model for binary data with random intercept. We implement the methods on a large motivating dataset on the individual longitudinal adherence to the breast cancer screening program of the Oslo region.

papers.intro:
Clustered binary outcomes arise when individuals are nested within centers, members belong to the same household, or repeated observations are collected from the same individual. Responses within a cluster may remain associated after accounting for measured covariates. Accounting for this dependence is important both for inference on covariate effects and for predicting individual outcomes. Two widely used approaches to modeling correlated discrete responses are marginal models and random-effects models (Molenberghs and Verbeke, 2005). Marginal models specify the population mean response separately from the association structure. Under this approach, Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) had provided an influential framework for estimating such models without specifying a full joint distribution (Liang and Zeger, 1986).

Responses within a cluster may remain associated after accounting for measured covariates. Marginal models specify the population mean response separately from the association structure. Under this approach, Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) had provided an influential framework for estimating such models without specifying a full joint distribution (Liang and Zeger, 1986).

Random-effects models introduce latent cluster-specific quantities that aim to capture residual heterogeneity and induce dependence among responses. Within this approach, Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) extend generalized linear models to clustered data, retaining the familiar interpretation of regression coefficients while allowing flexible dependence through the random-effects structure (Breslow and Clayton, 1993). Predicting these latent effects supports model diagnostics and comparisons between clusters (Skrondal and Rabe-Hesketh, 2009). The latent effects may also be of direct interest, as in small-area estimation for the prediction of area-specific risks (Jiang and Lahiri, 2001; Jiang, 2003; Rao and Molina, 2015) and in identifying clusters with unusually high or low outcome risks Neuhaus et al. (2025).

(2025).

Despite these advantages, GLMMs has several potential drawbacks. Parameter estimation can be computationally demanding. In logistic-normal GLMMs, the likelihood requires integration over the random effects, generally without a closed-form solution (Demidenko, 2013; Jiang and Nguyen, 2021). Common strategies include Laplace approximations, marginal and penalized quasi-likelihood (Breslow and Clayton, 1993), adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature (Liu and Pierce, 1994; Pinheiro and Bates, 1995), and Monte Carlo likelihood methods (McCulloch, 1997; Booth and Hobert, 1999). These strategies require to balance computational cost against approximation or simulation error. Quasi-likelihood methods can be inaccurate for binary responses with small clusters or substantial heterogeneity (Rodríguez and Goldman, 1995), while quadrature becomes expensive as the dimension of the random effects increases. Alternatives to design models with tractable conditional and marginal relationships were investigated such as marginally specified logistic-normal models (Heagerty, 1999), bridge distributions (Wang and Louis, 2003), and specialized link–distribution combinations (Kazemi and Hassanzadeh, 2021). Explicit marginal means, however, do not by themselves imply a closed-form joint marginal likelihood.

Random-effect prediction presents similar challenges. For known model parameters, the posterior mean of the random effect given the observed cluster data minimizes expected squared-error loss. Replacing the parameters by their maximum likelihood estimates yields the empirical Bayes posterior mean, also called an empirical best predictor (Robinson, 1991; Skrondal and Rabe-Hesketh, 2004; Skrondal and Rabe-Hesketh, 2009; Jiang and Nguyen, 2021). For non-normal outcomes, its computation typically involves a ratio of integrals, evaluated using quadrature or Laplace-based approximations such as those of Tierney and Kadane (1986). Skrondal and Rabe-Hesketh (2009) discuss posterior prediction in multilevel generalized linear models, including the use of adaptive quadrature to evaluate posterior moments. Other proposals target prediction in the specific GLMMs logistic settings. Tamura and Giampaoli (2010) investigate procedures based on empirical best prediction and Tamura and Giampaoli (2013) develop a computationally simpler prediction method based on regressing fitted random effects on aggregated group covariates. In the context of prediction, Sun et al. (2018) propose classified mixed logistic prediction that links new observations from a validation data to clusters available in a training data through a classification step.

(2018) propose classified mixed logistic prediction that links new observations from a validation data to clusters available in a training data through a classification step.

A less developed literature obtains analytically tractable likelihoods and random effect predictions by combining binary response models with positive distributed random effects. Conaway (1990) used a complementary log-log link and log-gamma random effects to integrate the likelihood analytically. Coull et al. (2006) extended this work to multivariate gamma random effects, allowing more flexible dependence while retaining computational tractability while Zhang and Chan (2014) adoped correlated exponential latent effects. Rice et al. (2019) model repeated HIV-testing indicators using a shared frailty framework. For this application, they specify the frailty distribution within the power-variance-function family, which includes the possibility of a point mass at zero to represent potential never-testers.

(2006) extended this work to multivariate gamma random effects, allowing more flexible dependence while retaining computational tractability while Zhang and Chan (2014) adoped correlated exponential latent effects. Rice et al. (2019) model repeated HIV-testing indicators using a shared frailty framework. For this application, they specify the frailty distribution within the power-variance-function family, which includes the possibility of a point mass at zero to represent potential never-testers.

Following these methodological developments, we propose a class of models for clustered binary responses based on a shared gamma frailty and a flexible, covariate-dependent reference probability. The term shared gamma frailty is inherited from the survival-analysis literature. In our framework, indeed, the random effect does not enter the linear predictor additively. Instead, it acts multiplicatively on a non-negative function of the covariates. The proposed class has several advantages. First, likelihood inference, marginal probabilities, and posterior predictive quantities are available in closed form, avoiding numerical integration or Monte Carlo methods and leading to a straightforward implementation. Second, the joint distribution of binary responses within a cluster has a computationally simple expression. Third, the reference probability, or more generally the covariate-dependent function defining the model, can be chosen flexibly according to the scientific setting and the predictive objective. Finally, specifying a logistic reference probability preserves the usual interpretation of regression coefficients and facilitates a direct comparison with the logistic random intercept GLMM, one of the most widely used approaches for clustered binary data. The proposed model can therefore be considered as a computationally tractable alternative to the logistic random intercept GLMM.

papers.title: Scrambled Multiply-with-Carry Pseudorandom Number Generators
papers.abstract: Multiply-with-carry (MWC) generators are very fast pseudorandom number generators whose quality depends on the choice of a multiplier, and is usually assessed by applying the spectral test to an associated multiplicative congruential generator. The special form of the modulus is shown to impose structural limitations on the lattice structure of every MWC generator, which the generalized MWC generators of Goresky and Klapper mitigate; in the tests reported, a scrambler made of a single xor removes them. Since these limitations make the usual worst-case criterion useless, candidates are ranked by a weighted geometric mean of their figures of merit, which does not depend on their normalization, and multipliers are suggested for generators with 64 to 256 bits of state. Along the way, some errors in the literature are corrected. In the end, MWC192X is proposed: a 64-bit generator with 192 bits of state that passes all known tests, and emits an output in half a nanosecond. Analogous 32-bit generators are proposed for GPUs.

papers.intro:
Congruential generators are among the oldest and best understood pseudorandom number generators (PRNGs): their outputs have a lattice structure that can be analyzed precisely with number-theoretic tools (Knuth, 1998). This paper is about a family of very fast generators whose analysis reduces to that of congruential generators: generators with carry.

Marsaglia and Zaman (Marsaglia and Zaman, 1991) introduced in 1991 add-with-carry (AWC) and subtract-with-borrow (SWB) generators, which extend lagged Fibonacci generators by propagating a carry (or borrow). Tezuka, L’Ecuyer, and Couture (Tezuka et al., 1993) showed that they are, in disguise, multiplicative congruential generators (MCGs) with a huge modulus, whose lattice structure is very bad in dimensions larger than the lag (see also (Couture and L’Ecuyer, 1994)), a defect that Lüscher’s RANLUX generator (Lüscher, 1994) mitigates by discarding most of the outputs.

papers.title: Schauder estimates for quasilinear parabolic equations with general Orlicz growth
papers.abstract: We develop a unified approach to Schauder estimates for scalar parabolic equations \[ \partial_t u-\operatorname{div}\big(\mathcal{A}(x,t,Du)\big)=f(x,t) \] with general Orlicz growth and coefficients that are Hölder continuous in the spatial variables and merely measurable in time. Combining intrinsic gradient estimates with a perturbative argument, we establish quantitative local bounds and Hölder estimates for the spatial gradient in the supercritical range and, for locally bounded weak solutions, throughout the full admissible growth range. Our results extend the Schauder regularity theory for parabolic $p$-Laplace type equations to a broad class of possibly nonradial operators with Orlicz growth, while simplifying the regularity arguments and treating singular, degenerate, and mixed growth laws within a unified framework.

papers.title: Strichartz Estimates and Scattering for the Massless Reduced Dirac-Fock Equation
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish Strichartz estimates for the reduced Dirac-Fock equation for 3D massless spinors, linearized around non-localized equilibria. Our analysis covers both the random field and the density matrix frameworks. As an application, we deduce scattering for the corresponding nonlinear problem with a high-frequency cut-off.

The Dirac-Fock equation has been extensively studied in the time-independent setting. The existence of critical points of the corresponding energy functional was established in [14, 38]. We refer here to critical points rather than minimizers due to the unboundedness from below of the energy functional, a consequence of the negative spectrum of the Dirac operator. This difficulty was addressed in [13] by analyzing the nonrelativistic limit, which yielded a well-defined electronic ground state energy. More recently, a new definition of the Dirac-Fock ground state was introduced in [39], a framework that has since been extended to a relativistic model for crystals [7]. In the time-dependent framework, the theory is far less developed. Global-in-time existence for a generalized Dirac-Fock evolution arising from the Bogoliubov-Dirac-Fock model was proved in [24], and recent works have extended this well-posedness result to relativistic electron-nucleus dynamics [33] and to a two-dimensional massless analog relevant for graphene [3].

papers.title: Universal Online Convex Optimization With Delayed Feedback
papers.abstract: We study universal online convex optimization with delayed feedback. We develop a single algorithm that simultaneously adapts to general convex, strongly convex, and exp-concave losses without prior knowledge of the curvature class or parameters. Our regret bounds match the best known dependence on the time horizon $T$ and delays up to doubly logarithmic factors: roughly $\sqrt{T + d_{\mathrm{tot}}}$ for convex losses and $σ_{\max}\log T$ rates with curved losses, where $d_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total cumulative delay and $σ_{\max}$ is the maximum number of simultaneously missing observations. Our main technical contribution is a delayed meta-learner with a second-order excess-loss guarantee, which enables curvature-adaptive aggregation of delayed base learners. In addition, our new exp-concave base learner yields a sharper regret bound which improves the state-of-the-art delay dependence by replacing the maximum delay with the potentially much smaller $σ_{\max}$, while retaining the complementary $\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{tot}}}$ dependence.

papers.title: Spatially developing drag reduction across a finite oscillating wall
papers.abstract: The spatial evolution of a turbulent boundary layer at $Re_τ= 652$ developing across a finite spanwise oscillating wall is investigated with normalised oscillation period of $T^+ \approx 101$ and amplitude $A^+ \approx 7$, yielding a drag reduction of 32\%. The spatial distribution of skin friction is estimated adopting a recently introduced near-wall data nonlinear regression method based on the arctangent function, which circumvents the requirement of high wall-normal resolution to capture the viscous sublayer. The method viability is assessed against reference DNS data, and the trends of measurement errors from experimental data are well reproduced. The local impact of the control action is examined by evaluating the spatial development of scalar fields of turbulence statistics as well as conditional quadrant analysis to link the onset and recovery transients to turbulence events. The boundary layer response is observed to follow an exponential decay law for the skin friction spatial evolution. The decay length-scale corresponds to $0.6$ boundary layer thicknesses $δ$ for the onset transient and $0.9δ$ for the recovery one. The same exponential fit applied to the Reynolds stresses yields a response within $0.5δ$, with the exception of the shear stress peak, that requires a significantly longer distance.

A proven active control strategy for a turbulent boundary layer is that of imposing a transverse, oscillatory motion of the wall. First developed by Jung et al. papers.title: A Twisted bidifferential, second fundamental form of Prym map and projective structures
papers.abstract: Given a point $[(\widetilde{C},C)]$ of the moduli space ${\mathcal R}_g$, where $\widetilde{C}$ is an étale double cover of a smooth curve $C$ of genus $g \,\geq\, 7$, we construct a twisted meromorphic bidifferential $\widehatη_P$ on $C\times C$ with a pole on the diagonal. It is shown that the second fundamental form $ρ_P$ of the Prym map from ${\mathcal R}_g$ to ${\mathcal A}_{g-1}$ at $[(\widetilde{C},C)]$ is given by this $\widehatη_P$. This allows us to compare $ρ_P$ with the second fundamental forms of the two Torelli maps, to ${\mathcal A}_{2g-1}$ and ${\mathcal A}_{g}$, at the points $[\widetilde{C}]$ and $[C]$ respectively. It is shown that $\widehatη_P$ induces a projective structure on $C$ that depends on the double cover $\widetilde{C}\, \longrightarrow\, C$; these projective structures together give a ${\mathcal C}^{\infty}$ section $β_P$ of the bundle of projective structures on the moduli space ${\mathcal R}_g$. Finally, it is proved that the $(0,\,1)$-component of the differential of the section $β_P$ is the pullback of the Kähler form of the Siegel metric on ${\mathcal A}_{g-1}$ via the Prym map. This is a key ingredient in the proof that this section $β_P$ is not the pullback of a section of projective structures on ${\mathcal M}_{g}$ and, in addition, that it differs from the known projective structures on ${\mathcal R}_g$.

papers.title: Reasoning as a Distribution: Generative Plan Latents for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies increasingly reason before acting, but existing reasoning models compress this intermediate decision into a single representation. When several plans are valid, this commitment hides alternatives that could otherwise be selected or revised. We introduce the Generative Plan Latent (GPL), which represents the reasoning state as a low-dimensional conditional distribution over plans, such as which object, grasp, or route to use. This makes the reasoning state addressable: without retraining the VLA, plans can be sampled (coverage), selected on request (steering), and reweighted by deployment outcomes (outcome adaptation). We test all three on SimplerEnv manipulation with $π_0$, and extend the analysis to RoboCasa, LIBERO, and a maze domain. Steering the plan raises the fraction of executions that follow the request from 0.48 to 0.94, while the same guidance on the native action distribution shows no reliable gain. Finally, we show that an explicit plan is most useful when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation.
papers.intro:
Vision–Language–Action (VLA) policies increasingly place a reasoning stage between perception and action (Zawalski et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026a), and this intermediate state empirically improves policy success rate. This intermediate state is attractive because it can separate what the robot decides to do from the motor trajectory that realizes that decision. Yet existing reasoning models represent this state as one vector per observation. This raises the question: should a model expose one committed decision per observation, or a distribution over valid ones?

Vision–Language–Action (VLA) policies increasingly place a reasoning stage between perception and action (Zawalski et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026a), and this intermediate state empirically improves policy success rate. This intermediate state is attractive because it can separate what the robot decides to do from the motor trajectory that realizes that decision. Yet existing reasoning models represent this state as one vector per observation. This raises the question: should a model expose one committed decision per observation, or a distribution over valid ones?

The distinction matters whenever the observation leaves more than one decision valid. Consider a robot facing two identical cubes, with an instruction that names neither: nothing favors one target over the other. The same ambiguity is pervasive in everyday tasks: whether to pick up a can or push it aside, how to grasp a mug, or which route to take. A reasoning state that must produce a single decision necessarily collapses these alternatives. Averaging them may yield an invalid plan between the cubes; choosing one avoids this failure but still hides the equally valid alternative. The missing property is therefore not simply validity, but a representation that preserves the alternatives so they remain accessible at inference time, allowing preferences or outcomes to dynamically select the most viable strategy at deployment without retraining (Figure 1). We call a reasoning state addressable when, at inference time, the policy can be: sampled to obtain distinct valid decisions (coverage), conditioned to select among them a single decision (steering), and reweighted by outcome to adapt the decision in closed-loop (outcome adaptation). The limitation of prior designs is therefore a lack of addressability. This is not the usual action-multimodality problem: robot learning has already developed generative action models precisely to avoid averaging incompatible motor trajectories (Section 2). The unresolved question is whether the upstream decision should itself also be represented as a distribution.

We introduce the Generative Plan Latent (gpl), which replaces a deterministic plan readout with a conditional distribution pθ​(z∣c)p_{\theta}(z\mid c) of plans zz given a VLA representation cc. This distribution can be sampled, steered toward a requested mode, and reweighted from deployment experience, all without retraining the underlying VLA. We show that the plan provides a substantially stronger handle than the action distribution for expressing an external preference. Under matched executors, selecting a requested plan increases the fraction of executions that follow it from 0.48 to 0.94, whereas applying the same inference-time intervention to π0\pi_{0}’s native action distribution yields no reliable improvement. Because these alternatives remain explicit, deployment outcomes can also change which plans are preferred without updating the plan generator or VLA. This benefit is conditional: an explicit plan can influence behavior only when it carries decision information that the executor cannot already recover from the observation. We call this the redundancy principle. In a controlled test, changing only the demonstrations to reduce this redundancy increases the plan-selection effect from +0.19 to +0.65. Finally, these capabilities do not depend on hand-designed plan coordinates: they persist when the plan representation is learned directly from demonstrated behavior.

papers.title: Perceives but Doesn't Brake: A Perception-Action Binding Gap in Reasoning Driving VLAs
papers.abstract: Reasoning-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) driving models can perceive and reason about safety-critical hazards yet fail to translate that evidence into safe actions. We characterize this failure as a perception-action binding gap: hazard information is available inside the model but exerts insufficient control over trajectory generation. Using matched simulated counterfactuals and logged driving replay, we show that in-path hazards are actually encoded in the visual representation, but longitudinal plans are dominated by ego-speed history and respond only weakly to hazard proximity or the model's own reasoning trace. Further analysis shows that the trajectory generator is capable of braking but sometimes fails to do so due to the perception-action binding gap. Without retraining or modifying any weights, we inject a hazard-conditioned energy into the frozen flow-matching sampler of Alpamayo-1.5, restoring the missing coupling at generation time. With exact obstacle geometry, guidance cuts footprint intrusion from 58.1% to 14.5% and recovers safe braking whenever sufficient stopping distance remains, eliminating collisions entirely in our braking-relevant closed-loop battery. It also reverses the diagnosed dependence of the plan, from tracking ego speed to responding to obstacle range. These results separate hazard perception from hazard control in driving VLAs, show that unsafe behavior can arise even when the model has both the evidence and the ability to act on it, and propose a simple fix for bridging this binding gap.

Reasoning-augmented vision–language–action (VLA) models are increasingly designed to do more than map observations directly to actions: they perceive the scene, produce an explicit reasoning trace, and then generate a driving trajectory. This architecture suggests a natural safety premise: if the model correctly identifies a hazard and reasons that the vehicle should respond, that evidence should influence the resulting action. However, on simulated scenes containing a stationary obstacle in the ego lane, a state-of-the-art reasoning VLA [1] generates trajectories that enter the obstacle footprint on 58.1% of samples, and its selected actions collide with a reconstructed version of that obstacle in most closed-loop rollouts, even though a comfortable stop was still possible. Crucially, the failure does not arise because the hazard is absent from the model. The obstacle is recoverable from the visual representation and is often explicitly identified in the model’s own reasoning, yet neither source of evidence exerts sufficient influence on the generated longitudinal plan. Instead, the plan remains strongly governed by the supplied ego-speed history. We call this dissociation between accessible hazard evidence and its influence on action a perception–action binding gap (Figure 1); here perceives means recoverable from the model’s representation (formalized as availability, Section IV), not awareness.

This distinction matters because an unsafe action can have at least three different causes. First, the relevant hazard may not be represented at all (availability). Second, the trajectory generator may be incapable of producing an appropriate response even when the hazard is known (action-side sufficiency). Third, the evidence may be available and a safe action may be expressible, but the evidence may have insufficient action authority: changing the hazard does not sufficiently change the generated plan. These cases imply different remedies, yet standard driving metrics typically conflate them.

We disentangle them with matched simulated interventions that vary visual hazard content, obstacle range, ego-speed history, and textual reasoning while holding competing inputs fixed. Hazard information is available throughout, yet longitudinal behavior is far more sensitive to ego history than to the hazard itself, under closed-loop control in AlpaSim/NuRec [2] as well as open-loop scoring.

Next, we ask whether the missing coupling can be restored without retraining the policy. We inject a differentiable hazard energy into the frozen flow-matching sampler of Alpamayo-1.5, steering trajectory generation during flow integration while leaving all model parameters unchanged. Supplied exact obstacle geometry, this reduces footprint intrusion from 58.1% to 14.5% and changes the governing dependence of the generated plan: trajectory reach becomes primarily responsive to obstacle range rather than ego speed. Controlled CARLA sweeps further show that the remaining failures are those in which insufficient stopping distance remains.

Finally, we ask how far this intervention can be driven by signals already present in the frozen model, rather than by privileged geometry. Lightweight readouts of the visual cache estimate both when an in-path hazard is present and where it lies. The key is to preserve the spatial structure needed for that estimate: on sites held out in both geometry and appearance, a spatially aware readout reduces footprint intrusion from 65.0% to 11.7%, approaching the 6.0% obtained with exact geometry, with no measured reach loss on matched clear scenes. Thus, much of the safety constraint needed to restore perception-action binding is already recoverable from the model’s own representation. Autonomous binding is therefore feasible within the evaluated visual domain, while robust semantic triggering under domain shift remains open.

Our contributions are threefold. First, our primary contribution is to identify and causally diagnose a perception–action binding gap in a reasoning driving VLA. Across logged driving, matched counterfactuals, and closed-loop replay, we separate hazard availability from action authority and show that longitudinal planning is dominated by ego-speed history; to our knowledge, this is the first causal, rather than correlational, separation of hazard availability from action authority in a reasoning driving VLA. Second, we show that the missing coupling can be enforced at inference time without retraining. A differentiable hazard-conditioned energy steers the frozen flow-matching sampler toward safe braking and, when supplied an accurate constraint, shifts the plan’s dependence from ego speed toward obstacle range, demonstrating action-side sufficiency. Third, we show why standard logged evaluation can miss such a failure. Because a binding gap is a failure of hazard-conditioned action response rather than average prediction quality, standard logged evaluation can miss it: safety-critical states in which a moving ego must brake for a stationary in-path obstacle are rare because human drivers typically avoid them.

papers.title: The Gagliardo-Nirenberg equation on Riemannian manifolds
papers.abstract: We establish geometric and analytic rigidity results for the Gagliardo-Nirenberg equation. On a complete noncompact Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature, the existence of a positive critical point of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg quotient forces the manifold to be Euclidean and the solution to be extremal. No minimizing assumption or volume growth hypothesis is required, thereby strengthening earlier rigidity results. In Euclidean space, we prove that all positive solutions of the normalized equation whose nonlinear mass on expanding annuli has sublinear growth are extremals. The linear threshold is optimal, as shown by explicit profiles that are constant in one direction. We also prove a sharp pointwise estimate involving the solution and its gradient, valid without assumptions at infinity, with equality at one point characterizing the extremals. The proofs use weighted divergence identities and a reflection argument controlled by annular mass. Explicit constructions reveal the geometric and variational limits of rigidity: nonflat quotient critical points exist beyond the curvature hypothesis, while the normalized equation admits positive solutions even under strictly positive sectional curvature and maximal volume growth.
papers.intro:
The classification of positive solutions to nonlinear elliptic equations is closely connected with the equality cases of sharp functional inequalities. An extremal satisfies an Euler–Lagrange equation, but the converse requires a rigidity theorem: a critical point need not minimize the functional. On a Riemannian manifold, there is a further question of whether the existence of such a solution determines the ambient geometry. In this paper, we address these questions for the Gagliardo–Nirenberg equation, proving rigidity for critical points under nonnegative Ricci curvature, a sharp annular classification in Euclidean space, and a pointwise estimate with rigidity in the equality case.

On complete Riemannian manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature, these questions combine analytic classification with geometric rigidity. For the critical semilinear equation, classification and rigidity results were obtained in [5, 11, 21, 41] under suitable assumptions (growth or finite energy) or when the Riemannian manifold has dimension at most five (see also [32, 43]). In each case, a nontrivial solution forces the manifold to be Euclidean. Differential identities involving a suitable power of the solution, its Hessian, and the Ricci tensor make it possible to obtain this conclusion without relying on Euclidean reflection symmetries. Related rigidity phenomena have also been investigated beyond the Riemannian critical Sobolev setting. For singular or degenerate critical equations arising from Caffarelli–Kohn–Nirenberg inequalities, see e.g. [10, 7, 14, 18]. In CR and sub-Riemannian geometries, Liouville-type rigidity and classification results were obtained in the Heisenberg group in [4, 20, 25, 29, 36], and on Sasakian manifolds in [8]. These results illustrate how identities adapted to the equation can turn information about a single solution into rigidity of the underlying space.

papers.title: Optimal power concavity of the variational mean curvature via singular $1$-Laplace problems
papers.abstract: Let $Ω\subset \mathbb{R}^N$ be a bounded convex domain and let $H_Ω\leq 0$ denote its variational mean curvature, in the sense of Barozzi, Gonzalez and Tamanini [PAMS, 1987]. We prove that $-H_Ω$ is harmonic convex, that is $1/H_Ω$ is a convex function in $Ω$, and that the exponent $-1$ is optimal in the class of convex domains. This strictly improves the concavity of $H_Ω$ obtained by Alter and Caselles [Nonlinear Anal., 2009], who also proved, by geometric methods, a closely related property for the classical mean curvature under Minkowski interpolation of convex bodies. Our approach is analytic: the result is deduced from a concavity property of the solution of the singular $1$-Laplace Dirichlet problem $$\begin{cases} -Δ_1 u = {u^{-γ}} & \quad \hbox{in $Ω$}, \\ u = 0 &\quad \hbox{on $\partial Ω$}, \end{cases}$$ for $γ\in (0,1]$, whose unique positive solution is $u=(-H_Ω)^{-1/γ}$. We show that $u^γ$ is concave, and we obtain this by proving that the solutions $u_p$ of the approximating problems $-Δ_p u_p = u_p^{-γ}$ are $\frac{p-1+γ}{p}$-concave on every bounded convex domain, without any boundary regularity, and then letting $p\to 1^+$. Explicit examples show that no Hölder continuity of $H_Ω$ up to $\partialΩ$ holds uniformly in the class of convex domains with $C^{1,1}$ boundary.

papers.title: Balmer breaks in accreting super-massive black hole binaries
papers.abstract: We show that truncated circumbinary accretion disks around super-massive black hole binaries can produce Balmer breaks. For binaries interacting with surrounding disks in a truncated, non-accreting phase, gas accumulates at the cavity edge, and can create conditions conducive to generating spectral discontinuities from $n=2$ hydrogen bound-free absorption. We develop a simple model for predicting the presence of a Balmer edge and estimating the break strength, and we find that the strongest discontinuities are expected for binaries with periods of months to years and total masses $\gtrsim10^6\,\Msun$. These systems share considerable overlap with those binaries anticipated to appear in upcoming time-domain surveys---like LSST and the Roman HLTDS---as periodically variable quasars. We estimate that for typical feeding rates of a few tenths of their Eddington rate, a few-to-10\% of periodic binaries at $z\lesssim1$ should show prominent Balmer breaks, and that this fraction increases for the more massive black holes that can be discovered at higher redshift. We suggest that black hole binaries that truncate their accretion flows will appear as periodically variable sources, and will additionally be intrinsically X-ray weak, deficient in ionizing emission, and in favorable cases, produce notable Balmer edges in their spectra. This combination provides a complementary observational test for massive black hole binary candidates.

papers.intro:
Spectral discontinuities from atomic bound-free transitions provide important diagnostics of the physical conditions of emitting material in astrophysical sources. The most prominent examples are the Lyman and Balmer edges of atomic hydrogen, whose appearance and strength depend sensitively on the temperature and ionization state of the emitting material. The Balmer break is particularly informative because substantial absorption from the n=2n=2 level of neutral hydrogen is produced only over a relatively narrow range of thermodynamic conditions. Balmer discontinuities are typically prominent in the spectra of A-type stars and, in integrated stellar populations, provide a useful tracer of intermediate-age stars [7]. As a result, the strength of the Balmer break is commonly used to constrain the ages of galaxies and stellar clusters, recent star-formation histories, and redshifts [29, 36, 47, 37, e.g.,].

Strong hydrogen bound-free discontinuities are not generally observed in the continua of AGN [2, 57], despite predictions from classical accretion-disk atmosphere models [35, e.g.,]. In particular, models for computing accretion disk emission by summing stellar spectra [34, e.g.,] or constructing vertical atmosphere profiles [39, 48, 55, 4, 14, e.g.,] can produce prominent hydrogen bound-free edges—though non-LTE effects, Comptonization, relativistic corrections, and more detailed treatments of the vertical disk structure can weaken or suppress these features [54, 24, 25, 22, 23, 5]. The general absence of prominent Lyman edges in observed AGN has become known as the “Lyman edge problem”, though Balmer breaks have been observed in some sources [31, 32].

Recently, in detailed radiation magnetohydrodynamics simulations, Kaul et al. [30] argued that such edges are suppressed in observed systems because of the low gas densities (and vertically inverted dissipation profiles) in magnetically supported disks. However, in similar radiative transfer calculations, Liu et al. [40] demonstrated that AGN disks can produce prominent Balmer breaks, provided they are truncated at a radius where the disk effective temperature is qualitatively similar to the surface temperatures of typical A-type stars (and for even cooler temperatures in sufficiently low density atmospheres); though they comment that there is not an obvious reason for disks to truncate at such specific radii.

Hydrodynamical simulations of thin-disk accretion onto (super-) massive black hole binaries, though, have recently demonstrated that the rotating binary potential can halt circumbinary accretion flows on scales of the binary semi-major axis [46, 60]; but that tidal and hydrodynamic heating of the inner-disk (i.e., at the edge of the central cavity) can keep these systems detectable in upcoming optical and infrared time-domain surveys [9, 58]. For binary configurations most relevant to identifying periodically variable sources in such surveys [6, 8, 12, see, e.g.,], disk truncation occurs beyond the near-horizon scales where the standard ultraviolet, big-blue bump is generated. This generally suppresses the ionizing continuum and makes an observable Lyman edge unlikely, but for sources that remain sufficiently luminous at optical wavelengths, it is possible that accreting (super-) massive black hole binaries with truncated accretion disks may present with notable Balmer edges in their spectra.

In this work, we estimate which accreting binary systems—assuming they truncate their accretion flow—would do so at disk radii that would result in a prominent Balmer break in the associated optical spectrum. To accomplish this, we detail in Section II our disk modeling, and in Section III our heuristic estimator for when Balmer breaks occur. In Section IV we apply these to estimate which combinations of binary mass, period, and feeding rate result in Balmer breaks and compare this with those binaries expected to be found in upcoming time-domain surveys like the Large Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Roman Space Telescope’s High Latitude time-domain Survey (HLTDS). We discuss or findings in the broader context of electromagnetic searches for (super-) massive black hole binaries and conclude in Section V.

papers.title: DDELenS: Tomographic Weak Lensing Simulations with Dynamical Dark Energy
papers.abstract: We present a suite of 128 cosmological simulations in $w_0w_a$CDM cosmologies with massive neutrinos, designed to enable simulation-based inference of dynamical dark energy parameters from weak gravitational lensing and other cosmological observables. Each simulation follows $1024^3$ dark matter particles in a $512\,h^{-1}$Mpc periodic box, with cosmological parameters sampled using a Sobol sequence over the ranges $Ω_m \in [0.28, 0.35]$, $σ_8 \in [0.74, 0.90]$, $w_0 \in [-1.0, -0.5]$, and $w_a \in [-1.5, 0.0]$, motivated by recent results from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument survey. The nonlinear evolution is computed with $\texttt{PKDGRAV3}$ using the N-body gauge to consistently incorporate relativistic corrections from massive neutrinos, photons, and dark energy. For each cosmology, we generate 10,000 ray-traced convergence maps at six source redshifts $z_s \in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 1100\}$ using $\texttt{LensTools}$, and additionally provide halo catalogues and projected halo overdensity fields for galaxy--lensing cross-correlation analyses. We generate 100,000 realizations at the fiducial cosmology for the construction of the covariance matrix. This simulation suite provides a foundation for field-level inference and non-Gaussian statistics with next-generation weak lensing surveys such as the Rubin Observatory LSST, Euclid, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, as well as CMB lensing experiments including the Simons Observatory.

The nature of dark energy remains one of the central open questions in cosmology. The first data release of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI DR1), combining baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) [9] and full-shape power spectrum measurements [8, 10] from galaxy samples spanning z∈[0.1,2.1]z\in[0.1,2.1], found a mild but statistically inconclusive preference for dynamical dark energy — specifically w0>−1w_{0}>-1 and wa<0w_{a}<0 in the Chevallier–Polarski–Linder (CPL) parametrization — when combined with cosmic microwave background (CMB) data. This preference strengthens upon inclusion of Type Ia supernova (SNe Ia) datasets [27, 84, 1, 78], some of which already show independent hints of departures from a cosmological constant. With two additional years of data, BAO measurements from DESI DR2 [5, 6] further consolidate this preference even without external datasets. More recently, a joint analysis of supernovae, BAO, weak lensing, and galaxy clustering from the full Dark Energy Survey (DES) dataset finds a 2.2​σ2.2\sigma preference for dynamical dark energy, increasing to 3.0​σ3.0\sigma when combined with DESI DR2 BAO and CMB data. A 2.6​σ2.6\sigma preference still persists when supernovae are excluded from the combined analysis, providing a cross-check independent of supernova photometric calibration [2].

Accurately predicting the clustering of matter in dynamical dark energy cosmologies is itself a significant theoretical challenge. While Einstein–Boltzmann solvers such as CAMB [62] and CLASS [61, 22] provide highly accurate large-scale predictions, they break down in the nonlinear regime. Fitting functions such as Halofit [91, 21] and HMCode [71] extend these to smaller scales, but they are insufficiently accurate for next-generation surveys. A complete description ultimately requires N-body simulations that evolve all species simultaneously11 1 We do not include the nonlinear clustering of dark energy perturbations in our simulations as they are subdominant relative to matter fluctuations [85, 38].

On the emulator side, a number of efforts — including COYOTE [55, 54, 60], EuclidEmulator2 [57], BACCO [16], CAMELUS [63], CosmicEmu [59], CSST [34, 35, 98], Aemulus [42, 43, 70, 97], and Goku [96] — have provided accurate nonlinear predictions of matter power spectra for beyond-Λ\LambdaCDM cosmologies, though these have largely focused on the matter power spectrum or halo mass function rather than weak lensing maps. Approximate methods such as COmoving Lagrangian Acceleration (COLA) have also been employed for emulator construction [83]. On the simulation methodology side, Nefertiti represents the first hydrodynamical simulation to self-consistently incorporate nonlinear dark energy clustering [24, 23]. In this work, we employ a pipeline combining PKDGRAV3 [79] and CONCEPT [40, 39], in which dark energy perturbations are evolved linearly while gravity is solved at full N-body precision, offering an efficient and self-consistent framework for dynamical dark energy simulations.
