Despite this progress, no existing weak lensing simulation suite covers dynamical dark energy in the w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM framework, motivated by recent DESI results, with the full machinery needed for field-level and non-Gaussian inference. Current surveys such as DES [3, 4], KiDS [94], and HSC [73] have already demonstrated the constraining power of galaxy weak lensing beyond the power spectrum and constraints on w0w_{0} from some of them. CMB lensing measurements, for example from ACT [81, 68], SPT [95], SPT-3G [74], Planck [12, 30], and their combination [82], have also provided cosmological constraints through the lensing convergence power spectrum (see Refs. [66, 32] for forecasts beyond the power spectrum, for example). Next-generation experiments — including the Rubin Observatory LSST [37], the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope [13, 88], Euclid [57], and CMB lensing from the Simons Observatory [11, 7] — will deliver datasets of sufficient statistical precision to demand accurate, field-level forward models. In this work, we present such a suite. We combine PKDGRAV3 [79] and CONCEPT [40, 39] for nonlinear N-body evolution — incorporating relativistic corrections from all linear species via the N-body gauge — with LensTools [77] for fully ray-traced convergence maps and ROCKSTAR [20] for halo finding. We generate 10,000 ray-traced convergence maps at six source redshifts for each of 128 cosmologies sampled with a Sobol sequence over (w0,wa,Ωm,σ8)(w_{0},w_{a},\Omega_{m},\sigma_{8}), along with halo catalogues and projected halo overdensity fields suitable for galaxy–lensing cross-correlation analyses.

Despite this progress, no existing weak lensing simulation suite covers dynamical dark energy in the w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM framework, motivated by recent DESI results, with the full machinery needed for field-level and non-Gaussian inference. Current surveys such as DES [3, 4], KiDS [94], and HSC [73] have already demonstrated the constraining power of galaxy weak lensing beyond the power spectrum and constraints on w0w_{0} from some of them. CMB lensing measurements, for example from ACT [81, 68], SPT [95], SPT-3G [74], Planck [12, 30], and their combination [82], have also provided cosmological constraints through the lensing convergence power spectrum (see Refs. [66, 32] for forecasts beyond the power spectrum, for example). Next-generation experiments — including the Rubin Observatory LSST [37], the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope [13, 88], Euclid [57], and CMB lensing from the Simons Observatory [11, 7] — will deliver datasets of sufficient statistical precision to demand accurate, field-level forward models. In this work, we present such a suite. We combine PKDGRAV3 [79] and CONCEPT [40, 39] for nonlinear N-body evolution — incorporating relativistic corrections from all linear species via the N-body gauge — with LensTools [77] for fully ray-traced convergence maps and ROCKSTAR [20] for halo finding. We generate 10,000 ray-traced convergence maps at six source redshifts for each of 128 cosmologies sampled with a Sobol sequence over (w0,wa,Ωm,σ8)(w_{0},w_{a},\Omega_{m},\sigma_{8}), along with halo catalogues and projected halo overdensity fields suitable for galaxy–lensing cross-correlation analyses.

papers.title: Programmable nonlinear rotation of acoustically levitated chiral stars
papers.abstract: Acoustic levitation enables objects to be suspended and manipulated without physical contact, providing a versatile platform for studying the dynamics of freely suspended matter. Yet levitated objects, from droplets and thin films to particle assemblies, frequently rotate spontaneously, and this axial rotation often remains difficult to predict or control. There is no general understanding of how the shape of a levitated object determines whether it rotates, in which direction, or how its rotation changes with acoustic amplitude. Here, we establish how particle geometry and acoustic amplitude govern spontaneous rotation of acoustically levitated objects. We work with a family of shapes we call ``chiral stars'', within which we systematically vary handedness and number of arms. In a symmetric acoustic field, stars that preserve in-plane mirror symmetry do not rotate, while those that break it spontaneously rotate with a direction set by handedness. Beyond this symmetry requirement, we demonstrate that geometry, as encoded by the number of star arms, couples with acoustic amplitude to produce complex, nonlinear dynamics, including spontaneous reversal of rotation direction. To explain these behaviors, we develop a minimal torque model constrained by independent measurements of rotational drag, which captures the observed responses across all star geometries. We then demonstrate predictive power by designing a ``hybrid star'' with a prescribed amplitude-dependent response and reversal voltage. Our results not only establish how particle geometry and acoustic amplitude combine to govern rotation in acoustically levitated systems, but also reveal unanticipated higher-order couplings with the acoustic field. Beyond explaining spontaneous rotation, they open a route toward programmable rotational dynamics in acoustically levitated matter.

papers.title: On the average of class numbers of indefinite binary quadratic forms
papers.abstract: We prove that the sum of class numbers of primitive indefinite binary quadratic forms with integer coefficients over positive nonsquare discriminants less than $X$ is $O(X^{3/2}\sqrt{\log\log X}/(\log X)^{3/2})$. This improves the longstanding classical upper bound $O(X^{3/2}/\log X)$ and implies the same upper bound for the corresponding sum over real quadratic fields. Our main input is a uniform upper bound for the number of small fundamental solutions to Pell's equation. In particular, we prove that, for almost all nonsquare positive integers $D$, the fundamental solution $\varepsilon_D$ of $t^2-Du^2=1$ is larger than any fixed power of $D$.

papers.title: On the Accuracy of Approximate Leave-One-Out with Blockwise Nonsmooth Regularization in High-dimensions
papers.abstract: Approximate leave-one-out (ALO) refers to methods that provide computationally efficient and statistically accurate approximations to leave-one-out risk estimation. These methods have recently attracted increased attention because of their connections to other important problems, including machine unlearning and data valuation. For empirical risk minimization, ALO methods often rely on a few Newton steps and therefore require smooth loss functions and regularizers. In high-dimensional problems, however, regularizers are frequently non-smooth. This has motivated the development of heuristic ALO methods for non-smooth regularization, whose empirical accuracy is often strong but whose theoretical justification remains limited. In this paper, we study the accuracy of a heuristic ALO method for a broad class of non-differentiable penalties that promote block sparsity in the proportional high-dimensional regime. Assuming uniformly bounded block sizes, we prove that the expected average absolute discrepancy between the exact leave-one-out loss and its ALO approximation is $O(\log^{3/2}(en)/\sqrt{n})$. Our proof technique differs substantially from existing approaches and relies on obtaining sharp bounds on the number of active groups whose status changes between the full-data and leave-one-out estimators. In addition to yielding stronger guarantees under weaker assumptions than prior work, our analysis provides new insight into the stability of sparse estimators under perturbations of the training data.

papers.title: The Effect of Field Line Tracing Height on Wang-Sheeley-Arge Solar Wind Predictions at Earth
papers.abstract: (Abridged abstract): A key component of the widely used Wang-Sheeley-Arge model is the tracing of magnetic field lines in the solar corona, as that largely determines the modeled open/closed field regions and in turn the predicted large-scale solar wind structure. We demonstrate that by slightly raising the height from which magnetic field lines are traced from the photosphere (R$_{su}$), we can improve the prediction of solar wind high-speed enhancements (HSEs). We find a higher R$_{su}$ produces more accurate estimates of the HSE start time, duration, and peak speed, and enables the detection of HSEs that were missed with the standard R$_{su}$. These improvements are primarily associated with changes in the great-circle angular distance, while the flux tube expansion factors remain largely unchanged. A higher R$_{su}$ produces smoother open-field boundaries and reduces small-scale fragmentation within open-field regions. These morphological changes lead to more stable magnetic footpoint mappings and consequently more robust GCD calculations. To assess the statistical relevance of these findings, we extend the analysis to 53 Carrington rotations and perform a multi-metric evaluation of model performance. The results indicate that higher R$_{su}$ improves HSE predictions while reducing false alarms. We thus find that the choice of R$_{su}$ represents an important and previously underexplored parameter that can help enhance our ambient solar wind modeling and forecasting capabilities.

papers.title: Localizing binary neutron stars with the Einstein Telescope: a full Bayesian comparison of the triangular and 2L configurations
papers.abstract: The Einstein Telescope (ET), the European next-generation gravitational-wave observatory, is at a decisive stage: the choice of its detector configuration is still open, with profound implications for its scientific output. We provide a quantitative basis for this choice by comparing two candidate configurations at their proposed sites: the triangular design ($Δ$) at the Euregio Meuse-Rhine site, and the 2L design, with interferometers in Sardinia, Italy, and Lusatia, Germany. We present the first realistic estimates of sky-localization uncertainties for binary neutron star (BNS) mergers, moving beyond Fisher-matrix forecasts to full Bayesian parameter estimation that captures the multimodal structure of the sky posterior. We focus mainly on the high-frequency interferometers alone, providing an expected scenario for the first years of ET operations, as the more challenging low-frequency instruments will come online later. BNS injections span different sky positions and luminosity distances between 40 and 2000 Mpc, corresponding to signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) from 12 to 720. Our analysis relaxes the long-wavelength approximation and includes Earth's rotation and higher-order modes, all of which improve sky localization. We find that the $Δ$ configuration localizes low- and moderate-SNR sources in eight degenerate sky modes spread across both hemispheres and over the day and night sides of the Earth, with 90% credible areas reaching $\sim 2 \times 10^4 \, \mathrm{deg}^2$. In contrast, the 2L configuration recovers a single dominant mode that contains at least 50% of the posterior probability and is one to two orders of magnitude smaller in area. This represents a substantial advantage for multimessenger follow-up campaigns.

papers.title: Unified Sharp Bounds on Probabilities of Causation
papers.abstract: Probabilities of causation (PoCs) have developed steadily, from the binary measures first introduced by Pearl to the non-binary setting recently studied by Shu et al. As the theory has matured, PoCs have found applications in a growing range of areas, including personalized medicine, marketing and legal attribution. Shu et al. proposed closed-form bounds for multi-valued treatments and outcomes and proved them valid, but left their sharpness in high dimensions open. We close this gap with a mathematical proof. We further show that $\PNS$, $\PSub$, $\PRep$ and $\PN$ are all special cases of a single, more general formula. Combined with their equivalence classes, this settles the question of sharp bounds for discrete PoCs from experimental and observational data: in every dimension, they are given in closed form by a single theorem.

papers.title: AC/DC on a Budget - Alternating Sparse Phases
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art neural network sparsification relies on alternating dense and sparse training phases. While computationally expensive, dense phases are critical for performance. Our empirical analysis reveals the mechanics behind this gain: upon reintroduction, previously masked parameters receive disproportionately large gradients that drive essential mask rewiring and parameter sign-flipping. Building on these insights, we optimize the performance-to-FLOPs Pareto frontier through three innovations: (1) zero-initializing masked parameters during dense phases to promote relevant sign flips, (2) shortening dense phases, and (3) replacing the dense phase entirely with a sparse rewiring phase that updates only the active mask and a small, high-gradient fraction of out-of-mask weights. Evaluated on CIFAR100 and ImageNet, our variant ARC (Alternating Rewiring Compression) matches baseline AC/DC performance at a fraction of the computational cost, establishing a superior performance-to-FLOPs frontier also compared to standard sparse-to-sparse algorithms. Experiments with GPT-2 on OpenWebText further show improvements in validation perplexity and average zero-shot performance

papers.title: Media Intelligence Platform: Multimodal Detection of Synthetic and Manipulated Content
papers.abstract: The rapid progress of generative artificial intelligence has led to a significant increase in manipulated multimedia content, including synthetic faces, forged videos, AI-generated images, fake audio, and locally edited images. Existing detection approaches are typically designed for a single manipulation type, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios involving heterogeneous media sources. In this work, we present the Media Intelligence Platform (MIP), a unified web-based framework for multimodal media forensics integrating specialized modules for fake video detection, face morphing detection, AI-generated image detection, audio deepfake detection, localized image manipulation detection, and text analysis. Its modular architecture enables flexible integration of heterogeneous models and supports future extensions for emerging manipulation techniques. Experimental results on representative benchmark datasets demonstrate reliable detection performance across multiple media modalities while providing a practical and user-friendly interface for forensic investigations. The platform highlights the potential of unified multimodal systems for comprehensive deepfake detection in real-world environments, and is accompanied by a public demonstrator released with this workshop submission to support reproducibility and community evaluation.

papers.title: Attosecond Quantum Optical Spectroscopy of Topological Materials
papers.abstract: High-harmonic generation (HHG) provides an ultrafast probe of quantum materials, yet conventional spectral observables do not generally furnish a common signature of band topology. Here we show that quantum-light-driven HHG opens an additional information channel through the photon statistics of the emitted harmonics. Using the Haldane Chern insulator and the time-reversal-invariant Kane-Mele topological insulator, we calculate helicity-resolved equal-time intensity correlations and identify a common enhancement of high-order harmonic correlations in the topological phases. For the Haldane model, a dichroic correlation constructed from opposite helicity channels reverses sign with the Chern number. These signatures originate from the distinct nonlinear response sampled by quantum fluctuations of the driving field and are absent from the corresponding mean harmonic spectra as a common classifier. Our results establish photon-correlation spectroscopy as a route to interrogate topological matter with quantum light and provide a bridge between strong-field solid-state physics and quantum optics.

papers.title: On the superbursts as photodisintegrators of ashes from the rp-process -- Numerical simulations of superbursts with MESA II
papers.abstract: Context: Superbursts are energetic explosions in the crusts of neutron stars in Low-Mass X-ray Binaries (LMXBs). At temperatures above 4 GK, photodisintegration of heavy rp-process ashes may play a major role alongside $^{12}$C fusion. Aims: We investigate how photodisintegration of rp-process ashes affects superburst properties and the initial $^{12}$C abundance required for ignition. Methods: We simulate superbursts with MESA v.24.08.1. Besides the canonical fuel of $20\%$ $^{12}$C and $80\%$ $^{56}$Fe, we test different $^{12}$C abundances mixed with scaled rp-process ashes. Results: Superbursts can ignite with only $10\%$ $^{12}$C when the remaining $90\%$ consists of rp-process ashes. Their luminosity is comparable to that of the canonical fuel, whereas $10\%$ $^{12}$C mixed with $90\%$ $^{56}$Fe yields lower luminosity. $^{56}$Fe remains the most abundant ash nuclide. Although photodisintegration drives nucleosynthesis, neutron, proton and alpha captures release energy at late times. We also find that $A=64$ nuclides or $^{20}$Ne help reduce the $^{12}$C abundance needed for ignition. Conclusions: The composition of accreted material - not just its $^{12}$C content - substantially affects superburst ignition, luminosity and nucleosynthesis.

papers.title: Subjective Valuations Make It Hard to be Fair: The Complexity of Resource Allocation to Groups of Agents
papers.abstract: We study the parameterized complexity of finding an EF1 allocation of indivisible items in the group-sharing setting, which has received increasing attention in recent years. There, items are not allocated to individual agents but rather to one of two (or possibly more) groups, and agents within that group all share the assigned items. We consider both the "fixed" (EF1-Fix) and "variable" (EF1-Var) group cases, where in the former the assignments of agents to groups are prescribed. While both are NP-hard in the classical sense, we show that their algorithmic behavior differs significantly from the parameterized perspective. As our main results, we: (1) prove that both cases are NP-hard even when the number of agents is a small constant; (2) circumvent this hardness by establishing fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Var w.r.t. the number of "subjective" items, that is, items which are viewed as chores or goods by different agents---but rule out an analogous result for EF1-Fix; and (3) establish fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Fix w.r.t. the number of item types, but link the existence of an analogous fixed-parameter algorithm for EF1-Var to a fundamental open question in the setting of Integer Linear Programming.

papers.title: Budgeted Admission from Timestamped Capacity Records in Shared Clusters
papers.abstract: A cluster admission gate can receive a capacity record that no longer matches current schedulability. We study one exogenous binary schedulability unit under a bound on the joint probability of admission and unavailability. For a symmetric Markov state, we derive the stationary admission frontier for a fixed observation delay and apply finite likelihood allocation to a delay-tagged delivered record. A one-sided exact binomial endpoint calibrates each fitted policy, and exact enumeration confirms the per-policy confidence target in every tested parameter cell. A separate deterministic guard charges every unresolved admission against the realized allowance and bounds unavailable-state admissions at every prefix under truthful outcome feedback. An executable admission procedure composes the allocation and guard. The controlled system binds source sampling, NATS delivery, randomized admission, Kubernetes objects, and API-derived outcomes in one append-only record. Independent audit finds no missing event, identity mismatch, or state mismatch in the completed functional block. A separate CPU request-accounting check preserves Job and Pod identity across an unschedulable-to-complete transition.

papers.title: Evolving Agent Interfaces
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents' trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s.

papers.title: Interaction-Gated Time-Frequency Learning for Parameter-Efficient PPG-Based Heart Rate Estimation
papers.abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) enables low-cost and non-invasive heart rate (HR) monitoring but remains sensitive to waveform distortion, physiological variability, and measurement interference. Temporal waveform characteristics and frequency-domain periodicity provide complementary information for HR estimation; however, effectively exploring and integrating these representations within a compact model remains challenging. This paper proposes TF-IG, a parameter-efficient interaction-gated time-frequency learning framework for PPG-based HR estimation. TF-IG employs a dual-branch architecture in which a temporal branch captures pulse morphology via dilated depthwise-separable convolutions, while a frequency branch extracts cardiac periodicity information from bounded log-spectrogram representations. To combine the two domains, we introduce an interaction-gated fusion module that explicitly models feature agreement and discrepancy, while also learning feature-wise weights to balance temporal and spectral information. A parameter-shared regression head further maps the temporal, spectral, and fused representations into the final HR prediction space. Experiments on the benchmark BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset using a subject-exclusive training, validation, and test protocol show that TF-IG achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.227 BPM, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.060 BPM, a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9934, and 92.28 percent of estimates within 3 BPM, while remaining parameter-efficient with only 84.6K parameters. Ablation results further demonstrate the complementary contributions of the temporal and frequency branches, interaction-gated fusion, and shared regression head. These results indicate that explicitly modeling cross-domain interactions provides an effective accuracy-complexity trade-off for lightweight PPG-based HR estimation.

papers.title: LoWAgent: A Low-Resource Multilingual Benchmark for Web Agents
papers.abstract: Web agents are typically evaluated on English-language interfaces, leaving their ability to operate across the world's multilingual websites largely unexplored. This gap is especially significant for low-resource languages, where standardized resources for evaluating web agents remain limited. To address this gap, we introduce Low-Resource Web Agent Benchmark (LoWAgent), a benchmark for evaluating web agents across different low-resource languages (LRLs) in comparison to the default, English. LoWAgent evaluates web agents across English and four LRLs: Hindi, Bengali, Urdu, and Amharic. The benchmark comprises of six fully localized websites, instantiated across five languages to yield 3,000 task instances. We evaluate three closed-source and five open-source models across all five languages on all six websites. Our findings show that both closed-source and open-source models experience performance degradation for LRLs compared to English, with substantially greater performance drops observed among the open-source model agents. We further evaluate the robustness of the models on realistic interface disruptions, such as cookie notices and advertisement pop-ups, and find that these further degrade agentic performance. Finally, we show that post-training on a small subset of LoWAgent traces can significantly improve low-resource language agentic task performance, demonstrating the usefulness of our benchmark.

papers.title: African Languages AI Safety Readiness Report
papers.abstract: With the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) across languages and domains, AI safety has emerged as a critical global concern. However, due to resource constraints, research and development efforts tend to prioritize a limited number of high-resource languages, leaving many others, especially those spoken in Africa, underrepresented. While existing research on language "resource-ness" has largely examined whether sufficient resources are available to develop language technologies, the question of whether languages are adequately represented in AI safety research has received attention only more recently. This report examines the readiness of African languages for inclusion in AI safety discussions, drawing on existing literature and data. It considers four factors: the availability of AI-relevant resources, including text data; national AI policy support; performance on established text benchmarks; and speaker population. Based on these factors, languages are grouped into four readiness categories: fully ready, mostly ready, emerging, and foundational support needed. This classification is intended to inform the inclusion of African languages in AI safety benchmarks, highlight varying levels of preparedness, and guide strategic investment in data development, policy, and community engagement for underrepresented languages.

papers.title: Adversarial Benchmarks and BenchDoor Attacks: Exploiting Benchmark Incentives for Backdoor Attacks
papers.abstract: Machine learning benchmarks act as guideposts for model development and spur the creation of training datasets intended to improve benchmark scores. We introduce BenchDoor, a family of data poisoning attacks that exploits this incentive. Beyond preserving benign performance, BenchDoor requires benchmark gains that encourage adoption of data that also implants a backdoor. The adversary either manipulates a benchmark's training or test data, creating an adversarial benchmark, or supplies an independent training dataset while leaving the benchmark unchanged. We formalize five attack scenarios, including training on rewritten test examples and applying similarity-based decontamination. Across multiple-choice Q&A, text classification, and open-ended Q&A with Qwen and Gemma models, BenchDoor achieves positive benchmark gains for all 30 evaluated configurations, with held-out attack success rates of 82.33% to 100.00% at poisoning rates of 2% to 10%. Both objectives remain achievable after synthetic data generation and similarity-based decontamination, with attack success rates of at least 90.33%. These findings show how benchmarks can serve as attack vectors both through their own data and through training resources that deliver improvements on them.

papers.title: Contextual Candour: Role-Aware Graduated Disclosure for LLMs over Mixed-Sensitivity Contexts
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly operate over mixed-sensitivity contexts, where they must reason over information ranging from public to confidential while disclosing only what the user is authorised to receive. Existing approaches enforce access control as a binary decision: either fully answering or refusing, without regulating how much or what kind of information is revealed if access is granted, leading to over-refusal or unintended leakage. We introduce graduated disclosure, an access-control formulation in which the level of detail and sensitivity in a model's response is calibrated to the user's authorisation rather than treated as a grant-or-deny decision. We model graduated disclosure as a disclosure-aware generation problem and propose a reward-based optimisation framework that shapes responses toward level-appropriate abstractions while penalising unauthorised factual leakage, including paraphrases and approximations. We evaluate our approach on enterprise and clinical benchmarks and compare it with prompt-based, gating, and supervised baselines. Experiments show that our method substantially reduces information leakage while preserving correctness and utility. These results suggest that disclosure control must be integrated into the generation process itself to enable secure yet useful LLM deployments.

authors.name: David Pape
authors.institution: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

papers.title: ClawMMU: Protection-Coherent Virtual Memory for Stateful LLM Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents keep long-term memory, much of which comes from web pages and tool results. Agent harnesses, the software that runs the model, do not record who may act on this memory, so an instruction hidden in a fetched page can be treated as the user's own instruction. We propose ClawMMU, a protection layer that labels every piece of memory with its owner, scope, origins, and authority. ClawMMU checks these labels whenever content enters the model's context, is written to storage, returns from storage, or drives a tool call. Its central rule is that information may rise in authority, but authority never lifts itself. Because the checks depend on where content came from, not on what it says, memory attacks become classical protection faults that the harness stops even when the model is fooled.

papers.title: Causal Discovery for Linear Models with Latent Confounding via Multi-domain Identifiable Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Causal discovery with latent confounding is particularly challenging, but a common setting in real-world data. In this work, we focus on linear causal models with latent confounding, represented by acyclic directed mixed graphs (ADMGs). Existing methods that fully identify ADMGs typically assume non-Gaussianity or graphical constraints, such as bow-freeness. In contrast, we propose Linear ADMG Learning (LinADMG), a framework for learning ADMGs for linear causal models through identifiable representation learning. Rather than relying on non-Gaussianity or bow-freeness, LinADMG leverages multi-domain settings to identify the noise variables. We show that the identifiability of the noise variables is sufficient for recovering all direct causal relations, and that, under an additional latent-confounding no-cancellation condition, LinADMG can identify the whole ADMG. We implement LinADMG with four identifiable representation learning approaches from the literature and validate the methods on simulated and semisynthetic datasets.

papers.title: Identifying Dependent Components from Multi-domain Linear Mixtures
papers.abstract: We study a linear mixing model with dependent latent components, assuming multiple data domains. Most existing models assume that the components are independent or at least uncorrelated, in line with independent component analysis (ICA). Some recent work allows for dependent components, but then makes specific assumptions such as parametric forms of dependencies, multi-view settings, or interventions, or does not recover the individual components. In contrast, we consider a multi-domain setting in which domains differ through domain-specific scalings of the components, while the distribution of the underlying latent components is the same across domains. This approach can model data collected, for example, from different sensors measuring the same process, different laboratories conducting the same experiment, different experimental conditions, or different subjects that might differ in biological or physiological factors. We show that, under sufficient domain variability, latent variables and mixing functions can be identified from second-order statistics alone. We propose the Multi-Domain Covariance Matching (MuDo-CoM) algorithm that generalizes previous methods of joint diagonalization. MuDo-CoM is validated on simulated data and a real-world fMRI dataset.

papers.title: Good-$Γ$ Numbers: A Shell-Optimized Route to the Thermodynamic Limit in Quantum Monte Carlo Calculations of the High-Density Two-Dimensional Electron Gas
papers.abstract: Single-particle finite-size errors remain a central obstacle in quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations of periodic systems, conventionally reduced via twist averaging (TA). Here we introduce Good-$Γ$ (GG) particle numbers as system sizes $N$ at which the $Γ$-point Hartree--Fock (HF) energy of the high-density two-dimensional uniform electron gas (2D UEG) lies anomalously close to its thermodynamic-limit (TL) value. All results in this work concern the 2D UEG in its high-density Fermi-liquid regime, $r_s=1$--$4$. We systematically investigate the kinetic- and exchange-energy errors, $ΔKE(N)$ and $ΔEX(N)$, that underlie this one-body finite-size-error cancellation across four densities and both spin polarizations. We then compare diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) energies extrapolated to the TL from GG-$N$ sequences against twist-averaged extrapolations at the same densities and polarizations, finding agreement to within a fraction of a millihartree in every case, independent of whether a $1/N$ or an $N^{-5/4}$ extrapolation form is used.

papers.title: The $m=2$ amplituhedron is a positive geometry
papers.abstract: Amplituhedra are semi-algebraic sets of fundamental importance in particle physics. Their discovery initiated the field of Positive Geometry. We settle a central conjecture in this field: we show that the $m=2$ amplituhedron is a positive geometry. Our main new tool is a Hodge-theoretic criterion for being a positive geometry, connecting the work of Brown--Dupont with the original setup of Arkani-Hamed--Bai--Lam.

authors.name: Rainer Sinn

papers.title: Local Inference of LLMs on Long Contexts: A Data Systems Perspective
papers.abstract: Large language models can solve complex problems across a variety of subjects, such as mathematics and coding. For such complex analytical tasks, models with a long context perform better. Serving models with long context is currently mostly done on powerful systems with multiple GPUs, which are too expensive for most users. An alternative is local inference, or serving a model on a user's own machine, which removes per-token costs and rate limits, besides keeping sensitive data private and giving users full control over the models they run. The common understanding, however, is that local LLMs need compression (e.g., quantization) to run on a single GPU. In this paper, we set out to study the limitations that prevent serving long-context models for single users, besides the capacity issue. Rather than characterizing a single model on one GPU, we analyze how different models behave across several GPU generations. This lets us uncover not just individual bottlenecks but broader trends in where inefficiencies arise. Our analysis confirms that, as expected, self-attention dominates the runtime for long-context inference. More unexpectedly, our evaluation reveals that the current structure of self-attention leaves key GPU resources significantly underutilized, and the newest GPU is often the least well served. Many of these findings are fundamentally data management problems, from paging the KV cache to improving cache utilization and synchronization in the GPU, which is why we bring this study to the Data Systems community. To engage this community, we present our findings as a series of experimental observations and formulate recommendations for future work.

papers.title: Interruption-Aware Recurrent Reinforcement Learning for UAS Navigation Under Temporary Overrides
papers.abstract: Safe autonomous navigation of UASs requires tactical deconfliction to address conflicts that strategic coordination cannot prevent. This task is challenging under partial observability, when sensor or traffic data are missing, delayed, or degraded. Geometry-based methods can offer separation assurances but face limitations in dense encounters. Recurrent reinforcement learning has therefore been proposed to learn navigation policies that integrate observation-action histories to optimise long-term safety-efficiency trade-offs. However, operational safeguards may require a remote pilot, onboard detect-and-avoid system, or runtime assurance mechanism to temporarily override the learned policy. A research gap remains in understanding how these interruptions affect recurrent policies when the agent regains authority. Benchmark evidence shows that interruptions make task variables less decodable from the recurrent hidden state and increase post-interruption collision risk. The findings suggest that altered recurrent context prolongs post-handback degradation through an action-observation feedback loop, in which changed actions alter the flight path and subsequent recurrent updates. To address this vulnerability, we propose three interruption-aware architectures that condition recurrent processing on interruption context through separate feature streams, dedicated interruption memory, or gated environmental features. Across simulations, all three architectures preserve more decodable task information than a standard recurrent policy. Moreover, the strongest architecture reduces post-interruption collisions by 74% and interruption-induced mission failures by 69% relative to the recurrent baseline, without degrading interruption-free performance. These results show that safe interruption does not guarantee safe handback, and support interruption-aware recurrent design for resilient UAS autonomy.

papers.title: Soft elasticity of soft shells
papers.abstract: Soft modes of a shell are one-parameter families of non-trivial deformations that preserve the elastic energy. We identify all soft modes of the soft shells described by the variational theory of put forward by Sonnet and Virga (2025). They are seen to be strictly connected with the Bonnet families, a special class of solutions to the problem posited by Bonnet, who asked whether there exist non-trivial isometries that preserve the mean curvature. Differential geometry deems as equivalent all surfaces in one and the same Bonnet family, but continuum mechanics is interested more specifically in soft deformation modes and the shapes they traverse, as they may describe ways to ignite fluctuations of soft shells that ideally require no energy to be activated. We give a general criterion for the existence of soft modes and a method to construct them based on a cascade of path integrations. We apply both criterion and method to some exemplary cases.

papers.title: Classification of SNC $(p,k)$-planes with Hodge structures of K3 type
papers.abstract: A SNC $(p,k)$-plane is a $(\mathbb Z/p)^k$-Galois cover $π\colon X \to \mathbb P^2$ with a simple normal crossing branch locus. In this setting, there exist several intermediate quotients $Y_1, Y_2,\dots, Y_{φ_{p,k}}$ corresponding to subgroups of $(\mathbb Z/p)^k$ of index $p$. We focus on the case where each $Y_i$ is either a surface with geometric genus $0$ or $1$, with at least one with geometric genus $1$. We classify all SNC $(p,k)$-planes satisfying these conditions obtaining that an extensive list of cases are minimal regular surfaces of general type with positive geometric genus. Moreover, these assumptions allow us to have strong control over the weight-$2$ Hodge structure of the minimal model of the covering surface $X$. Therefore, we also prove that Tate and Mumford-Tate conjectures hold for such surfaces. As an independent result of our methods, we obtain a classification of SNC $(p,1)$-planes with geometric genus $1$, which turn out to be precisely all K3 surfaces, and a classification of SNC $(p,1)$-planes with geometric genus $0$, which turn out to be instead rational surfaces.

papers.title: Schauder estimates for ratios of elliptic solutions under zero set inclusion
papers.abstract: Let $u,v$ be two nontrivial functions that solve $$ \mathrm{div}(A\nabla u)=\mathrm{div}(A\nabla v)=0\qquad\mathrm{in \ }B_r\subset\mathbb R^n,\quad n\geq2,\quad r>0, $$ with $A$ symmetric, uniformly elliptic and Lipschitz continuous, and assume the zero set inclusion $Z(u)\subseteq Z(v)$. We prove that the ratio $w=v/u$ continuously extends, together with its gradient, across $Z(u)=\{u=0\}$. In particular, $w\in C^{1,α}_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_{r})$ for any $α\in(0,1)$. Furthermore, given any integer $k\geq2$ and $α\in(0,1)$, if $A\in C^{k-1,α}(B_r)$, then $w\in C^{k,α}_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_{r})$. The estimates are uniform in classes of coefficients $A$ with prescribed ellipticity and regularity bounds, and in normalized classes of denominators $u$ with uniformly bounded doubling constant.

papers.title: Make the Adversary Spend More Energy: Generative Deception against Language-Model Attackers in Critical Infrastructure
papers.abstract: Language-model attackers consume computational resources as they explore and interact with a target, creating an opportunity for cyber deception to impose costs. Whether such engagements favor the defender requires measuring both sides. We evaluate an autonomous language-model attacker against a decoy that uses a defending language model to analyze attacker commands and select defensive responses. Across 330 sessions, eight model pairs, two attacker profiles and three counter-injection levels, both sides run on identical GPUs and their energy is measured above idle. With runtime thinking disabled, the attacker-to-defender energy ratio has a 95% interval above one in 41 of 48 configurations under an allocation excluding attacker diagnostic calls, and in all 48 when those calls are included. Token ratios remain within approximately a factor of two in configurations without generation-cap truncation, showing that token counts can obscure substantial energy asymmetry. Counter-injection increases attacker tokens by approximately 9% per level without a detectable pooled change in energy consumption. Enabling thinking on both sides increases defender energy by 8--17 times and reverses the exchange for one model pair in the original campaign. We use these findings to motivate a proposed SCADA deception architecture with private physical state per identified adversary and deterministic protocol and process emulation.

authors.name: Alessandro Cantelli-Forti
authors.institution: Consorzio Nazionale Interuniversitario per le Telecomunicazioni

papers.title: A counterexample to the fractional Michael-Simon inequality
papers.abstract: We show that the fractional Michael-Simon inequality does not hold for general smooth hypersurfaces and for the range of 0 < s < (n-1)/n in the case p=1. We construct a family of smooth hypersurfaces, whose fractional mean curvature is nonnegative everywhere, which violates the inequality in the limit. The same construction yields a counterexample for every 1 \leq p < \infty for the range s < (n-1)/(np).

papers.title: Improved automatic speech-based cognitive assessment using neuropsychologically calibrated diagnostic labels
papers.abstract: Although automatic detection of cognitive impairment from conversational speech is a promising way, it becomes less accurate, as large real-world datasets often contain unreliable diagnostic labels due to self-referral and limited clinical verification, and here we investigated whether neuropsychologically calibrated diagnostic relabeling improves it. We analysed 138 hours of conversational speech from 720 participants, recalibrating unreliable diagnostic labels using attention, executive function, and memory performance via external clinical thresholds, Gaussian, and normative z-score calibration. Transformer-based classifiers were trained using both original and recalibrated labels and evaluated internally on 150 clinically verified participants and externally on Pitt, ADReSS and PROCESS-2 datasets. Memory- and MoCA-based z-score calibration produced the greatest improvements. Using our internal dataset, $F_1$ increased from $0.70$ to $0.83$ ($+13\%$) and from $0.54$ to $0.66$ ($+12\%$) for binary and multiclass classification, respectively. For external validation, the increases are $+4\%$, $+5\%$ and $+9\%$ on Pitt, ADReSS and PROCESS-2 corpus. Neuropsychologically calibrated relabeling substantially improves speech-based cognitive assessment, highlighting label quality, rather than model architecture, as a critical bottleneck in clinical AI for dementia screening.

authors.name: Daniel Blackburn
authors.institution: Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

papers.title: A MUSE Study of Stellar and Ionized-Gas Kinematics in Central Group Galaxies
papers.abstract: Understanding gas accretion and feedback in low-mass galaxy groups bridges the gap between isolated ellipticals and cluster-dominant galaxies. We present new Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE) observations of 17 nearby brightest group galaxies (BGGs), revealing diverse origins for their gas reservoirs. Warm ionized gas, traced by Halpha and [N II], is detected in 77% (13/17) of the sample, with morphologies including rotating disks with or without tails and diffuse emission, rings, and filaments. Unlike brightest cluster galaxies, most BGGs host regularly rotating stars, whereas their gas displays diverse kinematics. Nearly half of the rotating gas disks are aligned with the stars, consistent with internal recycling. However, tails, diffuse emission, or rings in three aligned systems may retain signatures of past accretion or interactions. The remaining disks, ring-like structures, and most filamentary systems are misaligned, supporting gas acquisition through mergers, interactions, or halo cooling. Compact disks are consistent with centrally concentrated, low-angular-momentum gas, possibly linked to residual cooling. Most filamentary systems lie near the precipitation threshold (tcool/teddy ~ 1-2) and preferentially occupy the turbulence-dominated region of the k-plot, supporting condensation consistent with chaotic cold accretion. All galaxies with detected X-ray halos, including those without warm gas, exhibit low central entropies (<30 keV cm^2) and short central cooling times (<3 Gyr). These conditions alone cannot predict multiphase gas, suggesting that AGN- or interaction-driven perturbations and turbulence-induced thermal instabilities help regulate condensation. No single mechanism dominates: BGGs are transitional systems in which internal recycling, environmental accretion, and cooling-driven condensation coexist, linking isolated ellipticals to cluster-dominant galaxies.

papers.title: A Brezis--Merle inequality for the biharmonic operator with Dirichlet boundary conditions in four-dimensional balls
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish a Brezis-Merle type inequality for very weak solutions of the biharmonic Dirichlet problem in the four-dimensional unit ball. By combining this inequality with moving-plane arguments, we obtain uniform a priori estimates for positive solutions of semilinear biharmonic equations with exponential nonlinearities in both the subcritical and critical regimes. As an application of these estimates, we prove the existence of a positive solution by means of topological methods. We also extend the analysis to a class of non-variational cooperative systems.

authors.name: Federica Sani
authors.institution: University of Modena and Reggio Emilia

papers.title: Beyond the Mean: A Two-Stage GAMLSS Framework for Physical Activity Bout Patterns and Survival in COPD
papers.abstract: Physical activity patterns in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) are typically summarised using simple metrics such as total daily activity or mean time spent in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity. In many studies, this activity is further characterized through physical activity bouts, defined as periods of at least 10 consecutive minutes above 3 metabolic equivalent tasks (METs). However, such summaries overlook the highly skewed, heterogeneous and patient-specific nature of bout-related variables, which may contain clinically relevant information. We propose a distributional modelling approach for accelerometer-derived bout-related physical activity outcomes based on Generalised Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape (GAMLSS). The framework models multiple parameters of the outcome distributions, including location, scale, and the probability of observing no bouts, allowing the analysis to extend beyond average levels of activity. In a second stage, the estimated distributional parameters are incorporated into a survival analysis to investigate whether information beyond the mean is associated with patient prognosis. The proposed framework is illustrated using accelerometer data from a cohort of 512 COPD patients and considering bout-related outcomes such as minutes accumulated in bouts per day, total number of bouts, and area under MET in bouts per day. The resulting distributional parameters were significantly associated with mortality and provided information beyond average activity levels, particularly through differences in variability across patients. These findings suggest that information contained in distributional parameters beyond the mean may be relevant for understanding the relationship between physical activity patterns and survival.

papers.title: On the spectrum of the biharmonic Steklov operator with Neumann boundary conditions acting on forms of the unit Euclidean ball
papers.abstract: We compute the spectrum of the biharmonic Steklov operator with Neumann boundary conditions acting on differential $p$-forms over the unit Euclidean ball. We apply it to test how far one of Kuttler-Sigillito inequalities is from being optimal.

papers.title: An Open Reliability Atlas of Sensitivity and Failure Modes in the Pulse Physiology Engine
papers.abstract: Pulse is an actively maintained open-source adult-physiology simulator, yet its maintainers report no formal sensitivity analysis of its operational inputs. We present the first open reliability atlas across its critical-care envelope: Morris elementary-effects sampling of seven inputs, four severity scenarios, male and female bodies (1,280 simulations). Sensitivity is skewed: three inputs carry a median 93% of each output's total. A four-flag classifier reveals failure modes: two operator-actionable, one sex-stratified. Tidal-volume oscillation (20.6% of runs) is consistent with patient-ventilator dyssynchrony; locking the VC-AC trigger to -2 cmH2O collapses that variability. At FiO2 = 1.0, transient hyperoxia makes 120-second runs underestimate plateau PaO2; 300-second healthy-lung reruns give a median 643 mmHg. Solver divergence was all-male in an input-extreme regime (20/1,280); reducing the male blood-volume baseline to the 4,082 mL floor eliminated it. Runs and flags are released openly, showing users which regions need checking before training on Pulse output.

authors.name: Arnaud Wiedemann
authors.institution: Centre Hospitalier Régional et Universitaire de Nancy

authors.name: Cyril Schweitzer
authors.institution: Centre Hospitalier Régional et Universitaire de Nancy

papers.title: Agentic Communication Networks: When Agents Become Network Entities
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents are moving from application-layer components to active participants in networked systems. They not only generate traffic but also perceive context, express intent, invoke services, coordinate with other agents, and act under task, policy, and resource constraints. This evolution exposes a mismatch between emerging agentic interactions and conventional endpoint- and traffic-centric network abstractions. This white paper introduces Agentic Communication Networks (ACN) as a network-centric paradigm for the time when agents become first-order network entities. At its core, ACN reshapes networking around three fundamental aspects. First, agents are represented as identifiable and governable network entities with explicit identity, authority, and lifecycle. Second, agentic services are expressed through intent, capability, context, policy, and task state, allowing the network to capture what an agent seeks to accomplish and under what conditions. Third, agentic execution becomes an explicit network concern as tasks involve multiple agents, services, tools, and distributed capabilities across heterogeneous infrastructures. Based on these shifts, the paper defines the scope, principles, architecture, and research directions of ACN, positioning it as a networking foundation for autonomous agent ecosystems.

papers.title: A Catalog of Dispersive Ionospheric and Plasmaspheric Arcs from Cislunar and Lunar-surface GNSS Radio Occultations
papers.abstract: This dataset is a catalog of 263 dispersive arcs induced by ionospheric and plasmaspheric occultation observed in GNSS signals recorded by the Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment (LuGRE) payload during Blue Ghost Mission 1 (BGM1), in cislunar space and on the lunar surface. Occultation arcs are identified and classified as ingress, egress or tangent by combining independently GPS and Galileo dual-frequency observables and computing the rate of the total electron content (ROT) and ROT index (ROTI), and are validated through a geometric criterion based on the grazing altitude of the tangent point. No distinction is made between the ionospheric and plasmaspheric contributions to each arc, which is treated as a single dispersive signature. For each arc, the catalog provides timing, grazing altitude, summary ROT/ROTI/$Δ$STEC attributes, the geomagnetic activity level, and time series of leveled slant total electron content (STEC), not corrected for instrumental biases, ROT, ROTI, tangent-point position and local time. The HDF5 (Hierarchical Data Format version 5) file contains a header with dataset-wide metadata and per-class statistics, and one entry per arc. It enables rapid selection of occultation arcs for statistical studies and targeted analyses, and complements ground-based and low Earth orbit radio-occultation data during the declining phase of solar cycle 25.

papers.title: Hidden engines in tidal disruption events: multimessenger signatures in a lepto-hadronic framework
papers.abstract: Tidal disruption events (TDEs) provide a unique laboratory for studying transient accretion, outflows, particle acceleration, and the possible connection between stellar disruptions and high-energy neutrinos. Motivated by recent candidate TDE-neutrino associations and by the forthcoming sensitivity of multimessenger facilities, we investigate under which physical conditions TDEs can be detected in MeV, GeV, and TeV gamma rays, and in high-energy neutrinos. We develop a lepto-hadronic emission framework and apply it to three representative sources: AT2019dsg, AT2019ehz, and ASASSN-14li. For each source we explore a set of physically motivated models that vary the proton and electron spectral indices, the minimum Lorentz factor of non-thermal protons, the particle energy partition, the acceleration efficiency, the magnetic compactness, and the presence of a compact corona. We compute the broadband spectral energy distributions, the associated muon-neutrino spectra, and compare them with reference sensitivities for COSI, Fermi/LAT, CTAO, and KM3NeT/ARCA. We find that hard proton spectra and/or large minimum proton Lorentz factors are the most favourable conditions for TeV gamma-ray and neutrino detectability, while GeV-bright models can be predominantly leptonic and neutrino quiet. AT2019dsg and AT2019ehz can reach the CTAO and KM3NeT benchmarks in hadronically favourable configurations, whereas ASASSN-14li is more naturally bright in the MeV-GeV band and constrained by its radio synchrotron emission. Our results highlight the importance of combining MeV, GeV, TeV, radio, and neutrino observations to distinguish between transparent, hidden, and lepton-dominated TDE emission regimes.

papers.title: Inverse domain uncertainty quantification in hemodynamics: sampling virtual patient cohorts under constraints
papers.abstract: We consider the following inverse domain uncertainty quantification problem: given a prescribed value or measurement of a hemodynamic biomarker, characterize the distribution of vascular geometries compatible with it. The problem is formulated as a Bayesian inverse problem in which a high-dimensional latent parameter encodes the cardiovascular shape and accounts for inter-patient variability. The parameter-to-observable map composes a conditional LDDMM stochastic interpolant generating the aortic surface with a high-performance numerical finite element solver for the unsteady incompressible Navier--Stokes equations, from which biomarkers of interest are evaluated. The map is nonlinear, high-dimensional and computationally expensive. To address the problem, we compare three ensemble strategies: ensemble adjusted Kalman inversion (EAKI), adaptive Bayesian updating with structural reliability (aBUS), and a Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao (WFR) sequential Monte Carlo scheme. The first two approaches are derivative-free. For the third method, we introduce a novel differentiable flow-matching surrogate that reduces the cost of a single forward map evaluation at the price of a distribution shift depending on the training distribution used for the surrogate. We apply the framework to the generation of virtual patient cohorts matching prescribed pressure drops along aortic geometries affected by coarctation, and we validate and compare the three methods on synthetic data.

papers.title: Proliferation Transitions for Quantum Doubles of Groups
papers.abstract: Proliferation transitions are phase transitions between a 2+1d topological order $\mathcal{T}$ and another $\mathcal{T}/\mathcal{A}$, obtained by condensing anyons in an algebra $\mathcal{A}\subset \mathcal{T}$. We consider such transitions in quantum doubles of groups, $\mathcal{T}=D(G, ω)$, for finite groups $G$ possibly with three-cocycle $ω$, for which condensable algebras are fully classified. Given a condensable algebra $\mathcal{A}$, we represent $\mathcal{T}$ in terms of a Symmetry Topological Field Theory (SymTFT), that is tailored to the $\mathcal{A}$ proliferation transition. The SymTFT bulk is constructed from the Müger center of the subcategory generated by the algebra, i.e. the category of transparent lines, which can be bosons or fermions. Properties of the transition can then be inferred directly from the algebra classification data. For gauged Landau-Ginzburg (LG*) type transitions, we show that they do not only depend on the anyons in $\mathcal{A}$ through their field content, but the cubic interactions are fixed in terms of the multiplication structure of $\mathcal{A}$. Applied to twin algebras, which have the same anyon content but different multiplication structures, we show that twins result in distinct proliferation transitions.

authors.name: Sakura Schafer-Nameki
authors.institution: Mathematical Institute of the Slovak Academy of Sciences

papers.title: The ALMA REBELS Survey: The [C II] Luminosity Function of UV-Selected Galaxies at $z\sim7$
papers.abstract: Luminosity functions (LF) are some of the most basic quantities providing insights into galaxy evolution across cosmic time and enabling a direct comparison between observations and simulations. Here, we present the first [CII]158$μ$m LF at $z\sim7$ from a sizeable UV-selected ALMA sample. Our analysis makes use of 27 galaxies with significant [CII] emission line detections in the epoch of reionization from the REBELS (Reionization Era Bright Emission Line Survey) ALMA Large Program and its pilot programs. We used these line detections and similar from ALPINE to calibrate UV luminosity-$L_{\mathrm{[CII]}}$ and stellar mass-$L_{\mathrm{[CII]}}$ relations at $z\sim7$. Given the challenge in precisely defining a selection volume for the REBELS sample itself, we rely on published UV LF and stellar mass function (SMF) determinations at $z\sim7$ and three complementary approaches to derive the [CII] LF. The UV LF-based method provides a lower limit on the [CII] LF, due to its missing the most dust-obscured systems. Our SMF-based estimate yields a Schechter function with a characteristic luminosity of $L^*_{\mathrm{[CII]}}=10^{9.11^{+0.11}_{-0.27}} L_\odot$ and a steep faint-end slope. From $z\sim7$ to $z\sim5$, our inferred [CII] LF shows an evolution of +0.3 dex in normalisation and +0.1 dex in $L^*_{\mathrm{[CII]}}$. Our results indicate a general underprediction from models of the abundance of [CII] emitters at high-redshift and thus potentially the number densities of massive yet UV-faint systems implied by our SMF-based method. Additionally, they suggest that 63% of the star formation rate density occurs in massive [CII]-bright systems and that $\sim$60-90% of [CII] emitters at $z\sim7$ may be missed by bright UV selections. This highlights the importance of surveys focusing on especially massive, UV-faint sources at $z>6$.

papers.title: MoSAIK: Motion Search with Artificial Intelligence in K-space
papers.abstract: Object: Motion artefacts remain a major limitation of routine two-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) brain MRI, reducing diagnostic confidence and often necessitating repeated acquisitions. MoSAIK (Motion Search with AI in K-space) retrospectively estimates in-plane rigid-body motion directly from standard multi-coil TSE k-space. Without a motion-free reference, external navigators, or additional acquisitions, MoSAIK infers motion from k-space self-consistency violations and incorporates predicted parameters into model-based, motion-aware reconstruction rather than synthesizing corrected images. Materials and Methods: Selected complex coil data were represented as log-magnitude and phase channels. A decoupled convolutional embedding and Transformer encoder estimated phase-encoding-line-indexed rotation and two-dimensional translations. Training used motion-free clinical acquisitions with simulated motion; four held-out subjects were evaluated. Component-wise errors assessed estimation; SSIM and PSNR in silico and entropy focus criterion (EFC) in vivo assessed reconstruction. Results: Motion estimation errors were low for both rotation (MSE $<$ 0.2 deg$^2$) and translation (MSE $<$ 0.2 pixels$^2$), with Pearson correlations of approximately 0.96 and 0.94, respectively. In every in-vivo acquisition, more than 75% of slices showed information gain relative to uncorrected reconstructions. MoSAIK reduced visible artefacts while preserving anatomical detail. Discussion: Transformer-based k-space motion-trajectory estimation enables fast retrospective correction of standard clinical TSE brain MRI.

papers.title: Optimal Algorithms and Hardness for Max-Cut in Bounded Degree Graphs
papers.abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves an $α_{GW} + \tildeΩ(1/d)$-approximation for Max 2-LIN(2) in weighted instances where each vertex appears in at most $d$ constraints. This improves on the $α_{GW}+\tildeΩ(1/d^2)$-approximation guarantee of [Hsieh-Kothari, ICALP'23]. We also show a matching Unique Games hardness under randomized polynomial-time reductions, thereby proving that the gain on $α_{GW}$ is optimal up to $\mathrm{polylog}(d)$ factors. Here, $α_{GW} \approx 0.878$ is the approximation ratio of the Goemans-Williamson algorithm. Our results resolve an open question due to Raghavendra and refute his conjectured optimal approximation ratio of $α_{GW} + \tildeΩ(1/\sqrt{d})$. Our local improvement scheme can be thought of as using an adaptive (based on the neighbors) shift applied to the Gaussian before using the GW sign rounding. This allows us to implement a ``soft but simultaneous'' flipping decision at each vertex as opposed to hard but sequential flipping decisions in prior works. Our hardness results are based on a new sparsification lemma for graphs produced by the reduction from Unique Games [Khot-Kindler-Mossel-O'Donnell, SICOMP'07] that preserves the optimal values up to a factor of $1 \pm ε$ while subsampling to an average degree of only $\tilde{O}(1/ε)$. This is the first example of a CSP in which the optimal advantage on degree-$d$ instances is asymptotically smaller than $O(1/\sqrt{d})$ [Trevisan, STOC'01]. A key idea in the proof of our sparsification theorem establishes new bounds on the number of ``nearly optimal'' cuts in the output of the KKMO reduction. This step, in turn, relies on a new, robust inverse Majority-Is-Stablest theorem.

papers.title: Intrinsic Curvature Controls Spontaneous Entanglement of Elastic Rods
papers.abstract: We report results from an experimental investigation on the role of intrinsic curvature in the spontaneous entanglement of elastic rods subjected to controlled tumbling. We examine two distinct entanglement mechanisms, knotting and locking, in a statistical ensemble of straight and helical rods with varying arc length and natural curvature. Our primary finding is that natural curvature exerts a dominant, non-monotonic influence on knotting, with a critical curvature that suppresses knot formation and significantly reduces the probability of knotting relative to equivalent straight rods. In contrast, locking is largely insensitive to curvature and scales primarily with rod length. These results, obtained for the macroscopic experimental system studied here, identify geometric parameters that govern distinct entanglement modes in tumbled elastic rods and may inform entanglement processes in microscopic filamentary systems such as DNA.

papers.title: Stop Paying by the Letter: Accelerating Full-Chip RTL Simulation with Host-Side Tokenized Logging
papers.abstract: Firmware diagnostic logging (printf) is an essential debug instrument in full-chip SoC design verification, yet it imposes a heavy tax on cycle-accurate RTL simulation: formatting a 30-character, 1-argument message on a simulated CPU and serializing it through an MMIO aperture costs 3.04 to 15.23 $μ$s per call (15.27 $μ$s unweighted / 15.08 $μ$s print-weighted critical-path mean on Suite A). Unlike embedded tokenizers that target flash footprint and wire bytes with offline decoding, RTL simulation is governed by a two-regime cost function---cross-fabric SoC paths are dominated by MMIO bus stalls (84.7% of call latency) whereas local subsystem paths are dominated by on-core vsprintf formatting (61.7%)---and requires live, zero-simulation-time string reconstruction to drive UVM scoreboards. We present a host-side in-simulation tokenized logging architecture for heterogeneous multi-core SoCs that eliminates both bottlenecks with zero firmware call-site edits. Using link-time ELF format-string virtual addresses as tokens over a fixed 32-bit word-aligned slot protocol across Arm, RISC-V, and DSP cores, on-core logging collapses to a single-pass specifier scan and $(1+S)$ MMIO word writes. This removes all on-core radix conversion ($C_{\mathrm{fmt}} \to 0$), 85.0%--94.5% of deployed bus transactions, 84.6%--93.3% of MMIO bus-stall cycles, and 63.5%--90.9% of total on-core logging cycles ($2.74\times$--$11.03\times$), while a SystemVerilog monitor reconstructs bit-exact strings in zero simulated cycles ($Δt_{\mathrm{sim}} = 0$). Across 858 matched full-chip test pairs (1,716 paired runs across 1,972 runs), we achieve 100% output parity with zero simulator memory overhead, saving 1,314.85 CPU hours (-26.18%) per regression pass, cutting median test CPU time by 41.51% (Suite A) and 21.33% (Suite B), and shrinking traces by 42.84% and waveforms by 28.82%.

authors.name: Rohit Kumar
authors.institution: All India Institute of Medical Sciences Raipur

papers.title: Neural Closed-Loop Identification of Nonlinear Systems with Stability and Generalization Guarantees
papers.abstract: Neural networks are expressive models of nonlinear dynamics, but identifying such systems from closed-loop data raises two difficulties: the feedback loop correlates inputs with measurement noise, biasing standard open-loop estimators, and the identified model must be stabilized by the data-collection controller, so that its closed-loop behavior matches the true plant's. We derive a complete parameterization of all nonlinear systems stabilized by a given controller, generalizing the classical dual-Youla parameterization to the nonlinear setting. Building on this characterization, we propose Internal Controller Identification (ICI), a computationally tractable framework for identifying potentially unstable systems while ensuring closed-loop stability by construction; in the linear case, our indirect method reduces to an open-loop identification problem, for which standard consistency results apply. The framework accommodates contextual information, letting a single certified model identify a family of systems, and supports a PAC-Bayesian training objective that, when data are scarce and prior knowledge is available, bounds the identified operator's expected prediction loss. Experiments show that ICI identifies open-loop unstable plants where uncertified baselines diverge, outperforms direct methods under weak excitation and feedback-correlated noise, generalizes zero-shot to environments unseen during training, and, with limited data, avoids the overfitting of empirical risk minimization while providing a non-vacuous generalization bound.

papers.title: Diffusion MRI protocol design for reliable parameter recovery: a unified framework across biophysical models
papers.abstract: Reliable microstructural parameter estimation in diffusion MRI (dMRI) critically depends on the acquisition protocol. Yet, common protocol design criteria may not fully reflect estimator bias, parameter constraints, and nonlinear fitting behavior in complex inverse problems. Here, we introduce Protocol Optimization via Loss Assessing Parameter Recovery (POLAR), an end-to-end framework that searches the continuous acquisition space and directly minimizes multiparameter recovery error through noisy signal simulation and the chosen model fitting. We demonstrate POLAR spanning distinct microstructural environments: the Cylinder-Zeppelin model for white matter, Neurite Exchange Imaging (NEXI) for gray matter, and Cellular Exchange Imaging (CEXI) for permeable cells. Across independent held-out parameter sets, POLAR consistently outperformed model-specific reference designs, reducing RMSE by up to $50\%$ for Cylinder-Zeppelin and $74\%$ for CEXI, while reducing NEXI exchange time bias by $70\%$. These gains across distinct biophysical models, acquisition settings, and reference design strategies demonstrate the benefit of optimizing acquisition protocols through the downstream parameter-estimation problem. POLAR provides a flexible, model-specific and estimator-aware framework for designing dMRI protocols tailored to the microstructural parameters and experimental conditions of interest.

papers.title: Classical spin liquids in the kagome Ising model, and their link with magnetoelasticity
papers.abstract: We investigate a nearest-neighbor Ising model on the kagome lattice coupled to elastic lattice distortions. By integrating out the lattice degrees of freedom, we derive an approximate spin-only description in terms of a kagome \(J_1\)-\(J_2\)-\(J_{3}\) Ising model with interactions extending to third nearest-neighbors. Using tensor network methods complemented by classical Monte Carlo simulations, we revisit its zero-temperature phase diagram and characterize the ground states studied more than thirty years ago. We discover three phases with extensive zero-temperature entropy and algebraically decaying spin correlations. Importantly, these states are not confined to fine-tuned points or frontiers between phases, but occupy extended areas of parameter space. Their quasi long-range order is reflected in Bragg-like peaks in the structure factors; we relate this, and other properties, to diverse phases found in Ising and Heisenberg models. Finally, we trace the trajectories generated by the magnetoelastic coupling through the effective-model phase diagram, explaining the emergence of self-frustration for the unfrustrated magnetoelastic model with ferromagnetic interactions.

papers.title: Sprinkling for random regular graphs and Kim-Vu's sandwich conjecture
papers.abstract: We show that the uniform random $d$-regular graph model on $n$ vertices is, in total variation distance, asymptotically close to the union of $d$ uniformly random edge-disjoint perfect matchings, provided that $n$ is even and $ω(1) = d \leq n^{1/10}$. This confirms a conjecture by Hollom, Lichev, Mond, Portier, and Wang for this range of parameters. This result has a couple of interesting consequences. First, this shows that random $d$-regular graphs on $n$ vertices exhibit sprinkling properties for some range of parameters, thereby confirming a conjecture by Isaev, McKay, Southwell and Zhukovskii in that range. Second, we give a short alternative proof of the upper side of Kim-Vu's sandwich conjecture in the sparse regime.

papers.title: GraphCast-Mamba: Learning Non-Markovian Corrections for Weather Forecasting
papers.abstract: Unresolved atmospheric processes can introduce history dependence beyond the short input windows used by many weather forecasting models. We introduce GraphCast--Mamba, which augments a frozen, pretrained $1^\circ$ GraphCast backbone with a trainable Mamba correction branch combining graph message passing and Mamba layers. The branch retains a temporal memory state across successive six-hour forecast steps, learning corrections informed by temporal context beyond GraphCast's two-frame input. Training is confined to the correction branch, using ERA5 data from 2015--2021. After 2,500 optimizer updates, including warm-up, the selected model achieves substantial improvements relative to the uncorrected GraphCast backbone. It reduces the GraphCast loss (normalized weighted mean-squared error; MSE) by 14.42% when aggregated over the full ten-day forecast and by 21.66% at day 10 (240 h after forecast initialization). At this final forecast lead time, root-mean-square error (RMSE) decreases by 7.09--14.60% across all 11 evaluated variable groups, spanning temperature, wind, pressure, geopotential, specific humidity, and precipitation. These results demonstrate broad improvements in ten-day weather forecasts through a short correction-training schedule while retaining the pretrained backbone.

papers.title: Local well-posedness of wave kinetic equations associated with water waves
papers.abstract: We prove two conceptually different local well-posedness results for wave kinetic equations associated with water-wave systems. For pure gravity waves with 2D interfaces, we establish a classical well-posedness theory in weighted Sobolev spaces: regularity is propagated, and solutions depend continuously on the initial data in the same topology. For gravity-capillary waves with one-dimensional interfaces, the situation is fundamentally different. We prove well-posedness in weighted $L^\infty$ spaces (in the sense of existence, uniqueness, and continuity in a weaker topology), but we also show that, in general, any additional regularity of the initial data is instantly lost. Moreover, continuity in time and continuous dependence on the initial data fail in the weighted $L^\infty$ norm, even for smooth compactly supported initial data. This instability is caused by degenerate three-wave resonances, which produce singular collision rates and arbitrarily short relaxation time scales. The distinction between the two theories reflects a fundamental difference in their resonant geometry.

authors.name: Yu Deng
authors.institution: University of Shanghai for Science and Technology

papers.title: PaPi: Parallel Picard-Duhamel Integration for Fast Neuro-Spectral Architectures
papers.abstract: Neuro-spectral architectures (NeuSA) are a class of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) that have proven effective for solving time-dependent PDEs in the frequency domain. However, training and inference often rely on costly numerical integration of the learned vector field, typically using sequential Runge-Kutta time stepping, which limits temporal parallelism. We introduce PaPi, an integration scheme inspired by weakly nonlinear flows that enables time-Parallel inference through exponential integration and a Duhamel-Picard scheme. We show that the Duhamel-Picard iteration converges exponentially for all flows, and provide explicit error bounds that depend on how close the flow is to linear. Experiments show that PaPi accelerates training and inference by up to two orders of magnitude, achieving training times of under one second for low-dimensional PDE learning problems, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy.

authors.name: João M. Pereira
authors.institution: Institute of Mechanical Engineering and Industrial Mangement

authors.name: Daniel Yukimura
