papers.title: StreamEval: Evaluating Interactive Streaming Video Generation Models
papers.abstract: We introduce StreamEval with four key features: (1) First interactive streaming video generation benchmark. (2) Fully open source. Benchmark data, evaluation code, protocols, and scoring rules are publicly available. (3) Comprehensive coverage. Five tasks cover avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing, with 300 scripted cases lasting 15 to 300 seconds. Ten metrics assess task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination. (4) Monthly updates. We will evaluate new and updated models and publish leaderboard results monthly. Results from 37 models show that high visual quality and identity retention do not necessarily coincide with reliable request execution or sustained state consistency. The leaderboard is available at https://streameval.ai.
papers.intro:
As streaming video generation advances, enabling real-time interaction with generated video is becoming increasingly important [72, 59]. Systems that generate video incrementally can accept new user inputs while a session is in progress [63, 5], supporting conversational avatars, controllable virtual worlds, and live video editing. Such settings require more than plausible individual frames or clips: generation and responsive control must remain aligned with incoming inputs as user requests and the surrounding context evolve over time.

Such settings require more than plausible individual frames or clips: generation and responsive control must remain aligned with incoming inputs as user requests and the surrounding context evolve over time.

Sustained interaction requires systems to execute new requests while preserving relevant prior content and state. A conversational avatar must respond in context without losing its identity or dialogue history; a generated world must accommodate new controls without disrupting unaffected scene content; and a video editor must apply, update, or remove edits while tracking an advancing source stream. Each request carries timing and scope requirements, defining when a change should occur, what it should modify, and what must remain intact. Evaluation must therefore assess both task execution and state consistency throughout a session alongside visual fidelity and audiovisual coordination.

Existing benchmarks examine complementary aspects of these requirements. VBench and EvalCrafter assess visual quality and temporal behavior, while T2V-CompBench examines compositional alignment [21, 41, 51]. WBench and WBench-Editing evaluate multi-turn control, successive edits, and content preservation within generated worlds [68, 36]. StreamAV-Bench assesses interactive updates and state retention in streaming video generation [39], and LongV2VBench examines editing quality over sustained source streams [59]. VideoFDB evaluates full-duplex conversational agents through their perception and generation of nonverbal audiovisual cues [44]. Its focus on conversational dynamics complements task-directed evaluation of request execution and state preservation. Building on these efforts, we bring avatar interaction, world generation, and real-time video editing into a unified benchmark with explicit, task-specific execution and preservation criteria.

We introduce StreamEval , spanning five tasks across these domains: digital-human dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing (figure 1). The benchmark contains 300 scripted test cases, each representing a 15–300 s interactive session. A test case bundles the initial portrait, scene, or source video with a sequence of timed user requests and explicit criteria for what the output should change and preserve. For example, an editing case may change one object, update another while retaining the first edit, then remove an edit to restore the source. Inputs arrive incrementally, so the system must respond as the session unfolds. Ten task-specific metrics evaluate performance along four complementary dimensions: task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination. This framework structures evaluation across tasks while respecting differences in model input interfaces and metric applicability.

We evaluate 38 models on 300 test cases across five interactive streaming video tasks. Vidu S2 Avatar obtains the highest reported Dialogue score in digital-human dialogue. By Overall score, Vidu S2 Avatar leads avatar performance, MemFlow leads world generation, and Vidu S2 Editing leads both instruction and reference editing. Individual metrics reveal complementary strengths: LiveTalk obtains the highest Quality score in avatar performance, while JoyAI-Video-Edit obtains the highest Preservation score in instruction editing (section 3.3). These results highlight distinct model strengths across tasks and interaction requirements. Looking ahead, we view real-time interactive video as an important challenge for bringing omni-modal models to diverse application settings.

papers.title: Present but Hard to Read: Probing Latent Reasoning with Minimal Pairs
papers.abstract: Probing studies of latent reasoning often read a model's state where the answer begins and take a failed probe as evidence that a value is absent. We test this with a digit copied from the question, in the looped model Ouro-1.4B and the standard transformer Qwen 2.5-1.5B. Comparing prompts that differ only in that digit shows it is present at the last prompt token, in a code shared across questions (readout about 0.9). A probe that sees one prompt at a time, the usual setting, barely reads it: 0.36 in Ouro and 0.19 in Qwen even after 5,249 training questions. The digit's change is small rather than crowded: random noise lands on equally busy directions, while a random word in its place moves the state far more and is readable. Since every varied token leaves a trace, a successful probe is ambiguous too. We give a protocol, including a synthetic null for generic mixing, for testing computed values against copies and mixtures of the inputs. In pre-registered studies of two-step problems it finds a small signal for the unwritten intermediate a+b just before Ouro writes the answer's last digit, and its sign follows the operation, though mixing alone produces much of that sign-following part. Holding that value at another problem's from the first loop on does not move the written digit toward the other problem's, while the same patch of the answer does: the value is readable but not used.
papers.intro:
Looped transformers apply one block of layers repeatedly (Geiping et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025), and one hope is that the extra loops work as a hidden chain of thought. Two kinds of evidence are used to test this: accuracy without written steps should rise with the number of loops, and the values the model works with should be readable from its states. For Huginn, Lu et al. (2025) found neither. Its answer-only GSM8K accuracy stayed at 3–5% across recurrence counts, and a logit lens showed no intermediate values. For Ouro-1.4B, accuracy alone cannot settle the question. Answering directly after the question, its GSM8K accuracy rises from 6.5% after one loop to 23% after four, but almost all of the gain comes at loop 2, where Ouro also improves on benchmarks that need no reasoning (Appendix A). To see whether the loops compute intermediate values, one has to look inside.

Probing studies of latent reasoning read the state at the position where the answer begins, which we call the summary position, and interpret failed readouts as evidence against latent intermediate values (Lu et al., 2025; Yu, 2024). Looking inside this way runs into a problem that is not specific to looped models: at the summary position, a standard linear probe barely reads even a digit copied from the question. We find: • The digit is present but hard to read (Sections 3.1 and 3.2). Minimal pairs, prompts that differ in a single token, show that it is there in both Ouro and Qwen2.5-1.5B, in a code shared across questions. A probe that compares a question’s ten variants reads it at about 0.9. A probe that sees a single prompt, as probing studies do, reads it at 0.12–0.24 with tens of training templates, and more than 5,000 distinct training questions lift it only to 0.36 in Ouro and 0.19 in Qwen (Figure 2). The two probes answer different questions, whether the digit is there and what it is in a new prompt, and here the answers come apart. A failed probe at such a position says little about whether a copied value is there. • The change is small, not crowded (Section 3.3). The digit’s directions are as busy as those of any change at that token, random noise included. What differs is size: a random word in the digit’s place moves the state far more and is readable, while random noise whose variants start as far apart as the words’ arrives as small as the digit. A pre-registered follow-up finds that this is not a matter of linear gain: what reaches the last token depends on which token is present. • A protocol for computed values (Section 4). Every varied token, needed or not, leaves a trace, so a successful probe says little more than a failed one. The protocol compares a candidate value with what copies of the inputs allow, ranks it against every combination of the inputs at a prime modulus, and compares it with its sign-flipped twin, with mixtures of the output being written, and with what generic mixing produces in synthetic states. • What it finds in Ouro (Section 5). In three pre-registered studies of two-step problems, a small, sign-specific signal for the unwritten a+ba+b appears just before the answer’s last digit, and when the operation is swapped, the better-read sign follows it. As a label, a+ba+b is the same as the answer plus cc, the answer is readable as early, and synthetic states that only mix the inputs with the answer give about half the signal, so it may be largely such a mixture. Replacing that value with another problem’s does not move the digit Ouro writes toward the other problem’s, even when it is held fixed from the first loop on, while clamping the answer does in 91% of pairs: at that position, and in the subspaces tested, the value is readable but not used. Appendix C gives the status of every analysis, including which were pre-registered.

papers.title: ECG for laboratory values:A comprehensive physiological and technical analysis
papers.abstract: Laboratory measurements are essential for clinical decision making but typically require invasive blood sampling. Recent research suggests that ECG recordings may contain information beyond cardiac rhythm and provide information related to laboratory values. This thesis investigates NT-proBNP prediction from ECG recordings and patient metadata using a multimodal deep learning framework, while considering the physiological plausibility of ECG-based prediction. It also compares a 1-lead configuration using lead II with the corresponding 12-lead configuration. Additional experiments on glucose, hemoglobin, and potassium are presented in the appendix. Regression, binary classification, and three-class classification experiments were conducted using MIMIC-IV, with the three-class task based on clinically established thresholds. The 12-lead configuration consistently achieved better performance. Regression reached a mean absolute error of 534.98 pg/mL for 1-lead and 514.27 pg/mL for 12-lead. Binary classification achieved AUROCs of 0.849 and 0.876, respectively, while three-class classification achieved macro-averaged AUROCs of 0.738 and 0.752. The results indicate that precise NT-proBNP regression remains challenging, whereas broader concentration ranges can be classified more effectively. The findings are consistent with the physiological hypothesis that ECG characteristics and NT-proBNP concentrations reflect shared cardiovascular processes. ECG-based NT-proBNP prediction may therefore provide complementary information, particularly for classifying broader concentration ranges. However, laboratory measurements remain necessary, and validation on independent datasets is required.

This chapter introduces the motivation of ECG-based laboratory value prediction and the clinical need for noninvasive approaches to obtain information related to laboratory values. Furthermore, this chapter discusses the role of machine learning in this context, the existing research and the contributions of this work.

Laboratory values have a crucial role in modern healthcare and are indispensable for clinical decision making. They provide information on the health status of the patient and are routinely used for disease diagnosis, treatment planning and monitoring the effectiveness of therapies[15]. Biomarkers that are measured through laboratory testing, such as NT-proBNP, hemoglobin, potassium and glucose, support clinicians in evaluating a wide range of cardiovascular, metabolic and physiological conditions[43, 52].

Despite their clinical importance, many laboratory values require invasive methods, such as blood sampling. Although blood sampling is invasive, it remains one of the most widely used testing methods[38]. It requires trained personnel, laboratory infrastructure and processing time for the results to become available. This contributes to the costs associated with laboratory testing for both patients and healthcare providers. Furthermore, repeated blood sampling increases workload and may cause discomfort for the patients, especially when frequent monitoring is required[69]. Hence, an approach that can provide clinically relevant information faster and causes less discomfort for patients is in demand.

Common applications of machine learning in healthcare include image analysis and analysis of biological and clinical data[19, 50].

ECG signals have become an important data source for machine learning. Recent research suggests that ECG contains information beyond cardiac rhythm analysis and may reflect broader physiological and pathological processes[5]. Since ECG signals can be obtained easily and without invasive procedures using wearable devices such as smartwatches, they represent a promising data source to be used with machine learning. Furthermore, multimodal machine learning is used by combining multiple data sources, such as physiological signals and patient metadata. Multimodal machine learning is therefore more suitable for use in the medical context, because it mimics the multimodal decision making of clinical experts[34]. These developments have motivated the application of multimodal deep learning for predicting laboratory values from ECG signals and patient metadata.

papers.title: A sub-Earth-sized TESS planet candidate in the nearby M-dwarf binary GJ 774, most likely orbiting GJ 774 A (TIC 351339274)
papers.abstract: Small planets transiting the nearest M dwarfs are the terrestrial planets most accessible to detailed characterisation. We report a sub-Earth-sized transiting planet candidate in the wide (17.6") M-dwarf binary GJ 774 at 12.86 pc, most likely orbiting the M2.5 primary GJ 774 A (TIC 351339274). The signal was a SPOC multi-sector threshold-crossing event (MES = 7.95) and is not a TESS Object of Interest. In eight TESS sectors (2019-2026) a 1.28-h transit recurs every 4.225138 +/- 0.000010 d with a box-mean depth of 365 +/- 32 ppm in A's light. The 2026 data, which entered neither the SPOC search nor our selection, show it at the ephemeris predicted from 2019-2023 data (304 +/- 43 ppm; none of 10^5 phase-scrambled versions of the 2026 data is as deep). The per-target false-alarm probability is < 0.03 at 95%. Odd/even, secondary-eclipse, archival-plate and Gaia radial-velocity tests exclude unrelated blended eclipsing binaries and eclipsing companions on 4.2-d orbits, and hierarchical eclipsing binaries are improbable. The stars are 0.85 TESS pixel apart, so the TRICERATOPS false-positive probability (0.26) is set by a planet on GJ 774 B. B is disfavoured because its own light does not dim enough: PRF-deblended photometry gives 109 +/- 115 ppm in B's light, against 1089 ppm required if B were the host. Conditional on a point source at A or at B, the joint host model gives P(A)=0.59-0.97 (0.97 for the native target-pixel baseline). Over all sectors the PRF photometry is consistent with A, but in the out-of-sample 2026 data 40% of the deficit appears at B's position, an unexplained 2-3 sigma (PSF-model and depth dependent) tension with host A. On A the planet has R_p=0.70 +/- 0.06 R_Earth, S=15.0 +/- 1.8 S_Earth and T_eq=548 +/- 16 K. It is not validated; resolved ground-based photometry of the pair would test host B directly.

papers.title: Who Approved This? Coding Agents, Human Accounts, and Merge-Gate Evidence at a Fintech Startup
papers.abstract: From 3 October, every non-bot merge into our main branch passed a non-author review gate, yet 71 of those 263 merges (27%) rested only on an approval that a coding agent had submitted through the technical lead's GitHub account, and the platform recorded each one as an ordinary approval by the lead. We report twelve weeks of agent-driven development at Bashi AI, a fintech startup preparing for a SOC 2 audit: 786 merged pull requests, 657 of them associated with agents by explicit markers or by inference, analysed from platform records and saved agent-session transcripts. In the gated phase, an agent session submitted every approval the lead's account gave on a colleague's pull request, and issued nearly all of its merges; the records cannot show who decided any of them. We recompute, for every merge, a core gate property: a non-author approval and a passing required check, both before the merge and both on the exact revision merged. The recomputation confirmed the gate wherever branch protection applied and found where it did not: agents switching enforcement off around individual merges, a merge script that recorded failed checks as passing, and an agent collapsing a stack of pull requests through unprotected branches. The engineers' survey answers show that one engineer's approvals also rested on review agents, with the person validating findings and deciding, and both engineers say review mattered when it tested a change against something outside the diff. We draw lessons on recording decision authority separately from account identity, keeping agents' credentials away from the controls they operate under, and checking evidence at the branch and revision where integration happens.
papers.intro:
A pull request approval on GitHub records an account, a revision, a state, and a time. Separation-of-duties controls read that record as evidence that a second person examined the change, which assumes that an account stands for a person. With coding agents, that no longer holds: an agent can write a change, ask another agent to review it, and submit the resulting approval through a developer’s account; the repository then holds an ordinary approval from that developer.

papers.title: An Asymptotic for Non-Wieferich Numbers
papers.abstract: A cyclic number is a positive integer $n$ such that $\gcd(n, \varphi(n)) = 1$. Erdős showed that the number of cyclic numbers up to $x$, $C(x)$, has $C(x) \sim e^{-γ}x/\log_3(x)$ asymptotically as $x$ tends to infinity. We define Wieferich numbers to be odd, positive integers $n$ such that $(n, (2^{\ell(n)}-1)/n) > 1$, where $\ell(n)$ is the smallest positive integer with $2^{\ell(n)} \equiv 1 \mod n$. Franco and Pomerance showed that non-Wieferich numbers have density zero among the odd integers. We show that the counting function of $n \leq x$ in the symmetric difference of non-Wieferich numbers and cyclic numbers is $O(x/(\log_3(x))^2)$, under a mild assumption on the counting function of Wieferich primes.

papers.title: Two-Colour Zig-Zag Numberlink on Rectangles: A Forbidden-Pattern Characterization, a Constructive Polynomial-Time Algorithm, and a Lean Verification
papers.abstract: In Zig-Zag Numberlink, pairs of endpoints in a grid must be joined by vertex-disjoint paths that together visit every cell. The problem is NP-complete when the number of pairs is un- bounded (Adcock et al.). For a single pair it is the Hamiltonian path problem in rectangular grid graphs, solved by Itai, Papadimitriou and Szwarcfiter. Two pairs on a rectangle form the paired 2-disjoint path cover problem. We settle the case of two pairs on rectangles with the endpoints anywhere in the grid. If both sides of the rectangle are at least 11, an instance is solvable if and only if no entry of a finite catalogue of forbidden patterns occurs. The catalogue consists of a parity condition, an alternation condition on the border, a handful of local corner and edge patterns, 65 listed corner configurations, and a rule that propagates forced routes out of the corners before testing alternation. If a side is at most 10, a frontier dynamic programming algorithm decides the instance in time linear in the long side. The characterization is construc- tive. Solutions are built by deleting empty lines, splitting the rectangle by straight cuts, and splicing the pieces back together, in time O((R+C) RC). Both directions of the characterization and the correctness of the dynamic programming algorithm are verified in Lean 4. The finite case analyses, which are window certificates for the corner configurations and a check of all irreducible instances with sides 11-22, are carried out by the Lean compiler via native decide. We describe the algorithm, the catalogue, the proof structure, the compromises made in the formalization, and implementations in Python, JavaScript and C that produce identical output.
papers.intro:
Numberlink is a pencil puzzle. The player is given pairs of numbered cells in a grid and connects each pair by a path along edge-adjacent cells, so that no two paths share a cell. The zig-zag variant, popular as the mobile game Flow Free, additionally requires every cell of the grid to be used. Adcock et al. [1] showed that Zig-Zag Numberlink is NP-complete when the number of pairs is unbounded.

With a single pair, the problem asks for a Hamiltonian path between two given cells. Shade the cells of the rectangle like a checkerboard. Itai, Papadimitriou and Szwarcfiter (IPS) [4] showed that if the rectangle has an even number of cells, a Hamiltonian path between two cells requires them to have different shades, and if it has an odd number of cells, both must have the majority shade. A pair that meets this condition has a Hamiltonian path unless it belongs to one of three small families of exceptions, which occur only when a side has length 11, 22 or 33.

Since the catalogue is a finite list of patterns, checking it takes time O⁡(R+C)O(R+C) when both sides are at least 1111. When a side is at most 1010, the dynamic programming algorithm takes time O⁡(max⁡(R,C))O(\max(R,C)), with a constant that depends only on the short side.
